I have been listening to Alan Watt's lectures for over a year now and just started reading the book "The Way of Zen" by him. He gives such a coherent and easy to understand way of percieving the universe and your life as the whole of Being as opposed to being a poor little stranger in the Universe. If you really listen, this is such a liberating way to live life - to just flow with the divine dance. What's really special about this game is that it brings such depth and color to this feeling and really brings his teachings alive through you experiencing the universe in a simulation yourself. Also, many of these lectures I've never heard before and may not be found on youtube or by searching the words on Google as it's not transcripted. It's a good place to hear his teachings if you don't have hundreds of dollars to spend buying his lectures on the Alan Watts library :) My only criticism though, is that I went into the "Golden gate" a second time and it seems near impossible to get out even though the first time you were able to. Any help with this problem would be appreciated :) Anyways, if you're debating getting this game or not, DEFINITELY recommend it whole-heartedly!!!

This game is very short, but still an excellent experience that I recommend highly.  I beat it in about an hour, but there is an additional challenge mode with no checkpoints that I did not play through.  I imagine that could easily take another hour or two.
The levels are well designed and provide a fun challenge without being completely infuriating.  Lots of checkpoints mean that deaths aren't too devastating (although if you want it to be devastating, you can of course play the challenge mode I mentioned).  You'll need amazing timing throughout the game, and having the music synchronized with the obstacles is an effective and satisfying way to make that doable.  The boss battles are AMAZING.  Very fresh mechanics are introduced during the boss fights (three total) and the final one in particular was exciting, challenging, and made a great climax for the game.
My main complaint is that, like I said, the game is very short.  I would like to play more like this, but I'd rather have a short game that is awesome all the way through than have a game with time-wasting filler.  Even with such a short playtime, I feel it is worth the money to have this experience.

I would only recommend this game if you already played this game in the past and really liked it.  If this game is new to you, it will be incredibly frustrating.  To create your economy, you are forced to build your buildings in a specific order.  There is no wiggle room, the game will only allow you to create building type 15 after building type 14, but only after you built 13, and so on.  It's a tedious process, and it takes your serfs about 4 minutes to build each building if everything goes smoothly, which it never will.  Serfs get stuck in roads...a lot.  The end goal of a healthy economy is to build a large enough army to beat the overwhelming forces of your enemy.  If you lose the 30-40 troops you are assigned at the beginning of the mission, it will probably take 1-2 hours to replace that army, and that may not be enough to kill the 300-400 enemies that you will be facing.  Also, winning a battle is always going to involve having one of your archers lure the enemy force into your carefully prepared army lines with militia in the front and archers in the back.  Over and over and over again.  That is the only strategy that you are expected to use or that will work.  You have to be quick about it too, because your troops will get hungry and have to be fed about every 15 minutes or they will die, which means you need tons of food and plenty of serfs to walk the food all the way across the map to feed your massive army.  Once in battle, the controls are clunky, the soldiers are incredibly hard to direct, and the archers must be positioned perfectly or they will be unresponsive.  If you do get this game, save your game a lot, because you do not want to lose many of your soldiers in battle.  Each soldier is a huge investment in time and resources. The game crashes a lot as well, there seems to be an issue with the sound causing crashes, so you may want to turn the sound off.  Be prepared for a lot of micromanagement and 20 very long levels in both campaigns.

This game is fun to play. It has a pretty good grasp on third person movement mechanics, allowing you to go around parkour-style. The only real annoyance I found was that because the game uses surface snapping, sometimes the players character will try and do completely the opposite to what you want. Like jump up and over a wall, falling down off the other side.
The action mechanics are less free-form, focusing more on the use of combo moves. However, there are enough of them to unlock such that it does give a good illusion of freedom of movement during fighting. I did find the odd point in the game where some of the combos didn't really stack up right, especially in very crowded areas.
This game can be rather violent and graphic at times. Does a good job of potraying a seedy gang-controlled city. This draws a contrast with GTA, which you initially might compare it against, in that it is less satirical and more serious. There are however a wide range of missions and storylines and mission types to keep you entertained, as can be found in GTA.
In the graphics department this game is fairly good, although there are some obvious bug, such as random pedestrians getting stuck in walls. There are also some times when the game's framerate drops for some reason, I can never reproduce it though. It may be to do with playing in windowed mode vs fullscreen. I would suggest sticking to fullscreen to ensure this doesn't occur.
The most annoying thing in this game is the bug at the start of the game, which several people seem to have encountered, where the NPC you're following stops moving. When it happens, just let the characters sit there and wait it out, the game will resume in about 10 seconds.
Overall, a pretty good game, with some nice characters, some less nice characters, and some downright evil. A bit rough around some of the edges, but still worth playing.

This is a bad game. It aged very poorly. The camera is terrible, the controls are terrible, the auto-aiming system is astoundingly terrible, and so on. These are all massive flaws that existed at the time, but which people ignored because the game was innovative.
The difficulty is ridiculous at times, mostly due to the bad mechanics. It took me ages to complete one early mission where I had to stop a car and kill the two guys in it. I'd stop them, try to get my gun to lock on, fail, and get stunlocked to death by a shotgun.
When you're running in one direction, the camera follows you. You also can't change the camera direction while moving. This means that if an enemy is chasing you and need to kill them, you have to completely stop, turn your camera, and hope you're able to target them with the horrible targeting system before they kill you. Spoiler: you won't be able to. You'll die.
If you played this 15 years ago, congrats! You were able to play through a horrible game because you didn't know any better. Now you have wonderful nostalgia and can view the game through the rose-tinted lenses of nostalgia.
If you've never played this game, don't start now. It sucks. It sucks really, really hard. Play Sleeping Dogs or GTA V or any other more modern, better refined sandbox game instead. This one belongs in the past.

GTA 3, when released in 2001, changed the entire gaming landscape. Around 1999, shortly after the release of the top-down GTA 2, Rockstar decided to cash into the trend of 3D gaming, and started development of GTA 3. What was once a cheesy, cartooney 3D city evolved into the living monolith the 3D Rendition of Liberty Ciy was. Taking place in 2001, while robbing a bank, an unnamed thug (known as Fido in game) is fatally shot by his girlfriend, Catalina. This man goes through various friends, enemies and betrayals to get to his goal of killing his girlfriend at a dam in a dramatic final mission. Liberty City is a giant. Consisting of three large islands and a huge green inaccessable countryside, Liberty City is stunning visually. The game has a decent array of weapons, with some of these weapons being an overpowered shotgun and Carbine Rifle, a sniper rifle, an undersized AK-47 and a well rounded Micro Uzi. With these weapons come mechanics. Though GTA 3 has generally solid mechanics, it does have setbacks, like inaccurate auto targeting (Classic Control Method) and the inability to crouch. Driving mechanics are quite good, with a big heavy army truck being hard to spin out following a fender crash, and a Viper based sports car spinning two 360s as the result of such collision. GTA 3's radio selection, while not nearly as good as the one in Vice City, is still decent. I was often listening to Head Radio, Double Clef, K-Jah or Flashback FM. If you loathe the entire game's soundtrack, this PC version supports custom radio stations, which can be accomplished by dragging your mp3s in the folder of the same name in the game directory. Additional PC features include choosable skins for the player, and full aiming with any weapon, something the PS2 version of the game did not support. There is alot more content and easter eggs in this amazing game that will keep you busy. Though you will find more fun in Vice City, that is not putting down GTA 3 at all. Even if you do get bored of the main game, the PC versions of both games support major mods, like the RealGTA mod for GTA III. No matter which way, GTA 3 is worth the wait and the money.

While EVERYTHING is good, there is one huge problem which I absolutely hated - the Story Mode cutscenes and audio. On the console versions, they were perfect... well - I didn't notice any problems. However here, the sound is AWFUL! It destroys the rather amazing story mode that MK actually has. The cutscenes also look rather blocky and not nice. There are some very hard-to-find fixes to be found on the internet (which actually replace the cutscenes), but this is still really awful and shouldn't be this way. The world is big (not as big as new GTA versions but it was at the time), the options are seamingly endless, the sand in the sandbox is deep (again not as much as new GTA games but was very much so for the time).
The fact that the character you play speaks no words is in itself, a very interesting dynamic to the game. It makes you more aware of the other characters, the missions, the world; everything is embellished with great detail because of your silence. You carry out bloodthirsty murders, arsons, and robberies with cold indifference to your actions. It's kind of chilling to think about.
The violence of the game was disturbing to lots of people and it is pretty bloody. The concept of a free-range murderer is kind of frightening, but the game is very much a game so there is nothing to worry about. Have fun blowing cars up. It's just a game.
The story is very obviously borrowed from gangster movies like The Godfather and Goodfellas and such. This is a bonus though, as everything seems very familiar to you, like you are already a made man.
Excellent game, and playable all the way through.

I did not like this game at first.  It was an earlier alpha version when I bought it and thought it was really boring.
However, after a few updates this gem really started to shine.  I have made myself stop playing it until the final release so I dont get burned out before the final features are in place.   Most of the things I did not orginally like about the game have been smoothed over.  It still seems at first glance to be a pretty dull game.  But once you start making some progress and start to understand your enemies as well as the strengths and weaknesses of your own troops this game gets pretty fun.
The best game I can compare it to is X-Com.   You manage your company and roam the map on a strategic level.   Then when you get into combat you will go to a tactical screen.   The armor, weapons, and individual troops can be managed on a strategic level.   Those decisions will have a huge effect on combat and should compliment the tactics you prefer.  Different kinds of enemies including goblins, orcs, human bandits, and the undead will force you to use different tactics.  Thus keeping every battle from being the same.   The AI has a knack for finding your weak spots and exploiting them.  So having a firm grasp of what your own weaknesses are can sometimes mean the difference between an overwhleming victory and a catstrophic disaster.   And unlike X-Com, you wont be constantly having those infuritating 98% "gimme put" shots that miss and wreck your game.

Right from the start, the vast landscape of this truly remarkable world is thrown completely open to you, and it constantly finds ways to draw you into the slightest details hidden in the environment. This review will be updated as I progress through the game.
Venetica is an enjoyable RPG that is flawed by a lack of polish and some technical issues, but is worth checking out due to some unique gameplay elements and an interesting world.
The story of Venetica is reasonably unique (especially since it is told from the perspective of a heroine). The story and world is fully voiced, and although the dialogue (especially the choices you are given) is a bit "off" at times, overall it suits the world of Venetica.
The gameplay in Venetica consists of exploration, combat, and occasional puzzles. The combat in Venetica isn't bad; but it is held back by a horrible camera, especially since much of the combat consists of dodging enemy attacks. The puzzles scattered throughout the game are reasonably simple but contribute to the game's diversity and help keep the overall adventure engaging.
The game's presentation is done reasonably well, although there seems to be some optimization and frame rate issues with my more than capable PC. The world looks good and is packed with objects, but it has a lot of small areas and tight locations that are made even worse by the poor camera.
Overall the game is definitely worth checking out (especially at its low price). If you are a fan of Action RPG's and don't mind a few technical issues, pick this one up.
+ Detailed World
+ Unique Story
+ Gameplay Diversity
- Bad Camera
- Occasionally Strange Dialogue
Overall So Far: 7/10

I've racked up almost 170 hours in Battle Brothers in the last year and a half or so, so I guess it's high time to say my piece on it.
Short version:
Battle Brothers is a really damn cool game and you should get it.
Altogether-More-Words-Than-Really-Necessary version:
Back when I bought it, Battle Brothers was considerably more barebones than it is now, and even still it was good for many hours of fun. Since then, every single update has only improved and enhanced the game, and every new campaign I've started has been more fun than the previous one. Today I sincerely rank Battle Brothers among my favourites in the turnbased tactics genre.
Audiovisually the game is a very pleasant, coherent package. The visual design is delightfully free of overwrought pomp, improbable anatomy and questionable ergonomics; The equipment, characters and monsters look down-to-earth and credible. The detailed, hand-drawn, slightly cartoony art style is delightful and plays wonderfully together with the calm and simple, yet catchy and evocative soundtrack, perfect for the game's setting of gritty medieval fantasy. A great example of "less is more", a beautiful balance of form and function.
Combat is where the art department's prowess does the most good for gameplay. Eventhough the charming boardgame pawn-like character sprites themselves are static, it is never unclear what is happening or who's equipped with what thanks to the clear, detailed graphics and elegant little visual cues. Thanks to this and especially the meaty sound effects, the combat feels startlingly visceral for such a boardgamey affair.
While Battle Brothers does not have any sort of central story, it does have a decent amount of writing. Not only is you picking up and turning in contracts presented in short narrative text boxes, there are also random events that might pop up during your travels. And although the setting of the game is gritty, it is not altogether grim. The writing has a dry wit to it, a kind of rascally tone that is just perfect to set the tone for a story of a rough-and-tumble band of mercenaries.
All that said, the cruxes of a tactics RPG like this are still character development and combat, both of which Battle Brothers does commendably. The level of complexity is just right to offer plenty of choices and variety without being overwhelming or opaque. Character perks have tangible, meaningful effects and the math behind them and the character stats is simple, consistent and easy to grasp. The various kinds of weapons have various pros and cons, and any choice is viable in one situation or other. Armor is where I would perhaps like to see more factors in play, as currently it is merely a balancing act between protection and fatigue, with helmets also having a penalty to vision range to consider.
And then there are the titular (anti)heroes of the game; your very own battle brothers. Eventhough they are procedurally generated and the pool of different background stories is sorely limited, the various professions and character traits bring a surprising amount of character to them, and there's a myriad little emergent moments to be found with them. Torsten, the dimwitted but brave farmhand who alone held three orcs at bay with his spear; Baldur, the retired soldier who took up arms again to join you just to be immediately stabbed to death by goblins; Bjarne the nearsighted beggar you hired on as disposable frontline fodder but is now your most fearsome axe murderer; I could go on and on, but you get the picture.
Overall, the level of polish in this game is admirable. There is very little technical jank; sometimes buildings in the city screen flicker a bit and the as-of-yet nonfunctional buildings are a bit of a sore thumb, but that's all I can think of. The UI is pleasing to the eye, responsive and easy to use save for a couple tiny niggling issues.
Of course, being Early Access, there are still a number of things to do to flesh the game out further. Fortunately the devs are quite forthcoming with information regarding their plans and the development process. It is apparent that they know exactly what sort of work the game needs and have the competence and motivation to do it, and do it right. As such, I have nothing but confidence that this gem of a game will shine all the brighter when it is finally finished.

Left 4 Dead is easily one of the best games ever made, a must have for your steam library. Left 4 Dead is overflowing with replayability, you'll want to come back to replay the same campaigns over and over in online co-op , survival, or versus mode.
Playing as either Zoey, Bill, Francis, or Louis you will fight your way through 7 campaigns filled to the brim with zombies and a variety of weapons to use to slaughter them. While you gun down a horde of mindless common infected, a few special infected will hunt you down, and if they get you, you'll require your team's help to survive the attack. As well as being able to play as the survivors, you can go online and play the insanley fun versus mode. In this mode you play as the team of survivors and try to make it as far into the campaign as ou can, while another team plays as the special infected and gives their best effort to kill you as quickly as possible. Still not satisfied? Go into a survival match with your friends and try to hold out against an endless amount of common infected and special infected in an effort to get the best time amongst your friends online.
Left 4 Dead is a great game... BUT, if you only have the money to get either Left 4 Dead 1, or Left 4 Dead 2, buy the second one! You'll get more content, as the second game contains all Left 4 Dead 1 campaigns, the campaigns for Left 4 Dead 2, a bigger online community, new special infected, steam workshop compatability and a new scavenge pvp mode. However if you're looking to play the original in all it's glory, Left 4 Dead is a great purchase, and is well worth the money.

I have been trying out a lot of different RPG games lately, trying to find one that can grab and hold my attention. And so far, I have found that Venetica is one of the few RPG games that I have tried recently that can hold my interest enough to make me want to keep playing it. So, with that said, here is my humble review of Venetica.
The graphics in Venetica are decent enough, I suppose they aren’t great. The scenery is quite wonderful though, very panoramic at points. It’s a great game if you are into screen shots of your character set against a backdrop of an awesome scene, especially vast cityscapes. The game is a tad cartoonish, with lots of exaggerated colors and characters, but still realistic enough to let you get lost in its surroundings.
Additionally, I loved the voice acting in this game. I’m pretty certain that Venetica is a German-made game, and obviously it’s set in Italy, and the voice actors are British, which is very cool. I thought the voice work was terrific and I especially liked how the main character Scarlett was portrayed.
I will not try to review the combat in Venetica except to say that I found it easy to master and I enjoyed the varied and unusual skills that my character could earn along the way as the game progresses. I'm an older, more casual gamer and Venetica's combat style suited me just fine.
The best part of the game for me was the terrific main protagonist Scarlett. She is an absolute delight! She’s really likeable and she’s lots of fun to play the game as. She’s tough without being mean spirited and she’s pretty and smart as well. The only thing that would prevent me from proposing marriage to her is that she’s the “daughter of death”. This would then make our children the “grandchildren of death” and I think that would sort of make our family reunions a bit awkward. Anyway, I do totally wish that there were more awesome female characters like Scarlett in PC gaming. There certainly should be, anyway.
Anyway, I enjoy playing Venetica quite a bit and I think it’s worth a play if you dig 3rd person RPG games like Fable or Gothic. The devs seem to be quite responsive to any posts or questions that I’ve seen in the game forums, and that’s a big plus, too. Some players have experienced a crash or two, but the devs remain engaged and involved on the Steam forums and there’s a decent community of gamers around to help out, too.
Thanks for reading my review and I hope you’ll give Venetica a try, if this sort of game is your thing. Scarlett is way too good of a character to pass up, if you ask me.

Venetica: a nice story rich RPG that takes place in late medieval Venice filled with fantasy and magic. The heroine of the tale is Scarlet a young strong willed maiden who travels through the astonishing city of Venice and countryside seeking to avenge her fiancee who gets killed in assault by mysterious folk.
Being quite generic RPG the game Venetica contains all the basic elements: side quests, various enemies (Robbers, skeletons, giant bats), different weapon types etc. The fighting system works fine combining dodging, hit chains and some special attacks and/or magic which are unlocked from skill trees. Just enough to make combat strategic and active.

The story stays facsinating the whole playthrough and most of the characters are interesting and voice talents know their job.  I still would have hoped deeper contacts to some characters whose potential is wasted after strong introduction. There is two different ways to conclude the game and this is determined by the moral choices the player commits - usually cases are quite black and white.
All in all Venetica is a solid 20 hour long package which might not surprise or dazzle, but is good enough to provide a fix for lesser or stronger RPG hunger.

This is going to be a continued review. I'll post here from time to time, updating on the things I see changed, and on my own opinions. Remember, though, this is EARLY ACCESS, so a lot will surely change.
I'm loving it so far, even though the game is still quite raw on the edges. The base game is there for the most part, and it works quite well. You can access the menus, work with the main interactions, produce, buy, sell, compliment people, etc. Moving around is a joy. The game looks great, even with graphic options 'turned down'(you can disable a few elements, but no quality sliders as in other games, as far as I've seen - I'll search later on today). Each profession and character presents a little backstory in the form of a text (A nice touch!) and the voice acting presented so far is quite enjoyable. Game mechanics, at least in the first hour, work just fine. Buildings have a few improvement options (btw, some of the menus for them still lack textures) and you get to expand property from the get-go. NPC presence works well at suspending disbelief, and the city looks quite alive most of the times.
But despite my sweet spot for the series and THQ as a whole, there are some miles to walk till this one is ready. For example, we still have no female voices, some of the customization options are limited (granted, they're still as varied as in former games, so I can't tell if the devs are putting in more or leaving it as is - it's not essential, anyway), the help documentation is still being written, some text boxes are wrogly sized (although perfectly functional), there's some clipping around against objects in the world and  once or twice the avatar just bolted for the end of the map, despite being ordered to go to the market (through clicking). I haven't seen options for eating or sleeping thus far (but I'm at the very beginning of the game, remember) and it seems that the actions available could use a bit more variety (we'll see if we get more during gameplay).
All in all, I think this game is building up quite well! A recommended experience (as are the other games in the series), waiting to see the inevitable improvements THQ will be bringing around this time!

I have played every game in the Fallout series to completion multiple times. Fallout 4 is a good game, but does not stand up to earlier games
Lets start with the good
+Deeper customization for weapons and armor
+A large, interesting, open world to explore
+A better character appearence customization
+Better gunplay
+There's a fun settlement building system not seen on earlier titles
+A larger weapon arsenal
+Wide range of armor
Then there's the bad, or what Fallout 4 did wrong
-Lacking morality system seen in earlier titles
-less choice of and ending, really its one of two endings
-Less unique-ness to unique weapons and armor
-less interesting of a story (Fallout 3: son looks for his dad, ends up changing the future of the capital wasteland forever and kicks some super advanced faction out of the wasteland, Fallout: New Vegas: you're a mailman who was shot in the head and ends up having the fate of 2 major factions, a city, and the rest of a wasteland on their shoulders, Fallout 4: Dad looks for son, some super advanced faction is the boogeyman of the area and you can decide what happens to them (deja-vu?)
-Dialouge simplified, you dont really know what you are going to say and what the effects are
-Dialouge has little to no impact on what happens in the story
-perk system simplified but in the wrong way
-worse character development and ability customization
all in all, Fallout 4 with its flaws is not a bad game, it just could've been better.
TL:DR If you're looking for a story and expierence, I suggest Fallout: New Vegas. if you're looking for just something to run around and have fun, you're in a good place

I orignally saw this game being played by Video Game Dunkey. His commentary and gameplay seemed to peg this game as a silly explorative game that seemed to parody other explorative games.
I was wrong.
This game is surprising deep. While it does have some hilarity (like how some animals move for example) it's primary focus is a philosophical exploration on... well everything. And nothing. And how that's still everything. And nothing. And the circle keeps going and going and going as Alan Watts (who I had to Google to figure out who he was) narrates through findable sound clips.
The gameplay is also circular. You start as something and can ascend or descend into something else until you've discovered everything. The turtorial helps you unlock other things you can do like grow big or small, create flocks, transform into things you've already discovered, add and subtract, or dance to make babies.
The one thing I had a love hate relationship was the Autoplay. I'd get up to go to the bathroom as a frog and I'd come back to find myself as a damn planet. Little did I know that autoplay progresses you through the plots of the tutorial so it did it to get me closer to my ultimate goal. Once I understood this, I was more ok with it and even let it help me get out of the Golden Gate, as I was at a loss for what to do. After the tutorial was completel, I found that autoplay didn't seem to progress you to anything anymore which I found disappointing as I was hoping it'd give some direction when it came to finding everything possible in the game.
Beat the game in 5. Completed it in 10. It's a relaxing and fun gaming experience that I whole heartedly recommed.

Ever wanted to be something other than human ?  This game lets you be a huge number of non-human things.  And possibly a human too, though I haven’t seen any yet.  Probably not everything as the name suggests, except in a metaphorical sense.
I started off as an Elk.  According to reviews other people started off as other animals.  I could wonder around a grassland and see other animals and things I’d expect to see there.  After a short while I learned how to overhear what they were thinking, which was usually something abstract and not in line with the kind of thing they were.
A short while later I learned how to become one of the things I could see.  There are two options: you choose "something a little bigger than me" or "something a little smaller than me" and the game highlights nearby options.  So from an Elk I could turn into a pig or a tree.  And then do it again and again.  Each time you turn into something new the game adds this thing to a categorised list.  You can look down the list and see a short description of this thing, usually the opening paragraph of Wikipedia or Simple Wikipedia.  The game has no real end but you might consider that being everything it’s possible to be would be an objective.
As each of these things you can "sing" which means making a noise that that thing might make (some always make the same noise, others have a few different ones).  You can also meet others of your kind and form a group — a flock of swans or an, erm, alphabet of black letters — and dance or perhaps have babies.
So you can go smaller and smaller and smaller until you’re an insect or a large rock.  Once you’ve spent some time as the extreme you learn how to descend or ascend scale.  At which point you’re a grain of pollen or an island, seeing a whole lot of new things that exist at this scale.  You can become those, and also travel down or upscale again to the point where you can change scale again.  The game does implement the wrap-around scale theory, where if you continually get bigger and bigger you eventually wrap around to tiny.  The detail of at what point and how this happens is interesting.
There are other powers you are told of when you’ve done each thing long enough.  So if you want to be a gigantic rabbit rampaging through a city, or to have the game rampage for you, you will eventually learn how to do it.
That’s it, really.  If you want to know what kinds of galaxy there are, get to galaxy scale, become a galaxy and look around you.  IF you see something you like become it.  If you want to learn about it, read the descriptive text.  But it’s not an encyclopaedia.  You can’t zoom straight to being an otter in its habitat, you have to work your way to it, and it’s possible there are no otters in the game.  I haven’t found one yet.  In three hours of playing I’ve been 317 different kinds of thing, which is about 22% of them all.  I calculate there are about 1500 different types of thing in all.
If you don’t do anything for a while the game goes into autoplay mode where it does the same sort of thing you’d do.  You can configure this so that, for example, is it or is not allowed to change scale.  So if it starts on an alien planet you get a tour of an alien planet and nothing else.  Or you might prefer that it changes scale frequently so you get a complete tour of the universe at all scales.  Something I didn’t see mentioned in reviews is that there’s an autoplay mode called "documentary".  In this mode, the game shows the text description of whatever it happened to be playing at the moment.  This is one of the best educational screensavers I’ve ever seen.  And, of course, if you find something you like you can take over at that point.  Possibly an interesting tool for teaching kids about the world.
In its ability to change scales this game reminds me of Katamari Damacy.  But there’s nothing else really like it.  It has no pace of its own.  You can play it with some objective in mind or meditatively, just to concentrate on something and keep your thoughts away from troubling things.
So if you ever wanted to be a stapler, a bacterium, a trumpet, a sun, a wolf, a fence, an oxygen atom, a cake, a wood splinter, a radio antenna, a lenticular galaxy, a campfire, a skyscraper, a motorcycle, a clump of grass, a grain of pollen, a dinner plate, a mushroom, a child’s alphabet block, a wedding ring, a plane tree, a castle, a bowling ball, the Cassini probe, a flake of skin, or an old boat, this is your chance.

Sleeping Dogs is an outstanding game that takes the open world elements from Grand Theft Auto and combine it with the melee combat system from the Batman Arkham games and you have a game that has a gorgeous world and satisfying combat. The game takes place in Hong Kong and the world is full of realistic details; just walking around you hear everyone speaking in Cantonese and the radio is filled with Cantonese songs. The streets are littered with stores and vendors trying to get you to purchase something; the world is full of these little details which makes the game feel alive. The combat and open world driving is very satisfying and fun. The real highlight of the game is the story, where you are an undercover cop moving up the ranks in the Triad. The story missions are all varied and are full of twists and turns. Overall, the game takes about 40 hours to completely 100% the main game and to finish the 3 large DLCs and the various small DLCs which add some additional missions/content. There are tons of collectibles to find and lots of areas to explore, so if you're a fan of open world games this is a must play with an awesome story and amazing martial arts combat. By the way, check out who voices the characters in the game, you will be surprised to see how many famous actors/actresses are in this game!

The overall concept and story is nice, but there could definitely stand to be some improvements to the design.

Stategically one will often find it appropriate to switch between weapon types depending on your oppenent or situation; however, instead of having one dedicated block button you must assign each of the block "skills" to a quick slot. Not only is this awkward in the heat of battle there aren't enough quickslots to begin with, even without needing one for each block. These quickslots are the only means of using your powers and require you to swap them out in the pause screen frequently and is very tedious. Three; this game is riddled with glitches. It's a shame, because under the problems there is definitely a great game that's fun and even had the potential to be much better with a few added touches, but the issues it suffers from make it difficult to appreciate. Skill trees are divided in two - physical and spiritual skills, which you can only buy with xp at certain trainers , in a similar fashion to other german arpgs like Gothic and Risen 2 as far as I remember. On the physical side of things we have all the combat skills including block (yep block is not available from the get-go , but ist probably the second skill you will buy)
On the spiritual side you have your "magic" abilities. Im not big on "magic" so I wont get into that but I will say this: Scatlett , the daughter of Death , has a crow who shows her the way to the next objective. Coincidence? I think not!
Overall not a bad game so far , there are some puzzles here and there , combat is ok , and visuals , although a bit dated , are pleasant.Controller support is ok with a 360 controller, the layout is not the most common one with A being attack and X being roll and B - block but you can change it in the settings.
Almost forgot. If you have trouble with game messages not popping up (tutorial and hints and such) enable them in the options and disable the steam overlay , that fixed it for me.

Positives:
+ Atmosphere. It's a mostly gritty and cruel world and the dialogue is well written, with a dark sense of humour.
+ Characters. Each brother you hire has a unique combination of background, genetic traits and different bonuses to skills which they can learn more easily. You choose what they should focus on as they level up and there are plenty of interesting talent synergies.
+ Strategic choices. Besides character customization, you also pick your battles and you have the opportunity to tweak your brothers' equipment based on your experience with the given fighting conditions and type of opponent.
+ Combat. The mechanics are good, the stakes are high and it's satisfying to see your plan pay off.
Negatives: (I'll try to keep this updated as the game is being developed)
- Can't see details about a brother before you hire them. You have to pay them a sum up front, only to immediately fire most of them because they're no good (if you wish to min/max).
- Difficult to know if you're strong enough to take on a given enemy type unil you've tried and failed. Brutal for a new player.
- Some game mechanics are really unclear until you read the wiki. Like what difference do the little stars you see on skills do, or what does a person's professional background matter, besides the skill adjustments? Why not show min/max rolls for different skills on level up?
- Too slow strategic map movement. It needs a fast forward mode, with auto-pause on enemy sighted, for example.
- On my campaign map, patrol missions always take me across mountains at some point. The algorithm seems to need some tweaking.

I recommend this game, because i'm biased. However, be expressively warned of bugs like insane frame rate drops (can be fixed by restarting the game), random, unexplaineble and reproducable, but avoidable, crashes, which as far as I believe, won't be fixed anytime soon or ever. Luckily, there are no plot stoppers though. I understand that others down-vote it for that, but I won't.
So, the combat is really fun in my book (haven't really tried magic), the voice acting ranges from okay to "meh", RPG-mechanics do their job, meaning: don't expect anything deep character-development-wise and the quests are okay (nothing groundbraking there). Graphics won't excite anyone, but it is no bother, because lighting, overall art- and character-design and effects are mostly quite alright to look at. Only most textures are downright abysmal. for today's standards at least. It even lures you into thinking that your choices in dialogues matter, they really don't, but that's not that big of a deal for me. A neatly told plot is better than incorporating branches no one really cares about.
And Venice as the setting sure doesn't hurt.
Sounds kinda mediocre, right?
It is.
Deck 13, the german adventure developers aren't known for Crysis-like eye-openers or action driven shenanigans, they are known for dialogues, characters and the fun of telling stories through a game. So, all things considered, they did pretty well with this semi-open world game out of their comfort zone. Because it has its heart in the right place. Which matters a lot to me.
I think "charming" would be the appropriate term. This game is that.
Also, Scarlett.
One of the best, most likeable and prettiest butt-kicking female protagonists in gaming ever. Take note, Sarkeesian drones, you might have a shining example at hand. For all I care, most of all those big-breasted polygon bimbos, which serve as eye candy and selling point in games, can go to hell. They have nothing on her. Nothing!
And I will start fist fights over it. I said, I'm biased, leave me alone.
Sure, this game isn't exactly afraid of the "sexy-factor" at times (sales matter), but it doesn't dwell on it and i'm not complaining about sexy in general anyway, because that would make me a hypocrite. Also it is low-poly anyway...
But I think I might have a very irrational crush on virtual Scarlett, in case you haven't noticed. *sigh*
Again. Because I pirated this game back then, liked it and had a second playthrough on Steam just now for a trip down memory lane. And to atone for my pirating sins, of course. By paying for it.
And because of Scarlett. Well, mostly because of Scarlett.
Did i mention her?
(On a sidenote: the effort put into keyframing her hair animations still astounds me for some reason, i know of no other game that did this so well, or, at all.)
I would love (even beg) for a sequel to this game to happen. Because all-in-all, it's actually one of my favorites and from a purely subjective POV, i am just digging the hell out of it, with all its nooks and crannies. Why else would i have bothered to babble on about it in this review, anyway?

I have 290+ games on my steam account, and until I got this game I never saw a reason to review any. This game is as if mount and blade and X-com had a baby and that baby became a drug addict and dreamed about necromancers and cultists.
Despite being in early access I have not come across a single bug or crash. One time it hung while loading, but thats the extent of the technical issues.
The game consists of two parts, an overland exploration part where you go from town to town performing contracts for local lords and the battle phase. Battle is clearly the focus of the game and is where it really shines. Different weapons have different abilities, different armor is either heavier or lighter, and your men all have backgrounds and skills that determine thier capabilities. Seeing a plan come together and gradually routing a force that is far superior to your own is hugely satisfying.
The "fantasy" element is very under-accented and its perhaps what draws me in the most. From what I can see there is no way for you to access magic yourself and you generally only see fantastical elements in the forces you fight, Necromancers, vampires, direwolves, and the undead. But from time to time you will gain an artifact item. They are unnaturally light or strong or whatever, but being so rareis what really makes you treasure finding them.
The game is still in early access and it shows in a few ways. There is no overarching goal, and while i personally prefer it that way the late game certainly feels a bit listless at times. There are also some slight balancing issues, where for example a long axe has a reach of two and can oneshot most enemies, but an equally pricey long bow is basically useless unless wielded by a master bowman and even then it dramatically underperforms against armor. For the most part the dev has stated that all these issues will be adressed, and I believe them.
Overall this game is amazing and can only get better. For 20$ I have already recieved entertainment value exceeding a AAA title. Just get it.

Fable, & Fable 2
You play as young Scarlett who is the only non blood relative in her hometown. She doesn't know who her parents were or what secrets will unfold in the coming times. The village is attacked and some blame the only outsider. The one who raised you will offer you know information about your past so you must seek it out on your own. You love dies, but you feel he is somehow helping you. You must go out and kill those who seek to kill you. You will level throughout the game, but can only use skill points at the proper trainer. You can specialize into melle combat, or be more twilight/magic orientated. You will get weapons, and armor throughout the game. The different weapons are used for different purposes. Hammers can blast down certain doors for example. The armor you find must be taken to a smith where you will pay to have it fitted to your body shape.
Magic and Twilight powers  are quite interesting. The dead will also help you along your quest in ways you may not expect initially. The game does have gamepad support, and I had zero issues getting my 360 controller working after I set the game to use it. It does also support 1080p resolution and other graphic options. The game itself comes off very lighthearted once the first 30 minutes of the game or so are over.
I admit it... I laughed as your love dies because the whole scene just felt terrible. I don't even feel the voice acting is bad as much as it being to over acted for the animations and graphics the game has. In that sense it comes off a lot like fable because in Fable I can't say I felt a thing when your village burned to the ground. The combat itself is very lacking. They teach you to roll in combat early on, but honestly I just walk away instead because I find it works better. I'm not saying its totally broken, but it is pretty weak. The graphics in the game itself feel more like it came out toward the end of original XBOX era. Bugs still exist in the game, and I've actually heard some can make it so you can't finish the game if you aren't careful.
The first half hour to hour of the game is easily the worst experience in the game. Once you get into this title it can actually be pretty fun. If you enjoyed the first fable, there is a descent chance you'll enjoy this. I am a bit bias, but I'd go with a balanced build that leans slightly toward magic. The game does offer some replay factor since you can only join one faction once you get to Venice. You may also enjoy playing around with different character builds.
I value the game at around $10 because even with bugs and flaws it can be a fun play for a old school Fable fan.

I'm writing this review on March 1st, 2016.
As far as I can tell, this game hasn't had a single update.
Here is Back to Basics Gaming and their developer associate speaking of a major update, written on June 10th, 2015.
Achievements, I think. Cool ! I'll actually have some goals when i play this.
A few months roll by, and nothing. Naturally, people are wondering what the heck is going on? This is before Back to Basics Gaming had a really solid reputation for publishing early access titles that never get finished.
The Developer, "Mint Age Studio" actually has another game in early access, that was released about two months earlier.
So they actually have another game on their plate, that they were busy with.
Not a good idea to have two unfinished games up for sale at the same time, in my opinion. Finish one, then start another, I say.
January 2016 rolls around, and apparently the developer can't finish the game as promised.  They are having financial issues.


hmm, now i thought the reason selling a game in early access, was to raise funds to finish the game? So if they've got two games in early access, and neither can be finished because of a lack of funds, what the hell are they doing on the store? It also wasn't a brilliant idea to have two games being developed at the same time, without funds to finish either of them. (Unless.. the plan is to never finish. Just take the money and run)
More and more people are beginning to smell something is off. Back to Basics Gaming doesn't have any answers for customers, and eventually the Developer, Mint Age Studios, admits he isn't working on EITHER of his early access games (This, and Escape Machines, that game that launched a month and a half before this one)
because he doesn't have any money for it, despite having two games published by Back to Basics Gaming being sold on steam. Is Back to Basics Gaming keeping all the money? Where has it gone? Both games have trading cards and are getting money from market transations.
The Mint Age developer starts getting pretty hostile, in the mean time, at customers.
So, Back to Basics Gaming publishes this guy's two games relatively close to each other. They launch in early access, for a price. And 9+ months later, he has no money to finish the games, so he's starting a NEW game, which he plans to sell and use that profit to pay for his previous two games which he couldn't otherwise finish.
What the heck kind of business strategy is this? It smells, and it smells bad.
Dan @ Back to Basics Gaming, has literally said nothing in regards to any of this as far as i know. I can't find an offical comment or response to Mint Age's declaration of stopping development on both games.
It was only a few months later, that Back to Basics Gaming would publish a different developer's game which shortly went from an update promised within a few weeks, to 4-5 months
You can read the story of that, in my review for that game.
During all this, Back to Basics Gaming published another game called "Flesh Eaters" (unrelated to Eaten Alive)
This also missed its release date by at least 6 months and counting.  Meanwhile, the developer has gotten two new games greenlit in the mean time. Both published by Back to Basics Gaming. Why is someone working on 3 games at once, especially when they can't even finish the first project? Keep in mind, this is a DIFFERENT developer than Mint Age and unrelated to the Eaten Alive devs (Space Cat Studios)
Back to Basics Gaming has also published "Lup", more recently. In tradition with most everything early access, it has missed its release date by 2 months and counting.
yeah i own a majority of their entire catalogue, and this game is in many ways, not an isolated incident with them. I would recommend avoiding Back to Basics Gaming. They can't be trusted to deliver on their promises, and you have a decent chance of the developer missing multiple deadlines or just completely walking away.

Ever wanted to be something other than human ?  This game lets you be a huge number of non-human things.  And possibly a human too, though I haven’t seen any yet.  Probably not everything as the name suggests, except in a metaphorical sense.
I started off as an Elk.  According to reviews other people started off as other animals.  I could wonder around a grassland and see other animals and things I’d expect to see there.  After a short while I learned how to overhear what they were thinking, which was usually something abstract and not in line with the kind of thing they were.
A short while later I learned how to become one of the things I could see.  There are two options: you choose "something a little bigger than me" or "something a little smaller than me" and the game highlights nearby options.  So from an Elk I could turn into a pig or a tree.  And then do it again and again.  Each time you turn into something new the game adds this thing to a categorised list.  You can look down the list and see a short description of this thing, usually the opening paragraph of Wikipedia or Simple Wikipedia.  The game has no real end but you might consider that being everything it’s possible to be would be an objective.
As each of these things you can "sing" which means making a noise that that thing might make (some always make the same noise, others have a few different ones).  You can also meet others of your kind and form a group — a flock of swans or an, erm, alphabet of black letters — and dance or perhaps have babies.
So you can go smaller and smaller and smaller until you’re an insect or a large rock.  Once you’ve spent some time as the extreme you learn how to descend or ascend scale.  At which point you’re a grain of pollen or an island, seeing a whole lot of new things that exist at this scale.  You can become those, and also travel down or upscale again to the point where you can change scale again.  The game does implement the wrap-around scale theory, where if you continually get bigger and bigger you eventually wrap around to tiny.  The detail of at what point and how this happens is interesting.
There are other powers you are told of when you’ve done each thing long enough.  So if you want to be a gigantic rabbit rampaging through a city, or to have the game rampage for you, you will eventually learn how to do it.
That’s it, really.  If you want to know what kinds of galaxy there are, get to galaxy scale, become a galaxy and look around you.  IF you see something you like become it.  If you want to learn about it, read the descriptive text.  But it’s not an encyclopaedia.  You can’t zoom straight to being an otter in its habitat, you have to work your way to it, and it’s possible there are no otters in the game.  I haven’t found one yet.  In three hours of playing I’ve been 317 different kinds of thing, which is about 22% of them all.  I calculate there are about 1500 different types of thing in all.
If you don’t do anything for a while the game goes into autoplay mode where it does the same sort of thing you’d do.  You can configure this so that, for example, is it or is not allowed to change scale.  So if it starts on an alien planet you get a tour of an alien planet and nothing else.  Or you might prefer that it changes scale frequently so you get a complete tour of the universe at all scales.  Something I didn’t see mentioned in reviews is that there’s an autoplay mode called "documentary".  In this mode, the game shows the text description of whatever it happened to be playing at the moment.  This is one of the best educational screensavers I’ve ever seen.  And, of course, if you find something you like you can take over at that point.  Possibly an interesting tool for teaching kids about the world.
In its ability to change scales this game reminds me of Katamari Damacy.  But there’s nothing else really like it.  It has no pace of its own.  You can play it with some objective in mind or meditatively, just to concentrate on something and keep your thoughts away from troubling things.
So if you ever wanted to be a stapler, a bacterium, a trumpet, a sun, a wolf, a fence, an oxygen atom, a cake, a wood splinter, a radio antenna, a lenticular galaxy, a campfire, a skyscraper, a motorcycle, a clump of grass, a grain of pollen, a dinner plate, a mushroom, a child’s alphabet block, a wedding ring, a plane tree, a castle, a bowling ball, the Cassini probe, a flake of skin, or an old boat, this is your chance.

[This review is from a guy who has had the game while it was in early access and is playing again with the game's official release.]
In a world filled with procedurally generated games, very few come near and far to what Starbound accomplishes as far as quality. If you enjoy games such as Terraria and Minecraft, you will absolutely enjoy this. This game has it all; exploration, farming, multiplayer, mining, crafting, quests, weapons, gadgets, boss battles, spaceships, multiple worlds, and more!
The gameplay is very similar to Terreria, where you have your character on a 2D plane and you explore the world arround you. Unlike Terreria, you are able to use a space ship to travel to different worlds, all unique in atmosphere, lore, and residents all while keeping your equipment and items throughout your entire playthrough of that character.
There are a TON of items you can collect in this game ranging from several different types of dirt and wood to different types of drops monster can give you to make certain type of equipment ranging from armor, tools, or weaponry. You will most likely get two daggers that look the same, but one will have poison damage and another will do fire damage which effects the type of damage per second (DPS) you will do.
The music and sounds in this game are -- excuse the pun -- out of this world! You will hear various orchastrated sounds for background music durring the day in certain bioms, certain areas underground, space, etc which all sound fantastic and make every world you visit feel new and different.
You can access different quests along your visit to these planets and outposts which you may choose to complete. The game has a main story which I have not yet complete so I can no comment on the quality of it, but from what I've seem included cutscenes and a neat story about saving the universe from a giant space cthuthlu.
Overall, I absolutely reccomend this game to every person who likes exploration, crafting, building, and space. Everything  in this game ranging from music and sound to gameplay has been fine tuned and really gives so much of a unique experience that no two people will end up on the same planet when starting the game.

Sleeping Dogs is great. It's just serious enough, just funny enough to ride the perfect line between tense and fun, funny and dramatic.
Like many other GTA-wannabes, Sleeping Dogs mixes up the formula with its setting. Modern day Hong Kong feels much like the usual cities we've driven through, with the biggest exception being driving on the left side. And this is actually a huge problem! It took me many hours to adjust, and even then making turns felt wrong. My whole intuition was off. One of those little things that helps contribute to the larger whole: this city is different, it's
.
The game that feels the closest to Sleeping Dogs is probably Mafia II. There's similar writing, gameplay, cinematics and style. But Sleeping Dogs improves nearly every aspect of the system. Not least of which is the story. Unlike Mafia II's abrupt, non-ending, Sleeping Dogs actually finishes the plot in a believable and satisfying way. (And not having to watch your spedometer or gas levels are big pluses too.)
The worst area is probably the guns. Not being able to carry more than one primary is a real shame, and slows down the combat pacing considerably. This is a primarily melee-based game, which I found quite boring during the early hours when your moves are limited. Luckily you can upgrade to open up more options. That helps, but it's still the weakest part of the game. The moments when you get nice weapons and plenty of ammo given to you by the story really shine by comparison.
The best part is the cinematic sequences. The voice acting is great. The direction and cinematography are better than you'd expect. And the in-game engine rendering the scenes makes them look surprisingly good. There are some awesome lighting effects. Sadly, this does not translate to the open world. The detail might be turned down because of draw distance, and the camera being so pulled back certainly doesn't help. There simply aren't a lot of natural shots that look great when you're roaming around, which is a missed opportunity - because there could be.
Not having a fast travel system was annoying. Some of the songs on the radio seemed to be way too overplayed (just like real life!). A few of the achievements required stupid amounts of random grinding ("Gambler" anyone?). And the DLC consisted of a few thin excuses to put you back in the ring. But these are relatively minor gripes on a polished package. I eagerly await a sequel.

Just finished the game for the first time in years. I've always played it on my PS2 when I was a kid, but never had the chance to actually beat it.
GTA III is a fantastic game. It's one of the fathers of 3D open-world gaming. You can see elements of this game in current generation open world games, like GTA V or Watch Dogs 2. It plays a big role in videogame history, for sure.
It has some limitations, but I think that's exactly what makes this game special and different from the other titles.
For example, GTA III lacks a map - yeah, you just can't pause and open the map so you can mark and travel wherever you want to go. In order to go to an Ammu-Nation store, for example, you need to know your way to the store before going there, without the help of a map or a blip. It's a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥sometimes, but I actually think that's lovely. In the last missions of the game you probably already know Liberty City better than your own real city and that is pretty much fantastic. The game lacks many basic functions that were later introduced in GTA San Andreas and other titles, but this doesn't turn the game into a bad game. Not even close. Its limitations create a unique and pretty nostalgic feeling.
Also, it is locked on something like 25FPS. And no, you can't unlock it to 60FPS without breaking the whole game while doing it. If you disable the built-in frame limiter, the game simply goes nuts. Physics, cars, AI, pretty much everything breaks up. There's a simple and functional workaround for that, I'm writing it on the next part - so let's talk about its flaws.
The PC version have some flaws when played out-of-the-box. Wide-screen resolutions are stretched 4:3 and man, it looks like♥♥♥♥♥ You need to patch it with a fan-made fix in order to play it in real 16:9 Widescreen, then it gets lovely.
Also, PC textures are not very good. They're pretty much the same as the PS2 version and they're kinda ugly IMO. But there are patches fixing that without transforming or changing the game experience.
The original XBox version of the game had way better lighting effects, textures and pretty much everything enhanced. There's a fan made patch that inserts these XBox upgraded assets into the game, too, so you can play the DEFINITIVE version of the game without modding it and changing the experience as a whole. It stays original and as a bonus, way more beautiful.
Also, this mod also fixes the stupid framerate lock. It upgrades the 20FPS slow♥♥♥♥♥experience to a very smooth, beautiful 35FPS one. Yeah, I know you must be laughing at me right now, but trust me. I mean, please, trust me. This game is absolutely fantastic at a locked 35FPS, man. I really couldn't believe I was playing something so smooth at that framerate. Really, frame-pacing is ROCK SOLID and the smoothness is great.
You can check how to enhance your game experience with this game on PCGamingWiki. They have a very good article just about these patches and fixes.
To end this long, tiring review, I must repeat that GTA III is a AWESOME game. It's legendary and every videogame fan should play it because it plays a gigantic role in videogame history.
It may not be as good as San Andreas or the modern ones like IV (which is the best, IMO), but it still packs a lot of nostalgia and a great experience. I truly recommend everyone to play it, because it is simple, PLAIN AWESOME.

A nice narrative-driven action RPG with very beautiful and colourful visuals. Bastion has you visit different stages in a quest for collectible items to help you restore the hub area (called The Bastion), which is a small flying fortress.
The gameplay is similar to most other isometric action RPGs with hack and slash elements. There is a variety of enemies, weapons, and special skills. The game offers a nice hub area management, so you get to see it improving with each mission you. You raise important buildings, such as the forge, distillery, etc, which allow you to upgrade your weapons, buy stuff, accomplish memorial challenges, and even activate shrines of peculiar deities that make enemies stronger in exchange for earning you more of the game's currency with each kill.
In addition to regular missions, there are also proving grounds associated with each weapon you find. These proving grounds provide you with unique challenges, and depending on how well you do, you get a prize. Each weapon's challenge is different. For example, the hammer's challenge requires you to smash 100 objects as fast as possible, whereas bow's challenges requires you to destroy all targets in as few shots as possible, and so on.
I liked the variety of weapons the game had. It diversified the gameplay and allowed you to choose your preferred playstyle since each weapon acts differently and is useful in different situations (I personally enjoyed destroying things with a Galleon Mortar).
For an action hack and slash game, it has a fairly good story. Don't expect something super tense and immersive, but you can be sure that you won't just be going from area to area with no goal. The narrator who speaks whilst you're out adventuring is also fun to listen to (and in my opinion way better than in Supergiant Games' other title Transistor).
Overall it's been a fun game to get through. The presence of a couple of story choices in the final mission seemed a bit strange, since the rest of the game didn't have those, so this addition seemed a bit off, and some parts of the game could feel a tad repetitive, but otherwise there's nothing much to complain about.

UPDATE 2 : after some hours, the game is just unplayable and every loading screen freezes, forcing me to restart the game. It's a pain. Changing this review to not recommended.
UPDATE : it seems like you can avoid most CTDs by putting the game in Winp XP SP3 compatibility mode. Now I can recommend it, as it solved the problem for me, but keep in mind there is still a risk.
PROS :
- a nice, lovely heroine ( who looks a lot like the old Lara Croft, no ? )
- simple but effective combat system and camera auto-lock
- nice ideas like being able to switch between the world of the living and the world of the dead. You can find secrets, and even do it during combat to escape your enemies or sneak behind them. You can also break fragile doors with a hammer.
- you can't wear the armors you find directly, because they are fitted for the big guys you fight, not a petite heroine like Scarlett. So you have to ask a smith to make them fit for you.
- as the left click is used to attack AND loot, you can't loot whith a weapon in your hand, so they added CTRL+click to do so, which is nice.
CONS :
- ugly graphics and textures, especially the environments ( we can see the texture seams, some normal maps are inverted, we see the separation between the meshes EVERYWHERE, etc. ). I know it's a game from 2009 but common guys, it looks so amateurish.
- CTDs, CTDs everywhere, the game is just unplayable ( half of the forum posts are about people getting CTDs )
- performance issues even with a GTX 660ti which can handle Skyrim on high settings
- physics make the game stutter ( reinstalled physX, doesn't change anything ), breaking a pot will put your PC on it's knees.
- any loading screen has a random chance to freeze for no reason, so you better save all the time
- sometimes the environments don't load, everything is black, need to quit the game.
- the "big open world" seems to be a big lie. The first levels are just corridors, and Venice is kinda small and separated in several areas.
Overall the game is so ridden with bugs, i don't know if I can finish it, but I'll try.

Okay so I've been keeping an eye on this game for a lot of time, and trust me, the dev team is probably the most dedicated and enthusiastic people I've ever seen in the industry, to the point where they would patch a bug few hours following it's report. They are simply awesome people, props to them.
Now, the game...
It's a turn based strategy game with a level of RPG that might not be the most inmersive but it surely makes the player feel involved in the story. Gameplay wise it's pretty straight forward, without excesive menus, inventoy tabs, abilities or commands that may scare more casual players away.
Yet it has some complexity to it, with a definitively strong strategy element and a brutal learning curve. Your company will probably get slaughtered again and again until you get the hand of it. It is so rewarding when your men return without casualties from a mission, or when you manage to save your most valuable brother from the fangs of certain death.
Another great asset is the artistic style of the game, which is very unique and nice looking. The models are hand drawn and very detailed, and you'll probably end up trying to collect every gear piece just for the looks.
Gameplay wise, and even if it's a turn based game, feels very agile and enjoyable, with a very nice interface and level design. The campaign map is randomly generated, something that makes every game feel more unique. It has a functional economy going, and actions have consequences, much like in M&B series.
Overall, it is a great choice for enjoyment, I'd recommend it again and again.

So this game came out a while ago, never knew it existed until a few days ago.  A combination of the low price tag and not having anything else to play drove me to buy this game, I did some preliminary research and bought knowing that it would be fun, but not expecting a masterpiece.  This is what I saw:
Graphics:
This is one of those games that isn't going for photo-realism.  Instead it offers a vary stylized world like Dishonored, Borderlands, or Fable to name a few.  Because of this, I believe the game has aged very well, it's not supposed to look like real life so the fact that it doesn't have Crysis 3 visuals doesn't bother me.  That being said, if you are a very visual person and you don't like stylized graphics the visuals are really going to bother you here.
Gameplay:
The gameplay is realtime, and is primarily based around striking and dodging.  It's about hitting without being hit.  Later you learn how to block, but I never really found it as effective, especially when fighting groups.  The combat is great in some places and not so great in others.  When you're fighting other humans like assassins or soldiers the game is really fun, because your enemies will block and dodge back at you so it's not a slugfest, but beasts and monsters are another story.
If I had to say what I liked least about the game it would be fighting monsters because they don't know how to block or dodge.  What that means is that all you have to do is hit first and keep slugging away at them with your combo chain.  I suppose the developers realized this made monsters incredibly easy, and decided that to compensate they would give monsters a ton of health, which only serves to make the slugfeast even longer and more irritating.
That being said, the combat in general is fast and easy to get into, while at the same time not being mindless.  I've only played the game once, it should be noted that there are many magic abilities that I never got to go for physical combat skills, so I can't really comment on how they add to the experience yet.   I intend to explore that on my second playthrough.
Story:
The overall story of Venetica is not exactly an original one:  you live an ordinary life until your world is turned upside down by trained killers hunting for you and kill at least one person you love causing you to swear revenge.  Then a long journey to eventually hunt down and punish those responsible.  But in Venetica it is all the things that happen along the way that in my opinion make this game a treat to play.
There are many choices and decisions Scarlett will have to make throughout the course of the story ranging from the important to the arbitrary, that really help you flesh out who your Scarlett is.  Ethical questions frequently arise such as "this person tried to turn me into the guards, but he claims his family would be hurt if he didn't, do you believe him?  Even if you do, is it safe to let him live?" Having played through to the ending I'm only going to say that these choices don't have much barring on the ending.
I expect a lot of people will be bothered by this.
Having said that, I appreciate all the choices being in there because at least for the first playthrough it makes me stop and ponder these moral delimas and issues of trust, and allows me to immerse myself in the story more and make Scarlett to be who I imagine her to be rather than the developer telling us who she is and what she stands for.  Or even worse... the silent protagonist.
Worth mentioning:
Sometimes what you have to do to advance in the story isn't exactly straight forward, and the game definately does not hold your hand at times like these.  You may need to consult a guide one or more times throught your first playthrough to get through.  I wouldn't worry too much about that though, I myself only needed to consult a guide twice, nevertheless, the more you know...
Overall:
I bought this game, as I said above, mainly out of boredom.  I knew it would be somewhat entertaining, and I was assured by other reviews that it is quite a long game (and it definately is, my first playthrough clocked in at 20 hours).  I could not be happier with what I ended up getting.  The world is engaging and the combat is (for the most part) fast and fun, and I really enjoyed all the choices to make on the way through the story.  If you don't mind stylized visuals, and you like swords and necromancy, I would recommend giving Venetica a try.

TL:DR just read the few sentences of the review
This contention that "the game is fine because we can mod back in all the fun stuff the devs were too lazy to put in the final game" is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ one, at best. You're right, no one is stopping you from doing that, but at the same time, the amount of core gameplay elements that are missing from Starbound don't justify the idea that we can just mod in a few new things to suit the game to our liking. It's not like the game has loads of engaging content and we just aren't happy with what it has.
The reality is that the devs took a lot of the content out to make the game feel as if it is fininshed at first glance, and simply didn't develop the story or other gameplay elements enough at all.The story is literally one of the most superficial and bland storylines that I have ever seen in a game, the grand array of techs that were once in the game has been reduced not even to a mere semblence of what it once was, the new tiered planet system makes the already bland storyline seem ever more flat, there is litereally no endgame whatsoever and the already lifeless storyline just drops off.
The "story" lieterally consists of you "scanning furniture" for missions and the Esher lady just repeating the same 3 quotes over and over again to reassure you that you are "being helpful" and not getting screwered over by a flat/lifeless storyline. It's almost like the devs were literally trying to trick the players into feeling like the story is more than what it is. That's the problem really is that I just don't feel enough to care about the story or any of the characters I meet. So Chucklefish didn't really even fool me into making a connection with the story. Which is sad.
I can't interact with any of the NPCs (button mash E to gain the same response every time), they don't even react to theft, the storyline NPCs say the exact same quote every time you talk to them... etc. the planets are tiered so exploration also feels procedural and not immersive. The structures are the same. The morphball tech is not fun to use. It feels like the devs literally changed the game to aclimate to the tech and just  trashed all of the other techs that were actually fun to use. Where did the Blink tech and so many others go? What happened to the non tiered planet and star systems that actually felt somewhat immersive? This game feels randomly generated to the point where it just kills immersion. Couple this with lack of features and depth to the characters and personailites you meet, and really the WHOLE UNIVERSE itself... and it just feels like a lifeless procedural void of repititon.
The idea for Starbound is great, and there are many great things about it. But it isn't finished by any means. The devs need more content for this game to be on board with other games in it's tier. And that fact that they released it like this for "1.0" is distrubting to me as an early backer for Starbound.
If you can't enjoy purposeless building on random planets (which are really all nearly the same) then I can't recomend this game to you. Just honestly. At the start it feels great - in the middle you are trying to convince yourself that its still pretty good - and in the end when the flat and lifeless story abpruptly drops off, you are left with nothing but what you have already seen: the endless procedural void that is Starbound.

I liked a lot of things about Everything. The mechanics, the procedural world, the discovery path, the narration all work really well together to make up the message and theme of the game.
What I did not like, to the point of disrecommending this game, is that its theme is fundamentally about death in the most mundane and therefore most scary way. And that this came without any warning of any kind from the game's marketing, reviews, etc. which are all about how it's "joyous" and "quirky" and "silly" and "relaxing". Rather, I find that it's about Alan Watts trying to convince me that it's OK that I will die, because "I" as an entity is a constructed concept anyway. Well, I like me as an entity, and constructed doesn't mean not real!
So I can't recommend a game that, again, without warning triggers a bout of severe existential dread and anxiety right before I have to go to bed.
It's like going in for a fun kids' movie but getting a melancholy art film about dying. and kids.

I definitely recommend this game for everyone who's interested in philosophy and enjoying a journey without purpose but only to understand the levels and perspective of existence itself.
