I currently have 145 games on my Steam account, and this is the first review I've bothered to write. After spending over 200 hours on this excellent and relatively cheap game, I thought that it deserved a recommendation. I can only think of a couple of games that I've ever spent more time playing.
This game does not feel like early access. I've only experienced one bug. It caused a crash. I reported it and the devs fixed it the same day and released a patch the next day. I havn't seen any other bugs.
The game has a very nice atmosphere. The events and missions are well written. They sometimes present you with difficult choises, often without any clear "correct" answer. What if this guy is lying? What if he's telling the truth?
The game is challenging. Combat is exciting and dangerous. Be prepared to see several of your favourite brothers die. When they do, just hire some new brothers. You'll grow to like the recruits soon enough. Maybe they'll even live longer than their predecessors.
I used to think that the character progression was not well implemented. That has been improved in the latest patch. You can now chose 3 stats to improve on levelup, and the perk system has been completely redone. I noticed some negative reviews because of the previous system. Some of the reviewers had spent considerable time playing. How can you not recommend a game that has entertained you for 50 hours even if you don't like one small part of it?
Now my only complaint is the lack of purpose or long term goals in the late game. When you have a full warband with good gear and several levels, you could always try to improve them further but I feel that I'd like something else to motivate me at that point. This may be improved when faction wars are implemented. It'll take you a long time to get to that point, and the journey is worth the money.
I see no reason not to put your money in at this stage unless you don't like turn based strategy games or you don't want a challenge.
Edit: At more than 300 hours now, I've seen another crash bug once and a few minor mistakes.

I can fully recommend this game, even in it`s EA-state. If you enable beta-patches you get a very stable, very entertaining game already filled with more than enough content.
Battle Brothers is a Mercenary simulator with an open world, heavy rpg mechanics (leveling of your troops, gearing them up...tons of loot, etc.) and a turnbased tactical combat which already is top notch.
This all takes place in a beatifully crafted 2d world (great art-style), accompanied by an amazing soundtrack (classical strings, percussions, etc.), meaty feeling sound effects and troop permadeath.

Managing your ressources (food, repairmats, healing stuff, arrows/bolta and ofcourse money), growing your band of mercs and fightint all from bandits to the undead, while exploring a world filled with lore and many little stories already makes a great game. if you like rpgs, medival-sims or turnbased tactical game buy it and thank me later.

The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth is a game that defies explanation. The story is horrifying and is difficult to explain to casual players. The graphics are grisly and purposely dated. There is no instruction guide in the game outside of the first room you log into. Yet this game is what all rogue-likes should aim to be.
The depth of the mechanics are incredible: you collect items in the game and they synergize with one another. Find a bomb? Cool! Then you find an item that makes all your bombs blow up into five tiny bombs. Cooler! THEN you find a bomb that shoots your attack in all directions when they blow up, so all your bombs do that.
There are thousands of combinations and they, along with the random layout every time you load, make this near-infinitely replayable. Some runs are 10 minutes of overpowered glory. Some runs take over an hour of intense effort to fufill. And there are hundreds of little secrets and tricks to learn as you play, along with a tremendously welcoming and helpful community.
Buy this game if you like action/adventure and want a constantly changing challenge. Just don't look at the plot too hard. It's better that way.

This certainly isn't the game for Everyone. I'm pretty sure more people will hate it (or get bored quickly) than like it, but that's ok. Those people have their games, and Everything really worked for me.
It's a surreal sort of game with amazing depth. The amount of different types of things the game has modeled and accounted for is staggering - I've spent much of my game time thinking, "Wow, that's in here, too? (It really does have Everything)".
There isn't much to *do* in the game, and that's going to rub people the wrong way. This isn't a game about gameplay, it's more about exploration (and even that runs out after a while) and peaceful contemplation. The lectures by Alan Watts constantly pulled me forward in the game - little snippets of reward for pushing far enough and exploring enough. This is a great midnight game when the lights are out and the house is asleep and you just want to peacefully drift through and think about things.

Conversely, the "bosses" are enjoyably faster paced offering a decent challenge. And whilst they merit praise, they cannot hold up the rest of 140's sluggish experience.
The art style is rather bland in my opinion, I understand it's meant to be minimalistic but that doesn't mean there shouldn't be any flair to it (see Electronic Super Joy and INK). Finally, as a fan of various electronic genres; I simply don't get the fuss about the soundtrack.

For twelve years, you have been asking: Who is John Galt? This is John Galt speaking. I am the man who loves his life. I am the man who does not sacrifice his love or his values. I am the man who has deprived you of victims and thus has destroyed your world, and if you wish to know why you are perishing-you who dread knowledge -I am the man who will now tell you.”
The chief engineer was the only one able to move; he ran to a television set and struggled frantically with its dials. But the screen remained empty; the speaker had not chosen to be seen. Only his voice filled the airways of the country-of the world, thought the chief engineer-sounding as if he were speaking here, in this room, not to a group, but to one man; it was not the tone of addressing a meeting, but the tone of addressing a mind.
“You have heard it said that this is an age of moral crisis. You have said it yourself, half in fear, half in hope that the words had no meaning. You have cried that man’s sins are destroying the world and you have cursed human nature for its unwillingness to practice the virtues you demanded. Since virtue, to you, consists of sacrifice, you have demanded more sacrifices at every successive disaster. In the name of a return to morality, you have sacrificed all those evils which you held as the cause of your plight. You have sacrificed justice to mercy. You have sacrificed independence to unity. You have sacrificed reason to faith. You have sacrificed wealth to need. You have sacrificed self-esteem to self-denial. You have sacrificed happiness to duty.
“You have destroyed all that which you held to be evil and achieved all that which you held to be good. Why, then, do you shrink in horror from the sight of the world around you? That world is not the product of your sins, it is the product and the image of your virtues. It is your moral ideal brought into reality in its full and final perfection. You have fought for it, you have dreamed of it, and you have wished it, and I-I am the man who has granted you your wish.
“Your ideal had an implacable enemy, which your code of morality was designed to destroy. I have withdrawn that enemy. I have taken it out of your way and out of your reach. I have removed the source of all those evils you were sacrificing one by one. I have ended your battle. I have stopped your motor. I have deprived your world of man’s mind.
“Men do not live by the mind, you say? I have withdrawn those who do. The mind is impotent, you say? I have withdrawn those whose mind isn’t. There are values higher than the mind, you say? I have withdrawn those for whom there aren’t.
“While you were dragging to your sacrificial altars the men of justice, of independence, of reason, of wealth, of self-esteem-I beat you to it, I reached them first. I told them the nature of the game you were playing and the nature of that moral code of yours, which they had been too innocently generous to grasp. I showed them the way to live by another morality-mine. It is mine that they chose to follow.
“All the men who have vanished, the men you hated, yet dreaded to lose, it is I who have taken them away from you. Do not attempt to find us. We do not choose to be found. Do not cry that it is our duty to serve you. We do not recognize such duty. Do not cry that you need us. We do not consider need a claim. Do not cry that you own us. You don’t. Do not beg us to return. We are on strike, we, the men of the mind.
“We are on strike against self-immolation. We are on strike against the creed of unearned rewards and unrewarded duties. We are on strike against the dogma that the pursuit of one’s happiness is evil. We are on strike against the doctrine that life is guilt.
“There is a difference between our strike and all those you’ve practiced for centuries: our strike consists, not of making demands, but of granting them. We are evil, according to your morality. We have chosen not to harm you any longer. We are useless, according to your economics. We have chosen not to exploit you any longer. We are dangerous and to be shackled, according to your politics. We have chosen not to endanger you, nor to wear the shackles any longer. We are only an illusion, according to your philosophy. We have chosen not to blind you any longer and have left you free to face reality-the reality you wanted, the world as you see it now, a world without mind.
“We have granted you everything you demanded of us, we who had always been the givers, but have only now understood it. We have no demands to present to you, no terms to bargain about, no compromise to reach. You have nothing to offer us. We do not need you.
“Are you now crying: No, this was not what you wanted? A mindless world of ruins was not your goal? You did not want us to leave you? You moral cannibals, I know that you’ve always known what it was that you wanted. But your game is up, because now we know it, too.
“Through centuries of scourges and disasters, brought about by your code of morality, you have cried that your code had been broken, that the scourges were punishment for breaking it, that men were too weak and too selfish to spill all the blood it required. You damned man, you damned existence, you damned this earth, but never dared to question your code. Your victims took the blame and struggled on, with your curses as reward for their martyrdom-while you went on crying that your code was noble, but human nature was not good enough to practice it. And no one rose to ask the question: Good?-by what standard?
“You wanted to know John Galt’s identity. I am the man who has asked that question.
“Yes, this is an age of moral crisis. Yes, you are bearing punishment for your evil. But it is not man who is now on trial and it is not human nature that will take the blame. It is your moral code that’s through, this time. Your moral code has reached its climax, the blind alley at the end of its course. And if you wish to go on living, what you now need is not to return to morality-you who have never known any-but to discover it.
“You have heard no concepts of morality but the mystical or the social. You have been taught that morality is a code of behavior imposed on you by whim, the whim of a supernatural power or the whim of society, to serve God’s purpose or your neighbor’s welfare, to please an authority beyond the grave or else next door-but not to serve your life or pleasure. Your pleasure, you have been taught, is to be found in immorality, your interests would best be served by evil, and any moral code must be designed not for you, but against you, not to further your life, but to drain it.
“For centuries, the battle of morality was fought between those who claimed that your life belongs to God and those who claimed that it belongs to your neighbors-between those who preached that the good is self-sacrifice for the sake of ghosts in heaven and those who preached that the good is self-sacrifice for the sake of incompetents on earth. And no one came to say that your life belongs to you and that the good is to live it.
“Both sides agreed that morality demands the surrender of your self-interest and of your mind, that the moral and the practical are opposites, that morality is not the province of reason, but the province of faith and force. Both sides agreed that no rational morality is possible, that there is no right or wrong in reason-that in reason there’s no reason to be moral.
“Whatever else they fought about, it was against man’s mind that all your moralists have stood united. It was man’s mind that all their schemes and systems were intended to despoil and destroy. Now choose to perish or to learn that the anti-mind is the anti-life.
“Man’s mind is his basic tool of survival. Life is given to him, survival is not. His body is given to him, its sustenance is not. His mind is given to him, its content is not.

For the developers, please dedicate your awesome skills and craftmanship in developing this game. You have my full support!

You the survivor have to find your son, rescue the commonwealth, save the minute men, help the brotherhood of steel and keep yourself alive. On a modern machine the graphics look good, but I would throw in a couple of mods and it is far more enjoyable experience. I have no interest in the creation club so cannot comment on it. I do see it has recieved criticism, but I generally avoid "micro" transactions on these kinds of products.
I am enjoying the game a lot, there are some bugs and sometimes you get faulty cameras during cut scenes. There are some strange quests that make you wonder what bethesda were thinking about when they wrote them. The crafting system needs to be modded to really make it worth your while, so does the settlements system. Some of bethesda's logic is a bit silly. I the player should be able to scrap the buildings too and use them to construct new dwellings without mods.
Companions are hit and miss at times, but they are worth dragging along for backup as you will fnd yourself outnumbered a lot of times in the Boston wasteland. There are several factions to join, but eventually one will go against the other and you will be forced to choose. The perks system is not as much fun but it is there, Some of the perks are useless though, however everyone plays differently.
Game seems to run okay on most settings (high or over), not experiencing any slowdown. Mods for weather really do make a difference you should try it if you get the chance. Lot of fetch quests, but there are some good stories if you stick it out.Exploring is always rewarded with side quests, so if you have the time, do so.
Would I recommend the game? Yes,
Would I recommnend modding it? Definately Yes
If you want the dlcs, wait till their super cheap or on sale before purchasing them, they tend to be poor value for money. If I had to say buy one, I would go for Far Harbor, that would be my next acquisition. Rest are a bit meh!

Sleeping Dogs is my favorite in the GTA-format game genre. You play as Wei Shen, an undercover cop with a vendetta against one of the Triads' bosses - a red pole in the Sun On Yee, a notorious gang with their hands in just about any criminal activity in or surrounding Hong Kong.
This game plays like a movie, and in fact you can sit and watch all of the cinematics pieced together into one movie-length video on youtube if you so choose. But for someone like me, who has by the way, seen the game played four times in different LPs, and watched the feature-length "film" of the cut-scenes, just watching won't be enough. There are dozens of cars and hundreds of potential outfits, collectible items, and a lot of open-world exploration.
The love that I have for Sleeping Dogs is unmatched by nearly any other fixed-plot game*. That old cliche goes something like - I laughed, I cried, I ___. Well, the first time I finished Sleeping Dogs, I laughed, cried, and wanted more. So I rewatched it, and then rewatched it again, made a few gifsets, bought lots of DLC... You know the drill. When you become attached to a story in the way I've become attached to the story of this game, you can play it 500 times and never lose interest.
10/10.
*I consider a "fixed plot" game to be a game wherein I, the player, have no hope of altering the main storyline in any way, shape, or form. The plot will play out as it is designed to, and I am there to enjoy the ride.
I highly recommend this game if you are a mortal kombat fun. Also use a gamepad to play the game it's easier that way.

I purchased this game because I had a 90% off coupon and when I saw the screenshots it reminded me of the original Warcraft game, which I loved.
Being familiar with RTS I decided to skip the tutorials and jump straight into the game, which was a huge mistake because I couldn't figure anything out on my own.  Part of the issue was there was no way to tell what you had selected.  Most games will highlight or box the unit or building that you have selected so if you have multiple units or buildings of the same type you know which one you've selected.  Also useful for when the units get closely bunched so you know you've selected the correct one.
After quiting the main campaign and going into the tutorials I was still confused about several key points.  First, I didn't see anywhere in the tutorial that told you the "sign post" of a building had to be connected to the road instead of any portion of the building (as was true in Warcraft 1).  This led to frustration as I had half a building constructed and a bunch of laborers sitting around doing nothing because the road didn't touch the right part of the building.  It didn't seem possible to rotate the building to change where the sign post was.  It was also offputting that laborers and serfs aren't rolled into one job.  Having a laborer wait at a build site because he didn't have materials was disappointing, especially if the build site was right by the storehouse.
I feel as if the combat tutorial was also far to short for the complexity of controlling combat units.  It would have been nice to include the paper-rock-scissors hierarchy of which units are strong against each other.  It was hinted at by telling you to attack certain units with a specific unit type but I believe there were only two instances of this.  There was also no explanation for how to train additional combat units.  It took a bit of playing around to figure out that you had to train a recruit at the schoolhouse then train him into the appropriate class at the barracks, but only if you have the appropriate equipment.  Another thing missing from the tutorial was facing and lines.
The combat in general also seemed somewhat clunky.  In the combat tutorial I had units charge past the enemy archers I was trying to attack, taking heavy casualties while they essentially encircled the enemy.  I also had a line of archers, facing forward, not auto-attack a lone enemy unit as he walked right up to them and slaughtered half the line.  It's not bad to have a lot of options and depth in combat but units should also use common sense.
Overall, this game appeals to people that like to micromanage, and could be good if it had a little bit of tweaking.  If you're looking for fast action this is not the game for you.

I bought this game several months back and play it on and off as it updates and so far I am very impressed. It is an early access game but I have the utmost confidence in the developers. They have a project with a goal. Nothing too ambitious and at the same time it is not underwhelming. They take their time while working at a timely pace.
As for the game itself, Battle Brothers is a Turn Based Strategy game about managing a company of mercenaries in a high fantasy setting with bandits, goblins, orcs and even zombies (among other things). It has a leveling system that works by character as well as a permadeath system. You gain loot, exp, and gold from completeing missions or clearing out enemy bases that randomly spawn on a radomly generated map. As you complete missions you gain reputation with the various factions generated with the map. If you fail missions you lose reputation.
The interface: It is clear and easy to grasp, the game is so simple to get into it barely needs a tutorial. Buttons are clearly labeled and inventory management has a sorting option, making it a breeze to go through your stash.
The combat: The combat is almost like a mix between your standard TBS game and chess. There really aren't many animations and the characters are 2D game pieces. It has various weapons and fighting styles as well as skills that characters gain as they level up. So far it is balanced but not equal in that there is balance, but each enemy has a different fighting style that you have to adapt to. It can take a lot of trial and error if you don't read a guide (which I do not personally consider a bad thing)
The AI: I am actually very impressed with the AI. Human enemies are fairly unpredictable, goblins are sneaky opportunists, while orcs use brute force and shock and awe. It puts you on the spot to choose a fighting style and formation to fit the type of enemy.
Graphics: They are on the low side. If 2D characters over a hex background are a dealbreaker for you, this game may not tickle your fancy the way it did for me and many others. They are smooth and demand very little however. Most up to date computers should be able to run this game with no problems. While it is 2D I actually enjoy the art style used for characters and weapons.
Cons: My only real gripes are the lack of story, lack of depth in the faction system, and repetitiveness. While I have a lot of fun with this game, it is easy to slip into a grind where you are running missions just to replace the men and equipment you lost on the previous mission.
Overall: This is probably my favorite game this year so far. I have had a great deal of fun with this game and look forward to what is to come of it. I'd give this game 2 thumbs up if I could.

Note: I have around 1500 hours in L4D2 at the time of writing this review.
Left 4 Dead is a well-known zombie shooter set in a variety of locations. Each campaign has 4 survivors, who have to reach the safety vehicle or area on the other side and have to fight their way through tons of infected. There's also a versus and survival mode.
PROS:
+ Teamplay can make a real difference. Good communication and teamwork seem to be more important than skill
+ It's not too much the same as L4D2; some mechanics, items, statistics, sounds and visuals are different
+ The game is nearly a decade old and still does not feel obsolete or outdated. It's also not completely abandoned, either. If anything, this game should have won or at least end up as a finalist of the "Test of Time" Steam award
+ The Source engine and console make adjusting the settings to your likings easier and is a comfortable engine to play with
+ L4D is harder than L4D2 due the lack of variety in items and overall difference
CONS
- While L4D seems to be less dense in hostile population than L4D2, there's still a fair share of people who aim to ruin your fun
- The game is, unavoidably, largely inferior to L4D2, especially since the content is nearly halved in comparison if you "downgrade" to this game (half the maps, half the infected, half the weapons, half the items and no mutations)
- While you may find some people to play with, the servers can be a little empty, especially if you want to avoid the lower difficulties
- Unlike the sequel, addons in this game are just as annoying to configure as in most games. Don't expect the same support L4D2 has to offer
Some consider L4D to be completely inferior to L4D2 due the lack of content, while veterans find it to be the complete opposite. I find both games really enjoyable either way and I often find myself launching L4D when playing the old maps, just for the nostalgia or refreshment.
One tip, you can't block trolls like in L4D2, so if you encounter a troll, just kick or shoot them.
10/10 Buy now, even if not on sale.

Overall for an early access title it is not bad, i have only had about 2 hours on it so far and no CTD, just some texture glitch which made all the buildings turn black, its a bit laggy in areas... but overall it went fine.
I have a reasonable amount of hours, online and offline of the guild 2 (over 100) and would have to say i am a good supporter of the series and mastered it well. With one of the overhaul mods for guild 2 which fixes some of the major issues we had with it, it is easily one of my most favourite games. So, the comparison...
I recommend this title so far as if you want to support the developers in further "finishing" the game by investing into it, then by all means invest, if you are looking for a complete feature game, without no annoying glitches then i would wait a few months and see how it develops... Surprisingly people dont understand sometimes what early access is, they think it should be bug free and "playable" , it doesnt have to be "playable" in the truest sense of the word, as you are basically alpha testing it for them and investing more into the project..
Now thats out the way time for the features, its ok.... so far from what i have seen it remains relatively true to the guild 2 in terms of concept ( build a business, by and sell and then go through political intrigue) and is enjoyable to a point... before it gets a bit arcade like. This may be expanded in time and i am sure it will, but there are 2 things which i hope they are looking to change otherwise unfortunately i will be put off from playing once released and that is.....
1 - in 2 hours i went from a poor shacked up guy that just rolled into town to a patrician with the ability to buy a super house and expand my business no end.... this felt like there was no depth or meaning to what i am doing, not only that but it was all automatic. No more going to the town hall and having to invest my xp / time / money to move up the ladder, just sit back and in no time become a royal. No real strategy to what i need to do. I didnt feel connected to my characters or my businesses like i did in the guild 2. It took me a good 15 hours to get a few levels up in the guild 2 and it felt an achievement, if this automatic upgrade based on XP stays, they have missed out, IMO, a large fun part of the game. ( fingers crossed it is only place holder )
2 - The use of complex interactions, intrigue and the political system. The guild 2 i believe ( with the overhaul mods ) did this to near perfection, the ability to bribe your way into office, throw fancy banquets to woo your allies and to use your dungeon master to torture someone when it was their time due at council to challenge your position and ultimately you retain your seat etc etc, i have yet to see any form of social interaction like this, maybe need more time to dig deeper, but from what i have seen of the UI and the options that are open to use at this moment it looks like this complex system is not there yet, fingers crossed it comes in because at the moment it lacks any form of depth.
So far these are 2 important game "breaking" features that i hope they add in time, based on my time testing it so far. But all in all i can recommend this early release with the premise of all in depth features, and more, being developed in the near future to a standard that made the guild series a truly unique master piece. So like i say, if you want to support them and have a quick blast at it, roll on, but for the most part i think people who cant deal with parting their money for something that is not ready, just wait out and keep popping back.

Sanctum 1 and 2, aside from similar enemies, are essentially two separate games. I think the main thing I like about this game is the different... um... classes? Heroes? that you can pick in this game. You can also augment your character with perks.
This game is far more FPS-like than the original game - you can jump over tower blocks (gone are the televators), enemies will attack you, and you have health. There are bosses that can destroy your towers, further cementing the emphasis of the FPS role. You also have a limit to how many towers can be built, and tower blocks are a separate resource.
Sanctum and Sanctum 2 are still the only games in this genre (perhaps still the only game if you specify FPS?) that deliver a satisfying experience. The only thing that comes close is Dungeon Defenders, which is more RPG-like and not as "action" filled as Sanctum 2 is.

It's games like these that make you appreciate modern real time strategy games. I understand the tags say Strategy, Medieval, Simulation, and City Builder, but it felt like a RTS. Modern real time strategy games have much better UIs, with less clutter, and more easily identifiable units/buildings. They also tend to give you more information about what your choices will lead to.
This game grants you almost none of that. It has a very poor UI, with a lack of easily identifiable information, like what each unit or building ultimately leads to. If you are a newcomer to the game, good luck. I can't comment on the graphics too much, as this seems to be a very old game, but even still, they're not that great.
The game is extremely slow paced. There are many different units and buildings to place, and I can't help but feel like less would be so much more in this game. I figured the serf would fill multiple different roles, but no, you have to build a schoolhouse to train the different types of workers. This is a convenience of modern RTS games, where you just have a one size fits all worker unit. This game affords you no such convenience. You also cannot command the serfs individually.
I honestly could not sit through very much of this game. It's just so boring, with a high barrier of entry. Taking the time to learn every unit, and everything that each building does is too much for such an old, obsolete game. There's nothing to be had here, except maybe nostalgia for those that played this many years ago.

Incredibly solid turn based tactics RPG even at this point in early access. Sandboxy much like Mount and Blade, there's no particular goal to the game other than playing it and building your team up. And much like Mount and Blade, everything else is in service of the combat.
Ideally the sandbox will become a bit more reactive and lively before release, but even as-is it's rock solid on the combat alone.
The final update hit so the game is by and large as it will be at launch, and I feel it's time to update this review.
You actually have goals, now. The ambitions system gives you bite-sized goals to strive toward, giving you additional renown (Increases your pay for contracts, gives you more/better contracts) and a morale boost to your mercs when you hit them. You also have late game crises as your ultimate goal, so the game even has a win state.
The sandbox did become more reactive and lively. Enemies/monsters have more of an impact on the settlements and the economy, and contracts seem more legitimate rather than purely spawned for your amusement.
The combat's still as great as it ever was, though slightly improved by balancing done to the perks and morale system.
TLDR summary: Possibly the best turn based tactical I've played, dethroning X-com/Xcom. Already gave it my seal of approval in early access and it's notably better now.

Introduction: I find myself typing this review thinking more about the conceptualization of existence, than the anime itself. Above all, there are two standards I hold true for anime. There are anime that simply entertain for the sake of enjoyment, and there are anime that stretches the boundary of human imagination. Serial Experiments Lain falls in the latter category and for this reason Serial Experiments Lain stands out as a true classic. Serial Experiments Lain pushes the envelope of what the perceived notion of what can be done with television as a medium. The show doesn’t just provide entertainment; it provides insight, and profound views and beliefs about technology and the role it plays in society. With that said it's time to get on with the review.
Story: Given that Lain’s story progression is very disjointed, if the execution were to be even off by the slightest, the show would have been ridden with plot holes. Lain however doesn’t need worry about plot and story in the same sense as other anime, but instead relies on the atmosphere and the characters to tell the story. What little plot Lain does have, the show works with it fabulously. Now some may argue that Lain is completely plot driven, but to each his own. Personally I believe that Lain strays as far as it can from bland episodic story telling, and in essence is similar to Citizen Kane in the aspect that the story has little to do with the show. Lain above all is a character study, and the plot only moves forward under the characters.
Art: Despite the art being off center in terms of traditional anime, it hardly deters from the overall enjoyment of the series. It is important to note that the series actually benefits from the unique art style presented in Lain. Art is not a big pulling factor for Lain, so if you are a fan of high quality art, you may be in for a rough ride.
Sound: The series relies on a minimalist approach to sound and music. Dialogue is sparse, but very profound. Sound effects are seldom used but with brevity, and has a lasting impact on the viewer. Once again, this lack of a quality that would normally be detrimental to an anime’s enjoyment, but becomes one of Lain’s strengths. The sound of the electricity running through power lines, the empty sound of Lain typing on her keyboard, and the scarce use of music. These are all memorable pieces of sound effects that adds to the overall impact of the show.
Character: Now this is where Lain shines brightest. In a vast wasteland of mundane same-old, Lain sticks out as an anime that takes its characters to a level that most anime can only dream of achieving. The character of Lain is perhaps the most deep and relevant characters in anime today. To explain upon this point, one would have to watch the series and comprehend the various themes and motif’s on one’s own. But in order to be brief, Lain’s character can be summarized as ascending from human status, to near God like power through the prowess of the internet. Ahem, I mean, “The Wired.” It’s a simple concept and seems like it has been done before, giving credit to the argument, and it probably has. But the beauty here is the cast of side characters that surround Lain. Her sister, her father, mother, and friends, are all extremely deep characters, that although don’t appear to be, are actually extremely poignant in their own right.
Enjoyment & Closing: If watched with an open mind, Lain will do more than simply entertain. It is truly revolutionary anime for its time, and the amount of depth in the show is utterly staggering. Never in my years of watching anime have I seen a show as thought provoking as Lain. If one were so inclined to contact me, we could talk for hours upon hours of the religious symbols, and religious references that run about the shows course. We could then change the subject to comparing Lain’s character to that of philosophy of the Jungian Shadow. We could converse and discover deeper and more universal meanings as time progressed. Lain is such a show that the viewer doesn’t just watch it. The viewer must be pushed to think, and who doesn’t want to do a bit a of thinking once in a while?
Honestly, one of the best early access games I have ever had the pleasure of playing. It feels like a complete game and the devs are still updating! Worth full price imo.

plays with a new innovative style, challenging gameplay, and a nice variety of levels. For each of the 13 levels, there are three available modes (plus two game modes: Easy and Normal) — Campaign, Heroic, and Iron; every level also has their own restrictions that decide which towers you can use and the max level they can be upgraded. The Campaign mode provides 20 lives, but Heroic and Iron mode offers only one life, essentially making the game many times harder.
There are four tower types — Archer Towers, Barracks, Mage Guilds, and Artillery Cannons. There are also eight tower upgrades that vary from Rangers to Barbarians. In addition, there are also 18 tower abilities that you can equip including Teleport, Poison, and Sniper Shot.
There are 30 monsters that range from Ogres and Yetis to Necromancers and Demon Hounds. Many people have a hard time memorizing each enemy’s ability, so there’s a handy Encyclopedia for the incompetent.
The best part of
is the visuals. In fact, the graphics are enjoyable to watch. Whether its mages dropping a lethal curse on crazed ogres, or troops in hand-to-hand combat with demon dogs, it’s a visual treat. On that note, the SFX are definitely worth mentioning, because when you activate Reinforcements, for example, a great voice actor actually yells out “Reinforcements!”, which is a great add-on to the experience.

I played Starbound a number of years ago and found it an enjoyable evolution of Terraria's sandbox/exploration concept, but it was clearly incomplete, so I set the game aside to wait for a proper release; I didn't even mind the long delay in development, since it suggested a better final product, but sadly the 1.0 release of Starbound still has an unacceptable lack of polish, and it fails to live up to the potential of being a successor to Terraria. It's in fact a clear step backwards from Terraria in many aspects:
The one upside of Starbound is the nice art style, but otherwise this release fails to live up to the hype or what could reasonably be expected from a game after 5 years in development. It's even questionable how much can be salvaged by mods, given the technological issues the game has. Overall, I wouldn't recommend this game in its current state; you'd have a much better time trying out Terraria instead and revisiting Starbound if/when it's actually designed with a proper vision.

Gather round, children, and I'll tell you a tell of gaming in the year of our lord nineteen hundred and eigthy four.  You see, back then, games HAD to rely on uniqueness to stand out.  Some where unique by having great graphics, others through innovative game play, while still others by challenge and re-playability.  In this age there came a game, on an ancient machine known only as a C64, a game called "Cliff Hanger".  It had the audacity to stand out by having something of a sense of humour and somewhat hazy rules that you had to suss out through exploration.   Comprised of a "scene", each level had to be explored and the rules and ways of beating it had to be discovered.  Failure simply meant that you watched fail animation that kind of made you smile.  And then this idea was lost to time, not quite enough to become legend, not too little to be utterly forgotten by those who were there.
Lost, that is, until now.
is a game about failure.  It's a game about exploration, and, ultimately, a game that you will step away from glad that you bought it.  The humour is on point, the presentation is solid, the music is engaging, and game play in interesting; it is worth the money the dev is charging.  It's not going to affect you, or change how you see gaming or narriative, or any of this, it's just solid, fun, silly game play.
Pros
----
- The graphical style is great retro-inspired chunky pixels
- It's pretty comical, with surprising outcomes for various actions
- Simple, stupid, fun
Cons
-----
- Once you've beaten it, you're probably not going back
- It's definitely not for everyone.  Hardcores will probably not enjoy it at all.
There's really not much more to be said about it.  On it's own terms, I'd give it a 8/10.

Starbound had around 3 years to become one of the best games ever created. So why do I feel like it was a better, more fun game before it's final release? I've played around 20 hours or so of the campaign, and I'm done, so it's definitely shorter than that. You may be saying, '20 hours? That's pretty good!' Wrong for three reasons.
Reason one; The boss fights take a long, long time to finish. So long, in fact, that I've seen people speeding up boss fight footage to make it finish quicker. And if you die? You need to restart the whole fight, and slowly tick away at their health bar once again. But you say that the weapons are too weak? Well, if you try to craft them yourself, they are even WEAKER than anything you may find. This wouldn't be a big deal if you didn't die towards the end of them a lot, making you do the whole thing over again.
Reason two; If I had known what I was doing, I could have knocked hours off. I'm not talking about speedrunning, I'm talking about the 'upgrade' mechanic that wasn't explained at all. Apparently, you can upgrade your equipment, such as your furnace, to create better ores. Perhaps the reason I didn't know this is because I played early access, but it wasn't explained at all either way, and I didn't notice the upgrade button until I looked it up. I instantly had much better equipment, and bursted through some of the planets I was having trouble at with ease using my new armor.
Reason three; IT WAS MORE FUN WITHOUT THE CAMPAIGN. I didn't put 200 hours in for the campaign; I put it in for the fun of exploring new planets, and the loot within their chests. It was more fun when you could summon bosses to wherever you are; have a lava battle with a giant robot, for example. Having their preset dungeons is stupid, and gets old quickly.
So is it worth buying?
For the campaign, no. The story is stupid, gonna be honest. At no time did I feel sympathy, sorrow, respect, or anger towards any of the characters. It's all the same for the different missions; meet a character, kill bad guys, fight boss, collect spoiler, and they join your clan. The final boss is stupid too. In the first mission (minor spoiler for the rest of this paragraph), they invade earth and destroy it, but at the final boss you see no way how they could have done this, because they are their own planet, and there is no space elevator to Earth.
For the workshop, yes. Eventually, I hope that they can eventually rip out the story, and let you play how YOU want to play, not how the game does. I've already seen biome additions, more dungeons, races, and etc. before the game was released, and I hope those can all transfer over here.
For exploration, yes... and no. You will not be limited by the story if you just explore, but some shops are closed until you do, and some quests cannot be completed. Planet explorers will have a fairly fun time, but village finders will not. Almost all the quests in the villages are the same. Here are the templates;
Can you give [person] X [item]? [Usually 2 or 3 more quests after this one]
Can you collect X [item]? [usually 2 or 3 more after this one]
My friend and I were going to talk about [something], but they never showed up. I think the [enemy] may have kidnapped them. Can you go to [location] to get them?
And then there's quests after the first quest is completed, but these are basically all you'll be doing at villages.
So, that's basically it. The recently added campaign sucks, and content was STRIPPED in the final release, such as some planets. HOWEVER, workshop and exploration can redeem this game. It will just take some time and patience. The reason I'm going to give this game a thumbs up is because it isn't a BAD game, and there's plenty to do without the campaign. But it's CERTAINLY not as good as it could have been.

Beautiful, calming, and insightful. This not a conplicated game, within a couple hours of play you'll have unlocked all your abilities. But that's really not the point. The graphics are style feel evoactive of Katamari Damacy in the best possible way, from the polygonally simple models to the way animals 'move' by comically shifting to a small set of angled positions. You can hear what's on a rock's mind or how a tower feels about its neighbors. And there are delightful and insightful audio clips scattered throughout. You're constantly rewarded for wandering, and while the game certainly doesn't have Everything it has a very large number of things to see and explore.
Sit back, relax, enjoy the soothing music and the contemplative audio clips and just let your mind wander. You won't regret it. I know what Early Access is. I can forgive a few imperfections here and there. But this game is VERY far from playable, let alone enjoyable. I'd look the other way if I could at least see that the core gameplay is an improvement over The Guild 2. Sadly it is not. And I don't see it becoming so. Even so I will keep an open mind and may change this review based on it's progress.
- Social standing is heavily dumbed down. Your rank is now a simple progress bar that fills alongside XP rather than through a combination of wealth, fame and bribing city officials in TG2. You don't even need to visit the city hall anymore. This means that your farmer that never leaves his farmstead will eventually become high nobility just because he farms. One moment you are harvesting some wheat and *poof* a magical letter from the Major sais you are part of the social elite.
- No building interiors. Even though they feature prominently in the promotion material and on the store page. This is a real shame because these were a major part of what gave TG2 it's charm. The game world has lost so much immersion because of it. No more hanging out in the Inn or watching dying plague victims in the hospital. No more watching characters being tortured or rotting in dungeons, dancing at lavish parties in patricians houses. No dramatic court cases leading to public executions, etc, etc, etc...
- Family life has been gutted. One of the most fun things to do in TG2 was courting your spouse, getting married and seeing the family grow together in the house with all those fun little animations. That is all gone now. The game taunts you by telling you that you need to get married ASAP in a loading screen. However peasants can't marry because the romance abilities are now locked behind social class levels. Do they mean to tell us that peasants didn't have children? The wedding is now a crappy cutscene that plays even though your character is still standing in the middle of the road on the exact spot where he met his wife three seconds ago. There is no courtship what so ever. 'wanna get married?' ... 'I never heard of you but since I like your face texture, sure! Let's do it stranger!' After that your wife will start to automatically pop out children because reproduction no longer requires physical contact between the husband and the wife. In fact, my character never even meets his(?) children because there is zero reason or incentive to visit your house.
- Terrible UI. Nothing feels intuitive! Even something as simple as accessing my character inventory was a chore to find out. In the last game I could click a building and the possible interactions for said building would pop up. The way it works now is that your character needs to walk all across the huge map and you hope the building does what your common sense tells you it should which more often than not leads to disappointment. For example I haven't even been able to figure out how to apply for an office at all. I can't talk to a clerk anymore because the city hall is just an outer shell without rooms inside. Buying stuff from the market interface is a complete pain in the♥♥♥♥♥because you can click until you are blue in the face but it won't register 4/5 times. Also it is very hard to know at which exact point in the sprawled out market your character or transport needs to stand to interact with it. Kind of a big problem in a trading game! You character has few abilities and even fewer social interactions compared to TG2, but for some reason they are all buried in far too many sub-menus with just one or two buttons in them. One of the few benefits of offering so little to do in the game should have been a slick UI at least, but even that didn't happen.
- Fake people and economy. At least in TG2 it took me the better part of a full playthrough before I started to see through the lie because at least it was a convincing one. My heart sank when I saw that TG3 is no better or even worse. The NPC's don't have daily routines anymore and just aimlessly wander around the map. Their job is to make it seem like they are part of a world where everything is interconnected but really they are useless as anything but eyecandy. No one but the player actually buys products at shops or those in the marketplace. The rest of the goods simply get magically added or subtracted over time. This becomes painfully apparent when you first start the game and the marketplace runs out of the precious starting supply of carts within the first few minutes while you can't afford to buy them yet. You don't see these carts entering into the traffic flow at all and there aren't a bunch of business owners crowding the marketplace scrambling to get them. You will be the only person standing there watching them simply vanish from the game for no reason. They aren't getting bought but rather deleted in a steady trickle. I know there will be rebalancing in the form of magical products being spawned/despawned, but is it really too much to ask that a game that focuses on trade uses actual supply and demand to distribute goods around the world? I'd love to actually compete against the other dynasties instead of the game playing pretend. If this is too hard to program then at least create a convincing illusion that the AI's are actually producing, transporting, consuming and thriving in a way that makes us believe they are following the same rules as the player. Make the NPC's actually stop at the market stalls and at the shops once a while, for example.
- Map size. They increased the map size while restricting our movement to just the roads that are unnecessarily long. This makes logistics an even bigger chore than it ever was before.
- Bugs & crashes. These are to be expected in an EA. Though I wonder why they were in such a rush to release it on steam in such an early state. Placing or upgrading buildings or even just clicking characters, which you'll agree are pretty important to be able to play this game will often result in random crashes.
- Text events. These are like chance cards in monopoly. In a board game these can work. Not so much in a simulator where I can see what my character is actually up to. So when a text event pops up saying how my character got insulted at the bar while he is sowing a field my immersion is broken instead of enhanced.
My starting character got an event saying he made money on real estate speculation. How? I own a shack and I juggle for a living. I stopped a murder? Again: how? I was just away making coffee. Did I miss something actually exciting? Stop telling me stuff that didn't happen! It seems like the text events try to sound spectacular to make up for how hollow the actual gameplay is.
Give us back the scrapped social interactions so we can make our own REAL events that made The Guild fun. Duels, romance, parties, wars... these were all fully animated and randomly occuring events in the Guild 2 that you could become part of and had real consequences in the game world. This new text feature is depressing to players who know what they have replaced.
- POTATO? WHAT'S A POTATO? You will learn to despise this phrase. It's the only full sentence your character knows. And boy oh boy does he love saying it! Over and over and over again. Fortunately the game allows you to dial the voice audio to 0%.
Overall verdict: Some of my complaints are fixable and some seem to be part of the new direction the devs are taking for this game franchise. The reality is that there are far better trade games out there and that by watering down the details and charm that made the Guild unique we aren't left with any reason to play this. Stay away from The Guild 3 for the next few months. You will not enjoy it in it's current state.
tl;dr : Very buggy, dumbed down and devoid of the charm that made TG2 a buggy but lovable mess. This time we just get the mess. Keep this game on your watch list for a few months, then check the reviews again.

This might be the best fighting game for PCs ever created. Mortal Kombat is not only a masterpiece, it is also a legacy, and this game does not disappoint even the most die-hard fans of the series.
I have played many games like this, starting from the Super Nintendo era, and none of them stood up to the level of Mortal Kombat III Ultimate... until this one. I can honestly say that I have enjoyed Komplete Edition the most.
It has good graphics, fun story, lots and lots of unlockable stuff, several modes, awesome combos, and Johny Cage. And like all Mortal Kombat games, we will see hectolitres of blood, tons of broken bones, severed limbs, heads, and spines here.
The port is pretty well done, and the fighting system is really tight and responsive. And it does not sell bonus characters and skins as DLC. (I am looking at you, Street Fighter X Tekken) Every fighter avalible feels unique, and there are no bad picks.
There are many hours of fun to be had in this game, with challenge tower, and all the Test your Might, Sight and other modes. It also has multiplayer, which unfortunately is not played by people very frequently.
There are some things it misses, though, like a single fight mode, in which you could choose your hero and your opponent, and I really hoped to see Li Mei in this game, but there are no big mistakes made.
But even the small ones are made up for, with brutal Fatalities. If there was one phrase to sum up a whole decade of gaming, it would be Duke's 'Come get some', but right after that it would be 'Fatality'. This installation of Mortal Kombat offers the player many different ways to kill their enemies, from decapitation to electrocution. Every fighter has two Fatalities of their own, and they are all really messy. Add to that stage fatalities, and you get the best gut-fest on this side of Milky Way.
Bottom line is, this game is a true Mortal Kombat, and is definitely worth buying, even at full price. Mortal Kombat Komplete Edition gets my nine out of ten.

On itself Sanctum would be great: Tower defense plus first person shooter, and there is even some sort of plot, even its if really cheesy.
However there are a whole bag of problems that ruin the fun:
1. the amount of money given at the beginning of each mission is uncorrelated to the amount that is actually needed to complete it. Sometimes way too much money is given, other missions will leave you with just 2 towers because thats all you can afford.
2. There is also no recompensation for playing alone, the money received is the same, meaning that some maps are only beatable with 4 players. Good luck finding them, there are not many active players left. Even less active players with a ping below 100ms.
3. The characters weapons are all horribly underpowered, and the characters themselves are very squishy and fragile, yet the towers too are too weak to deal alone with most enemies, forcing an uncomfortable compromise of pulling in and out of action quickly. And then you have the pleasure (in solo play) of having to race forward and backward across the map because there are often more than one core to protect.
4. No money is given during the waves for kills, which makes it hard to deal with bosses that destroy towers.
5. Speaking of bosses: Most will be armored head to toe, making them flat out invulnerable to any tower attacks, except lucky shots. So imagine having to do aimed shots (a whole magazine of them) on a boss while evading his minions and hoping that you do not die and that the other core wont be destroyed when you are finally done with this boss.
A challenge is of course welcome but rendering all your towers useless is a bit too much.
Considering that all those issues (and many more) have remained unfixed for now 4 years, this speaks ill of the developers skill or commitment to their product.

Sleeping Dogs was a game I bought in Steam's 2013 Autumn Sales, after being curious about this game for a long time and being aware that looking up YouTube footage might have spoiled the story for me, this sale was a good opportunity for me to just gamble on this one.
And it was jackpot for me. Having played Just Cause 2, GTA 1 to 4, Saints Row 3, L.A. Noire and countless other free roaming games, I was completely overwhelmed by how convincing Hong Kong was portrayed in Sleeping Dogs. Hong Kong, which in this review refers to the map in Sleeping Dogs, is a graphically pleasing platform that carries the player through a gritty storyline revolving around Chinese gangsters. Even though the city is small compared to most of the aforementioned free roaming city games, there is a healthy amount of detail put in every square foot of Hong Kong, making the city feel as big as it would have felt in real life. The city dynamics are downright convincing, you will encounter a large amount of variation among the residents, each with their own reason for being on the street. This, and the amounts of interaction provided for the player, is something that at the time of writing is not appreciated enough in the industry.
Sleeping Dogs features oriental themed music to reinforce that atmosphere. The genre of the background music as well as the radio stations vary from hip-hop to classic, all with Chinese roots. Luckily, a great majority of the used vocabulary is English, although you may encounter a Chinese swearword here and there. This is translated in the subtitles and may seem a bit forced, if not out of place. Personally I find it understandable considering a full English or Chinese transcript would've alienated the player from the casting in this context, or otherwise not being able to follow the story at all.
It's important that this appeals to the player as the emphasis of the game heavily lies on the implied Chinese gangster culture. This means that gunplay and car-craze is reduced to a minimum when compared to other games in this genre. Rather than mowing down your enemies it's more common to have to fight people barehanded, the use of several martial arts and enemies with different specialities makes this less linear than it may sound. I wouldn't go as far as calling this game less violent either, if anything, this game deserves its 18+ rating more than the others in its genre.
Having that said, the mechanics of the game definitely require getting used to, luckily this is achieved through a clever tutorial that gradually increases the freedom you have while playing.
To progress through the game there are countless of missions and events to participate in, and not all of these are fun to do. In fact, there's some dreadful shooter-on-rails included. Luckily this wasn't so common that it started to bother me more than I could take but these are things that make Sleeping Dogs far from perfect. It's a missed opportunity to go down in history as a classic, though looking back on what Sleeping Dogs did manage to achieve, it would be greedy to ask for much more. I already feel like a cheapskate having paid so little for what I got.

Great start. I've been following Beam in their updates leading up to the steam release and it's great finally experience what they've been working on. When I first plunked down into the ocean after a very quick and simple tutorial, I raced to an island and equipped my knife. I ran up to a tree and hacked away at it. I hacked the tree into logs. Then the logs into sticks.  I didn't know what else to do. I found a rock, and decided to just start piling all my stuff into one big heap.
That is when I noticed the dot in the center of my screen change. Click and hold brought up a crafting window with serveral options. Craft Crude Axe, Craft Crude Hammer, Camp Fire, I could make it all. I got a fire going and managed to balance a crab on the side and cooked it. I found some coconuts, banged them with my axe and drank it's milk. Then cut it in half and ate it. I kept piling stuff together and soon I was using my hammer to build a floor, then walls, and a roof.
My knife broke a long time ago, and my axe was about to break too. I happened to break a rock in half and I made a new knife, a new axe, and what? A SPEAR?
Next I'm in the ocean, stabbing fish and taking them to my fire and eatting them. I found sunken boats with chests containing flashlights and hammers.
The entire experience has been wonderful. It looks -beautiful-. I love how minimal the interface is. And how far the crafting and just how far you can break items down is awesome. I'm definately looking forward to being able to crafting and salvaging more things.
By this time, I've reached the limits of what the game has to offer me I believe. It's a wonderful start, and I'm definately looking forward to more.
Keep up the great work, Beam Team!

Unfortunately this game suffers from the same problems that a lot of games that rely on procedurally generated content have: a vast, infinite universe that is full of the same thing, over and over.
This wouldn't be so much of a problem, particularly for $15 at full price, except for the fact that all the quests, including the main storyline is the same thing over and over. It becomes an issue of whether or not this game is worth your time, and ultimately I think it is not.
To progress enough to fight each boss, you have to "scan" i.e. click on a few dozen items from one of the universe's cultures that you will spend several hours looking for. They'll be spread out over a number of different worlds, and it will take lot of searching for generally. Once you fight the boss, you're assigned another culture to scan items for. I've made it through four cycles of this and I'm uninstalling. There's quite a few more to go and I just can't do it again.
It's a shame, because there's a lot of decorative stuff to build a base with, at first it seems like just a ton of content to explore but each planet is disappointingly similarly composed, despite cosmetic differences.
At the end I'm left with the impression that I just don't care what the next boss is like, and making me scan more items makes me want to smash my head on the keyboard.

The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth is a game that defies explanation. The story is horrifying and is difficult to explain to casual players. The graphics are grisly and purposely dated. There is no instruction guide in the game outside of the first room you log into. Yet this game is what all rogue-likes should aim to be.
The depth of the mechanics are incredible: you collect items in the game and they synergize with one another. Find a bomb? Cool! Then you find an item that makes all your bombs blow up into five tiny bombs. Cooler! THEN you find a bomb that shoots your attack in all directions when they blow up, so all your bombs do that.
There are thousands of combinations and they, along with the random layout every time you load, make this near-infinitely replayable. Some runs are 10 minutes of overpowered glory. Some runs take over an hour of intense effort to fufill. And there are hundreds of little secrets and tricks to learn as you play, along with a tremendously welcoming and helpful community.
Buy this game if you like action/adventure and want a constantly changing challenge. Just don't look at the plot too hard. It's better that way.

There are a lot of reviews from people who have played 100+ hours from the initial alpha release in 2013 who are grumpy that every single thing promised three years ago didn't make it into the game.
If you have not yet played this game, if it's an entirely new experience, you have absolutely nothing to complain about. There's a great questline and progression system, with heaps of freedom to diverge and do and build whatever you want. Jumping around to different systems and planets is great. Plenty of character customisation with a bunch of different races and architecture to choose from. Combat is much improved from the early versions of the game. And you can find instruments and play whatever songs you want! The multiplayer could work a little more seamlessly but if you can forward ports it's not a big issue. Some planets/creatures are a little samey after a while, but I think that's just the nature of procedural generation and a big open world. The UI is a big finnicky, which is one annoying thing.
So if you're newly looking at this wondering if it's worth the money: definitely. Any early access game will be flooded with power users who have already siphoned hundreds of hours and are mad that there isn't anything big and new for them to do in the final release, but that's not really an issue for newcomers. I'd say if you like the progression and building of Terraria, I would definitely recommend this game too.

So I spent 2 years trying to complete this game, trying to get the achievements. I've grown to love this game, and hate it at times too.
This isn't just your typical rhythm platformer, but it's one that's filled with bright colours, pleasing aesthetics, and above all music that feels as though it's as much a part of the game as the ground, enemies, or player character are. The game will captivate you with it's charm, all the while making sure it's got you tightly enough that dying at particularly hard chokepoints don't scare you off.
It has a good learning curve, though seems to stop short of it's full potential. The 3 levels of the game are well designed, but can be quick to punish you if you are impatient. Of course, the checkpoints make sure you have a chance to attempt the hard parts very quickly again.
The mirror levels are the frustration point for the completionists, and where I feel the real challenge lies. You do the same 3 levels as before, but the opposite way and no checkpoints - if you die you go back to the level select. The game will punish you again and again, and only reward you for persistence, patience, and practice.
Overall I love 140. And I'm sad that I'm not going to be able to continue trying to beat it.

Sleeping Dogs somehow emerged as the sequel to True Crime: Streets of LA, one of the ♥♥♥♥♥iest PS2 games I ever played. How this happened, I have no idea, seeing as how there's a huge disparity in quality between the two, and one occurs in Los Angeles, while the other is set in Hong Kong. Sleeping Dogs is probably the best sandbox open world game I've ever played. Though it's kind of unfair to compare the two, considering GTA V is much larger in scope and has a multiplayer component, I believe Sleeping Dogs can stand up to its Los Santos counterpart, and even best it in many aspects. First, the driving is arcade-y but still maintains the tightness you would expect a racing game to contain. The visuals are absolutely drop dead gorgeous. Hong Kong rendered at night really makes me want to visit China, while Los Santos... makes me want to stay where I am. The gunplay and combat is decent, but GTA V has it beat due to its variety and excellent cover based approach. The map is fairly large and there were enough offerings to keep me interested when I wasn't doing story missions. The story itself is done really well. It's nothing that will confuse you or make you think too hard, but it's written really well and contains quality voice acting. The dynamic for the protagonist is one that always keeps things interesting, as he's constantly torn between his work as a police officer and his position in the triad. The ensuing tensions culminate in a finale somewhere between Scorsese's "The Departed" and a Jackie Chan film.

With the wide plethora of ghost related shows and movies, such as Ghost Whisperer or The Conjuring, and most is successful no matter if a lot of people hated it afterwards. So when it comes to games of course we will have ghosts in them too. For the most part I never see any quick cash grab games with ghosts like I do with zombies. Though with ghosts being very prominent in the horror genre, with them holding fear in our world, of course Dark Fall will fall into horror. And with this I do find it interesting how they handled the ghosts.
Dark Fall is really chill, not rushing things so you can take your time. You come to this abandoned train station and hotel so you can help your brother out. Who told you about some strange happenings while he was working on the area. Once you get there, you are confronted with the mystery of why people disappeared and soon figure out a way to release their spirits. You are literally put in to go through the story freely as you do not need to go through it in the order it wants but just to get to the end and achieve it.
This is heavy on the reading. Without being able to talk to anyone, all the history and clues resides in books, notes, and various papers scattered around. It does a wonderful job in this regard as you get the feel for all of the people who disappeared and the hotel you end up spending most of your time in. Many of the clues will also be revealed in your readings but you do get a sense of whether it will be important enough to jot down, or if you already got to the puzzle you will know what information you need to get.
And while yes some of the puzzles and items are far out there. I even had some troubles with finding solutions; some just being that I did not know I could view the contents or just missing a movement prompt and another to trigger a ghost to talk. But most of them are fairly easy to get through and figure out, especially the overarching one. I do like how they are all connected to the residents of the rooms at the time, especially since they hid all the scraps of paper with the symbols you end up looking for.
The greatest strength is definitely the atmosphere. Everything adds onto the atmosphere making this eerie. There is barely any music during the actual gameplay. Making a simple ringing of a phone send goosebumps as it slices through the silence. The only place that predominantly has some sound is the room hallways and I actually thought it was more towards the ghosts making it before I found a device that measured what activity is more likely to take place based on the distance you were to the ghosts. With this I love that the ghosts talked to you. With my previous experiences being the ghosts attacking you or being hostile, I like that these ghosts had no interest other than just talking. And well it sure spooked me the first couple times. One of my favorite moments was going into the room of Matilda, the actress. When you poke through some papers she reveals herself with an observation that you like poking through people’s stuff.
I, personally, do not find the graphics too detrimental to the experience. Everything is supposed to look old and it does well showcasing this. Though if you are someone that finds updated graphics vital to the experience you might not like how this looks.
It does have a weird window resolution, which will of course mess it up for your computer if you alt tab, but I never had any problems of the screen being unviewable due to this. Without changing my resolution, the hit box of items were still accurate and the movement arrows still showed but of course you will need to get used to where they generally show up at. Such as door ones being on the handle rather than being the door itself. Though of course I do have an average screen size/ resolution so those that have bigger or smaller sizes might run into this problem.
+ Atmosphere
+ Story/lore
+ Ghost interactions
+/- Graphics
- Weird fixed resolution

Having played the game for just over an hour, this review does not encapsulate a full opnion on everything the game has yet to offer, though I will do my best to give an unbiased opnion of what I have experienced thus far.
To begin, the game truly does have some impressive visuals. Few other games I have played have left me with a feeling of such awe and scale, or for that matter, immersion when interacting with or observing the environment. With realsitic textures and mostly smooth edges on things like trees and rocks, the game presents itself excpetionally well visually. Of particular breathtaking display were the rays of sunlight  and flecks of shade which I observed through the treetops on my small starting island. The best of all however, were the sunsets and rises. Each one made me pause from my activities on the island to simply stand and enjoy the beautiful view. As I said before, few games have delivered their environments so well. Additionally, the sea has been textured so as to look believably realistic and well-done, with excellent reflection effects for both the rays of the sun and the moon. All-in-all, a commendable and highly promotable visual delivery, with the one excpetion of a lack of bodily presence when looking down at your character, or any presence of a character shadow. I have not as of yet explored the ocean depths, so I can give no information on that aspect of the game at this time.
Gameplay is simplistic, yet satisfying. It comprises mainly of dynamically harvesting resources from the surrounding environment, dragging them into place using the right mouse-button and then left-clicking on an indicator which acts as a signal to inform the player that an item can be crafted. Though at this early stage of development there is little point to building a shelter, the time and effort it requires to build one, and the freshly dynamic crafting method of doing so, makes the process an enjoyable experience nonetheless, and I felt great satisfaction whilst looking upon my newly constructed abode, I felt that I had influenced the world around me, made an impact against nature in the never-ending struggle to survive. However, as enjoyable as the crafting system was once I had gotten a handle on it, the intial lack of any information in-game as to the mechanics left me confused and at times frustrated. Furthermore, the crafting mechanic is two-fold, comprising of crafting (orange object highlighting) and building (blue object highlighting) for which you need a hammer specifically,and is the method through which things such as rafts and shelter components are made, which is just as unexplained as the rest of the crafting. Perhaps a similar mechanic to that in "The Forest" of providing a survival guide in the life-raft from the plane would be a good idea? As it would allow for some basic instructions to be incorporated into the game without taking away from immersion. As a final note to the crafting mechanic, be aware that the way in which you build a raft is the same as building a shelter foundation (8 sticks) only you must build it in the water, and the option still comes up as "Foundation", which is a minor, confusing flaw.  Further on the subject of gameplay is climbing/platforming. During my first in-game day, I spent the larger portion of it attempting to get onto a wrecked vessel which had beached on my island, and the rest of the day trying to get out of the hull, which I had jumped down into through a hatch on the deck. There should be some time spent focusing on developing this essential mechanic during future development, as it will make for a much more polished and well-roundedly enjoyable experience. Lastly, the only in-game bug I experienced was when I built a raft in order to move to an island in the distance as my supplies were running low. While slowly paddling my way over, my raft disappeared and I was unceremoniously dunked into the ocean halfway between either island with sharks almost immediately to my left, which resulted in my death. To sum up, the gameplay is in definite need of expansion and refinement, though what the game does possess as of the writing of this review feels challenging without being impossible, and highly satisfying as well as amusing.
Sound is for the most part very well-done. With appropriate envrionmental sounds adding nicely to the immersion such as the gentle crashing of waves, the sand crunching softly beneath my as-of-yet invisible feet, as well as a well-balanced soundtrack with somewhat foreboding musical elements, adding a sense of urgency to the situation of survival and limited resources at your disposal.
As of today, January 24th, 2015, "Stranded Deep" is an intelligently made game with some solid core mechanics in need of further polishing, excellent visuals and with an exponential amount of potential which, if developed with care and competence, could become one of the best survival games on today's market. I look forward to the game's progression with optimistic, if somewhat cautious, hope and anticipation.
Overall Score: 6.5/10 (Not indicative of final rating)
P.S. One rather neat mechanic which could be added, I thought, would be the addition of a journal keeping mechanic, wherein players using charcoal from burnt-out campfires could write accounts of their in-game stories or write S.O.S's which when put in either your starting water bottle or washed-up bottles from the beach, could be thrown into the sea and appear in other players' games or be integrated into the end-game somehow.
Hoping this review is helpful to any and all who read it.
