I have loved and supported this series and looked forward to the release for years. Unfortunately, in 6 years* of development, the game is nowhere near ready for EA. If the devs believed this game to be in a playable state they were deluding themselves.
This is what the developers said this EA release was, vs what it actually is:
"...we're nearing completion and balancing/polishing the game..." - game is nowhere near complete. Requires much more than balances and polishing - large gameplay elements are missing. This release** is a sandbox Alpha test at best.
“The only differences will be those made due to feedback from the fans, and of course final fixes" - The ONLY differences? I certainly hope not (unless they are counting on the fans to finish coding and building the game themselves, like they did with The Guild 2)
“Early Access is fully playable but in need of balancing and (performance) optimization." - Outright lie.
All I could do with my character was buy a business and craft the same items over and over. No trade routes meant that I had to micro manage production by sending my transporter to the market to buy resources for my business constantly. If I stopped even for a few minutes, my business would run out of resources and production would cease.
I couldn't get court anyone, get married or, you know, build a dynasty.
I couldn't upgrade my business to craft more lucrative items.
Almost every option and action I clicked was broken/not working.
The UI is awful. It looks older and is less user friendly than UI from The Guild 2 (a game over 10 years old)
AI pathfinding is terrible (have they copied and pasted the pathfinding from The Guild 2? Characters are still moving along the ground without moving their legs and getting stuck walking into buildings... this is 2017...)
I could go on and on about what is missing and what an EA game
should include as an absolute minimum, but I'm just going to release this review unfinished and hope for the best.

*Game has been in development 3 years (going by announcement Sept 2014), not 6 years. I believe the engine has been in development 6 years - thanks to SCARRIOR for bringing this to my attention)
**My use of the term "release" should be read as Early Access (thanks to L|t|E|Luetti for letting my know of my incorrect terminology). My use of the word release was not intended as a technical term, more in a coloquial sense (in that THQ Nordic have "released" this version for Early Access), but thought I should clarify nontheless.

Music is often used to set the feeling for a game. In horror games you can rarely be sure if what you hear is harmless ambience or the playable character's sanity (or your own) going nuts. In action games, the battle music vary from epic choirs to hard rock, but the goal is to make the player FEEL the battle - with intense and up-lifting sounds, as if something large is behind the sounds.
Rarely music is made for other reasons than that. 140 seeks to experiment other variations, and that it has definitely done well.
140 is a rhythmic platformer game where the music guides you. It tells you how the environment warps, either for your favor or to kill you. Every time you catch one of those fleeing, round music machines and drag them to a check point, the world changes. The color theme changes, and the music gets a new addition while enhancing the already existing soundtrack. An another part of the level has now been unlocked, either by formerly static objects starting to move or you suddenly going all anti-gravity. Whatever happens, the new instrument in the concert that is 140's changing soundtrack tells you how do they work. Just don't forget that the music doesn't tell you when to jump!
140 was mainly developed by a person also involved in LIMBO. While playing the game, I could really feel the fact when failing the outwardly simple yet mind-bending timing requiring platforming.
The game includes three stages with one boss for each. The boss fights are the moments where you REALLY get tested! And if after clearing the game once you still seek a challenge, you might want to try the mirror worlds, where you get only one attempt to clearing each level.
In other words and in short, despite the game being short and looking simple both graphically and gameplay-wise, it still manages to bring in fresh experiences with well thought-out design. It's a kind of a game that you have to play to understand its worth.
However, as much as I want to blurt out fancy phrases to describe 140's greatness, it's still a short game. One can easily finish this game in one to two hours. But is that such a bad thing? I got the feeling that this game was experimental, and a well thought-out one, if I may be so shameful as to re-use my early wording. The price is also a good measurement of the game's length: the full price is a meekly $5, and every now and then I spot that it's on sale with 80 % off the price.
In short:
- Simple yet challenging, but still doesn't make it seem like it's impossible
- Fun boss fights that differ from usual platforming, even within this game itself
- Graphically fluid and simple
- The music, along with being used in a new way, is also pretty good 'n catchy!
If you thought platformers can not have anything new to offer, that everything has already been done, this game proves that there is still a lot to be done to reach that point.

Mount & Blade and X-COM had a baby.
It's not as pretty as either of those, however, rather unusually, I find it more immersive and challenging than either of those titles. For example losing a key soldier in this game is a lot more tragic and will have a much stronger effect on your combat capabilities than in X-COM.
When I lost a key soldier in X-COM, I bought another "blank page" soldier for next to nothing got a few kills with it and sorted. When I lose a key soldier in Battle Brothers I howl in horror, shout at the screen, tear some of my hair out, weep a little, then suck it up and carry on. There is of course the option to run-around quick-saving and just re-load when you fail, but that kinda kills the atmosphere of the game, for me at least.
This game, for me, is the definition of gameplay over graphics. I recently invested in a brand-spanking new GPU and here I am playing Battle Brothers, ha.
Please note that Goblins are going to make you rage, avoid them until you're stronger or just be aware that they are a real headache to fight. Been a lot of Q_Q about these opponents but I personally enjoy the challenge. I hope they don't nerf the difficulty too much, most games these days take <1 hour to master. I will admit, I do quick-save, but only before battles against goblins, cuz they will net you down and have their way with you, like... 20 inches of it with no lube. Don't say I haven't warned you. But they are beatable, fight them at night so their ranged weapons are less accurate, use shields to block some projectiles and never ever just try to rush them unless your men are SUPER tough.
If you want a challenging game that requires a lot of thinking aswell as being enjoyable and involves a lot of risk/gambles, I would definetly recommend this game.
If you can't handle a challenge and are going to cry about the difficulty go sit in the corner with the other 99% and play Call'o'Duty. Thanks.

While it almost seems too simplistic in its design, it is that very quality that makes it immensely replayable. Running from room to room in a Legend of Zelda-esque dungeon layout, trying to survive and reach the next floor until you reach the boss and win. And while the large variety of enemies, random floor layouts, and many secrets are enough to keep you hooked for a long time, the game truly shines with its large arsenal of random items.
A number of them synergize in interesting ways that lead to the screen going crazy with wavy beams, bouncing explosions, and all sorts of things. But even those that don't necessarily effect other items directly can still change the game up quite a bit. One item might let you fly, avoiding traps and rocks blocking your path. Another lets you go really fast - but maybe *too* fast? Explosions clear out rocks and reveal secrets but make it dangerous to take on enemies up close. And on and on the list goes.
Most rogue-likes, whether they be more action oriented like this or slower like the turn based ones, put plenty of focus on randomization and replayability. While you will certainly see the same room layouts time and time again, the incredibly vast item pool, secrets to unlock, and ease of jumping in for another game make this one of my top choices.
Definitely worth the money!

Basically Starbound is more or less Terraria-in-space with a gazillion procedurally-generated planets with each planet having a primary biome and up to several mini-biomes, as well as minibiomes underground. Starbound was started by some of the original Terraria devs.
Builtin-Pros:
- Good basic 2D block building framework
- IN SPACE
- Housing
- Farming
- Exploration
- Has multiplayer with dedicated servers
- Has a basic builtin wiring/electronics building framework allowing you to craft and place switches/sensors.
- Extensive Lua-based modding and scripting
Out-of-the-box Cons:
- Lack of weapon types. I mean there are a lot of generated variations but are all based on short sword, long sword, spear, axe, hammer, pistol, machine pistol, shotgun, grenade launcher, rocket launcher, auto rifle, sniper rifle. (moddable)
- Lack of useful/weapon craftables (most of it is cosmetic or food items) (moddable)
- Can get boring
- Depending on what kind of player you are, questing isn't very impressive, but at least there is more than before.
- No more drills (previously, in early beta you could get/craft destructible drills which made digging faster than using your matter manipulator, now the matter manipulator can get upgraded but the fastest speed is still not very fast compared to the old diamond drills). There is probably a mod which adds this back in.
1.0-Pros: (Pros introduced in 1.0):
- You can get ship crew now.
- NPC villages give quests with rewards.
- Hunger meter re-added (actually this was added back in during the unstable/nightly pre-releases).
1.0-Cons: (Cons introduced in 1.0):
- only 6 hotbar items per hotbar now (but you get 2 of them) and default-equipped quickslot removed
- Can't teleport back to ship unless the sky is visible (ok I sorta get that, and it's also probably moddable).
- Can't stack food items (this is due to food degradation but there is a mod for that now).
- Appears ore is more rare (probably to get people to travel more to get stuff rather than just farming one or two planets per star type).
You can walk around the planet as one of 7 playable races by walking continously in a given direction and you will end up where you started. Each planet as a reachable core made of lava or impassible solid (moons). The planets are located within star systems. You have a "ship" with expandable rooms which serves as your main base of operations that can retain all of your stuff when switching multiplayer servers and from where you can travel between planets, beam up and down from planets, and travel between the star systems.
I usually play this in single player, where I engage in farming (it's actually slightly more fun than the farming in Stardew Valley, imo), going to planets, looking for cool NPC villages or NPC dungeons.
I have been playing this since it was in Beta and on Steam Early Access. A couple of years ago, during the Koala series of beta releases, the universe was split into 5 sectors of varying NPC diffculty and you had to beat a boss to open up each sector but otherwise there was no questing. In the next release, codenamed Giraffe, each star was given a radiation type, requiring protective gear (for supplying air, radiation immunity, heat immunity, cold immunity) for each of the more exotic biomes (aireless, radiation, hot, cold). Bosses were changed so that they would reward the appropirate protection level so you could get to harder planets. Boss missions were handed out from a respawning NPC base which is beamable from your ship was added with additional quests. In 1.0, the complete backstory and lore was fleshed out and you get a single main quest-giver which lets you play out the "plot" involving some cataclysm and the various races. The protection gear is now craftable. NPC Villages also now give out quests which give you items as rewards and can reward crew members for your ships too.
1.0 lags less than beta for me, on GTX 770 and i5-4690 with 8gb ram. In beta I had to restart the client every few hours due to memory leak which seems to be improving (1.0.2 update released today supposed to fix another leak).
It's a great little game to get by on until No Man's Sky. The soundtrack by Curtis Schweizter is also very relaxing even out-of-game.

Open-world classic that inspired dozens of clones and made Rockstar one of the most successful developers of all time.
However, the PC port of this game was poor on release and it's aged like milk. I've made a list of problems and solutions I had while getting it running:
I had a lot of trouble getting this game to launch in Win10. I had to use both SilentPatch and the DDraw patch
to get past the Unhandled Exception c0000005 error and crash after the intro movie. EDIT: These patches also fix a bug where menu text is either invisible or very faded.
This is one of those old games where physics are tied to framerate. If you turn off the 30FPS limiter, car friction, jumping and running up stairs are totally broken. This is one of those things where someone at Rockstar could fix it in an afternoon but it's still broken after all these years. As far as I know, there's no mod or patch to fix this. You can limit the game to 60 with a graphics driver tool but the physics problems are still there.
The HUD doesn't scale well for widescreen. There's a "widescreen" option in the graphics menu but it doesn't work. You need to use a community fix
to get the game to look as expected at resolutions like 1080p (or anything bigger than 1024x768).
The Steam version of the game has a bug where lighting doesn't affect cars if you're running it on a modern version of Windows. The SilentPatch I linked earlier fixes this bug, but the widescreen patch I linked breaks it again. The best way to fix this bug is adding
.
GTA3 has decent support for DirectInput controls and that's good enough for me. There's plenty of people with Xinput controllers though. San Andreas recently got a patch to support them but GTA3 hasn't had that patch yet despite using the same engine.
is a mod that adds support along with the correct HUD buttons.
If you change mouse sensitivity in game (which everyone would, since it's designed for monitors with like 8 DPI), it only changes the X sensitivity while leaving the Y axis to go wild.
is a patch to fix that bug.
This one isn't a big issue (I don't use it) but this game was designed to take advantage of the PS2's hardware with stuff like real-time car reflections. They couldn't be bothered to port any of these enhancements to the PC version but there is a mod that restores PS2-like graphics to the game
(Read the instructions though!)
If you're a completionist, the in-game stats aren't useful at all. A member of the community made a 100% checklist that hooks the game (
) and tells you what you still need to do if you're trying to complete the game 100%.
Another not-huge issue but something to keep in mind before playing. As
points out, their huge game with 3 different islands has no in-game map, so you either have to memorise where everything is or follow their suggestion and
like it's 1999.
Just a final tip to top everything off, once you've got the game running you can delete the "movies" directory from the install folder and it'll no longer play the intro movies. A little nugget that will save you a few seconds after spending 20 minutes or more getting the game running.
I do love this game but I can't honestly recommend GTA3 to anyone until they fix some of these issues.

This review mostly concerns Fallout 4 pricing during Steam Winter Sale 2017.
But to be fair, I'll actually review the game below.
First, pricing (all amounts rounded up 1 cent, because what, you think I don't notice that $19.99 is actually $20? Seriously?):
Base game: $20 CDN (originally $80 CDN)
GOTY: $40 CDN (difference is $20 for all DLC)
Season Pass: $35 CDN
Far Harbour DLC (ONLY): $21 CDN
So, why can't I upgrade my base game to GOTY for $20? You seriouly expect me to buy the same game twice? Why is the Season Pass not priced to match the difference? Especially given the lukewarm reviews (at best) for the majority of the content. I can't even get the DLC Far Harbour for $20 at its sale price.
I would maybe understand the oversight if all the DLC were 50% off across the board, but the individual are only 40% discounted.
Greedy and arrogant pricing. Not recommended, unless your first FO4 purchase is the GOTY edition. Then, it's 50% off! Huzzah!
Now, Fallout 4 the base game:
It's a fun modding playground set in a post-nuclear wasteland. But, I had to mod it heavily to stay interested. The base game UI drove me nuts in like 10min (just like skyrim's UI). I'm told there's a story, but when the second (major) main quest marker is 2/3 away across the map, it takes forever to get there.
Granted I meander through openworld games like a cat chasing a laser pointer...

Sleeping Dogs is one of those hidden gems: it had a solid team of artists, good gameplay, got its 15 minutes in the sunlight and was never seen again.
The game stars undercover cop Wei Shen as he integrates into the shady side of Hong Kong, planting himself in the middle of a notorious triad in a time of conflict. Yet his cameleon act isn't simply an act, and he finds himself becoming a gangster in more ways than one, straddling the line between cop and criminal.
As an open-world sim, players have ample amounts of freedom to simply roam about and explore - outside of missions, players can relax and do whatever they want with no consequences. Partaking in missions is different, and parameters become much more strict: as an undercover cop, causing needless mayhem reduces score at the end of a mission, encouraging players to be at the top of their game when partaking in high speed chases and highway hijackings.
Trying to compare this game to any other is difficult. At first glance, it has the Grand Theft Auto feel of being able to set out, explore, hijack cars, evade cops, etc., but there is also a shadow of Just Cause 2 mixed in there in the game's movement and stunt system (you can even unlock Rico Rodriguez' outfit). The game's fighting is primarily hand to hand and resembles the Batman games, utilizing a sort of combo system with light attacks, heavy attacks, counters and grapples to take down thugs. The end result: players dishing out wild justice as a kung-fu gangster-cop in Hong Kong while also engaging in street racing, general mayhem, and Kareoke. Hand-to-hand combat, gunfights, street racing, some parkour elements, all set in a thriving Chinese metropolis; what's not to love?
But while the game has a feel similar to Just Cause 2, Sleeping Dogs trades Rico's exploration abilities for a higher degree of storytelling - Sleeping Dogs has a reasonably strong cast of characters with distinct personalities and motives, all which serve the overarching narrative. Yet while the story is not incredibly complex, it's also not entirely predictable; not every character is a deep ocean of mystery, but there's enough ambiguity in most of them that it's not always clear what they are going to do. The player does not dictate the game's story - Wei Shen's character is established and makes his own choices, but is just volatile and unpredictable enough to keep things fresh.
Speaking of choices, that is one of the game's weaknesses. The story is linear, which can be excused as it still manages to deliver a fresh and original narrative. Rather, it's the missions themselves which are regrettably constrictive, an unfortunate trait in an open world game that should ideally leave multiple solutions for the player to take, and Sleeping Dogs is very hallway-esque while inside story missions not involving car chases.
The combat is visually entertaining and fun to play, but there are some odd hiccups here or there; while the combat is not difficult and really feels great when the player gets a solid chain going, it lacks the rhythmic feel from the Arkham series that refined the free-for-all brawling style. As a result, while the player has high control over their attacks and enjoys a variety of options, it lacks the smoothness that pushes the combat from 'good' to 'great'.
Another downside is where and when suspension of disbelief happens. We know it's a video game and so a few things will be unrealistic for the sake of good gameplay, but there's a limit. For instance, when chasing an enemy on foot, they are prone to receiving speed boosts just to artificially extend the chase (or they will sometimes slow down to let the player catch up). Enemies will circle around the player and take turns fighting, or they'll stand and do nothing while Chen uses a long-winded environmental attack. Escorting vehicles will 'give up' on protecting their escort after enough are eliminated. Add in a few bugs where people walk into walls or dive in front of moving vehicles and you have a game with a good story but a difficult-to-believe everything else.
Other than that, Sleeping Dogs is a great game on a similar level as Just Cause - it's a game that got very little attention but turned out being fairly solid, and overall it is a very pleasant experience to mess with. I recommend that, should this game show up on sale for a couple dollars, that it be picked up immediately, as it is absolutely worth the few days/week it will take to fully explore everything this interpretation of Hong Kong has to offer.

This is a two part review. If you're seriously considering buying this, read this entirely. It will really help you out.
If the words "Planet Fusion" don't mean anything to you, skip to the second part.
Part I
When I was growing up, there was always one game in particular that stood out as an amazing game, and that was FusionFall. Looking back on it, if one were to take away the negative CN aspects from the game, it'd be a solid (minimum) 8/10. This game essentially improves on the design of FusionFall and morphs it into a TD game. If you've ever played FF and wanted a game with a more serious version of its tone, I will always recommend this.
The aesthetic of this game is very similar to parts of Downtown and Darklands. Giant spores reminiscent of the ones in the Tyrannical Gardens, gnarly trees like the ones found at the Dark Glade and beautiful scenery comparible to the Really Twisted Forest truly capture the art design that made FusionFall so memorable. And don't even get me started on the Swamp levels. Everything about those are so well designed that words can't explain them (seriously. It gives Rayman Origins a run for its money, and Origins is one of my favorite games of all time).
Did I mention the music? I loved FusionFall's music, especially during the later Wilds and Darklands levels. Sanctum 2's music draws on the same influences, but of course discards any of the more cartoony bits typical of FusionFall. Again, the Swamp levels reign supreme in the music department. It's well worth getting to the Swamp sections, I promise.
It is important to note that this isn't a complete copy of FusionFall and repackaged as a TD. This game has its own art style, characters, plot, gameplay, etc. In its own right, Sanctum 2 has merely adopted the art style of FusionFall and incorporated it into itself. Some parts of FF are missing: Fusion Matter, Infected Zones, Nanos (although Perks could count, the charm from having a mini caricature hovering around is non-existent here).
tl;dr: Sanctum 2 is a much darker, more serious and overall better take on the concept FusionFall built around, all wrapped up into a TD. If you enjoyed FF, you will probably enjoy Sanctum 2.
Part II
Outside of having the characteristics of FusionFall, Sanctum 2 does a great job standing on its own. Building on the idea of a FPS game, Sanctum 2 demands the necessity of quick thinking, advanced movement ability, and strategic logic to complete a level. This is even more true when playing with Feats of Strength: factors that make gameplay harder, but result in more XP.
Like said in Part I, the aesthetics in this game is unbelievably stunning. My laptop can't run very high graphics, but even with low settings on I was still blown away by the design, feel, and mood Sanctum 2 delivers. The natural world of Giant Trees and Swamp clashing with the modern technology planted onto Loek III by humans is also an interesting touch that draws on the struggles faced during the Industrial Revolution.
Gameplay is pretty simple FPS wise. Shoot things dead. Different lumes have different health stats obviously, but some are much harder to kill, however. Armorered Heavies are almost impenetrable aside from the backside, and Bobbleheads (one of the most frustrating lumes in game) can only be killed by attacking the head. Among typical lumes come with aerial enemies, including Pliskeplaskes, Spore Pods, and Spitflies that can force the player to experiment with other weapons and towers. Finally, no game would be complete without bosses, and Sanctum 2 is no stranger. Several bosses make prominent features: Hoverer Queens, giant forms of Hoverers; Walker Patriarchs, giant Walkers that can destroy blocks; and Super Heavies: giant Armored Heavies that shoot laser eyes that destroy anything in their path. Besides this, some other giants loom within the game, but I won't spoil the entirety of it ;)
With towers and weapons, Sanctum 2 is full of them. Rifles, giant tasers, and rocket launchers are all at the player's disposal. When it comes to towers, there's essentially one for every niche. Drones can pierce armor, Violators can put a massive dent in monsters with large pools of health, and Slow Field Dispensers make monster move slower, which can be a life saver.
Character development is also a pretty nice feature in game too. While Skye tends to be an arrogant prick half the time, she is a pretty good leader and a bond is almost always made with any player. Sweet is the much more innocent version of Skye and resonates well those not fond of vulgarity or pomposity. SiMo is a war machine that in the comics is seen as a sort of a father figure to all characters, even Skye. Haigen is a quiet but confident man that likes a challenge - both against lumes and against authority, but always works well with the others.
The maps in this game are truly a sight to behold. This is where all those amazing graphics and artwork are. Each level forces the player to think about every aspect of their game play - their character (which I will talk about in the next paragraph), weapons, towers, and their maze design. The main goal is to defend cores that power various objects on Loek III. Each core starts with 4,000 health, and depending on the setup, this is either a lot, or not enough.
Each character has their own advantages of using them. Skye does 2% more damage per successive shot, stacking up to 50 times. She can also double jump, which is what got me into playing her most (even though I really play more like SiMo or Haigen). Sweet can rocket jump if the player uses the REX, has more air control, jumps higher, and sets enemies on fire. SiMo has 60% less spread and does more damage on critical hits than any other character, and that also stacks as well. Haigen has far more health then the other characters and gets a 35% damage bonus if he's within reach of the enemy.
Now time for the complaints. I love this game, I really do. No game is perfect however.
A lot of the time, this game feels grindy, especially during the later levels. There are a lot of different types of lumes in the game, but only a few make an appearance during a wave, and sometimes not a lot of them show up in a single map.
The level system in Sanctum 2 really could've used a far larger number than 50. I say could've as the game has been out for almost four years now, and players at level 50 would all essentially have to start from 0 to get the highest level possible. I say 0 not technically, but metaphorically, as 50 is the highest level one can get. When in multiplayer, Level 50s can be deceptive. One could progress through the entire game, and start from the beginning using all five Feats of Strength, and make it an eighth of the way through and reach level 50. I've played with Levels 50s that are amazing at their craft, and ones who spam Orbitals nonstop and wonder why they can't progress. A much larger level system is something I personally would like (this was also a problem in Fusion Fall, but with 36).
Another thing I wish could happen is regular updates. I discovered Sanctum 1 in the summer of 2013, and while I never had the chance to buy it until 2015, I fell in love with the design. I bought Sanctum 2 instead, and was amazed at the work put into it. However, writing this review in 2017, it has been 3 years since the last update, and I wish more work could be put into it. I can't blame CSS though, Sanctum 2 is pretty much as good as it can get. Some balancing would be nice, but like a game I play a lot, TF2, I guess there isn't much else to update.
So that's my review. I absolutely love this game! I'd recommend it to any FPS player that's getting bored of typical FPS game play. Even without DLC (which I did buy at the same time as Sanctum 2), this is an all around great game. I recommend getting the DLC, which doubles the size of the content in game. If I had to rate Sanctum 2, at LEAST 80/100. Get this game.

Darklands meets Mount & Blade. You roam around a procedurally generated map adopting quests, random events and contracts as a means to feed, sate, equip, heal, repair and maintain your company of hired men. Much like xcom they can be outfitted to any equipment you want, upgraded (if they survive) in a small manner of RPG mechanics, and given their own name and appearances of your choosing. Yes, you can make your party of friends and equip them to survive, only to be torn down by ghouls in six minutes.
Roaming the map feels a lot like Darklands. You go from village to village and encounter some kind of contract, alement or quest. Admittedly it's a thin herd of options right now but as early access trudges on, so does the feature list. Today they just added an entirely reworked world map, economy, and politics system -- and there's more to come.
Combat is turn based and tactical. It's simplistic and easy to be punished for and needs some balance tweaks, (RNG is very real for some weapons) but it gets better every update. Permadeath is a feature -- you can and will lose your company, either entirely or partially, almost every fight. One whirring arrow can catch your eye and that's that for your favorite level 4 merc.
Enemies include ferocious, unique Orcs. Terrifiyng undead/ghouls, and enemy mercs/bandits/robbers/militia that stand in your way. Fighting each 'faction' feels unique and punishing. Orcs will slaughter, take double turns, cut off your heads. Ghouls will rise back up RIGHT next to you and kill you. Humans use evasion, tactics and flanks.

Update one year later:
On the eve of launch, this game is ready for prime time. Watch your let's plays on youtube and decide for yourself. But don't watch too much. The devs have added some nice random events and decision points that should be enjoyed on your own.
As said below, this development team has been highly active and transparent with its community. The roadmap and timelines have been followed throughout the entire process. Whenever they've put out an update, any bugs found have been immediately squashed.
The art, sound, metagame, tactical combat, skill tree's, mercenary backgrounds, weapons, armor...everything has been improved and tweaked to make this game one of my favorite tactical point and click games.
They've listened to customer feedback and implemented many positive changes...this team really understands how games should be made with their audience in mind.
It's highly enjoyable and stable before launch. They're just polishing and tweaking the balance in certain areas. Well worth twenty bucks folks. If you like tactical, team-oriented, turn based combat with light economy management and a world map that changes based on your action or inaction...check this game out!
====================================================================
Man, this game is quickly shaping up to be a great turn-based strategy game with solid meta game mechanics. The devs provide regular updates, videos, and accept feedback (everything you would want from a developer and a game in early access).
In less than a year, they have made major improvements to a game that started out as a quirky turn-based combat game. Definitely worth the 20 bucks I spent (maybe even less, as I think I may have picked it up on sale). Check out some videos to see if its mechanics work for you.
+regular updates; great communication from developers about the ever changing state of the game
+nice battle mechanics: high-ground, terrain, fatigue
+fleshed out over-world map; even in it's early access state
+quirky battle animations and characters (as you suffer blows in combat, your characters get nicked, scratched and can be beheaded. Also, some cool back stories and achetypes, suitable for the mercenary company you are building.
+permadeath
No cons with it being early access for me. The current build seems to be stable and the economics seem to be fairly balanced. The game is still evolving, but I can fully recommend this game baased on developer involvment with the community, regular updates, and the current state of gameplay.

I've been with Binding of Isaac since the beginning and what a ride it's been. From beating Mom for the first time to unlocking the final item and your '1001%!' achievement, this game has never once lost replay value. The sheer variety of items, characters, monsters, and other tweaks have kept me always coming back for more. Furthermore, this game is surprisingly open to new players. You don't *have* to unlock everything, you don't *have* to beat a certain boss to have a successful run, and you don't *have* to play the daily runs - the game is only as difficult as you make it.

My only caution would be against the difficulty: This game is a roguelike, a game designed to be difficult to people that want it all. You will die repeatedly. You will lose runs you thought a sure thing. You will get stuck on a challenge or objective. If any of these are a turn-off for you, proceed with caution...but you'll probably enjoy it anyways.
If not? Buckle up, and get that '1001%!' badge. It feels so good.
On a technical note: The soundtrack is excellent, the atmosphere is delicously discomforting (as it should be, given the setting!), and the controls are exactly what they need to be: simple and intuitive.

Bastion is another indie game which is put on a pedestal for its presentation, even though its presentation is not nearly as revolutionary as it advertises itself as being. Once again the actual narrative is very thin on content, and the voice over narration is what people refer to when they discuss its "amazing story". The actual content of the game consists of walking on linear cubic paths in a void while engaging in very bland and unengaging 3rd person combat. The monotone narrator talks through the whole game, giving a greater sense of setting to the game than there really is by describing lore about the floating hallway you're traveling even though there is zero visual evidence of any the levels you're occupying as being a real place in any way.
The narrator itself is novel but not very engaging. He speaks with little to no inflection, and it can be easy to not pay attention to anything he says since you're too busy killing enemies on the current floating hallway void. The narration is supposed to be a revolutionary advancement for video game story telling, but it doesn't seem like the voice over is very noteworthy when there is basically no variation in what the player does, and the whole level is a literal linear floating void. The plot itself is vague and immaterial, and doesn't seem to go anywhere.
I really did give the game a go, and wanted to see what it would present next for a short while. The painterly art style is nice enough, even though the ambigious levels meant that changing areas amounted to pallet swaps. The music is also very nice and might be the best part about the whole game. What really got me though was the bland and easy gameplay, and Bastion's answer to giving the player more. The idols are a very good idea, games such as The World Ends With You and Kid Icarus Uprising certainly show how controllable difficulty can be done. The first few idols add some expected increases in challenge to the enemies you fight, such as increased health, faster attacks, and more damage. None of this really makes the game any harder, and the idols that come later basically consist of sabotaging the player, by making enemies randomly not take damage, and even inflicting slow movement on the player for attacking. I admit that the game was pretty difficult with all of these modifiers turned on, but what an artificial and tedious form of difficulty it was. If the only answer the devs have to players who want more interesting combat is "play the game with one hand behind your back" then they shouldn't even bother.
I recommend for anyone curious about Bastion to play the demo first before purchasing. This is definitely not a must buy, and you should decide for yourself whether Bastion's various presentation gimmicks are as worthy of the praise it has been given. Do note as you play that the combat you experience at the beginning is an accurate representation of the whole game, and the game will never add new mechanics or interactions with the world other than new weapons. If what you played in the demo is what you would like to do for 8-10 hours straight, then feel free to buy it.

One of the most completely immersive exploration survival games out there,
the beginning plane crash scene is a bit rough though , it's quite a turn off with
the unaccessable pilot cockpit and the martini ingrediants magically turning into a
glass of martini, let alone the jet engine explosion which didn't really have any affect
on me.
BUT let's forget all that, they are minor issues waiting to be fixed. Let's focus on this games
potential. And boy does it have potential, When you begin gameplay you are put on a raft
right next to an Island. Let's just take a quick look around us, first thing I notice is the immersive
graphics, but don't get me wrong it's certaintly not next gen. When we dock on the island we are
confronted by a mass of ingrediants, hundreds of conbinations of items which can produce food,
structures tools and weapons. Using my environment around me as my life source was very
satisfying especially as everything was completely physics based and could be moved around with
total freedom. There is no crafting guide, but the aspect of experimentation in this game
immediatelly came to light, I found myself throwing different resources on top of eachother and
before I knew it I had built myself an axe, and after quite the struggle, jumping around the island
like a chimpanzee I managed to get a spear into my hands. Before I knew it I was ready to explore
even further, out to sea, I was quickly surrounded by sharks so I sailed back to the island. But on
my way I noticed a rusty boat that had dug itself into the sand, in it was a container, I opened
it and found an oxygen tank and I threw it on my life boat and called it Oscar.
I asked myself what else could I find out in this vast ocean, the oppurtinities seemed endless and that really filled me with excitement. This game is something I've been waiting for, for a long time. The Forest never met my expectations, I've always wanted a survival game that completely immersed me not from zombies or aliens, but just from it's environment, I've always wanted to feel what it would be like to survive out in the wilderness on my own,with nobody else. This game has met my requirements, it's audio, visuals and inteligent crafting system and physics make the game a survival sandbox I have always wanted. If you liked the forest you will like this more, If you are familiar with open world survival than I would recommend this game over any other, except for skyrim ofcourse.

TL;DR:
Don't waste your time. It's fun for a few hours, but plagued by a cash shop that wants you to buy quality of life features or even straight up buy raw power in the form of rare items/pets.
The "I've got time to spare" rant:
Eh, so this is basically a twin-stick shooter fused with a minimalist MMO with permadeath. This is how your experience is gonna play out:
The first thing you will experience upon loading in is the third party site RMT advertisement bots in the central hub area. The second thing you will find is that you are surrounded on all sides with Cash Shop Items for you to buy (they give you 40 "Gold" for free, the real cash currency, but it isnt enough to even buy anything other than maybe a clothing dye). So then you go into a Realm (server instance) with a heap of other players, most doing their own thing killing the high level stuff because they are way more geared, no biggie, you start out grinding and farming.
This part of the game isnt too bad. It's one giant open field, and generally the further you get from the start area the harder the monsters are. On screen prompts generally guide you toward level appropriate enemies to kill, called "quests". Loot will drop for you to upgrade your gear, and its pretty much linear: the equipment is clearly marked with tiers (T0, T1, T2, etc). Occasionally a monster will open an entrance to an instanced dungeon you can go into that generally has better rewards assuming you can complete it. The overworld also has objectives the players in it need to complete to get to the actual boss, and when they are fullfilled all present players are teleported to an instanced dungeon with several stages to complete. When its all said and done and the last boss is killed, the realm is closed and a new one is opened and you can do it all again.
So you are grinding and then you get in over your head and you die. And then you realize its permadeath. Honestly, that's no big deal for me, I love rougelikes, and the occasional forray into hardcore Diablo 3 or Path of Exile, but I digress.
So you make a new character and load in again. Maybe you were smart and you put some high tier items in your vault, a persistent storage space, so you can start again with a bang. Unfortunatly, they only give you 8 slots of vault storage for free, but the room has space to expand your storage for like 5$ per 8 slots, with room for up to like, i don't know, a thousand slots maybe?
This is where it becomes appearant where the developers priorities for the game lay: to make money. The prices on items are ridiculously predatory and exploitive. Remember that this is a game with permadeath: when you die with a character, that stuff is gone. So when you load into the hub and see the Cash Shop stall where you can buy weapons and armor for 3$-10$, if you die with it, its gone. Thats money literally down the drain. It's 10-30$ for a PET! You can get the pets via normal means as well, but they are pretty strong once you get them leveled up and you can buy the rarer pets semi-leveled/fused straight up with cash.
So what is your alternative to buying items and pets? (because lets face it, the prices are absurd for items that you will lose on death) Store all the good extra loot you find in the vault.... except.... you only get 8 slots of storage. Oh, but you can buy more, 5$ a pop! Vault storage is quite honestly the biggest quality of life purchase you could consider. The game experience of someone playing 100% free and a person who bought a couple extra chests of storage is huge, because each class can only equip their specific kind of weapon or armor, so if you want 1 weapon and 1 armor when you start a new character after dying, you can have at most 4 sets of starter gear for the game's (I think) 17 classes. But what if you want to collect some rings and spell items too? As you can see, your base storage will fill up almost immediately, requiring you to travel back to the hub area repeatedly to micro-manage your 8 slots to prepare for death. If you never die, great I guess.
And speaking of which, you dont get to have more than one character slot without paying for that as well. I think it's like 10$. So you have a really hella geared Wizard but you kinda wanted to try a warrior too? Too bad. Your only choice, without paying, would be to put your wizard's gear back in the vault and kill him on purpose to try a new class, then level a new wizard if you ever wanted to go back to him.
Anyway, I've rambled enough about the Cash shop expoitation enough, my opinion on that is that the prices and quality of life improvements they want you to purchases are predatory. They want you to feel starved of basic features so that you spend a good 20$ at least on probably a second character slot and a couple extra vault chests. On the other hand, buying POWER via high tier gear and pets, while worrisome in terms of game balance, is largely ignorable. But the things like storage and character slots makes you feel like you are playing a trial version of a game that was meant to cost 20$ or so.
All that really brings me to the main problem I have with the game: the depth of gameplay is NOT proportional to what they seem to want you to invest in it. Its fine for a free game, the mechanics are very simple, the stats are simple, the upgrades are mostly linear. But you quickly come to a point where you are asking yourself, "Is this it? Is this all there is to do?" This game has been out for 5 years now. I played it several years ago and recently re-installed it to see how far it had come along, but it remains largely the same as it has always been. It feels like the devs just reached a point where they said, "OK this is good enough, we have reached the status quo, it should be just barely developed enough to start making money." The gameplay is just shallow, really shallow, for a game that has been out for 5 years and wants a lot of your money. It's like a game that was someone's pet project that ended up being pretty good and people liked it in it's beta form, but then as soon as they realized they could just make money without expanding the original premise they just got lazy.
Anyway, my final words on the game are: OK concept that is fun for maybe 10 hours before you are ultimately reminded that they want your money, not your high praise of a well designed game. I would not reccomend investing too much time into this game: it's too constricted by cash features for a free game, and doesnt have enough depth of gameplay if you were to spend money to turn it into a 10-20$ game. If you spend more than that then I dont know what to tell you other than you just made some lazy dev's day.

If you can describe this game in one word, it would be... immersive.  There is 3 campaigns that run alongside each other, one for the Alien, the Predator and of course, the terrified Space Marines.  Each campaign feels drastically different from each other, and how you play, and more importantly, how you feel while you play the said races, is rife with role playing moments.
As the Space Marine... you are prey.  While the Alien and Predator have melee and stealth kills, the Space Marine gets constant paranoia, in the shape of a motion detector constantly beeping and confusing you with the infamous lack of an vertical axis.  You will be shivering in your boots, as white dots flash on the screen and move around, and through your position.  You will eye the ceiling and the floor, looking for vents, grates, and hiding holes.  I dont know if it was just because I am not a very good shot, but every Space Marine level I played, I survived by the skin of my teeth.  I was low on health, ammo, and often let out an exasperated breath, and a sigh of relief after each level.  This is... perfect, exactly what Id want from a Space Marine campaign.
The Predator is FAR more relaxing then the Space Marine, or even the Alien.  You can cloak, and leap to ledges, roofs, trees, and watch your prey from a distant.  I pretended like I was recording the banter of my hapless humen prey, which you can hear perfectly, if you zoom in onto Space Marines from any distance (Again, very immeresive) even though, sadly, you cannot in fact record key words from your victims.  You can however, use a disapointingly limited selection of phrases, by looking at an enemy and pressing the E key, to lure them away from their friends, and into your clutches.  For full immersive effect, I recomend staying in infrared the ENTIRE game... unless of course, you want to see a grizzly stealth kill, or finisher of course.  When the Aliens show up... its a surprising shift in pace.  Instead of methodically picking apart the superior numbers and collective fire superiority of the Space Marines, you are suddenly ambushed and bum rushed by clawed, dark colored blurs scampering around the walls and attacking you from all sides.  A fight with an Alien ranges from easy when everything goes right, or very, very horrible, if the Alien manages to block your attacks, or keeps landing flanking swipes as it dances around you.  Fighting an Alien (Or 4) is always very exciting, and often cinematic!
The Alien... while the Predator feels like your simulating a hunter, stalking and slaying your prey... the Alien plays more like a coked out serial killer who can climb on walls.  While you cant cloak, you can climb and jump around the walls, and have "Alien vision" which basically means you know where everyone is at all times, as you can see enemies through walls, and even know if their hostile by the color of their glow!  (Guess we know why the Alien is almost always on the giving end of ambushes, even when your playing as the Predator.)  Besides wall climbing and jumping, you are fast.  Easily the fastest of the three, and you will use your speed to murder your way from Space Marine to Space Marine, taking the time to stealth kill purely out of sadistic satisfaction.  You can also knock people down with your tail at a distance with the right mouse button, a VERY effective way open victims up for a front facing execution, which is will be extremely brutal, as you are playing the Alien.
All in all, its a very fun game.  Its not perfect, the flamethrower for the Space Marine feels off, the Predators voice playbacks (Luring) is not only limited, but it adds some very strange distortion effects that doesnt sound good, doesnt sound anything like it did from the movies.  I often go into an elevator and into the next zone before exploring, accidentally as the Space Marine...  But these are mostly nitpicks.

Knights and Merchants is one of those games I grew up with, how ever saying that I have put allot of time into the game. Compared to the old version I have on the CD format the Steam version of it seems to be easy to gather food (by adding in the fishers hut) and dose have some fix's to the builders where they would stop working after you grew to fast. Though with this the steam version also made it longer on the missions compared to the old game.
To those who never played this classic I would highly recommend this to you, the game is based on building your town and getting an army up fast. Though if you grow your town to fast you will lose, you need to have about 6 farms, 6 wine farms, around 3-4 pig farms and 2-3 mills that will take care of your food for most of the game and lets you get plenty of pig skins to make the better units. I would also like to add that you need about 5 or wood cutters. You will run out of wood and stone fast, on the other levels once you get to about half point of the game you will need to get gold, I would say rush to that asap.
There is also a trick to winning the maps with out losing to much men, you make a single bow unit and put him close by to enemy units wait for them to come out of there base to attack your unit, then with draw him back to your line (that needs to be near by). With this tactic you can wipe out there main force. Sometimes this will not work if you don't have the right units to do it. Most maps will last you 2-4 hours so make sure you have time, and that you make 2 saves (one at the start of the level encase you screw up, and a mid map save or a save when you need to take a break). The game dose take time in fact allot of time, I have not beat the steam version and made it to the last level on the old school version before my old 497Hhz died.
Over all Pros and Cons:
Pro's
*Game has much needed fix's such as the builder’s bug and the resource bug.
*The AI dose not rush you as much as the old version (except on a few maps with just fighting units).
*You are able to do a mid map rush if you are a vet of the game.
*Added single maps where you can play AI with out the missions however you can not set up teams and the AI is highly lacking.
Con's
*The music is not the best is not the original and will sometimes lock up.
*The sound file's of the game will sometimes skip if you have the music on which can lock up the sounds.
*Increased the games time for most maps where it will take you an extra hour.
Over all I highly recommend this game to anyone that enjoys games like AOE (Age of Empires), Warcraft III. It is well worth the price of the game.

Darklands meets Mount & Blade. You roam around a procedurally generated map adopting quests, random events and contracts as a means to feed, sate, equip, heal, repair and maintain your company of hired men. Much like xcom they can be outfitted to any equipment you want, upgraded (if they survive) in a small manner of RPG mechanics, and given their own name and appearances of your choosing. Yes, you can make your party of friends and equip them to survive, only to be torn down by ghouls in six minutes.
Roaming the map feels a lot like Darklands. You go from village to village and encounter some kind of contract, alement or quest. Admittedly it's a thin herd of options right now but as early access trudges on, so does the feature list. Today they just added an entirely reworked world map, economy, and politics system -- and there's more to come.
Combat is turn based and tactical. It's simplistic and easy to be punished for and needs some balance tweaks, (RNG is very real for some weapons) but it gets better every update. Permadeath is a feature -- you can and will lose your company, either entirely or partially, almost every fight. One whirring arrow can catch your eye and that's that for your favorite level 4 merc.
Enemies include ferocious, unique Orcs. Terrifiyng undead/ghouls, and enemy mercs/bandits/robbers/militia that stand in your way. Fighting each 'faction' feels unique and punishing. Orcs will slaughter, take double turns, cut off your heads. Ghouls will rise back up RIGHT next to you and kill you. Humans use evasion, tactics and flanks.
Could talk about it all day. You've played this game before, but worse. Battle Brothers is a polished refinment and vision of a tried and true genre that is a staple to anyones collection.

On the eve of launch, this game is ready for prime time. Watch your let's plays on youtube and decide for yourself. But don't watch too much. The devs have added some nice random events and decision points that should be enjoyed on your own.
As said below, this development team has been highly active and transparent with its community. The roadmap and timelines have been followed throughout the entire process. Whenever they've put out an update, any bugs found have been immediately squashed.
The art, sound, metagame, tactical combat, skill tree's, mercenary backgrounds, weapons, armor...everything has been improved and tweaked to make this game one of my favorite tactical point and click games.
They've listened to customer feedback and implemented many positive changes...this team really understands how games should be made with their audience in mind.
It's highly enjoyable and stable before launch. They're just polishing and tweaking the balance in certain areas. Well worth twenty bucks folks. Bastion is another indie game which is put on a pedestal for its presentation, even though its presentation is not nearly as revolutionary as it advertises itself as being. Once again the actual narrative is very thin on content, and the voice over narration is what people refer to when they discuss its "amazing story". The actual content of the game consists of walking on linear cubic paths in a void while engaging in very bland and unengaging 3rd person combat. The monotone narrator talks through the whole game, giving a greater sense of setting to the game than there really is by describing lore about the floating hallway you're traveling even though there is zero visual evidence of any the levels you're occupying as being a real place in any way.
The narrator itself is novel but not very engaging. He speaks with little to no inflection, and it can be easy to not pay attention to anything he says since you're too busy killing enemies on the current floating hallway void. The narration is supposed to be a revolutionary advancement for video game story telling, but it doesn't seem like the voice over is very noteworthy when there is basically no variation in what the player does, and the whole level is a literal linear floating void. The plot itself is vague and immaterial, and doesn't seem to go anywhere.
I really did give the game a go, and wanted to see what it would present next for a short while. The painterly art style is nice enough, even though the ambigious levels meant that changing areas amounted to pallet swaps. The music is also very nice and might be the best part about the whole game. What really got me though was the bland and easy gameplay, and Bastion's answer to giving the player more. The idols are a very good idea, games such as The World Ends With You and Kid Icarus Uprising certainly show how controllable difficulty can be done. The first few idols add some expected increases in challenge to the enemies you fight, such as increased health, faster attacks, and more damage. None of this really makes the game any harder, and the idols that come later basically consist of sabotaging the player, by making enemies randomly not take damage, and even inflicting slow movement on the player for attacking. I admit that the game was pretty difficult with all of these modifiers turned on, but what an artificial and tedious form of difficulty it was. If the only answer the devs have to players who want more interesting combat is "play the game with one hand behind your back" then they shouldn't even bother.
I recommend for anyone curious about Bastion to play the demo first before purchasing. This is definitely not a must buy, and you should decide for yourself whether Bastion's various presentation gimmicks are as worthy of the praise it has been given. Do note as you play that the combat you experience at the beginning is an accurate representation of the whole game, and the game will never add new mechanics or interactions with the world other than new weapons. If what you played in the demo is what you would like to do for 8-10 hours straight, then feel free to buy it.

I've always had a hard time getting into sandbox games, but Starbound has felt different to me. While I liked the "idea" of being able to create my own fun in a digital sandbox environment, I was never able to get a whole lot out of it. Something about Starbound's charming looks and ideas made me decide to ignore my usual feelings and give it a shot. Here are some things I enjoy:
1. Planets and Biomes
There are a lot of different planets with a lot of some of the expected biomes with it: lava planet, forested planet, etc. What makes these interesting is the fact that within some of these planets are sub-biomes, villages, ruins, and colonies. These make sure that exploration always feels fresh and you always feel rewarded for exploring further.
2. Stories and Quests
The story is nothing special or groundbreaking, but I have found it pretty enjoyable, at the very least, as a guide on how to safely navigate through the steady progression of increasingly hostile planets. While the story is basic, there are many times where you will have to complete instanced levels and boss fights which are very fun. One moment you're doing a survival/horror style raid on an infected space station and the next you're trying to survive in a hunting party gauntlet with some killer alien wildlife. Most of these areas are non-linear too, encouraging replayability to find secret areas, gear, and furniture items.
3. The Feeling of Progression and Exploration
Gear is set up in an almost MMO style. As you get better gear, you'll use it to do missions and go searching for even stronger gear and it feels very rewarding. Another cool factor is that of all the unique races in the game have their own sets of gear to go with their style. Not really game-changing, but a nice touch. Plus there are a lot of novelty items that can be used as costumes like astronaut helmets, tuxedos, penguin suits, etc, so you can customize your look.
Outside the straight gear change though, there are also upgrades for your character that are pretty cool. A lot of them will be familiar to anyone who's played a 2D platformer, like a double jump and the very Metroid-Style ball form. There are a lot of other abilities I haven't even tried yet but I can't wait to use them.
There are a lot of features I haven't gone into detail about like the crew system, expanding your ship, and the variety of weapons you can use (so so many!), but if you have any interest in the game, give it a go. I've been really enjoying it since beta and I'm looking forward to see what the next updates will add to it!

Bastion is an amazing singleplayer experience that provides an exceptional story and impressive artistic design, with simple, but effective combat mechanics, amplified by it's interesting soundtrack. It was released in 2012.
Bastion is recieved high praise for it's story, which is told through a narrator. This form of storytelling was a new form of interactive media. In Bastion, a man narrates the actions of the protagonist, while also engaging the players in the lore of the world. This dialogue is vast, and there is a lot of narration throughout the game, which reveals the world to the players in an interesting and unique way. The interactivity can be seen when players simply play the game, which makes the game stand out. For example, if you flawlessly continue through a level, or if you defeat an enemy with a new weapon you found, or if you fell off a new level, you would get a unique piece of dialogue, adding to the theme of the game. There are hundreds of these conditional dialogue pieces, and even players that make mistakes can hear some unique dialogue as well, intensifying the bond between gameplay and narrative. Through this kind of narrative, players can learn about the world just by playing the game. Another example is the shrine. When you activate a god's shrine, it gives a short, but enticing, bit of dialogue that reveals a little bit more of the god to you. There's even a lot of text to go through, and lots of interesting descriptions to read about items that you find or use, and you are guaranteed to hear many different things by the time the game is complete. Another example of this narrative interactivity is even seen when picking weapons, as the narrator will make comments about the choice of weapons you have. Like if you pick a mortar and pike, or a mortar and carbine. Even the soundtrack is part of the story, as some music within the game actually is relevent to the game. On top of that, the soundtrack is quite good. The player also gets a little bit of choice through the story, as they can choose any weapon they have unlocked, activate any god to increase the difficulty, and there is an interesting moment where the player decides something. It's a post-apocalyptic world that feels like an adventure, yet there are moments where the player may learn about the sadder things in the world, as the game firmly grasps emotion, something that many games fail to do.
Bastion isn't a complex game. It has relatively simple controls, however, this doesn't mean the game is boring, by any stretch, as there are a good selection of different weapons, and players get the option to make the game more difficult. Players can also use 'drinks', which are passive effects that the player can choose to make them even stronger. Weapons are handed to the player as the game progresses, widening the level of choice players get as they move towards the end of the game, and players can also select upgrades for their weapons, and can choose which upgrades they want. For example, a player may opt for damage, or they may opt for more range. The combat itself is relatively enjoyable. Players can roll, use a shield to block and counterattack, use range or melee attacks, and pick from a variety of special abilities, and, as mentioned before, the game's difficulty can be increased for more fun, possibly making the game faster paced. The game is very easy to get into, which makes it a great choice for casual players, or people who don't have much time to begin with, as they won't have to deal with an unforgiving learning curve.
Bastion also has a very unique artistic style. It's a 2.5D game with great looking style throughout the entire game. There isn't a moment in the game that feels like it doesn't carry the theme of the rest of the game, and visually, it's easy to see that as players stroll through the menus, look at the loading screen, and explore the levels. Instead of the standard 3D world that you just walk around, Bastion's world is floating. Though there isn't really any platforming, it's a unique way to define current nature of the world, as it does become part of the game and the story. The top notch artwork complements the graphical style of the game, and at the same time, the game is not at all intensive to run. There aren't any super hardcore textures, and there aren't any hardcore lighting effects, as the game's graphic style makes it for it by being unique. This means that even 'non-gaming' PCs ( or Macs ) and Linux based systems can run this easily.
Personally, I believe Bastion to be a very solid title. It's not a triple A title, it's actually an indie game, and yet it's still recognized internationally to be a great title, despite being as small as it is. It's the kind of game that you have to try, even if you don't think you'll like it, and for good reason. Bastion is a great experience, and though you won't be getting hundreds of hours out of this title, every hour will be worth it, and worth a little bit more.

Got this game in Early Access on Janurary 2nd 2014, played a bit of it, then never touched it again. Fast forward to its release date, I saw a friend playing it on steam, checked the steam store, and saw that 1.0 had been released. So I downloaded the game again, started it up, and my oh my it was a pleasant surprise.
Now, let's get onto things in the game. First, THE MULTIPLAYER IS SO MUCH BETTER. You don't have to do any stupid bs to join games, just join via steam, it's really nice. You can teleport to your friend, go on their ship, see their stuff, etc. It works really well.
Secondly, let's see... The story? Yeah, the story. I loved the beginning scene, it gives you plenty of backround info, etc. The main story incorporates well into the game. Taking you to different planets to explore, telling a decently written story, giving you companions along the way, people to know. I am currently on the Avians looking for their stuff, but I need a radioactive EPP upgrade... So I guess I'll need a bit more titanium, meaning I actually have to explore for stuff.
Now, let's take a break and look at a lot of the negatives people have about the game.
First one I just read was about losing your items... Huh, my game must be glitched, it had 3 options, Casual - No Hunger, No item loss. Whatever the next one is that makes you lose items, and have hunger. Then permadeath, with hunger. I mean, c'mon dude, if you want to complain about item loss, make sure the game doesn't have a mode where you don't lose items.
And reading more reviews they all say things are missing but can never mention them? That's a load of bs if I've ever seen it, if it's missing say it in your review, don't skirt around it.
Now, putting this in here, one thing I don't like is the bliddy scanning everything that is required, it's boring, I just want to find 1 thing that gives me a cool clue, not click on a painting that somehow gives me a hint. Also, when I effing pause the game should to, and I play on casual, think of how bs that is for people playing w/ hunger.
I also found a complaint about the EPP things, about how they magically make you immune to a planets heat/fire/ice, etc... Well, it's for simplicity, would you really rather have to have 6 different damn things just to go on 1 ♥♥♥♥ing planet? No, hell no, no one wants that at all, just keep it bliddy simple.
Now, again I read another negative, and this one actually had valid points about things being taken out. Mainly temperature (not sure how this would affect the game at all, as there are ice planets and hot planets) and, star sectors... And I'm wondering, what the hell are star sectors? I read up about them, and they were mainly about difficulty... And I kinda disagree with that, I think it's better without star sectors. I like layered difficulty levels in games, but you should always have a chance to go there anyways, without requiring special things to just not die from the air or something. Of course, there are planets where those still happen, but you can go around them, or at least land near them, just not go on planets, etc.
Another thing to address is being compared to Terraria... I have played lots of Terraria, and I must say, these are similar in some ways, but are vastly different. In Terraria, you are stuck on 1 world, and 1 world only. Granted, you can make the world pretty big, and there is more on the individual world of terraria than 1 world in starbound. Quite a bit more I must say. But here's the big difference, starbound is about exploration, a lot of it. Sure you can make colonies on planets in starbound, set up a base, but generally your spaceship is your main base, as the game focuses on a lot of exploration as compared to Terraria's base building mining focus. And I would say Terraria does do many aspects better, and if that seems more your kind of game, get that instead. But starbound still does a lot of other things better, like exploration, survival, sci fi stuff, weapon design, and the story...
Also, Starbound has a story, so if you like stories, you'd probably like this.
Anyhow, I think this is it for now, I highly recommend this game, it's pretty good!

So, after watching a few videos of this game online, and having read numerous postive reviews here on Steam, I was definitely interested in this game. What sealed the purchase for me was the clear commitment from the devs to make this game the best it can be. I first heard about Stranded Deep about a month or so ago, and I was definitely skeptical at first. What kept me interested was the success of The Forest, which is one of my favourite games on Steam.
Once I heard that this game has been in development for over 2 years, the core gameplay is implemented, and that one of the devs' highest priorities is bug squashing, I decided to get the game.
Immediately, I was captivated. Unlike many other survival games out right now, Stranded Deep doesn't throw anything super natural or unnatural at you. The basic premise is that you're the survivor of what ppears to be a private plane crash somewhere on the pacific ocean. Your life raft drifts overnight to a series of small, tropical/desert islands with limited resources on them.
There are ship wrecks, coral reefs and deep ocean trenches to explore as well, with various fish, crabs, and even predatory sharks that will attack and kill you if you're not careful when skinny dipping!
The sharks are the only "enemy" in the game; there are no zombies, no mutants, no cannibals or anything in between.
Just you are the world.
You can die from dehyrdation under the burning sun, starvation, sickness and possibly physical injuries (don't eat raw crabs. Just don't. You'll thank me later).
My current character suffered a broken arm after climbing a palm tree and falling off. The game actually has a mechanic where you look at your wrist watch to see the time and days survived (press F). Pressing LMB from here will cycle it to show your vital stats (health, hunger and thirst). If, like me, you sustain a broken arm, when looking at your watch, the arm will actually look disfigured and legitimately broken. Props to the devs for this detail. It actually made me cringe when I saw it, and I'm not usually squeamish about anything, let alone video game content.
Graphically, the game is fantastic. It runs on the Unity engine, and with all (available) graphical settings maxed out, I'm getting 80-120 FPS on average (with FX 8350, GTX 770 and 8 GB RAM), so the game is very well optimised and runs silky smooth (the sparseness of the world obviously plays a part in this). The open ocean is rendered beautifully, lighting, shade and textures all look great and its approaching The Forest levels of fidelity.
Eye candy.
The controls are responsive if a bit glitchy, and the crafting system is very unique, and arguably realistic. You place items on the floor and put them together in various combinations to make anything from a basic fire to steps for your shelter (yes, basic base building is a thing in Stranded Deep, and it works well).
One thing in particular is probably going through your mind if you've been involved in PC gaming for any longer than a year; EARLY ACCESS.
Straight away, I would like to say that yes, this game is in alpha, and yes, it has bugs and glitches. However, they are not as bad as I was expecting.
In fact, I haven't noticed many at all. Like I said earlier, the game is silky smooth to play, and tbh, some of the glitches that I have come across are quite funny (and completely excusable for an alpha). For example, your character has no shadow, and when holding an item in your hands, the item casts a shadow on the floor, but your body doesn't. So when you're walking around, it looks like there's a floating knife :D
The only major glitch that I encountered was when my inventory and hotkeys froze up, and I couldn't use or do anything in the game. I had to restart the game.
The devs are committed to the game and will do their part to iron out the problems.
I have seen my fair share of bad/questionable alphas; WarZ and DayZ come to mind (the latter of which I actually enjoy, it's the pace of development of that game that has been sleep-inducing). Stranded Deep isn't one of them. It is an Early Access Alpha done right.
Not only that, but it's a pure survival game. You vs the wild. Nothing more.
If the devs stick to their guns and polish this game as they intend, we could be looking at a fantastic open world survival experience. It's already a tonne of fun, and despite the problems that it has, the potential is there.
I will be updating this review periodically throughout the year, until the game is fully released.
8/10- recommended if you are okay with Early Access and enjoy survival survival games, otherwise wait for beta or full release.

Man, this was a pretty sweet game. I will say that Aliens Versus Predator 2 from years back (this new game is a reboot, here) was better in my opinion. I beat that older one probably half a dozen times as well as its DLC. I loved the story, the levels, the weapons, and even the multiplayer, which is really something because I'm not big into competitive multiplayer, but I played AvP2 multiplayer for many, many hours.
So, this AvP here is good stuff. It's not superb, but I really enjoyed the single player campaign. The competitive multiplayer was pretty decent, though I never really could get into it for long. The campaign, as with the old games of the same name, is comprised of a colonial marine campaign, a xenomorph campaign, and a yaujta (predator) campaign. Each campaign was fun and felt different. I will even go so far as to admit that the xenomorph campaign, in my opinion, was drastically superior to the xenomorph campaign in the older AvP2. In that one, you were fast but kinda unstoppable, even up against guns that shred xenos in the films. Here, you die pretty easily to pulse rifle shots, so it's more of a stealth game when playing a xeno, remaining in the shadows on ceilings, hissing to draw solitary humans closer for a takedown...man, just thinking back on it I kinda wanna play it again.
The yaujta and colonial marine campaigns are good, too, featuring nowhere near as many weapons as AvP2 had back in the day, but the guns that are here are good, and the plot is decent enough. The gameplay is just really fun, and I feel like it will satisfy people far more than Aliens: Colonial Marines. I actually kinda liked that game, but AvP is drastically better, thanks to the gameplay variety of 3 playable races. I'm really going to have to play AvP again sometime. I've played through it twice since I first bought it, and I definitely had a good time; far better than with Aliens: Colonial Marines.
