This game brings back such memories.. Ah..
Anyway, nostalgia trip over, here's my views on this game.
Pro's and benefits:
This game has an indepth resource management system. Seriously, it's way better than anything to date. Your army can drain your economy rapidly depending on how big it is, so fielding smaller armies can be mutually better, if it may take longer to defeat your enemy.
Strategy is actually required for this game. No really, it's not a case of throwing a large army of 50 spear holders against a small force of 10 swordsmen with some archers behind, because that'll just get you murdered and that's a whole bunch of gold and resources gone. It's better to have small squads of 6, 9 and 12 with occasional 16 squads appearing now and then.
The nostalgic feel of this game is incredible! This game was made a good 10 years ago at the very least, maybe even earlier. Because it was made earlier and during the time that game developers actually had the balls to step outside the box and try something now, it created this game as well as many others.
The Cons/painful stuff:
Crash crash crash landings. This game SUCKS with the amount of crashes you can get. Seriously, there's an amazing amount of things you can do, and half of them will make you crash to desktop faster than the speed of light. (Note: this can be remedied via downloading the remake version on modDB. No free game for you though, you have to own the game to get access to the remake. Nice little touch of coding on the dev's part)
Time. THIS TAKES FOREVER!!! No really, you can be there for a good few hours figuring out one single mission. It can get really frustrating and at times I need to quit and relax my mind before I blow a brain tumor.
Final score:
I give this game a 4/5.
I'm giving it this score because considering everything that's great about this game, the crashes and amount of time it takes, as well as the sheer amount of difficulty some missions can have will result in rages and you not touching the game for a full week. However considering everything else about the game, it's really fun to play.
Notice: With the remake edition, multiplayer is available as well as a few other options, not to mention the crashes are at a minimum and you can increase time to X10 so waiting on your♥♥♥♥♥no longer becomes such a dull practice. Use the remake version if you want a better game in general. (again, you must own the game before you can use anything in the remake, and even then the remake isn't complete even today, so expect a few issues)

I had been keeping an eye on Northgard for awhile and when it went on sale for the Holidays, I couldn't hold off any longer.  I've been a fairly big fan of the Civilization series -- though, certainly not as intense of a fan as some -- and probably have 2-300 hours between Civ 5 and 6.  I usually played Civ 5 and 6 on the second hardest difficulty, since Immortal (hardest) required a lot of boring (from my perspective) cheese in Civ 5.  I was an absolutely MASSIVE fan of Warcraft 3 and its expansion Frozen Throne.  Massive.  That and Diablo 2 are probably my two most played games of all time.  Keep that in mind as you read.
When I first jumped into Northgard (NG), it felt a bit like Civ Lite.  It had some interesting features, but wasn't all that complex.  For example, NG has "lore" and an accompanying tech tree which functions in almost the exact same fashion as science/culture in Civ6.  The main difference?  Significantly fewer options.  My initial feeling was that the game was kind of shallow, it didn't seem like there was much to it especially since this "stripped down" Civilization feeling persists through some of the other core mechanics.
Like Civilization, there are different victory conditions.  Lore (basically technology -- science in Civ), Domination, Trade, I always forget the name of this other one, but it's essentially "influence" (you own 12 colonies, have a score of 1200, and build unique building).  Finally, each map has a "unique" victory condition.  For example, you might be asked to colonize this lava area, build a forge, and reforge Odyn's Sword.  You might be asked to capture Yddrassil (sp?), the World Tree.  I'm not sure how many different unique victory conditions there are, I can recall at least 3.  As with Civ, you can turn any of these conditions on/off prior to starting the game.  The only victory conditions I haven't won with are Domination (seems really hard on a big map with 5 other clans and the Unique feature (almost did this once, but it required 2000 food and it was heavily guarded).  I have been playing with all of them on so each of the "clans" can capitalize on what they are best at, but it might be worth considering removing them to avoid the temptation of taking the easiest path to victory.
This temptation leads me to my first, minor, qualm with the game: victory condition balance.  It is highly likely that I simply have not played enough games, and I have not played online yet (was waiting for dedicated servers, coming this month), but "Lore" feels like the easiest victory condition by far.  Not only does it give you a comparitive technological advantage (some of which are MASSIVE boons), but it's fast.  In my last game, I sprinted for a Lore victory and had won before any other Clan was more than 60% of the way to victory.  Trade also felt pretty easy with the proper initial sequence.
There are currently six different clans (hopefully they add more) each with their own unique bonuses.  At 200 and 500 (of the resource that I cannot think of the name -- one of the victory conditions above), the clan receives its first and second bonus.  You receive this resource from Lore, population, upgraded buildings, etc.  Additionally, each clan has some special lore features.  For example, the Clan of the Boar replaces the standard "herbalism" trait with one that boosts their unique "mender" unit.  Unfortunately, as far as I can tell, you cannot see their unique Lore technologies prior to loading into the game.  I played 3-4 games before I realized that some of the lore features were changing between clans.  I think it would be really convenient if these were shown in the UI when setting up a game, especailly for newer players.  I cannot speak on clan balance, because I haven't played enough.  There are a lot of posts on different forums, but there doesn't seem to be a lot of agreement.  I've spent most of my time playing Boar because I like being a recluse and pumping out Lore while turtling.  That's their specialty.
There are six different primary resources that contribute to your Clan's overall well-being.  These are: happiness (determines how quickly your population grows, or doesn't), Food (each unit has food upkeep, if you don't produce enough food you starve.  Can also be used for "great feasts" which temporarily boosts happiness and production of all resources, as well as grants fame [which I believe is the name of the resource that I keep forgetting]), Wood (used for building and to keep citizens warm during winter), Money (some buildings, some units, and standard Clan upkeep), and Lore (technology).  Stone and Iron are two valuable secondary resources (I call them secondary because there is a finite amount of them, though you can also purchase them in limted quantities through the marketplace) that are used for building and unit upgrades.  Your growth is also limited by housing.  I wouldn't consider this a "resource" in the same way as the others because it isn't generated through work, you just build houses.  Most of what separates a good player from a great player involves micro-managing your workers production of these different resources (Ex. pumping food out during the summer when you don't have a production penalty).
My favorite part of the game, and one that I really hope they expand upon, is the weather/event system.  Occasionally, you'll get hit by a blizzard during winter or an earthquake.  A blizzard hammers your food/wood supplies.  Earthquakes require you to have some extra wood on hand for building repairs.  The game will give you a warning a couple months ahead of time to encourage you to prepare.  If you don't, your clan gets sick, freezes, unhappy, etc.  I hope they expand this to include more negative events, as well as some positive ones such as "bountiful harvest" which gives you a temporary boost in food production or something.  Add tornadoes or cyclones, plagues, etc.  There's also rats in your food sometimes (mess you up if you don't have food silos) that can make your population sick.  Basically, this system throws a wrench in some of your planning in pretty interesting ways.  But by your 10th game, when you've faced your 15th blizzard, you're kind of hoping for something new.  Could throw in hurricanes too to impact trade victory conditions.  There is a lot of potential for this.
Right now there are three difficulties: easy, medium, hard.  I began on medium difficulty, but kicked it up to hard pretty soon after.  For me, there wasn't much of a difference.  On hard, it seems like the environment (wolves, Draugr -- think Barbs from Civ) is more aggressive, as are the other clans, and I have read that there are some production penalties in the form of additional unit maintenance costs, but it didn't seem all that bad.
I ran out of space to discuss, in depth, the colonization system.  Each tile has a limited number of buildings (2-4, 5 on your primary) and you can develop it to hold 1 additional building.  Smartly place your buildings.
As I come to a close, I want to bring this full circle and reiterate that my initial impression of this game was a stripped down civilization.  It seemed too basic to keep my interest.  But this is actually exactly why I like this game.  Civilization's late game has never appealed to me.  It gets to the point, for my taste, where things are super bloated, turns start taking forever, etc, etc.  I ADORE civilization's early/mid game, though.  This game is like Civ's early/mid game.  The match time is shorter (probably partially because it is RTS instead of turn-based), there is less complexity (though enough for important choices), and you're reacting to events in real time.  With a little more content (clans, more events) this game would go from good to great.  I'd probably give it 85/100 right now.  Everything functions, the gameplay is fun, but it'd be incredible with a touch more dynamism.  Overall, I'd highly recommend this title.

I can tell this game took heavy inspiration in its artistic approach from Age of Empires: Online, and it honestly makes me miss it.
In my opinion, where this game finds its strengths is also where it shows its flaws, such as:
-Randomly Generated Maps: While this does make each play through interesting by forcing you to rethink each time how to use the limited resources in front of you, it can also start you off with either an unfair advantage or a cruel hinderance to you- depending on the faction you chose and your prefered play style.
-Scouts: At first, I found it interesting to play an RTS that made them actually matter, until I am sitting on the border of the last two areas of my enemy, massive army in tow with my frost giant buddy, only to find out that, despite seeing his units move just outside of the fog of war, I am unable to pass over this wall of darkness. I suppose my men were too afraid after walking over piles of undead corpses on their way there.
-Micromanaging: This is something that I rather enjoy in games such as Stronghold, because it keeps you on your tows. However this game makes that burden a bit too heavy by making use of A.I. that will just stand there after constrcuting a building. This is done because only Villagers can construct buildings, yet if you assign them to a mine and that mine runs out, you have to command your now Miner unit to return to a House or your Town Hall in order to once again construct buildings. This becomes a most unwelcome challenge as you scramble for those precious resources that your clan has been sorely lacking.
-Combat: Plenty of others here have stated how mundane the combat is, so I won't dwell on this much. Honestly, with the limited spaces that these battles take place in, the game would not really have room (pun intended) for an in depth combat system, such as formations and the like. However, a wider variety of units would be nice, there are currently four including a hero unit.
All in all, the game is enjoyable, but some of the mechanics behind your unit management, and the somewhat aimless A. I. proved to be a bit irritating. However, I do recomend it. For a indie game, it isn't bad at all, and I believe it is worth the asking price.

Sleeping Dogs is one of the better open world GTA-style games you can find on the market. It stands apart from its peers thanks to its combat system, which focuses on melee combat (although there's still a fair bit of shooting, especially in main story missions). The main story is of medium length and quite enjoyable with its down-to-earth tone. Main storyline aside, there isn't much to do. There are "favors" which are essentially bite-sized errands, races and a number of repetitive jobs which earn you money to be spent on clothing and cars. There's numerous collectibles to be discovered, but they all become visible on the minimap eventually. Overall there's little fun to be had outside of main story missions, unless you enjoy racing of which there's plenty.
Graphically the game ranges from gorgeous to hideous, with the average being rather charming, provided you install the HD texture DLC which is free. Most textures look pretty good, but you'll often encounter the odd, hideous texture which looks like it came from 2006. Wet roads look absolutely terrific and overall there's plenty of work put into making rainy Hong Kong look good. Additionally, it's one of the better optimized games. With everything set to maximum except anti-aliasing which I set to the second highest preset, my GTX 780 scored 81 average FPS and 63 minimum FPS on the in game benchmark.
However the game suffers from a number of technical flaws. First and foremost, the camera when driving tends to do its own thing and when you're accelerating or reversing the camera will rarely look at the direction you're going. There were numerous instances of egregious popping with skyscrapers appearing out of thin air in front of my eyes. Much of the game revolves around using your phone. In order to take out your cell phone, holster your gun or just browse the upgrade menus, you have to use the arrow keys. Those can't be rebound.
Additionally the combat controls are wonky. The combat doesn't feel responsive, animations stop abruptly when performing a combo or whe countering an enemy in the middle of a combo. You perform light attacks by tapping left click and heavy attacks by holding it down. Occasionally your character will lock into performing heavy attacks only even when you just tap left click, forcing you to run around for a little bit until all animations end. Overall there's a jerky feel to it, which was rather disappointing.
The game crashed twice over the course of 28 hours of gameplay. A few times I had to restart missions because of the terrible pathing. Enemies wouldn't reach their predetermined positions because they couldn't get past minor obstacles, so the cutscene wouldn't progress, forcing me to restart. Likewise the character sometimes fails to walk over a small obstacle or gets stuck running. The switch between running and jumping animations is also jerky, which gives giving chase to somebody an unsatisfying feel. Additionally, the game will often start in windowed mode and it always enters windowed mode when you Alt+Tab, forcing me to enter the options menu every time to switch it back to fullscreen.
In summary it's a good purchase. The gameplay is fun if somewhat limited and the story is grounded and has an authentic feel to it. However its numerous technical issues prevented me from enjoying it to the fullest.

The Game:
Battle Brothers is a turn-based strategy game where you lead a mercenary band in a medieval fantasy world.
After a battle that goes wrong you become the captain of a small mercenary group and lead them in a low magic fantasy world. Your band will face dangers ranging from human bandits all the way to vampires. You will have to build them up from scratch through ways like looting defeated enemies, doing quests for villages or noble houses.
The game has 2 main parts. The large map where you travel around fighting enemies and doing quests and the battle area where the turn-based combat takes place. The large map is procedurally generated so different playthroughs aren't usually the same. From there you can go to towns to trade for provisions and equipment for your mercenary group, and recruit new members for your party. Each town has it's own economy and these are sometimes affected by quests or bandits. Different towns also give different kinds of recruits, so poorer towns usually have farmhands usually while richer ones have knights available. There are also random events while traveling the map. These usually happens depending on the backgrounds of your battle brothers. Some benefit others, some clash causing negative results. It makes traveling around the map more dynamic and less of a boring walk from one place to another.
The battle area is also procedurally generated so thinking on your feet is needed to win battles. You can field a maximum of 12 battle brothers at a time. Sadly there isn't much you can do with your formations so for me, that limits the tactical possibilities for the player. Permadeath is a major part of the game so a bad damage roll can usually end the life of a battle brother quickly if he isn't equipped well enough. There are a variety of perks and weapons to choose from making it easy for specialization of troops. Though not all troops are created equal, those from more well off backgrounds are usually better suited to combat and are better objectively.
In combat there are a lot of factors that come into play not just hp and damage. There is a morale mechanic in place which can sway the battle for better or worse in a single turn if you luck is good or bad enough. This is complemented by the multiple possible traits of each battle brother. Some traits make them more likely to hit opponents, some less likely to run away, though some traits are negative. These are assigned randomly when you first recruit them. Making the best out of every battle brother is key to surviving this harsh world.
Get this?
I highly recommend this game for fans of tactical games. The game forces you to keep making your battle brothers more efficient after every battle. The art style is not only gorgeous but also functional. It looks simple yet detailed enough that even after playing for a long time it doesn't get stale watching them act.
One of my favorite parts is that you can customize the name and face of each battle brother. So you can set it as an adventure with your friends, or a walking boy band. Even the design of the different armors looks great as you can see what each person has equipped giving a better sense of immersion.
I bought the supporters edition since the developers are active and communicate well with the fans. These kind of developers deserve the support since they're also survivors of the Steam early access system.
I didn't mention all the things about the game because I want you to see the rest for yourself since this is a great game from great people.

This game is full of so many surprises, amazing visuals, varied environments, fun combat, great base building tools, etc. For example, I was on a desolate planet after just barely using enough fuel for my FTL drive (faster than light drive) to get across the universe. Soon I began to see tiny windmills, a miniature hospital, convenience stores, and little houses... everywhere. I had somehow stumpled upon an entire subterranean city for gnomes that stretched for hundreds of meters in every direction! NOTICE: I AM COMING INTO THIS MORE OR LESS UNBIASED.
I didn't play the early access, so I'm reviewing PURELY based on full release first impressions. This review does not necessarily negate any reviews angry about early access period woes; it's simply a review from another perspective.
The short of it: 9/10 after a few hours of play. The most fun I've had with a game of its type since Dig or Die.
70TH HOUR UPDATE: This game is incredible. I've never had so much fun with a game of its genre in my life. Everything below was written after only a five hours of play, so I'll summarize my 70-hour impressions here: It's fun. It's robust. It's endless. It's the very definition of an excellent sandbox game. There are so few things this game could've done better I can't even think of any right now. If you enjoy the concept of freeroam sci-fi colonization and exploration, you won't stop playing this game for a long time. I have to update to 10/10 simply because I haven't binged a Minecraft-alike for so many hours in my life. Not even Minecraft.
The longer version:
I'm someone who loved Minecraft for a time, but always felt it wasn't quite living up to its potential. Especially on the roleplaying front. I'm also someone who loves the idea of carving your place in the world out of nothing, but my aversion to post-apocalyptic horror and zombie mayhem in such a game left games like Rust off the table for me.
I tried Terraria but it never fully clicked with me. Dig or Die offered a fun experience, though it grew stale after the third or fourth day (real world time, that is). Enter Starbound. I'd heard of it, but assumed I wasn't interested at first because it looked like another Terraria. Once it hit full release, I had another look and the features couldn't be overlooked, so I took the plunge.
After five hours of vigorous play, my impressions are very good. Visually, it's a charming and at times beautiful game, as far as games with this art style can be. The tiles are very well made and generally blend together well, while the backdrops on the worlds you'll colonize can be downright breathtaking (again, as far as pixels can provide). The core mechanic of the game is solid. From surviving monsters and treacherous falls, to staying dry in the rain and well lit at night, the basic build-and-survive aspect is everything it needs to be. I feel genuinely proud of my work when I manage to get my first base up and running to full efficiency, and that's what you ask for in a game like this.
Then there's the promise of so much more on the horizon. Thanks to trying to get multiplayer to work with my friend (it worked fine after one of us hosted a dedicated server for the other to direct connect to, by the way), I restarted three or four times early on, and each time I was dropped onto a planet that looked rather different than the last. On each world, different manmade structures - both functional and ruined - left me wondering about the possbility of intelligent life, and made for an interesting break in the natural scenery that was different for each new world. The color pallets, even some of the tiles, different worlds offered in different flavors. And with the prospect of repairing and possibly expanding my derelict shuttle... I have no shortage of goals, and I'm eager to see my way to them.
The mechanics take very little getting used to if you've played games like Terraria or Dig or Die before. You have something of an omnitool that allows you to interact with the world; left click breaks or places objects on the "front layer", while right click does so for background objects (generally walls). Space to jump, A and D to move left and right. S crouches. A few quality of life things have made the mechanics even smoother, such as the way diagonally-adjacent platforms become staircases, and the ability to craft rope that can be thrown onto a ledge via grappling hook, then ascended or descended at will. Flashlights and flares help tremendously in spelunking endeavors as well.
Already I've discovered a weapon chest full of very useful items, and an intriguing quest to activate an ancient power source. It seems the game has both scripted and non-scripted finds like these that make exploration even more than just a matter of finding new materials to craft with. I even noticed under a gravestone that a hole was dug out containing bones and a silver treasure chest. Dare I dig and find out what's in there, or just leave the dead to rest...? That's a decision I'll have to make.
How good is it as an endless sandbox game? Unfortunately, I can't say definitively, as I haven't even approached that content yet. But I will say that based on light reading and current experiences, the odds are looking quite good that it'll be enjoyable as an endless experience. I understand that apparently, promised content during the alpha was cut out as the game got closer to release, but going purely based on post-release screenshots and features details, I have high hopes for the endgame content.
As someone who wasn't at all paying attention to the alpha, I can only give my opinion on the finished product and the content that made it in. From my perspective as a totally new player, this game is very fun and I highly recommend it to anyone into this sort of Minecraft-alike. I can't speak to what was cut or how the developers handled the early access period, but for those who want a review of the final release, apart from early access... I highly recommend this game.

But that's all I'll say about Early Access. No need for lectures, everyone knows the drill by now.

It is still far too early yet to say how quickly the Beam Team will develop the game or how their interaction with the community will be now that the game is out. Their goal as it stands, is to have Stranded Deep complete by the end of 2015 and if other Early Access games are saying anything it's: "That's optimistic....But if you say so".

I wish the Beam Team well on their maiden voyage! Just don't crash into the ocean and disappear eh? ;)

Town of Salem is a murder-mystery game that pits 16 people together and requires them to achieve their factions' objective.
There are several factions in this game. There is your Town(the good guys), The Mafia(Bad Guys) and the Neutral(side with anyone you want). The objective of the town is to "lynch all evildoers", the Mafia's objective being to kill every other faction, and neutral can be different in terms of your sub role.
Each role is very important, and can mean the difference between a loss and a win. Within each faction, there will be groups of sub-roles, and within those groups it is the roles themselves. For example, within a Mafia, theres Mafia Deception, Mafia Killing and Mafia Support. Those within the Killing subrole is simply put ; can kill for the mafia. Those in support is basically make sure to support those doing the "dirty work" and make sure the Mafia stays hidden. Lastly, the Deception, where they can trick the "good guys", and manipulating them.
I would not go into a very detailed explanation about what each role does, but for sure each and every one of them has a big part to play. What I extremely like about this game ; just like any other murder-mystery game, is not knowing who to trust. Not knowing those that are on your side. Not knowing whether the person you have been collaborating with is even telling the truth. What makes ToS stand out is just the wide variety of roles ; and they made it where each one is important. Especially those in Town and the Mafia. Each role has their own special ability too, of course.
Customization also exists within this game. It allows players to cutomize their character, choose their house, and even have a pet. They can also buy "character scrolls", which when activated, will increase the chance of you getting that said role.
Once I first started playing ToS, I was immediately hooked. I have played much more on the browser(back then it was only on browser), and as soon it came out on Steam, I bought it immeadiately. For ToS, its a game where... its unique from others. That is why I really like this game.
Play it on browser first before purchasing it here. Personal opinion : 9/10

Remember AvP2? The great controls of the Alien, which can shred any foe to pieces within seconds? The Predator with its slower, but powerful strikes and great weaponry, melee and ranged? The fun Marine campaign with all the horror and huge arsenal of weapons? The many variations of enemies and environments? All of which kept you entertained for quite a while? Yes? Well, there's none of that in this game.
There's a blocking mechanic, which means that a Marine can repeatedly block the strikes of an Alien or a Predator. It's actually a very dominant mechanic in melee. Don't expect your shoulder cannon to actually hit the Aliens, they evade your shots quite often. The predators standard weapons are his claws. You also have the shoulder cannon, which is out of energy after a few shots until you refill it at a refill spot. There's mines, a throwing disc and a throwing spear. Oddly enough, the Predator can't crouch. Neither can the Marine.
The Aliens wall crawl mechanic feels way inferior to AvP2. In this game, you don't keep the button pressed to stick to walls, you hit it once near a wall. And then you hit it again in order to jump off (yes, you can't just let yourself fall off), it occasionally seems to be on even if you don't want it to be. The Alien is also way slower than what you've seen in AvP2. If you wanna silently kill someone from behind, good luck. You need to crawl slowly, which happens at the exact same speed as your victim moves. Pounce into a Marines face? Can work, but he can also (kid you not) hit you with the rifle and you'll just get smashed to the floor and need to get up again.
The Alien and Predator campaigns focus on the grab-kills. Which means you can get close to an enemy from behind and hit a key in order to kill silently. You'll actually have to do this quite often. The animations vary, but get really old really fast, can't be skipped and even put you in harms way. In case of the Predator, it means that he'll decloak, grab the person, decapitate it, look at the head and maybe plays with the spine, before putting it away. Yes, you're visible during that whole sequence which can take anywhere between about 3 and 7 seconds. Yes, enemies will attack you if you're seen during this. Yes, you'll likely die. Yes, it's frustrating.
The Marine campaign is the best and longest of the campaigns, but it's rather mediocre compared to so many great FPS out there.
There's no save option, just checkpoints. The Alien and Predator campaigns take approx. 2-3 hours each, so they're relatively short, even on hard. You'll also see the same places in each of the campaigns. On hard, with a couple re-tries, it took me about 10 hours to complete the game.
Maybe you may like it if you don't have any expectations. But if AvP2 set the bar for you, and you're looking for a more modern, but equally good game, you may wanna skip this.
Is this terrible? No. Is it good? Meh, too flawed. If you're interested, get it on sale. I certainly wouldn't pay 22€ for the whole pack.
Overall I'd probably give this something like 3 out of 5. It's kinda okay, but not great and the money is better spent elsewhere.

This game has had so many chances to be updated to a better game, scene as though it was made in september last year, but it's possibly the worst game I have played in a while, and that includes Ride to Hell...
Please note that I have only got passed the bit where you get out of the temple and the guy steals your flask but I had to stop playing as it was giving me a headache.  The game starts with you in a temple where you have to fight a man that looks like he was made out of cardboard by a three year old. The fighting is literally F to block and click the mouse buttons to kill the guy.  However, when you kill him, he disappears somewhere (I would probably find out where if I carried on playing).  The fighting in this game, to say it's a survival game, should be intense and exciting, but turns out to be a big pile of poop, pressing a button every now and then.
Then you are posed with the question of, should I save this woman?  Because in the game, he says that it could kill him if he saves her, but if you do save her, nothing actually happens to you or her... she just sits where she was for the next year or so.
The game tells you what to do but not where to do it, so either tell us what to do, or not at all.  It's really annoying having a survival game that tells you what to do after 2 minutes of exploration.  Then, when something actually happens, for example; you see someone, in a normal survival game, it starts to get really intense and exciting, but in this game, it zooms really weirdly taking all of the intensity out of it.
Then we get onto the buugs... where do I start?
First off, when I went down into the depth of the temple (a couple of feet down under ground), I found a gun and thought that this was a turning point for the game.  Maybe I could now choose whether to fight loud or go in really stealthy, but no, as soon as the next cut-scene comes, the gun was taken out of my inventory never to be seen again.
Secondly, when things start to fall, things hover in the air (again, could be part of the game) but for me, you can't get close to the rocks without there being an invisable wall.  This makes the 'survival' game really restrictive.   When I was trying to do a simple task of walking down the stairs, I couldn't as there was a rock above me.  I tried to crouch, thinking that maybe I needed to, but nope, that didn't work either.
This game is terrible and I wouldn't even wish it onto my worst enemy.
Whatever you do, do not waste £15 on this game.  I wouldn't even spend 50p on it, this game should be free, heck, they should pay us to play it.
How can I get my money back?

An absurd and sometimes obscene puzzle game that focuses on short visual gags and the most illogical solutions one can find to a problem. The strangest thing is that it works quite well either as a good bad game or just as a clever indie puzzle– with an excellent length/price ratio thanks to the continuous release of free new levels.
McPixel is the kind of game that you can hardly place anywhere. On one hand it’s obviously a joke title, full of obscene and sometimes downright reta
rded gags, completely illogical puzzles and an utterly insane basic idea: you have to defuse bombs at unusual places (including a lot of video game or movie themed levels) using the most absurd ways.
Still, despite the complete absence of logic, it works surprisingly well as a puzzle game, and the incentives to find all possible solutions can open up a few clever visual gags that really show how great imagination the creator has. It may not be a new Portal in terms of advancing puzzle games to the next level, but it offers a quick fun, and thanks to the many levels– including the free DLCs and community-created ones– it can last quite long, if you choose to stick with it.
Buy to support the devs not for a complete game.

140 is a music-based puzzle platformer that uses abstract shapes for all of the game objects.
This game is pretty, but lacks substance. The shapes are distinct enough that you can tell what's going on, and the game certainly is going for an interesting style, but it's all devoid of any meaning or significance, especially because the game has zero story. The music provides a nice beat for the game to go by, but it's repetitive and not very memorable. The controls work fine and the levels are competently built, but the game is very short, there's not a whole lot of challenge, and no part of this game stands out as being better than "competent" or "decent".
There's not much in this game that's done poorly, but there's also not much that's better than average here. It's really just kind of a waste of time. There's nothing worthwhile to experience in this game. It's not worth your time, and it's certainly not worth your money.
(I played a non-Steam version of this game. Steam does not accurately reflect the time I spent on it.)

Sleeping Dogs is a lot like playing Grand Theft Auto in a Hong Kong setting. It is an open-world, sandbox type of game that gives you no shortage of things to do. However, it's notable differences, mostly borrowed from other games, makes it stand up in its own merits and provides a very different feel than GTA.
First, the combat is very akin to the Arkham series of games. With an importance of countering attacks, identifying enemy types, while beating up large gangs at once, you get an intense melee experience.
What really sets Sleeping Dogs apart, is it's Hollywood-quality, action movie experience: The usual story of an undercover cop going into a gang war, and all the associated tropes. It all makes for great entertainment.

The Binding of Isaac series has been one of my ungodly addictions for years.  It embodies the perfect rogue style game, making each and every new start a fresh and horrific experience.  With each and every restart, I can't help but look forward to what new tools and strategies I must employ and alter to survive to the end.  It is an end that is never satisfying, but never disappointing.
The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth is not only infuriatingly difficult, but enticingly generous with each new game.  The potential for an item of immense power promises to the player an experience to remember, assuming another item you picked up previously does not destroy you in the process.
Never touch Bob's Brain unless you have Pyromaniac and avoid the Cursed Eye, a pedestal item.  Either will end, not in Isaac's tears, but your own.
Edit: It's almost 2018 and I still adore this game, sans Afterbirth+.  <3

Bastion is a game whose story is delivered by a third person omniscient narrator. The game starts in a broken world
suspended in the sky. A catastrophe or calamity, how it is referred as in the game, just occurred but you have no
recollections of any of the events. The narrator doesn’t speak about the characters emotional or psychological state,
he simply narrates the actions being portrayed. He is also the one who tells the player the story of the world that it
once was and what it is now. The entire context around the environment and the characters is being narrated whilst
the player is experiencing them at first hand. Gameplay is fun and soundtrack fenomenal.

This game is full of so many surprises, amazing visuals, varied environments, fun combat, great base building tools, etc. For example, I was on a desolate planet after just barely using enough fuel for my FTL drive (faster than light drive) to get across the universe. The planet was dead, or so it seemed. I was digging deep into the planets crust and through the dark labrinyths of hopelessness and despair I saw a glimmer of light. Naturally I had to investigate this strange occurance. When I drew closer I began to realize that the light was coming from a small streetlamp, a tiny streetlamp of all things!! Soon I began to see tiny windmills, a miniature hospital, convenience stores, and little houses... everywhere. I had somehow stumpled upon an entire subterranean city for gnomes that stretched for hundreds of meters in every direction! Not only that but the surroundings of the city where covered in gold, silver, tungsten, iron, and coal. I made sure to preserve the houses and buildings of the gnomes because Im a gentle giant and moreover, I couldn't believe what I was seeing.
This game is FULL of surprises, which makes it so unique. The game mechanics are solid and each surprise will keep you coming back for more. Its a solid game in every aspect and it only costs $15! Plus its not technologically demanding so you can pretty much run it on a graphing calculator.

TL;DR- From the devs that made our favorite goat game, Goat Simulator, Sanctum 2 is a Tower Defense FPS with a lot of potential and hours of fun both alone, and with friends.
I remember purchasing and playing Goat Simulator, laughing my a** off at the bugs, so I decided to check out the other games Coffee Stain had made, and I saw this one. This sat on my wishlist for a whole year until Christmas 2016, when I bought this game with money I'd gotten. I came in thinking this game was going to be another buggy game, but was hit in the face with new things to learn, an awesome UI, and amazing gameplay. This is worth your money and I'd highly suggest playing this with friends.
Now, no game is without its kinks. Singleplayer is brutal on the Campaign mode, and graphically speaking, it's a little intensive. The game has limits on towers, which can make things difficult real fast, especially on Survival mode. This game is also kind of dead, so playing with friends is your best bet sometimes. Otherwise, not much to complain about.

Recipe: Maple Bacon
Preparation time: 30 minutes
Yield: 4-8 servings
Ingredients:
- 3/4 pound thick cut bacon (16 slices)
- 1-2 tablespoons of Maple Syrup
Directions:
Preheat the oven to 400 degrees F.
Place a baking rack on a sheet pan and arrange the bacon in 1 layer on the baking rack. Bake for 15 to 20 minutes, until the bacon begins to brown. Remove the pan carefully from the oven; there will be hot grease in the pan! Brush the bacon slices with maple syrup and bake for another 3 to 5 minutes, until the bacon is a warm golden brown. Transfer the bacon to a plate lined with paper towels and serve warm.

The Fallout franchise; a series of games full of choices in a post apocalyptic world full of strife and death. Your choices throughout the games would change the outcome of the endings. Perhaps your character was a paragon for the greater good, or maybe they reveled in the chaos of the wastes and killed and murdered their way to the top. They could have even walked the fine line of good and evil, something sometimes harder than the other two options.
That is entirely♥♥♥♥♥♥upon in this game. Like Whose Line's philosphy; the points are everything and your choices don't matter! That's right! For every dialogue ever there are four dang options for you to pick and can be summerized as this: "Yes," "good yes," "funny/money/mean yes," and "not now but later." You can almost never say no to something. More on roleplay; you play as Nate or Nora, people from prewar times. Nate is a soldier who would surely hold many of the Prewar American Values  of old. Nora is a lawyer, who would surely hold many of the prewar American Values of old. So from a roleplay standpoint you are an American citizen with American beliefs from prewar America and it just wouldn't make any sense to become a murderous terrible person.
The gunplay is good, and the customization is nice. Settlements need work but at least it's fun building them.
TLDR: Better FPS than RPG. Bad game IMO. Mods make it better.

This is my first time leaving a review, so I'm going to try and be as thorough as possible. Also if you like watching video's more, you can see my first impressiong in this video on
To start off, I think the thumbs up-thumbs down binary choice of steam reviews is terrible, and lacks alot of context as well as "poisoning the well" for any nuiance that might see some people still interested and others not so much. So let's just say that while I can't give a blanket endorsement on this game to everyone, I do think there are people that will want to buy it in even its current state, and I'll explain more below.
So to start off, the game has several features missing from the original series. These have been promised in later updates, like Multiplayer for instance. I actually fully believe the dev team will follow through on its word to implement these features, but their roadmap seems a bit..optomistic. The game has numerous game-breaking bugs and broken features, and is not even feature-complete, much less polished. And I'm not talking about proposed features, I mean the currently implemented features are unfinished. There are skills that don't exist, skill tree's that are more developed than others, and occasional shader issues that will cause portions of the city to turn black. Saying that by Christmas we'll have multiplayer implemented seems overly ambitious, and I think will ultimately see a pushed back deadline or more broken features released.
Adding to that, there are major UI issues that make playing the game difficult. Tooltips are found by right-clicking and holding. Which is useful to know if you haven't played the prior Guild 2 games (or its been a few years and you forgot), but of course nothing will tell you this.
Localizations for tooltips and general game info is missing in many areas, and vague in others. While playing a Rogue for example, there is a skill that allows you to scout an area to rob carts from. The problem is that, when you use it, no new information is made apparent to the player. If there is a UI element that shows "THIS ROUTE IS GOLDEN FOR ROBBING", then its not made apparent. All I saw was that I'd gain experiance every time I used it.
Contrast that with one of the other elements of the starting Rogue Tree, Jugglery. You use this skill to dance around in the street and get a few coins thrown at you, and either little or no experiance. This...this is a drastic step down from the previous title. I liked the idea of pacing out the gameplay over time and truely starting from humble beginings, rather than launching your criminal career as a rogue by having a ready-made gang as soon as you buy your first building in the immediate start of the game. But why can't my character pick pocket? Why does that have to be a later skill? It makes the begining skill set of a Rogue seem pathetic.
I wanted to continue on towards a different issue. The team behind this game is apparently less than 20 people. The game itself is hugely ambitious, and that doesn't mean they can't accomplish it. After all they are recieving support from their publisher, including additional programmers. But the workload for this game is not small, and will likely require time to see through. I expected crashes, bugs, etc. I didn't expect to see so little actual features and gameplay comparatively finished.
Finally, I think the biggest problem with the game right now is its price. Once upon a time, game companies had open betas. It was a chance to do mass bug testing, drive up hype for a game, and generally get feedback. The problem with Early Access is that it means the dev's are charging for an open beta right now. And its not that cheap.
They will get all the positives of an open beta from this move, but they're killing alot of good will by having their release now. I don't think it will kill the game outright, but I think it was the wrong move overall. Because even after the Early Access, they'll still have the normal patching and updating taking place before the inevitable DLC and expansions, and I hope they have a solidly finished product by then or this could easily turn into a disaster.
So now for the final element of it all, would I reccomend this game? If you have disposable income and nothing higher on your list, I'd reccomend picking it up. Its cheap now, and I have faith in the developer to accomplish their goal of making the game. However, if you are looking for a more finished early access title, or you are low on cash and want something that is more likely to be enjoyable now rather than a few months from now, hold off and wait for a sale or for the final release date.
There is a solid framework for this game. The problem is that its not close enough to being finished to reccomend yet generally. But the promise of a good game is here, and I believe it will be seen through.

Even in its early stages, Battle Brothers is an engaging experience. Gameplay is a refreshing mix of a gritty, morally ambiguous open-world experience with methodical tactical combat ala classics like FFT. In a world filled with undead, orcs and more, you can expect that your mere human Brothers will die quickly, and often. Combat can be unforgiving, but gives you a real sense of reward when you manage to pull it off. XCOM fans will not be disappointed here.
Theme and art style are also well done. Brothers have this interesting chess piece-like feel to them (being represented by only disembodied torsos), but their randomly generated names, backgrounds and traits lend a surprising amount of character to each one. By the time your Brothers hack their way through a few battles, chances are that you'd have quite the soft spot for your mangy warband; with stories to tell your friends of the time "Reinhold the Torturer" made that sick Hail Mary arrow shot at max range or when "Otto the Fisherman" demolished 8 zombies all by himself.
As of current, there is a huge new update on the horizon. The planned feature list is tremendous, and the additions and overhauls seem set to add more gameplay value to the existing product. Definitely consider picking this one up.

When you combine the tactical combat and chance-on-hit mechanics of XCOM, world view and company managment on Mount and Blade: Warband, and random events of FTL, you get Battle Brothers.
Battle Brothers is a diamond in the rough. It's a game that has combined systems of others and has managed to create a fresh new gaming experience.
You are the leader of a mercenary company. Your job is to simply do what mercenaries do best: take on dangerous jobs for sweet, sweet money. You'll face goblins, bandits, undead, and orcs. There are perils aplenty, and to combat such things, you have to create a team that can be versatile in all combat situations. This is where the game shines, in the freedom of creating a strategic team that can survive any situation.
You can buy gear, hire more mercenaries with unique traits, and devise tactics to overcome your foes. In combat, it all pays off. But beware, for the game is brutal and unforgiving. Such is the life of a mercenary, to live and die for glory and gold.
The music is beautiful and crafted wonderfully, and the art-style of the game is charming and very fitting. What I love a LOT about the game are the small little descriptions of mercenaries you hire. They all have little backstories which helps me live inside this randomly generated fantasy world. I love it because I can create my own stories in the absense of a campaign. The writing is also simply superb and well-written.
Though it is early access, it is worth your time. I am looking forward to all of the updates that will be rolling out throughout 2016 and beyond. As it stands, Battle Brothers is worthy of praise.

Alright, so Starbound is finally out after so many years of early access. It was the first early access game I ever purchased, soon after it became available, simply because I believed in the concept. But it's been a rocky ride to 1.0 with lots of changes from that initial plan and, even though I'm giving it a thumbs up, the road still looks kinda rocky ahead.
Starbound is a mixture of a procedural sandbox game and something with a plot. The sandbox is similar to Terraria, but with different strengths and weakness. Terraria has more interesting enemies and combat in general, but I'd say that starbound feels stronger to me in the exploration department, and has a huge variety of collectables up if you're into that kind of thing. If you want to farm, explore surfaces, explore caves, capture monsters to kill stuff for you, do quests, learn about and talk to all the different races, you can find something to do. What kinks there are in the exploration system mainly result from the fact that the planets are tiered, like the equipment, which makes things rather awkward at the end of the time, but it's still pretty fun to run around and look at things in a way that Terraria can't possibly match.
Starbounds story isn't too special, at least not the main plot, and the most intriguing background pieces of information on each race were removed/rewritten before release, unfortunately, as the leading baddies of some races were sacrificed in the name of focusing on the big cosmic baddie. The plot mainly seems to be a vehicle for the developer designed missions, which are interesting to explore if not much of a challenge so far (I'm not too far in, but the last boss I fought killed me several times until I realized she wasn't really reacting to me most of the time and so I could win mostly by standing in a particular safe spot). How difficult the bosses are in each mission and what equipment you should probably have before doing it isn't really communicated all that well. Moreover, the missions/story seem like a place where they should have forgone the random quest reward bag in favor of cool, specific things, especially at the end of the game (where it would be nice to unlock some kind of sandbox God powers to reduce the grind and make movement easier), but nope, just the same random rewards you get for escorting a villager back to their friend. Still, it manages to not come off as incredibly cheesy, like Freedom Planet (which is great game for other reasons, don't grab your pitchforks please).
So overall I would recommend the game if you're looking for an easy-going romp through space. I wouldn't say it's amazing, but then I just spent my entire weekend playing it, so it's certainly good enough to recommend.
However, this is ONE LARGE CAVEAT that I noted at the top here:
Performance issues. If your computer is a 5 year old budget laptop like mine, wait before you buy. The devs are planning the next patch to be the one that fixes the performance issues and, I have to say, during early access I didn't have any problems. But 1.0 introduced a huuuuuge amount of lag and loading problems I never experienced before. It's never killed me but it really breaks immersion and is flat out inconvenient when you get to watch the edge of the world pop into existence after 15 seconds, or you teleport to the outpost and nothing can move (npcs, doors) but you and you have to wait 30 seconds before the game catches up and staggers forward for you. Weather effects never used to cause me more than a slight framerate drop but now, combined with whatever else the game is trying to do, they seriously cause my poor integrated-graphics machine to chug. It has been mostly playable, that's the only reason I've gotten as far as I have, but geez, it *really* freezes up my machine in a way it never did during early access.
That about sums it up. I hope this is useful for you guys.

I've always had a hard time getting into sandbox games, but Starbound has felt different to me. While I liked the "idea" of being able to create my own fun in a digital sandbox environment, I was never able to get a whole lot out of it. Something about Starbound's charming looks and ideas made me decide to ignore my usual feelings and give it a shot. Here are some things I enjoy:
1. Planets and Biomes
There are a lot of different planets with a lot of some of the expected biomes with it: lava planet, forested planet, etc. What makes these interesting is the fact that within some of these planets are sub-biomes, villages, ruins, and colonies. These make sure that exploration always feels fresh and you always feel rewarded for exploring further.
2. Stories and Quests
The story is nothing special or groundbreaking, but I have found it pretty enjoyable, at the very least, as a guide on how to safely navigate through the steady progression of increasingly hostile planets. While the story is basic, there are many times where you will have to complete instanced levels and boss fights which are very fun. One moment you're doing a survival/horror style raid on an infected space station and the next you're trying to survive in a hunting party gauntlet with some killer alien wildlife. Most of these areas are non-linear too, encouraging replayability to find secret areas, gear, and furniture items.
3. The Feeling of Progression and Exploration
Gear is set up in an almost MMO style. As you get better gear, you'll use it to do missions and go searching for even stronger gear and it feels very rewarding. Another cool factor is that of all the unique races in the game have their own sets of gear to go with their style. Not really game-changing, but a nice touch. Plus there are a lot of novelty items that can be used as costumes like astronaut helmets, tuxedos, penguin suits, etc, so you can customize your look.
Outside the straight gear change though, there are also upgrades for your character that are pretty cool. A lot of them will be familiar to anyone who's played a 2D platformer, like a double jump and the very Metroid-Style ball form. There are a lot of other abilities I haven't even tried yet but I can't wait to use them.
There are a lot of features I haven't gone into detail about like the crew system, expanding your ship, and the variety of weapons you can use (so so many!), but if you have any interest in the game, give it a go. I've been really enjoying it since beta and I'm looking forward to see what the next updates will add to it!

Got this game in Early Access on Janurary 2nd 2014, played a bit of it, then never touched it again. Fast forward to its release date, I saw a friend playing it on steam, checked the steam store, and saw that 1.0 had been released. So I downloaded the game again, started it up, and my oh my it was a pleasant surprise.
Now, let's get onto things in the game. First, THE MULTIPLAYER IS SO MUCH BETTER. You don't have to do any stupid bs to join games, just join via steam, it's really nice. You can teleport to your friend, go on their ship, see their stuff, etc. It works really well.
Secondly, let's see... The story? Yeah, the story. I loved the beginning scene, it gives you plenty of backround info, etc. The main story incorporates well into the game. Taking you to different planets to explore, telling a decently written story, giving you companions along the way, people to know. I am currently on the Avians looking for their stuff, but I need a radioactive EPP upgrade... So I guess I'll need a bit more titanium, meaning I actually have to explore for stuff.
Now, let's take a break and look at a lot of the negatives people have about the game.
First one I just read was about losing your items... Huh, my game must be glitched, it had 3 options, Casual - No Hunger, No item loss. Whatever the next one is that makes you lose items, and have hunger. Then permadeath, with hunger. I mean, c'mon dude, if you want to complain about item loss, make sure the game doesn't have a mode where you don't lose items.
And reading more reviews they all say things are missing but can never mention them? That's a load of bs if I've ever seen it, if it's missing say it in your review, don't skirt around it.
Now, putting this in here, one thing I don't like is the bliddy scanning everything that is required, it's boring, I just want to find 1 thing that gives me a cool clue, not click on a painting that somehow gives me a hint. Also, when I effing pause the game should to, and I play on casual, think of how bs that is for people playing w/ hunger.
I also found a complaint about the EPP things, about how they magically make you immune to a planets heat/fire/ice, etc... Well, it's for simplicity, would you really rather have to have 6 different damn things just to go on 1 ♥♥♥♥ing planet? No, hell no, no one wants that at all, just keep it bliddy simple.
Now, again I read another negative, and this one actually had valid points about things being taken out. Mainly temperature (not sure how this would affect the game at all, as there are ice planets and hot planets) and, star sectors... And I'm wondering, what the hell are star sectors? I read up about them, and they were mainly about difficulty... And I kinda disagree with that, I think it's better without star sectors. I like layered difficulty levels in games, but you should always have a chance to go there anyways, without requiring special things to just not die from the air or something. Of course, there are planets where those still happen, but you can go around them, or at least land near them, just not go on planets, etc.
Another thing to address is being compared to Terraria... I have played lots of Terraria, and I must say, these are similar in some ways, but are vastly different. In Terraria, you are stuck on 1 world, and 1 world only. Granted, you can make the world pretty big, and there is more on the individual world of terraria than 1 world in starbound. Quite a bit more I must say. But here's the big difference, starbound is about exploration, a lot of it. Sure you can make colonies on planets in starbound, set up a base, but generally your spaceship is your main base, as the game focuses on a lot of exploration as compared to Terraria's base building mining focus. And I would say Terraria does do many aspects better, and if that seems more your kind of game, get that instead. But starbound still does a lot of other things better, like exploration, survival, sci fi stuff, weapon design, and the story...
Also, Starbound has a story, so if you like stories, you'd probably like this.
Anyhow, I think this is it for now, I highly recommend this game, it's pretty good!

A fun, strategic game that focuses on psychology and trickery. It's like an online board game, really, it gives me board game vibes. It's purely multiplayer - no singleplayer in sight, and this is a free game - I recommend trying it online for free before buying it, as the only benefit to buying it is unlocking an exclusive character skin + 2,000 gold coins.
It revolves around two main teams (in the classic mode, there's also coven which is more complicated) - Mafia, and Town. The town actively searches for the mafia and tries to hang them (they can hang one mafia per day), while the Mafia actively kills Town (kill 1 per day) while trying to pose as a town so they dont get hanged. There's also neutrals, such as the Serial Killer, who can only win by himself, who is immune to basic attacks + kills 1 per day as well. And the jester, which wins by pretending to be someone bad or purposely giving wrong information to get hanged, after which they get to kill someone and automatically win the game, and lastly the executioner, who wins by getting his target hanged by providing forged information, however if his target dies, he turns into a jester.
That's pretty much it, it's a fun game, I recommend it. It's easy to learn and it's not too complicated, it might help to read guides online though.

Finally The game is out on steam, Knights and Merchants is a typical Strategy game Based on the feudal system in the middle ages or what we call as Feudalism, What made Knights and Merchants Stand out back then that its even alive today is that game has a strange charm about it, It has no epic story or huge cinematics but its rather simple and great implementation of the feudal system , If you have played settlers this is no strange game then, its very similar to it .
What i like about Knights and merchants is that game is well paced and restricted unlike the other games like age of empires where you can build up very quickly and rush others, KAM lays down a Strong System where you need to have specifc Buildings to progress to the next one , so Unless you have a strong economy setup , there is no way to build up a army Fast and rush, It retains that cumbersome slow system Feudalism was. You can Focus on the city Builiding and then make units.
It even has a feeding system where you have to feed everyone in your base constantly so , planning is very important , without the right balance people will go hungry and die eventually.
Everything is simple and Influences your game in a way.
Its a very unique old game , unless you master that starting tutorial the game will be impossible to play easily.
There are a lot of fan based Re-makes and fixes but i recommend playing the game as it is, Its a great challenge that way, specially For those not interested in multiplayer.
Do Remember to save a lot , The game tends to crash after a long stretch of gaming or music changes

When you combine the tactical combat and chance-on-hit mechanics of XCOM, world view and company managment on Mount and Blade: Warband, and random events of FTL, you get Battle Brothers.
Battle Brothers is a diamond in the rough. It's a game that has combined systems of others and has managed to create a fresh new gaming experience.
You are the leader of a mercenary company. Your job is to simply do what mercenaries do best: take on dangerous jobs for sweet, sweet money. You'll face goblins, bandits, undead, and orcs. There are perils aplenty, and to combat such things, you have to create a team that can be versatile in all combat situations. This is where the game shines, in the freedom of creating a strategic team that can survive any situation.
You can buy gear, hire more mercenaries with unique traits, and devise tactics to overcome your foes. In combat, it all pays off. But beware, for the game is brutal and unforgiving. Such is the life of a mercenary, to live and die for glory and gold.
The music is beautiful and crafted wonderfully, and the art-style of the game is charming and very fitting. What I love a LOT about the game are the small little descriptions of mercenaries you hire. They all have little backstories which helps me live inside this randomly generated fantasy world. I love it because I can create my own stories in the absense of a campaign. The writing is also simply superb and well-written.
Though it is early access, it is worth your time. I am looking forward to all of the updates that will be rolling out throughout 2016 and beyond. As it stands, Battle Brothers is worthy of praise.

If you are looking for a faithful Fallout game, you will be disappointed. BUT, if you play it for what it is, which is an open world first person shooter with RPG elements, you will enjoy it.

Small note regarding game requirments: it DOES work on Intel HD 3000 just fine, only thing lagging a bit is selling/buying stuff but I'm not sure if its caused by that.
Describing it briefly: it's Mount & Blade's type of wandering on map and general freedom of choice combined with Darkest Dungeon's high difficulty, turn based combat system and permadeath of every character.
A bit more in-depth: this is game about leading pack of maximum 12 mercenaries/sellswords looking for glory and coin. It's done by taking contracts from local people to raid places that are source of their problems (old ruins with bandits, orc's forts and so on), escort caravans or deliver messages to specific place. You can of course do the first one by yourself, but then you are missing opportunity to earn some gold.
Lets describe some game concepts and diffrences from sea of other tactical turn based games:
"Skillset" of every mercenary depends on what weapon and perks he has. With hammer you can crush your opponents armor very quickly, with axe - destroy his shield and deal more damage to armor, with two handed axe or sword - swing hitting everyone around character and so on. And of course with shield you can defend yourself, with bow - shoot etc.
And when we are at skillsets: character leveling looks similar to typical cRPGs - after level up (max 10 lvl ups) you can choose to increase 3 out of 8 statistics of mercenary: ranged/melee defense/offense, resolve, health, fatigue or initiative and take 1 perk that helps you survive, deal more damage or gives some kind of utility.
Some characters come with traits that can incrase specific statistics (optimist will have higher resolve, though guy will start with bonus health) or decrease (pesimist starts battles with lower resolve, greedy guy wants higher daily payment).
Backgrounds  - every mercenary has his background. One could be farmer, another miller, hunter, bowyer, retired soldier, disowned noble... depending on who he was before, battle brother could have diffrent modifiers to statistics and there could be events regarding those backgrounds. Bowyer wants to create amazing bow, sellsword ask for higher payment because another group would give him more, gambler wants to gamble with you... And this is STILL early access.
Fatigue system - I didn't like it at first, but then I understood why it was put here in the first place.
Every skill cost points of fatigue (beside action points like in most turn based games) - from something like 5 points to even 20+ for single use.
To put it into perspective - every character starts with around 100 points of fatigue to start with. Doesn't sound that bad? Every piece of equipment character is carrying decrease maximum amount of fatigue you can have during fight.
For example normal sword takes around 8 points, helmet from 5 to even 20 torso armor from mere 6 for armor that wont survive one hit up to even 40 for plate. You can end up with guy having 40 points of fatigue left during fight. Sure, enemies will have hard time hitting him, but before he even reach them he will be to exhausted to swing his sword once.
Yet after training the same character can have 2x more of said fatigue with the same equipment but it takes some time to do so.
Equipment - fair variety of armors... but I feel there is not enough weapons. Only 2 kinds of "standard" bows, 1 type of crossbow... At least developers said its going to change.
World map - feels similar to Mount & Blade, but there isn't much happening - most of the time it's going from A to B, attack enemies, tactical battle, go back to A to get your reward - rinse and repeat. There is no incentive to explore map too much, because at least for now there is no reward beside gold, resources and sometimes better weapon to begin with.
Quests - I saw only 5 types of them: go to another town/village to deliver message (♥♥♥♥♥♥ payment, most of the time its not even worth it) escort caravan (most of the time payment is low and forces you to stay close to caravan) destroy/find location (best/low payment) and sometimes killing specific group of enemies. New quest system is in development, probably much better than this.
For me this is one of the best (if not the best) tactical rpg-esque games I played (and one of few I bought for nearly full price). Feeling of nearly perfect battle when none of your 12 men died but you took 20+ enemies to their graves is priceless. If you are into quite difficult, brutal and unforgiving strategic game - this is something for ya.

This game is still very early in its early access phase, but the core game loop that's there is enormously satisfying. Think Darklands + Mount & Blade with a very attractive graphical presentation. Hand drawn procedurally generated world maps, spiffy looking characters you can dress up with a huge variety of weapons and armour, and, of course, hats. Medieval German low-fantasy tactical hat simulator.
There is also RPG-style character progression for each of the 12 members of your mercenary company, complete with talent trees, making it all the more painful when your favourite guy's head gets chopped off by an orc cleaver. Brutal, brutal permadeath, but that's okay because there's any number of gravediggers, rat catchers, farmers, hedge knights, beggars, and all kinds of other adventurers waiting to be hired. Did I mention there's a whole pile of character backgrounds? Complete with various other traits that will give benefits or penalties in combat, the whole setup vaguely recalling the character traits from Crusader Kings. For example, Cowardly will mean that the character will never gain high morale in combat, while Loyal will mean that the character will be far less likely to desert your company should your funds or supplies run out, while a character with a Houndmaster background will gain bonuses when handling dogues. Loads and loads of others that will incline the character this way or that, and it's up to you to build them in a way that will take advantage of those traits.
While the strategic gameplay is great, where the game really shines is the excellent hex-grid turn-based tactical RPG combat. Here, think X-Com + Final Fantasy Tactics (or so I've been told, not being privileged to have played FFT). Lots of depth in setting up combos with the aforementioned weapon variety and RPG-style character builds. Bonuses for high ground, standing behind trees for defending against missile fire, and so on. Each type of weapon has its own unique active abilities. Here, think GW2 but greatly simplified since you're not controlling only the one character. So, for instance, a shield will give you a bash and a defensive shield wall ability, blunt weapons like maces will have a basic attack and a stun, a warhammer will have a basic attack and an armour-break, a sword will have a basic attack and a defensive riposte, and a greatsword will have various AoE abilities that chop bandits up real nice.
In conclusion, I'm greatly enjoying this game, can't wait to see where they take it, and I'd venture to warmly recommend it to any fan of any of the above-mentioned influences as well as tactical RPGs in general.

Stranded Deep is very similiar to the Forest apart from it's a little less creepy (Sharks still make it creepy!).
The tutorial is nice, it starts you off on a plane and teaches you the basics of crafting before pluning into the ocean with nothing but a few basic supplies and your trusty life raft.
--- GAMEPLAY ---
The gameplay is pretty much what you'd expect, you have to gather supplies from sticks to crabs, and use them to survive for as long as you can. Almost all aspects of Stranded Deep feel exceptionally well done and polished and they've added some nifty features that make surviving a little easier. To gve you an example of a couple of these features: Any palm tree can be climbed to reach the coconuts that reside at the top or simply for a better view, by right lciking you can drag any material around, be it a freshly chopped tree or a live crab. This makes organising your resources a hell of a lot easier.
The building system is almost identical to that of Rust, you place a foundation and then add supports, walls, roofs and interior furniture to make it more functional. It is worth stating that you need t find a hammer before you can build structures, they can be found as random spawns on some of the shipwrecks you'll find populating the islands.
Another great feature is that you can use your lifeboat to travel between islands to gather even more resources or find the perfect place to set up.
--- GRAPHICS ---
The graphics are really very good, again, similiar in style and realism to the Forest.
--- SOUND ---
No complaints about the sound, the game is immersive, thoguh the rowing sound can become a little grating if you're sailing for any period of time.
For anyone that's interested, here's a link to a video showing off the features i've spoken about. if you have any questions, feel free to comment on this review!
