tldr; Death mechanics in survival drive home how much of a drag it is to mine and farm in a game built to be about mining and farming. Losing your character and/or progress appears to be a mini game of Russian Roulette as numerous bug reports and personal experience has shown this to be an issue.
I originally purchased Starbound in EA, pretty much day one. It
wasn't ready for prime time but wanted to support development for one of my favorite genres. So I left it on the back burner and waited for the release. At long last we are here and this is my first weekend experience with it.
Day one:
Started a brand new character in Survival mode. Like the new story mode, gave me a bit of direction. Big fan of Terraria and the updated graphics as well as the theme was satisfying.
I only played a couple hours when I first bought it because the game was large and felt empty, it was a sandbox and there were better out there. This time though, there's a central hub, an encouragement to build a home base (and house some tenants? Neat), cooking, fossil hunting, bug hunting, crafting. Maybe this is all there is to see. I mean admittedly the tech upgrade system for your person and Matter Manipulator feel a bit shallow and planets still feel a bit recycled but I was still committed to the sandbox mentality and make this game my own. After the first boss and a couple quests I settle in on a rainy and peaceful planet and start rebuilding a ruin, plant some crops and do some deep dive mining.
Mining - Typical Terraria experience but initial entry is faster. I like the matter manipulator for the reach and the number of blocks it takes out, although it requires a few upgrades before digging becomes 'fun' instead of a slog. Same cave features as the aforementioned game, chests, underground 'homes/ruins’, holy crap, gnome villages?! and the occasional challenge room, which are far from challenging and often even less rewarding. There are several biomes that I encountered, gnome, slime, tar... I'm sure there's more but some of them felt kind of... empty and the rewards for the chests you find is not anything to write home about. You can only find a slightly different flavor of the same weapon over and over again before you strap on whatever fits your play style and pretty much ignore the rest. After the first dozen chests, I no longer felt excited when I found a cave feature and its treasure chest, instead I'd tear it apart to learn a new 'blueprint' where you obtain knowledge to craft a new wall, background, etc. Rock, Paper, Shotgun had a great review about the sandbox mentality, which is what I read to get me excited to jump back into this game.
Alas, I dug too deep, all the way to the core of the planet, and there’s nothing down there except a lake of lava where I died.
Dying: There are penalties to death, and on Survival, at first glance, they seemed fair. Drop some pixels (currency), and your items. But here’s the rub, you don’t drop everything, from what I can tell just your ores/blocks and food. This is by far the worst items in the game to lose. I have two dozen useless weapons and guns in my inventory, take those!
Mining can be slow and accumulating enough ores for crafting is a milestone, ditto for farming and cooking. I gathered these ores, healing items and food over the course of several planetary stops, pillaging chests and crates and quests. These are the items that just happen to fall into your inventory while you’re exploring or finding enough tungsten to make that next tier of armor. Cooking is very much the same, you do it because you have to because when you starve you die. When you have a nice inventory of food and ore/blocks, you feel good about your progress even if the mechanic wasn’t 100% satisfying.
That’s when you quit. Yes, I could of done better with my inventory management and storage, but who wants to play around with an inventory system in this day and age? I want to manage my inventory as much as I want to… go mining and farming for the sake of mining and farming.
Day 2 - 3: I decided to give it one more chance. There’s no way to switch your current character’s difficulty because… programming is hard? feature creep? Intern was sick that day? So I started up a new ‘casual’ character. You’re pretty much locked into Casual with 10% pixel loss and no hunger bar, Survival with 30% pixel loss, hunger and item drop, and hardcore where I guess you just hate your life after you die. There is nothing in between. Want a game with pixel loss, no item drops and hunger? Tough. Luckily there’s a steam workshop for that and I was able to apply hunger to my casual character and get to experience the game without the heart break.
In a few hours I was right back where I started with a slightly different RNG weapon set up. My material manipulator and personal techs were all upgraded and I set out to start a new and better base on a forest planet. I explored a moon for fuel and even did some interstellar travel to new and dangerous planets with ore I needed to upgrade my work benches. Things were looking up, I was looking forward to future sessions, this might be my go to game for the upcoming week, the game I tell all my buddies at work to get on board. But I made a fatal mistake, I quit the game and saved.
Most games that leave beta can do at least one thing right, save your character’s progress when you quit the game. But if you go through the bug reports on Steam and on the Starbound forum you will see a disturbing trend. People are losing characters, worlds, ships for reasons like a game crash, power failure, solar flairs or in my case, saving and quitting.
And that’s where I’m done. My character is still there in the game folder but a JSON parsing error refuses to load him up so he can continue on with his adventure and that’s where I’m done. It’s been a good, albeit short run, maybe we can try this again in 3 more years.

At Release date 2015-01-23, the game shows a lot of promise already, at the start its fun trying to find out how you can survive on your little island and figuring out crafting recipes. But after you run out of resources its really hard to just go to another island and bring back stuff, since from a distance the islands look practicly the same. The Devs said theres no end goal right now, so to keep ourselves bussy we can do stuff like surviving, exploring, base building or fighting sharks... which haven't really gone successful for me yet.
The surviving part gets easy when you realize all you need to do is eat a few coconuts to get your fill of water and hydration.
Exploring gets tedious when rowing to another island takes ages and have a high risk of bugging your raft out so you are left out in the dangerous open water without refuge. But diving into the waters to search through the various ship wrecks around is quite exciting, especially when you realize a shark is just outside waiting for you to come out. Another bad point though is the very limited backpack space you have, and putting stuff in your raft just ends up with them disappearing eventually.
Base building/Home making isn't really a great option right now since you can only chop down coconut trees which are quite limited on your island, also rocks are also few on your island and as mentioned above, going back and forth between islands just fetching rocks is not a fun process.
So at its current state its not something I would play for hours with no end, but I feel that it has a great start already and would love to play more of it after a few feature updates.

A fun, strategic game that focuses on psychology and trickery. It's like an online board game, really, it gives me board game vibes. It's purely multiplayer - no singleplayer in sight, and this is a free game - I recommend trying it online for free before buying it, as the only benefit to buying it is unlocking an exclusive character skin + 2,000 gold coins.
It revolves around two main teams (in the classic mode, there's also coven which is more complicated) - Mafia, and Town. The town actively searches for the mafia and tries to hang them (they can hang one mafia per day), while the Mafia actively kills Town (kill 1 per day) while trying to pose as a town so they dont get hanged. There's also neutrals, such as the Serial Killer, who can only win by himself, who is immune to basic attacks + kills 1 per day as well. And the jester, which wins by pretending to be someone bad or purposely giving wrong information to get hanged, after which they get to kill someone and automatically win the game, and lastly the executioner, who wins by getting his target hanged by providing forged information, however if his target dies, he turns into a jester.
That's pretty much it, it's a fun game, I recommend it. It's easy to learn and it's not too complicated, it might help to read guides online though.

Battle Brothers is an interesting game. Similar to Mount and Blade: Warband, you trek from settlement to settlement with your band of sellswords, buying gear and recruiting new grunts who're down on luck and likely to be slain in battle. However, unlike Warband, each one of your men has a unique story behind him. Be he a lumberjack, deserter, daytaler or thief, each of your men has been driven to the mercenary life one way or another. Maybe he committed a crime and is on run from the law? Perhaps his village was burned down, and he has no way to support what's left of his family other than the work your outfit provides? Or he could've gotten a bad case of wanderlust and just wanted to see the world beyond his little farm. Regardless, he's a Battle Brother now, and one day he will die in rank with his brothers-in-arms.
I won't go into detail of how the combat in this game works, as that can be easily be discerned by watching a video or two. Sometimes RNGesus will bless your men in their hour of need, and at other times he will damn them and your entire force. RNGesus sometimes finds certain men he favours -- soon-to-be veteran soldiers who will form the backbone of your little unit, able to cut down swathes of foes and opening holes in the enemy line for the rest of your men to rush through. While sometimes combat can feel like a game of chance, when your men are truly trained and skilled, that feeling goes away. The only thing required on your end is adjusting tactics as the situation demands; certain foes may require particular strategies to defeat them.
Or gear.
You'll wish you bought a helmet for poor Adalbert, as he lays crumpled on the ground with his skull caved-in from that greenskin's axeblow.
Battle Brothers is still in development, and development is sometimes slow, but this game is certainly in a playable state as of the day of this writing. With upcoming plans for quests that have twists and turns tossed into them, on top of the moral dilemmas of attacking innocents or sending men off to die so others may escape, will make this a title well worth keeping your eye on. Even now, I'd still highly recommend this title to anyone interested in a turn-based strategy game.
Last, but not least, the decapitation animations are pretty frickin' sweet to watch. And since all the place names and your soldiers are German, everything sounds more manly and badass.
9 dead greenskins out of 10, a great title worth checking out -- even in early access.

Kingdom Rush is a solid tower defense game. It has recognizable enemies with a variety of strengths and weaknesses to plan for, plus an almanac to sort it all out. The towers are all useful and all emphasize some different approach. It has a sense of humor and flair. There is an overwhelming amount of dated pop culture jokes. Many levels also have some kind of Easter egg in the background, anything from clicking on sheep and goats to freeing a spider's next meal. But what really makes Kingdom Rush special is one of the four groups of towers, the barracks. What the barracks add to the game is soldiers, a human element, which can be made to rally anywhere in the radius of the barracks. What the soldiers do is engage a single enemy; each hold them in place until the melee is completed. This means, by placing soldiers, a chokepoint is created and other towers can be placed with that in mind. This also means that troops can be repositioned to stop enemies that are just about the escape. With this movement, along with the use of a hero that can made to rally anywhere on the map, the game becomes much more active and begins to blur the line between tower defense and real time strategy.

Battle Brothers... what's that about?
So, what can you do in this game right now:
1) Generate a world with different towns, villages, castles and etc
2) Start off with a 3-men mercenary company and work your way up
3) Earn money by completing different tasks: slaying, guarding caravans, defending villages against goblins, orks or werewolves.
4) Spend money on mercs wages, new equipment, provisions, medicine, ammo and repair kits
5) BATTLE. I must say, as a fan of turn-based tactics, I find the already implemented battle system in Battle Brothers very solid and fun. It's rather simple, but have it's "depth". Across the world of BB you will find a lot of nasty enemies: mentioned above werewolves, goblins, orks, also undead and other humans. They all got different tactics and gear and it's bringing more fun to the game.
6) Art style & graphics. Well, it's 2D and when you play a 2D game and it's not a "pixel throwback to 80s" it's all about art style. And to my taste, the style here is absolutely stunning. The work the artist did on the tiles, characters ... basically everything is not only well done, but done really VERY GOOD. (but ofc there is a room for improvement here)
Overall, these guys managed to create one of the best indies ever (also, one of the best EA titles), and it will become even more enjoyable in Februart 2016 with the big update coming, bringing new wordl map mechanics, fast travel, factions with their own politics and much more. So in the era of failed Kickstarter-funded titles and failed Early Access titles, this game is a jewel. I strongly recommend this game, hats off to the developers. Great job so far guys, keep it up!

Get KaM remake. The base game only has resolutions 800 x 600 and 1024 x 768. KaM remake allows a lot more, and you can even run in windowed mode if you so wish. The mod is compatible with this version, details and downloads are available at
If you liked the origional Settlers games (before 5) you will love this. (Personally I don't think much of the Settlers games, but that could be because I played this first).
KaM has more micromanagement than most strategy games that are not built around it (see the Tropico series and any of the Tycoons (Railroad, Rollercoaster, Airport, Lemonade Stand etc etc etc)), and contains a much more strategic realtime combat system, where you can't just constantly throw units away at your opponent until they crumble.
As a comparison to other strategy games lets look at food.
Most strategy games you need farms; food is now sorted.
KaM has 3 food types; bread, sausages and wine.
Bread requires; a Wheat farm, a Windmill, and a Baker.
Sausages require a Wheat farm (to feed the pigs on the...) Swine Farm and a Butcher.
Wine requires only a Vineyard.
However, so your non-military units eat, you need atleast 1 Inn. (The Inns can sit either 6 or 8 people I can't recall exactly so if you have a lot of non-militants you need more than 1 Inn...but you wont have to worry about that until later in the base game (Shattered Kingdom)).
5 useful tips. (Contains what some would consider a spoiler)
1: Ignoring military, I generally recommend 3 serfs for every 2 buildings. Its not exact but works well enough for the most part.
2: For highest efficiency each farm should have 14 fields close by.
3: On the first combat only mission STOP ALL YOUR UNITS. They will be slaughtered very quickly as they enter a valley. You will be fighting a much larger force, but use your head and you can do it.
4: Save often in different slots. This game is very unforgiving and something you did or didn't do an hour ago can make all the difference now.
5: Treat every military unit as Sacred. They can be costly and just a plain arese to replace.

I have a hard time recommending this game in it's current incarnate. In 2 hours of gameplay, I have barely been able to complete the first fight without losing 2-3 members of my team.
I can appreciate that this game is early access, and I am optimistic about the direction of where the game can go, but presently it just isn't fun. The RNG is too stacked against you, to the point where even Darkest Dungeon feels like a walk in the park comparatively. If I can't find, much less finish, 2-3 fights before I have lost my whole team to ♥♥♥♥♥♥ RNG, I can't enjoy your game.
Perhaps the biggest problem I have is the difficulty gauge. "Even" still feels like you're boatloads behind in terms of the ability to hit, do damage, etc. Yet "Deadly" wasn't too difficult at all. Somehow "Weaker" ends up mopping the floor with you though. This makes the risk vs. reward feel completely uncompelling, as you're entering fights with faulty information.
A few other things:
- I think there needs to be a +10% chance to hit, minimum, across the board. It feels lousy not being able to hit anything ever, period. At the very least, equipment that adds +hit% would be amazing
- Need more ways to make gold; walking in small squares is not exciting
- Really need to balance goblins
- Needs more factions to HELP you; having no caravans after day 25 is pretty awful
- Enemy bases that you discover need to not outscale you constantly. There's literally nothing worse in the game than seeing no enemy encampments you can fight, no enemy patrols you can fight, and no allies to help you fight so that you can level up characters
- Quests need to reward XP as a way to help get crap-tier characters levels without auto-dying
Lastly, and this is important, it's very possible to hit a stalemate as a combination of the above features. Multiple playthroughs now, I have gotten around 40 days into the game and been unable to level, unable to make real money (100-200 crown delivery quests are the worst and don't count), and unable to fight enemies. I restarted, figuring I did something wrong. Nope. This is a continuous thing. If you don't min-max with your party set-up and pigeonhole your play style, you'll hit this same brick wall over and over again. Please re-evaluate the pacing and flow of the game so that this doesn't happen. I should *never* hit a point where I am incapable of progressing any further.
Edit 3/1/2016:
Base chance to hit enemies is still so brutal and unappealing that I still can't enjoy the game. Even X-Com 2, a notoriously unforgiving game, has Rookies starting off with a 45-70% chance to hit. Battle Brothers is still sitting on a 13-44% chance to hit to start, which is inherently unfun.

Hire a small band of peasants to kill some bandits. Feel empowered at your early success. Make a few gold and build your team up. Things are looking good for you. GET UTTERLY CURB STOMPED BY ORCS, UNDEAD,  AND WEREWOLVES THE NEXT DAY.
You're going to die, best just to cry and let the impending sense of futility wash over you now before you even get started. It'll make things go by much easier.
Much like Xcom and Dark Souls, you'll literally live or die based on the ability to learn and adapt to the threats presented to you. The difficult curve is practically at the ceiling starting out. There is no forgiveness for mistakes here. If you see a brigade of bandits coming your way, but better haul your *** in the opposite direction. Just because you managed to hire 3-4 peasants to aid you in your journey, doesn't mean there aren't far more experienced, well armed, and capable soldiers out there ready to slaughter you. For that I applaud Battle Brothers. I always hated unjustifable weak enemies in games being slowly spoon fed to you just so you could level up to take on the next bigger meal.
Combat is much like any isometric turnbased strategy game. You move your units along hexes, the order of which being based on initiative, and then hack the opposing enemy to death. Units have different abilities based on the weapons and equipment they're carrying. For example, if you have a shield, you can bash enemies away from you, or create a one~multiple man shieldwall. Spears can be held outward, to counter any enemy that walks into range, axes can cut shields apart etc. There's a fairly good diversity of total moves, but each weapon generally only has 2-3.
The main resource in combat is stamina. Everything your men carries causes them to effectively slow down and tire out more quickly. While a fully armored knight might be very hard to kill, they're very slow, and in only a few turns, will end up doubled over, out of breath. Pacing your men and having them slowly accilimate to heavier gear is a sound strategy, and while you may be lighter than your advesary, you'll be more nimble and can run circles around them.
There are many tools at your disposal, and each has their own strengths and weaknesses. Clubs, spears, maces, axes, daggers, flails, billhooks, and bows and crossbows are just a few weapons of your arsenal. See a knight in practically impenetrable platemail? Bash his helmet in with a mace and hammer, or puncture it with a pick axe. Hell, use a dagger to seek the weakpoints in the joints of his armor and do pure damage. Are they in cloth or light armor? Run them through with a spear, cut them apart with a sword, or shoot them with an arrow. Having a wellbalanced team will lead to victory, as each opponent will carry a mix of different equipment.
Armor and shields are likewise, very diverse. Everything from cloth, hauberks, and multi layered full on KNIGHT armor is present, each with their own stamina requirements. Armor be heavy, not to mention bloody expensive. Not to worry however, salvage is a fairly big part of the game, and you'll regularly find gear off the poor sods you murder, though it will often be in disrepair. Go figure, slicing a guy in half can leave you with a destroyed suit of armor.
In terms of story, the game allows you to travel along a randomly generated map in any direction you choose. In towns you can purchase gear, hire new mercanaries, or take on missions. These missions however are fairly boring and practically boils down to find this, deliver that, destroy this camp, or escort a caravan. However, more content is supposedly on the way down the pipe for this part of the game. Factions, contracts, and other story telling events will be present. The developers have been very active with the game, so I would expect this portion of the game to improve drastically given time.

Looking for a great story driven, immersive open world action RPG?  Look no further.
Sleeping Dogs originally came out to little fanfare. It just sort of was THERE suddenly. I took a chance on it when I originally saw it, and it payed off. This is a good game.
The game itself follows the exploits of Wei Shen, an undercover cop sent in to infiltrate and bring down the Triads in Hong Kong.
And exploits indeed! You'll find yourself doing everything from making deliveries, to burning down rival gang warehouses, carting around women planning their weddings, singing karaoke, racing, and much, much more.
The gameplay itself is great, everything flows smooth, and looks good. If you're familiar with Grand Theft Auto, you'll probably feel right at home here, with a few exceptions.
One of those exceptions is the combat system. In most open world games there's very little melee. Usually a punch or a kick and that's about it. In SD, there's a fully features fighting system that's like a cross between Soul Calibre and Die Hard Arcade. It's fun, though it can be challenging. I found myself rather enjoying when fights came my way.
There's also a shooting aspect, which isn't particularly impressive, though quite functional.
There's also more parkour bits than in games like GTA. You'll find yourself running after suspects (or running away from them) at several points in the game, over rooftops and through back alley markets.
The graphics, as I mentioned, are quite good. The game is a few years old now and even without the high-res textures, Hong Kong has rarely looked more immersive. Tall buildings, bright lights, weather effects, you name it. It's all very convincing.
There are a few things to be cautioned about though. The game is VERY bloody, and there's a TON of language. It's not really surprising, given the subject matter, but the squeemish may want to hold off. Just in fights alone you can slash people with knives and cleavers, break arms and legs, slam faces into ventilations fans, and use a number of other environmental objects to deliver what are very clearly death-blows to your enemies. The majority of which are shown. There's also some even more grisly things which are more implied than shown.
The language would be a definite R rating as well. The characters in the Triad drop F bombs like they're going out of style.
The game lacks multiplayer, though it does allow you to compare scores and records with your friends. Silly things like longest wheelie, highest number of hit and runs in a row, largest amount of money collected from parking meters, etc are all counted, and the game will show you who of your friends has the highest record for you to beat, while you're doing it; so you have a reference.
The story itself is more or less linear, but solid. You do develop attachments to the characters and what happens around them. I would say it stands up a bit better than the GTAV story. The ending though did feel a little bit rushed. (I'll avoid any spoilers) Most all the writing and dialogue is pretty good, though the romance parts of the game fell pretty flat.
(I got yelled at by a girl for "cheating on her" with a girl I met all of one time, and I didn't even know I was supposedly dating the first girl.)
TLDR/
All in all, Sleeping Dogs is a fantastic game. It has some flaws but most of them are small and easy to ignore. It's definitely in my list of all-time great games. I highly recommend it.

Years later, Sanctum 2 is still a great title. Tower Defense/FPS hybrid was executed almost perfectly & it is difficult but not to the point of ragequit.  Graphics are a bit dated but not by much at all & it runs on both newer hardware & older setups.  It's easy to get lost in designing & redesigning the mazes (see: 3hrs in the zone) & the FPS is short, but satisfying.  Bosses are tough if you can't hit their weak spots & flying enemies can be incredibly frustrating if the maze isn't planned accordingly, but that just makes you want to play more to tweak what you've made.
All in all a great game & very fun one to play with friends who are also into the strategy defense genre.  If you're looking for a game that's FPS at it's core gameplay, though, you'll probably want to look elsewhere because despite there being a decent weapons/skills tree to unlock, it's not up to par with major label FPS.  Still a good community of players & closed parties is always a great thing. Atmospheric electronic soundtrack is very fitting. Definitely solid in all aspects.
I recommend this game to any of you who are reading these comments & leaning towards buying it.  Definitely a few bucks well spent!

It's been a long time but Starbound is finally released and it's a great successor to Terraria. To new people, this is essentially 2D minecraft with a notable difference: you can either play it like sandbox or adventure (questlines, planet explorations etc.) which gives it a speedrun potential.
It has a variety of melee weapons, guns, techs (player abilities) and vehicles to move around. Hell you can even tame any monster you encounter with capture pods which work like pokeballs; you weaken them before capturing. This game also has instruments that work like in LOTRO. You can play your own music solo or with people and it creates some funny Youtube videos. It has cosmetics and different races with their racial cosmetics and weaponry as well as plenty of lore. If these arent enough there are plenty of great mods.
TDLR: It beats Terraria and Minecraft together.
I keep coming back to this game and enjoying it. With so many things to unlock I do not see it getting old anytime soon.

-Different Modes [Classic, Ranked, All Any, Vigilantics etc]
-Skin and house designs

-Spammers
-Occasional incovenience (Servers down etc)

I found town of salem through a friend. Since then I played on browser and only recently have I got the steam version (for the coven). I have shown multiple friends this game who have gone on to show even more friends. The reason I love this game is because there are so many possibilities and its so strategic!

~Conclusion~
Overall, Town of Salem is a great game. With faster loading times on steam than online it makes it so much better. The coven adds in a whole new level when bought because it makes new roles do new things. Overall I rate it like this:
Graphics: 9/10
Gameplay: 7/10
Controls: 10/10
OVERALL: 8/10

This is NOT a free-2-play game.
It's a DEMO of a game. You find the exact same limitations in demos as the 'free version' of this game places on you.
To put it bluntly, you are not going to get more time out of this product than you are from a demo of any other game UNLESS you start buying boosters.
The question then comes, of course, is it worth it to buy boosters?
For me, looking at prices and taking my experiences while trying out the mislabeled DEMO, the answer became a resounding NO.
Doing the story missions (which I did to get every unlock possible in the demo) was somewhat ok. A bit repetitve at times, due to the limitations of the game, but at least the battles were somewhat balanced.
Ability to get cards for free seemed limited to the few you got in the limited amount of solo-play missions available. The only currency in the game is hard cash, and it's not something you can 'earn' by playing (not in any games I tried at least), but purely something you pay to get boosters.
Most of the time when I queued up for online battles against other players, it told me that nobody was available to play against. So I had to alt-tab and do random stuff in a web-browser while trying to even GET games going online against other players.
Any of the battles I tried against other players were horribly horribly mismatched. There was no way the deck I was supplied with as a 'freebie'(or demo player) would compete with the decks of people I met (every one of the ones I met seemed to have paid and played for a while, given their levels and cards).
Randomization also have a huge effect on battles, meaning what initially looked like a balanced battle (as the ones I encountered in the solo missions) can turn onesided very quickly by a combination of cards gotten and mana orb placement. Battles that are already onesided can become extremely pointless beyond hope because of this too (like where my level 3 drake was put up against a level 30 drake by the matchmaking).
Unless you are planning to spend ALOT of money over a period of time to buy boosters as time goes by, steer clear of this one. The variety also seemed close to non-existent in the games I played, despite meeting levels and drakes of different types.
The poor balance, non-varietyof battles, lack of ability to progress without paying for it (coupled with the prices per time you actually consider if you should purchase something) ultimately turned me off from the game once I found out that I had exhausted the demo of its potential in a matter of 4 hours...
Some cute ideas, but ultimately flawed in execution on how they go about trying to handle the 'distribution model'.

So I'm writing my first ever review for this particular game because I put a lot of hours into The Guild 2 and I would love for this game to succeed in the way I truly think it can. I don't think many of the negative reviewers are giving this game a fair shake. They have every right to not recommend the game and a lot of the common complaints do have merit.
Let me first explain why this is a positive reccommendation: The foundation and bones that this game is built upon have me very excited as to what this game can potentially be when it's fully fleshed out. I mean that's the point of Early Access right? To get a feel for a game during its development. In my opinion, the problems that the game has now should not take away from what we as players view as the game's potential. The potential is there. It's undeniable. Whether or not that potential is realized is up to the devs and I'm giving them the benefit of the doubt. I understand that's a risk not everyone will be comfortable with. The game takes everything that worked with The Guild 2 and builds upon it. They even add some other things so it doesn't simply feel like a remastered version of The Guild 2. You can already see it in this version of the game. It's going to be a solid entry into the series and I believe the best yet.
So let me now explain the bad, but really none of this should surprise anyone as the devs themselves have acknowledged that there are issues. The game is choppy. And by that I mean that it runs smooth in some parts and chugs in others. But again the devs said the game hasn't been optimized yet. To be honest I also haven't had nearly the FPS issues that other reviewers have had and I'm running a 1070 with a Phenom II Quadcore. The voices and sound are wonky. The voices are  bad and I actually thought they were pretty funny to be honest. I have to imagine they're placeholder voices as of now, they are THAT terrible. The UI is definitely confusing but I think that's something that will make more sense once tutorials are added. Some random bits here and there don't work or have placeholder text, all things that simply need to be patched out and in no way break the game. So yes there are bugs and issues with the game. If it were a full release I would have refunded the game already. But it's not. It's in Early Access and i believe the game should be treated as such. I think it's far too early to give negative recommendations based on bugs and issues that the devs themselves have acknowledged.
So in conclusion I recommend the game because of the potential that's there, not because it feels finished. If you want to get in a game's ground floor and see it grow, then stick around and see what The Guild 3 has to offer. I'm willing to bet my sterling game reviewing reputation that you'll be surprised. If you want a game that feels like it's only one or two patches away from being finished, then stay away from this game. The game is absolutely playable but it does have a few hiccups, which you know...it's Early Access.

Fallout 4 is a good game that could have easily been a masterpiece if not for a few glaring flaws, most notably among them the game's confused direction.
Fallout 4 sets itself aside from the art direction and tone of past Fallout games, favouring sleek looking "Synths" that look more like something out of i-Robot than any of the 50s sci-fi movie robots that long time fans of the series have grown to accept as being simply the way those technologies advanced in Fallout's alternative history. Seeing these machines, and new technologies such as teleportation, standing alongside the vacuum-tube computer monitors and flash-gordon jumpsuits really shows a desire by Bethesda to take the franchise away from itself, so to speak. Many of the things that exist in Fallout 4 in terms of art and tone simply don't belong in a Fallout game.
Survival in post-apocalyptic America doesn't seem so hard given how easily settlements are constructed, how many people will flock to them, and how simple it is to get access to food and fresh water by building a pump and planting some crops. One would think that if fresh water was so easy to access with a simple pump that the Water-Chip in the original Fallout wouldn't be so important, the G.E.C.K in Fallout 2 wouldn't have been needed to save the village, and the entire plot of the water purification project in Fallout 3 would be a little pointless. The settlement system makes many aspects of the game simply trivial, and the settlements themselves never come under any real threat. Building fully automated robotic turrets capable of mowing raiders and super-mutants alike down is no issue in Bethesda's newest take on post-nuclear wasteland survival.
These things being said about the game's confused tone, the gameplay itself is very good. While the more hardcore role-playing elements have been replaced by a rather trivial perk system that was hit and miss for me, the weapon and armour customization is a lot of fun, and the free "Survival" mode is a wonderful way to play the game, and if a player is so inclined to ignore the settlement system, provides a new level of immersion and difficulty to the game's wasteland survival that the previous Fallout games failed to master (My Fallout 1 and 2 characters would go weeks without eating food, and my Fallout 3 character used it to heal is wounds, oddly enough). The shooting elements are a massive improvement over Fallout 3 and New Vegas, with enemies feeling far less spongy, and guns behaving a bit more realistically. The world itself is also a real pleasure to explore. While I have seen this game criticized for having a smaller world size than Fallout 3 or Skyrim, I would argue that there quality of the world is greater. It is more full, and encounters and dungeons are more likely to tell a compelling story, as opposed to the dozens of generic bandit caves in Skyrim and identical raider hide-outs in Fallout 3.
The main story is driven through the selection of one of several factions. I found the motivations of only one of these factions compelling, without giving too much away. The game does give the option to try and work with several factions if one is indecisive, but eventually the player is forced to make a choice. The game's main story is very linear outside of a few key decisions, such as which faction you join and which ending you choose. Unfortunately, the story's biggest weakness is that the villains are the least interesting that the franchise has ever seen. The main villain's motivations are absurdly unrealistic, and I could not bring myself to believe that even an insane villain would come to the leaps of logic that he came to, and the entire evil organization that you work against throughout the entire main story does the rest of the game a serious injustice. Honestly, this game would be better without this main story holding it back.
The game's fun though does not come from the main storyline, thankfully. If a player just wanders the wastes and, in the case of the survival difficulty setting, just tries to level up and stay alive while completing the many side areas and talking to the many interesting NPCs throughout the wastes, it is hard not to enjoy this game. Despite all of its flaws in terms of tone and story, I simply can't call this game a bad game for how fun it is to explore the wastes.
Forget the story, the settlements and the factions. Enjoy this game as a lone-wanderer and make your own story, and you will certainly enjoy this game. That being said, this is definitely the weakest title in an otherwise very good franchise.

Caveat emptor: Early access, so there is always the risk a future update ruins everything
This is already a very solid game. Even disregarding the promised updates for early 2016 (settlement upgrades, persistent great houses, reputation, contracts and backstabbing).
Name your band of merry mercenaries! Tour the randomly generated countryside! Lure farmers and fishermen to your banner with the promise of gold! Take on contracts to escort a caravan from a to b! Watch with horror as all your men get slaughtered by goblins!
The game has 2 parts, the results of which feed back into each other. Much like much-belowed UFO: Enemy unknown (X-COM in the states). The overmap where you wander around, take on contracts, upgrade and equip your band, and the hexagon map where you fight turn-based battles. The overmap is servicable, but barebones. (At least until the devs deliver the upgrades they promised for early 2016). But it nonetheless provides continuity between the battles.
Battles are where the meat of the game lies, and they are a joy to play. There's a decidedly board-gamey feel to the battles in the best possible way. Information is displayed concisely and you seldom feel overwhelmed or uncertain about what's going on. Positioning is the name of the game, making sure your people are placed so their gear works well against the enemies they're facing and that you can deal the maximum damage while receiving the minimum in return. The AI is quick to exploit holes in your formation, leaving to many a vader-esque "NOOOOOO!" as permadeath claims your favourite battle brother.

140 is an interesting, if exceptionally short, abstract musical platformer. Each of the three levels in 140 has a unique song which evolves as the player makes progress. This musical evolution is important as the level itself will also shift and become more alive as new beats are added; platforms will activate, blocks will shift, and deadly static will move, all to the beat of the music. For such a short game, 140 packs a massive amount of creativity and style into each of its stages and a large amount of the enjoyment to be had from 140 comes from figuring out which rules each object follows and keeping track of which parts of the environment synchronize with which parts of the song.
While by no means the hardest platformer out there, 140 nevertheless often asks quite a bit of the player, so I am rather happy to be able to say that the controls are not only simple and intuitive, but very precise. Visually, 140 is a game composed of simple geometrical shapes and its various color schemes can at times be outright ugly, but the graphics never feel lazy nor mundane. This is a game for which a specific aesthetic was chosen and repeatedly pushed to its limits in various ways without being outright broken and, at the end of the day, the simple shapes and often-ugly color schemes compliment each other and work surprisingly well.
Although I have mentioned it in passing previously, the biggest downside to 140 really is its length. Players can beat the game in under an hour and, after that, there's just not much reason to go back. Yes, there are mirror mode stages with no checkpoints which unlock after beating the game, but reversed versions of the original stages with new color schemes are not particularly interesting and the lack of checkpointing (which is quite well-placed in the normal stages) feels like a lazy way to inflate difficulty and mostly just results in frustration and boredom. 140 is definitely a game which values quality over quantity and, while it has quality in spades, it's a bit tough to recommend a game which is quite this short for its normal asking price of $5.
Brevity aside, 140 is ultimately a wonderful and wonderfully creative game which fully embraces the beauty of simplicity in every way it can.

where they went wrong:
* dumbed down the dialogue options only giving you 4 things to say that dont really change the outcome at all and are paraphrased so you dont actually know what youre going to say until you say it.
* voiced protagonist ruins the immersion that other bethesda games had, in the sense that you cant role play very well because the voice and dialogue options mix together to limit you from being anything other than the role of the distressed parent looking for their son. i never realized how a non voiced protagonist allowed you to fill in the gaps and put yourself into the character and devise their own backstory, attitude, emotions, and motives. in fallout 4 you are told who you are, where you came from, how to feel, how to act, and what you should do... thats not an RPG.
*the main story is in your face every second of the game. with almost all dialougue options eventually leading into the fact that youre looking for your son and you need to find him. this and the limited amount of dialogue restricts the ability to role play your character the way you want.
*the leveling and skill system has been severly dumbed down compared to fallout 3 and New Vegas (seeing a trend yet? everything has been dumbed down or unnecessarily simplified to accomadate little kids playing on consoles, and the four button dialougue menu thats mapped just like a controller is proof of that.)
*dumbed down quests, most situations are solved by shooting anything that moves, compared to how in the older games you had many options of solving a problem or quest.
*paid mods... i dont care what you want to technically classify them as, they arent mini dlcs, they at most add one item or reskin for 5 dollars or more each, they cost credits, you get credits with money. its paid mods end of story. (better quality on nexus anyway)
*as for the actual DLCs,  alot of them are expansions to the base building mechanics that i personally think arent worth a DLC they should just be updated into everyones game, i miss when DLCs added giant new campaigns and huge amounts of new content and items, factions and new lands.
*power armor is handed to the player 15 minutes into the game, power armor has always been something that should feel like a great achievment you had to work for or go somewhere to get the training. while i do like how its treated like a vehicle you step in and out of, i just think the way they just gave it to us ruined what made it special.
with all of these aspects combined, bethesda manged to make a vast open world feel like a dumbed down linear action game with small amounts of RPG elements. rather than an open world RPG.

The original Sanctum was a cool game, even if it was kind of a mess. you placed towers atop walls, but the walls were so high up that you needed elevators to get up on top of them, so battles were largely either centralized at one spot atop the wall, or standing down inside your maze you built, armed with the game's somewhat poor weapon selection. Some of this might sound confusing if you don't know about Sanctum or Sanctum 2, but I'll explain a bit more. In short, though, the first game, though  pretty good for the time, is completely outclassed by its sequel, to the point of shelving it forever, in my opinion.
Sanctum 2 is a tower defense...and a co-op first person shooter, but a tower defense game at its heart. You can choose between 4 characters (5 with DLC) with different weapons and bonuses, and each can choose other weapons and you can equip a few little bonuses that make a big difference in the game. You fight from a first person combat perspective with guns, but it's a tower defense game over all. You place walls that are low enough you can jump on top of them easily, the enemy can't pass over them (except flying enemies), you build mazes/paths to make it take longer for the enemies to get to the core (glowy thing you're trying to protect), and place towers atop the walls that will have the most time/opportunity to kill lots of baddies.
In regard to the weaponry and towers, there are a bunch of weapons to choose from for combat, with quite a few of them being pretty good, and there are a lot of different types of towers. It's honestly surprising how many of them were actually good as well. You've got everything from super-powerful flying-unit-only towers to ground-only area of effect towers to towers that make mines you can manually lay out to devastate enemies, to single shot towers that deal positively insane damage across nearly the entire map...but they take forever to rearm. It's great just how many choices there are, and how many of them are actually quite good for various maps and enemies in the game.
The story exists. It's okay, though nothing amazing. The story is presented in silent (no voice acting) comic-style panels before each mission. Technically, you need the two DLCs to get the rest of the story, but honestly, this is one of those games where story isn't a big deal, and very little happens plot-wise in the DLC.
The graphics are nice enough with a pretty sci-fi asthetic, though humans look kinda...weird. Luckily, there aren't many of them. The music is very peaceful, "airy" stuff and nice to listen to while building your maze and placing your towers. There's also one of those fun digital voices you can do text-to-speech with in multiplayer, and that's good for laughs no matter how long you've seen/heard it. This game is fun alone or with friends, and I highly recommend it.

Let me start off by saying that Town of Salem is a free game to play on Blank Media Games' website, and that there really isn't much to gain by purchasing it on Steam, but I found that five dollars was a low enough price to help support the creators of a game that I've attained countless hours of entertainment from.
Town of Salem is an online game where a party of fifteen players is thrown into a town. Each player has a different role and goals, but the two main parties are the townies (who want to survive and lynch all evildoers) and the mafia (who want to kill everyone in the town). Thing is, you can't tell for certain what another person's role is until they're dead. So if you, say, were on the lookout at DarthVader's house and saw Rick Sanchez sneak in to kill him: good for you. Next you've got to convince the rest of the town to believe you and maybe get a doctor to cover you the next night in case the mafia decide to get revenge.
The Classic mode is enough to draw endless laughs and create a new mystery with each play, but other modes like Ranked and Ranked Practice add more roles like werewolves, arsonists, witches, and even more townie roles and tend to be more random in the roles it assigns every game, which makes things even more exciting.
It has a couple of problems, mostly pretaining to the community (which has a few gamethrowers to ruin the fun for everyone), but the developers have been working to fix things with the report system, and I can definitly see a severe drop in toxic and mean-spirited players compared to when I first began playing.
So, yeah, I recommend this game. It can take a few games to get the hang of it and know what you're doing, but it's worth it. If you're still on the fence, go play the free version yourself to see if you like it enough to support Town of Salem's creators, but if you're a fan of mystery and getting into all sorts of wacky situations, you're going to love it.

To be absolutely clear, yes, this game is available to play free on Blank Media Games' website. I played it there for a long while before I decided to purchase the game on Steam to help support the developers. I recommend you do the same to see if you enjoy it, if you haven't done so already. The game remains as fun now as it ever was, in my opinion.
To be absolutely clear: I play almost exclusively on All Any mode. I only played a small amount of Classic when I started out, I've never played Ranked or Ranked Practice because I have no interest in playing competitively. I can't speak for what the playing experience is like in those modes.
There are two currency types for purchasing from the store: merit points and town points. Merit points are earned by playing games. With a Steam purchase, you earn them at twice the speed, and on double merit point weekends, that increases to three times the speed. I've found lately that it seems to take no time at all to have enough to buy something from the store.
Town points are your standard currency that's bought with real money. Some items in the store are town point exclusive, but most are available with merit points too. Recently I noticed a couple of skins that were previously town point exclusive can now be bought with merit points. Don't worry about not getting anything without paying. There's plenty available for free.
On the matter of The Coven, it's not an update, although there was an update that was released alongside it. It's an expansion. It adds a lot of new content, which is why it's paid. The base game remains perfectly playable for free and is still going to be updated. I don't own The Coven yet, but I plan on purchasing it to further support the developers. And because it looks fun.
On the matter of actual gameplay, Town of Salem has a large variety of roles with a large variety of abilities. There is no generic "Townie" role; every role has unique abilities. The game has a Vampire role (a conversion role), but if you don't like that, the role doesn't appear in Ranked or Ranked practice, nor does it appear in Classic, and if you choose to play Custom, you can avoid games that include them.
Scrolls are available for purchase that will increase the odds of you getting a certain role (although this is not a guarantee). They're consumable; they burn up once you've gotten the desired role, and are purchased in sets of three. They're available for merit points, so everyone can buy them if they want.
I have no complaints about the game itself. The only complaint I have is the occasional behavior of the players, which is obviously unavoidable in any game. Occasionally, I see players get aggressive and insulting toward other people, or deliberately throw the game. In All Any mode, I don't see this frequently, but the problem may be worse in other modes.
Don't be surprised if people hound you for making mistakes. People in this game tend to get frustrated very easily. When the whole point of the game is deceiving and seeing through deception, you're bound to make mistakes, especially when you're new and still learning the ropes. I highly recommend keeping the wiki handy so you can look things up.
For me, it's been a lot of fun. There are a couple of roles I loathe playing, but with so many of them, that's bound to happen, and it all comes down to personal taste.
Like I said at the beginning, you can play this game for free. If you do that and find you really like it, then you can purchase the Steam version and get those double merit points rolling in.

For anyone with a passion for free roam games, Just Cause 2 is definately the game for you. Combined with the multiplayer mod, which requires just cause 2 in order to play, this game gives you the chance to cause chaos to the world around you. Now please note that this game was made in 2010 so around the edges it might not be that sharp, but it is still a very beatiful game. However, if the graphics bother you there is a great modding community.
If you find yourself walking in this game on foot you are playing it wrong; the developers made it easy for you to find a ride wether it's a motorcylce, jeep, sports car, jet, or even an helicopter evac. The free roam is great but the story is lacking. If the devolpers spent a bit more time i think this game could have really shined, but they didn't and that's why i'm here to tell you what they did do. The story missions are little more than a pointless dialog about the next thing they want you to destroy. the characters are shallow and are poorly scripted, but i can still follow the story even though i could predict the rest of the conversation after 2 mins. But when it comes to the combat its great it's a little slugish but fun nonetheless.
When u discover and capture a city, town, or base they will have side missions and goals. The missions can be anything from a racing in cars to flying in jets, but it's a great way to enjoy a break from story missons and mindless chaos. The goals, on the other hand, are nice but very had to find. There are vehicles parts, Weapon parts, and armor parts which are used in order to upgrade things that you can order from the black market. If you are in a huge area, you will often find it diffecult to hunt for these objects, being the only help is a little rader in the corner of the screen which is basically the equalivalent to a kid saying hot or cold. However, If you want a game where u don't have to worry about a set path Just Cause 2 is definately the game for you. Even the story stinks, the gameplay more the makes up for it. Town of Salem is an interesting and critical-thinking-inspiring game.
You're on a team, whether it's just you or multiple players, and your job as a member of that team is to make the streets of Salem yours to keep. In a word, no trespassing.
There may be other teams with more neutral backgrounds that you might like to keep hanging around after you've finished off everyone else. Just be sure that they still are who they say...!
Ever day and every night are critical points of the game, literally. Accusations are sometimes enough to destroy one player, and/or implicate the rest of your comrades. Make sure you save some face if you out one of your own.
Town of Salem games can be fast, when the right kinds of chaotic choices are made. Either way, long or short, you will definitely have a little fun playing.

I'd heard about this game through TV Tropes and TotalBiscuit, so when I happened to get it as part of a bundle I decided to try it out.
It certainly lives up to its reputation.
See, this game uses a titanic amount of memory, which... limits its framerate somewhat.  Forget advancing through the story.  Forget survival challenges.  Hell, forget looking for amusing glitches.  Simply moving from point A to point B is an aggravating ordeal.
I can deal with the abrupt instant kills, the gratuitous invisible walls, the overly simplistic stealth mechanics, and even those damned monkeys, but not when the framerate feels like my screen is grinding against my eyes.
The worst part is that this could have been bad in a funny way.  Like, for example, one time I tried to shoot an enemy from atop a pyramid, but not only did an invisible wall block my shot, the ricochet killed me!  I still didn't have my last trading card, so I spent the next few minutes killing myself against that invisible wall, just to pass the time.  Unfortunately, if this game is ever brought a playable state, most of the more entertaining problems will probably be fixed as well.  Too bad.
Anyway, don't buy this.  If you get it in a bundle, don't install it.  This game is painful to play.  Leave it be.

I was so excited for this game I grabbed it the minute I saw it despite the Mixed reviews.  It has SO much potential.  Beautiful graphics, pleasant music.
Unforunately, this is as far as the pros go at the moment.  The cons are extensive.
- You -can- play a female but the NPC voice is male no matter what.  Awkward?
- The game broke completely when I turned off full-screen like 5 minutes in (and had to restart).  Buttons were hovering inches away, menu options wouldn't work, then it just crashed.
- No tutorial in text or interactive or... anything.  Not even descriptive tooltips.
- Terrible, terrible 'navigation'.  Over-sensitive motion jumps OR no motion at all.  Can't figure out why.
- Terrible, terrible voice overs.  Picking that always-male voice was text-to-speech from the 90's bad.
- Price point.  For an early access in this condition, that price is outrageous.
Overall conclusion: Wait to see if there's progress before you buy.  If they fixed even the game-breaking crash, I would reconsider recommending this for people interested in supporting development but at this point you couldn't give detailed feedback if you tried.

Sharpen the pikes, reload the crossbows, make ready the hounds we are hunting goblins! Goblins are a plague upon the earth, their existence is unacceptable and as such we must exterminate them all.
Shouted The Black Wolf to his men, a extract from the writings of Roderick the Wise.
A tale of Devils, born in hell, but made to save mortal men.
Well my fellow adventure seeking travelers, I have come to you with a little story to tell. Have you heard word of a mighty mercenary band called Hellborn Battalion, led my Marius the Black Wolf, his brother Christian the Scholar, and their good friend Sebastian the Berserker. Together with their mercenary companions they traveled the land cleansing the forests of goblin filth, removing treacherous bandits from the roads and destroying vile undead abominations. This they had done so successfully for a long time until chance had it a encounter in the southern swamps, a band of Orcs was reported to be raiding nearby communities so the Hellborn marched forth to meet the threat, little did they know the Orcs might was more then just the stuff of legend. As the brave brothers fought of waves of Orc young it became apparent they were only the light infantry of the orc force and soon their orc warriors strode in, the true masters of the battle field. They lumbered forth wielding their mighty weapons clad in the cobbled together ruins of many a brave fallen knight armor. Keeping their archers safe while they rained down punishment on the greenskin fighters the Hellborn Battalion toiled to see their foes vanquished, shields splintered, spears cracked to pieces, swords were shaken and much blood was split. But finally it was the orcs who were defeated, shaken, tired and wounded the Hellborn Battalion rallied to their leaders for support. Marius and Christian thanked their brothers in arms for the brave deed they had performed, and made forward to celebrate their victory and lick their wounds. Not more then a week had passed however and a nother orc warband fell before the Hellborn, the strength of their leadership so praise worthy, that even a untrained apprentice with little equipment, who was only recruited to boost the Battalions ranks temporarily, survived the battle against all odds.
The company then prepared itself for the brave goal of removing another orc clan as they had made their camp near a important city hailed by the Hellborn as their home. The battle was more fierce and terrifying then any yet recorded, man and beast fought each other tooth and nail, but ultimately the orc warlord and his warriors were destroyed, and only one of the Hellborn Battalion lost his life that day.
To this day I hear proud merry talk in the taverns, markets and even noble courts of people claiming justified or not, they had associated with the valiant Hellborn Battalion, and spreading tales of their famed exploits. Where they may be now, I cannot say. But I know this, if there is an orc, goblin or undead in their path it wont be standing there for much longer. However while I hail them as heroes, I would prefer we have no use for them, for they are indeed the devils of the battle ground and where ever they go, danger is surely present.

I rate Mortal Kombat: Komplete Edition 2.5/5. It's almost OK and I'm really happy I bought it for only 6 dollars.
Okay, let's get the good things out of the way. This game has a large number (but not variety) of characters, difficulty levels and modes to choose from making this a highly replayable game. The graphics are pretty good as is the sound. I encountered no bugs. Every character has their own somewhat unique moves.
But...the characters are generally much of a muchness. There are ninjas, musclebound grotesques and scantily clad women (with one departure from this rule). Asides from those 3 basic character types (or within those character types) there is little variety. The voice acting is so bad it may be purposefully bad and the music is largely mediocre. The graphics are not amazing (they are simply good). This game is, like its predecessors, highly repetitious and, also true to its predecessors, the controls are quite obtuse and have a sharp learning curve (though this is the most user-friendly Mortal Kombat game I have ever played thanks largely to the lists of moves and their corresponding buttons made easily accessible from the pause menu allowing players to teach themselves new moves on the fly).
But (and perhaps worst of all) unsurprisingly there are numerous features and special arenas and character skins that need to be unlocked to be used (I'd guess about 50% of the total content this game has to offer needs to be unlocked by playing the game and earning "Kombat Koins") Locking up all this content from the start merely comes off as a hassle, particularly to someone like me who only wants to play this game casually and has little intention of ever playing it thoroughly (the lack of depth of this game's gameplay and shallow plot ensure that I will not want to play it thoroughly as the game does not intrinsically lend itself well to being played in such a way). Locking features and content up is not the same as creating a game which has true intellectual or artistic depth.
The menu system and the buttons assigned to them are extremely obtuse also. The totally obtuse Kombat Kodes system needed for using things you've previously unlocked persists as well (things you unlock should be accessible from dedicated menus, or rather in such a game as this, everything the game has in it should be accessible from menus and should never need to be unlocked. I paid for the game, now give me everything it has to offer so everything which was created may then impress me). As in all previous Mortal Kombat games, the arenas which have initially been made accessible are randomly selected when you begin a match. In essence, this game (Like all previous Mortal Kombat games) gives you a general lack of choice and a lack of access to the plethora of content that it may potentially offer. Not a surprise by any means but that does not diminish the fact that this aesthetic is an intrinsically irritating one.
This is an OK game for casual playing I guess but it lacks many nifty options which it could have had and is, as a direct result, more irritating and cumbersome than it needed to be and thus not as good as it could have been. This was no surprise to me however. I bought this game for 6 dollars (it was on sale on steam for 75% off) and knew what I was getting for my money. I write this review so you will know to not buy this game unless you see it for a similar price.

Northgard manages to bring new life to an otherwise dated genre. RTS games and 4X titles share many similarities, however, there are a few differences. Most noticeably how time, resources and research are handled.
Northgard manages to combine the best of both of these genres to make a seemingly simple yet complex system that keeps players on their toes.
The resource management is similar to titles like Endless Legend or the Sid Meier's Civilization series. Each unit effects your overall consumption and you need to balance everything in order to succeed.
The RTS genre comes in with mechanics similar to Age of Empires or Command and Conquer. Everything is in real time and you can individually select units to move them in and out of combat.
On a side note, you can really tell the developer cares about there community. They have released consistent updates that range from new clans to unique pieces of land that offer strategic benefits.
Overall I definitely recommend Northgard to any fan of RTS or 4x games. Northgard offers a new experience that is sure to impress.

The Steam release of Realm of the Mad God marks a new mainstream focus for the free-to-play browser MMO. It's a combination of Rogue, Robotron and Diablo, an isometric fantasy shooter where quests are handed to you on the fly, where you're never given a reason to stop running, shooting, or farming experience – until you die, and your character is deleted forever. It's simplistic and supremely silly, but also one of the most distinctive multiplayer experiences around.
Mad God knows how rudimentary it is, and the main reason it's enjoyable is that sense of being let in on the joke. It reduces MMO mechanics to the point of absurdity without rejecting them, revelling in the festive pointlessness of haring around with your mates blowing up an improbable number of elves.
Wide-eyed sprites and a looping up-tempo soundtrack contribute to this thrill of being swept up in a tidal wave of manic consumption. Being absorbed into one of Realm of the Mad God's 'trains' is something every gamer should experience at least once: a gang of players that reaches a critical mass where no monster can stop it, then tears through the world in a leaderless stampede. Such Skinner Box game mechanics would be cynical elsewhere, but when accelerated to the point of ridiculousness they become charming, like listening to a despot give a speech on helium.                                                                   It's easy to emerge from one of these trains with a max-level character, and for the committed this is where Realm of the Mad God actually begins. Collecting special potions from bosses maxes out your character's stats, enabling you to take on tougher bosses and eventually several variants of the Mad God himself. Then you die, and your character's achievements are totted up and served back to you as a 'fame' rating, which contributes to your account's total score.
It's a game that's happy to discard your efforts in a heartbeat, and that complicates the inclusion of microtransactions. Everything you can buy with real money is cosmetic, with the exception of dungeon portals that allow you to skip straight to a specific encounter. The cheaper items – armour dyes that cost between 25p to £1 – are lost with your character, while more expensive unlocks such as pets are permanently bound to your account. The game invites throwaway spending with the same anarchic spirit that encourages players to chase pretty green numbers in the wilderness. One is harmless, the other isn't.
If you rationalise the money you spend as a way of tipping the developers, it makes more sense. You're invited to participate exactly as much as you want, whether that's jumping in for 20 minutes or dedicating yourself to unlocking every class, buying every hat, and killing every god. It's your choice, after all – just don't be surprised if people think you're mad for trying.

Fragments and various components found throughout the game is used to upgrade your weapons. Once you complete your first play through, there are options to replay at higher difficulty and with all items unlocked.
I'd recommend buying the "Bastion Soundtrack Edition" for the OST.

From this early access it seems to be a very promising game. Crafting is actually puzzling, so far I've figured out how to make rock shards and a campfire. For some reason, I cannot combine a rock shard and a stick to create a spear, maybe I'm doing something wrong, maybe that's just not how you make a spear. maybe if I swing my knife at the stick enough times it'll make a spear, I'm just not sure). I think it's pretty nice that it doesn't just tell you how to do things, but it would be nice if there was a button to bring up what he/she already knows (not to craft from it, but just to tell you what tools and supplies are required for the items you've already crafted once, in case you forget what you needed.
Also for those claiming the sharks AI is off, and they lose sight of you, no they don't. They modeled the shark behavior in game off of real life sharks. In the real world sharks are not mindless killing machines, they are curious animals, one aspect to showing their curiosity is bumping things, they are feeling it with their lateral lines and trying to figure out what it is, in this game they may bump your raft, or even you. Once they can learn no more from bumping an object, they may bite, this is because sharks use their mouths a bit like you or I use our hands, not only are they trying to figure out if you are edible, but what you're made out of, if you taste good, how you react, etc. Wherever you are in this game, it's deserted, these sharks have never seen a human and will behave as if you are some unknown creature to them (which you are). They flee from battle because that is what real life sharks do. There was a popular scuba spot somewhere IRL and someone panicked when a shark approached him (it was a preserve and by all accounts the shark was not being aggressive, just swimming past), the man reacted by stabbing it with his safety stick, and hit it the gills and it died. No sharks were seen in that area for 5 years after, they shunned it because one man with a stick. So the sharks aren't losing sight of you, they're behaving like real sharks in the wild.
Long story short, pros and cons list for you:
Pros:
- interesting concept no mutants, zombies, ghosts, monsters or other unnatural creatures
- very realistic shark behavior
- reasonably low minimum graphic specs allow almost anyone to play the game
- doesn't hold your hand, lets you figure out things for yourself
- some minor bugs, but nothing game ruining (less buggy than most games out of early access on day 1)
Cons:
- No visible hunger/thirst bar I am not sure how to tell if my character is hungry or thirsty (that being said I didn't really try to starve myself). It would be nice to see a menu with, while maybe not full on bars to tell, just a little mention (maybe while looking at your watch) that you need something, with some status ailments.
- Keep seeing plants like "Yucca", can't figure out how to harvest it. Maybe I need those fibers to craft my spear.
- Cannot change the controls. My laptop touchpad mouse is broken, just the click functions. I can left click with the touchpad, but have no way to right-click, usually I just set the game that alt right-clicks but the game won't let me. Also with my laptop I have no "middle click" button so can't do that either. This will most likely be added in a future update.
- Apparently my character does not get hot or cold, nor tired. No need for the fire except to cook, and for light. No need to sleep (apparently can't sleep anyway). What's the point in building a shelter if I can't sleep in it? This will most likely be added in a future update.
- Not a lot of content, and no story yet, but each update will add more, and a story to get rescued is in the works.
All in all, considering it's early access the game shows promise. Beam Team is very good about updating pretty regularly. The game is enjoyable as is, but could be so much more, and I'm sure in the end it will be. I have great faith in the developers, as I've been following the game almost since it's inception, and I know the small dev team (2 people) will work their asses off to make it great. I can't wait to progress, it should be a fun experience. All in all 9.5/10 for early access.
-Stay Alive Beam Team! And congrats on the awesome game!

Few things genuinely terrify me so much as the Xenomorphs of the Aliens franchise. It’s the look, as well as behavior, of the monstrous Xenomorphs, designed by surrealist artist H.R. Giger, which sets my heart pounding and adrenaline flowing when I watch the movies or play the games, and hear that telltale ping of the Marines’ motion trackers. Then, their method of reproduction is just disgusting in itself.
That’s why I was immensely relieved to learn back in the 90s that a comic series had been released that pairs that horrific species with the bloodthirsty yet honorable Predators, and sets them against each other. It’s just unfortunate that humans are caught right in the middle of the masked, dreadlocked humanoids’ endless hunt against the grotesque monstrosities.
Many video games and several movies were also released that chronicled the struggle among the three species, but the most recent game, released in 2010 by SEGA and developed by Rebellion, is somewhat connected to the first recent movie. You can play as a Marine, which bears the most resemblance to a standard FPS, or as a Predator hunting both humans and Xenomorphs, or as the very species which terrifies me so, known somewhat confusingly as simply Aliens (the Predators are just as much alien to us).
Predators are vicious and brutal killers, but they didn’t know or care about humans; their prey was always the Aliens. But when we violated the Predators’ sacred hunting grounds, which just so happened to be on Earth, in South America (in the first Predator movie) as well as the various planets that were colonized by the Weyland-Yutani Corporation (in comics, movies, and games), the Predators decided we had to pay with our lives. This, along with the mindlessly ravenous Aliens, and corrupt corporate executive Weyland’s ambitious drive for more money (which involves preserving a Xenomorph specimen, just as the company wanted in Aliens), threatens humanity’s hold on the colony.
Multiplayer modes also exist, but due to the age of the game as well as most players being on consoles (Xbox 360 and PlayStation 3), I have not been able to test the PC version’s multiplayer. But according to the menus, standard (deathmatch, team deathmatch, capture the flag, etc.) as well as special modes exist. There does seem to be a great deal of potential for multiplayer, because of the diversity of the three species, but I haven’t been able to see it yet. I’m sure it’s great, though.
If you like science fiction stories that can turn quite horrific at times, I’d advise you to check out the Aliens vs. Predator franchise as a whole, as well as this game. It’s a little derivative at times (at least in the Marine’s story), but it’s still quite a strong title. I give it 4 out of 5 stars.
