I rate Mortal Kombat: Komplete Edition 2.5/5. It's almost OK and I'm really happy I bought it for only 6 dollars.
Okay, let's get the good things out of the way. This game has a large number (but not variety) of characters, difficulty levels and modes to choose from making this a highly replayable game. The graphics are pretty good as is the sound. I encountered no bugs. Every character has their own somewhat unique moves.
But...the characters are generally much of a muchness. There are ninjas, musclebound grotesques and scantily clad women (with one departure from this rule). Asides from those 3 basic character types (or within those character types) there is little variety. The voice acting is so bad it may be purposefully bad and the music is largely mediocre. The graphics are not amazing (they are simply good). This game is, like its predecessors, highly repetitious and, also true to its predecessors, the controls are quite obtuse and have a sharp learning curve (though this is the most user-friendly Mortal Kombat game I have ever played thanks largely to the lists of moves and their corresponding buttons made easily accessible from the pause menu allowing players to teach themselves new moves on the fly).
But (and perhaps worst of all) unsurprisingly there are numerous features and special arenas and character skins that need to be unlocked to be used (I'd guess about 50% of the total content this game has to offer needs to be unlocked by playing the game and earning "Kombat Koins") Locking up all this content from the start merely comes off as a hassle, particularly to someone like me who only wants to play this game casually and has little intention of ever playing it thoroughly (the lack of depth of this game's gameplay and shallow plot ensure that I will not want to play it thoroughly as the game does not intrinsically lend itself well to being played in such a way). Locking features and content up is not the same as creating a game which has true intellectual or artistic depth.
The menu system and the buttons assigned to them are extremely obtuse also. The totally obtuse Kombat Kodes system needed for using things you've previously unlocked persists as well (things you unlock should be accessible from dedicated menus, or rather in such a game as this, everything the game has in it should be accessible from menus and should never need to be unlocked. I paid for the game, now give me everything it has to offer so everything which was created may then impress me). As in all previous Mortal Kombat games, the arenas which have initially been made accessible are randomly selected when you begin a match. In essence, this game (Like all previous Mortal Kombat games) gives you a general lack of choice and a lack of access to the plethora of content that it may potentially offer. Not a surprise by any means but that does not diminish the fact that this aesthetic is an intrinsically irritating one.
This is an OK game for casual playing I guess but it lacks many nifty options which it could have had and is, as a direct result, more irritating and cumbersome than it needed to be and thus not as good as it could have been. This was no surprise to me however. I bought this game for 6 dollars (it was on sale on steam for 75% off) and knew what I was getting for my money. I write this review so you will know to not buy this game unless you see it for a similar price.

There have been a lot of Tower Defense Games over the past years. Be it games that follow the classic "watch your towers destroy a ton of enemies"-formula, like the Defense Grid series or Super Sanctum TD, while others tried to get the player more involved, like Orcs Must Die and it's Tower Defense/Third Person Shooter Hybrid gameplay or the Sanctum series that mixed TD with First Person Shooter and an emphasis on Coop.
Kingdom Rush is your classic Tower Defense game, where you watch the landscape from above, place your towers, upgrade them and hopefully put them on spots so all the evil monsters don't reach the Exit.
The game is set in a Fantasy Kingdom (so expect anything from Spiders to Gnomes to Ogres and Knights) as enemies) that is presented in a cute, comic art style and features a lot of humor with tons of references to movies like Army of Darkness (the mages in their tower quote „Klaatu Barada Nikto“) and during fights there are little text bubbles with words like "Pow", basically taken straight from 1966 Batman series. It's charming and thankfully not overdone.
On your journey, that leads you through forest areas and snow landscapes, you get coins by beating the missions which you can invest to upgrade the Towers, the Knights and your Spells. Unlike other games in the genre, Kingdom Rush is a bit limited in it's towers. You only get 4: The Archer Tower, the Barracks, the Magic Tower and the Artillery but it's enough and you can not only upgrade those up to Level 3 but also turn them into specialised towers. For example the Archer Tower can later on changed into a Musketeer Garrison or the Ranger Hideout, both of them have their advantages and disadvantages, so there is a learning curve in this game ot find out how the upgrades are and what works best in each mission.
Next to that are the spells. These can be activated and then have a cooldown. One is the reinforcements which spawns 2 pretty weak fighters but the cooldown is short and the other is Rain of Fire which, after you selected the target area, sends down a couple meteors.
And the last thing at your disposal for defense are the Heroes. You unlock them one by one by playing the Campaign and they are different in their type (like a Paladin, an Archer or Thor) and their abilities. You can send them around the map but they're best used right at the exit to kill any enemy that might gotten through your defense lines.
The game is fun and as expected, thanks to all the upgradable towers and the Heroes highly addicitive. The only criticism i can bring is the missing endless mode which is something that should be here since it's a standard game mode in Tower Defense and the music is a bit on the boring side, it's not bad but it doesn't stand out either.
All in all i just can highly recommend this game to every fan of the genre.

Battle Brothers is a turn-based tactics and sandbox that places you as the noncombatant head of a mercenary company. Players must juggle the logistics of supplying, paying, and equipping their mercenaries with a white-knuckle battle system that will leave you in a state of catharsis nine times out of ten.
I will be frank here; Battle Brothers is unashamedly a brilliant game, one that is consistently evolving to become even more than the basic concept. Already, we have four graphically, tactically, and musically different enemy factions to fight against, with a fifth on the way. The world map is simple and perfectly functional at this time, with the upcoming release bringing with it a beautiful new map; one with regions, towns, cities, and noble houses ready to exploit.
It does have flaws, however. The learning curve is more so a learning peak, and it can be very newb unfriendly at times (especially in regards to Goblins... yeesh, don't trust your gaming instincts with those greenskins). As of the time of writing (7th of November, 2015) one can expect a solid 8-15 hours of gameplay at least, with the expectation going in that this game will not hold your hand.
All in all, this is an excellent game, and one that shows the best side of Early-Access. Attentive developers, sizable updates, and the meat of the game already in. Worth a purchase for sure.

Bastion is a hack n' slash role playing game, however this game has some really interesting aspects that contrast from other games inside the same genre.
You play as "The Kid" someone that just woke up in the middle of a catastrophe that neither the player nor the character know anything about, however we can count on the strong presence of the Narrator to enlighten us during our adventure.
I want my first point on this review to be exactly about the Narrator, something that really standed out from any game I've ever played. We are used to games which story develops over time with strong interactions between characters, or with the environment however in Bastion, every interaction is very  subtle, and that's where the Narrator comes in, as someone telling and unfolding a story and interacting as much with the main character as with the player himself which is awesome. And the developers really hit gold here, since first of all the voice fits perfectly on the western theme that surrounds the game, and at the same time the voice acting is also amazing, since you can feel every emotion which helps create a certain empathy with this being, and that's something fundamental in this story.
Since we're talking about voices and sounds let's jump to the soundtrack, which after the Narrator is the best aspect of the game, since it manages to develop and transform according to the story which is phenomenal. You'll understand what i mean since it's quite rare to hear a soundtrack which contain tracks with lyrics, and even though I think that including something like that is risky since it could break the atmosphere of the game, it does exactly the opposite and traps you even more on this brilliant story.
Now onto the gameplay, this is up to you to decide if it is a good thing or not according to your standards but to me it felt like the combat and exploration is something secondary. Don't get me wrong, the combat is fun and this aspect of the game is very well developed with a big array of weaponry, abilities and upgrades. The developers even managed to make this part of the game more interesting with the fact that all the way to the last part of the game you unlock a new mechanic, however it didn't feel as good as the plot, which was what really kept me going.
The visuals are very interesting, the 2D visuals with the isometric camera really fitted into the style, nevertheless some models seemed quite odd, as an example the main character which on some drawings shows up as someone quite slim, when you look at the model you see someone quite bulky which doesn't make much sense. Same goes for Rucks which the model doesn't look that good either.
Something that also bugged me was the fact that you're being told a story and all of a sudden the game gives you the option to make a couple decisions on the final stage and to me it felt out of place, I think you should be either given more choices to make or none at all. Before I start this review, take into consideration that I've spent a good 1K hours on the browser version of the game and have alot of experience with it.
Realm of the Mad God at it's foundation is a great game with A LOT of potential. It has a unique concept and is (or
, depending on your current opinion about the game) a very fun and enjoyable game. We are also now getting frequent updates once again (doesn't make up for the years of missing content, though), so there's a lot of fun to have if you're willing to look for it.
It's everything ELSE that has been added on top of the original foundation of the game that has taken away most of it's charm and hurt the game and community as a whole.
Pets are considered by many to be the death of ROTMG and the begining of the "dark age". They've had nothing but negative effects on quite literally everything in the game and it's economy. There are many people in the community that spend hundreds on dollars on pets so don't expect DECA to remove this poison from the game anytime soon, as they wouldn't want to upset the whales (this games main source of income). Pets have also largely changed the game and made it ridiculously easier while also being the cause of the massive economy crash which heavily decreased the value of
, meaning that despite the fact that pets bring DECA alot of money, they also took away a large portion of revenue made from selling in-game items for gold.
Pets are the poison in this game and bring it down as a whole.
In ROTMG, you'll encounter a number of different types of people in the community, such as:
The guy who spends hundreds of dollars on pets, buys every vault chest and has a LOT of character slots. This person generally also uses a hacked client to ensure their own characters immortality, this is also the same person that creates a crap ton of "PPE" characters as a way to "challenge" their own godlike abilities and to squeeze as much enjoyment out of the game as possible. However, this isn't to say that every whale spends hundreds on the game, the more common ones, which I like to call "baby whales",
spend about $60-100 on the game. This, however, isn't to say that every whale is completely blind on what they are spending their money on, many of them are selfaware and do not mind spend hundreds as long as it keeps them entertained for a long period of time.
If you haven't noticed already, there's a lot of these fellas hanging around in the review section for this game, defending DECA and ROTMG to death. Many of these blind fanboys tend to be "baby whales" and spend a good chunk of money on the game, then proceed to tell people that you don't need to spend a cent on the game and it's still "really fun". They, however, usually don't hold this "f2p is fun" argument up for very long and end up contradicting themselves by saying things like "The only thing you need to buy are vault chests and character slots," Because they themselves have spent no less than $30 on them.
You will also find that a number of ROTMG fanboys will claim to be "F2Pers" and use that to attempt to win an argument about ROTMG not being a Pay2Win or Pay2Play game, however through my experience I've never once spoken to somebody that hasn't bought in-game gold or spent money on a third-party website that sells in-game items and accounts. One big thing fanboys and whales (the blind, unselfaware ones atleast) have in common is that usually support the Microtransaction business model and will commonly call it the "future of gaming monetization" and then proceed to go on about how every AAA game will soon have them. These people are the reason why we are seeing lootboxes appearing in $60 ganes more and more.
There seems to be a quite a few of these types of people hanging around in the ROTMG community, yesterday there was some guy roleplaying sexual intercourse between his own pet and pets owned by other players, while another person was roleplaying himself having forced sexual intercourse with some other guy. Public Nests (the dungeon) seems to be where alot of these weirdos hang around, with alot of them roleplaying sexual intercourse with the bees and...
things. The amount of times I hear things like "impregnates queen bee", "turns bee into mother bee", "deepthroats stinger", "is turned on by queen bee", "cums on queen bees belly" or "rides queen bees stinger" in this dungeon is absolutely ridiculous.
Majority of the people who play ROTMG will fall under these two catergories of players, but it wouldn't be fair to say that every single member of the community does.
As soon as somebody enters the Nexus (the lobby for ROTMG), they will be quick to notice the huge amount of bots advertising third-party websites that resell in-game items and accounts to make profit. These sites are in somewhat of a cold war with DECA at the moment (and they were with Kabam too), with the most ever being done to stop such sites being adding an setting in the options menu for players to filter out messages from low-star accounts. In fact, it honestly suprises me that these sites are still up and running and haven't been shut down yet by DECA (like how Valve sarted shutting down CSGO gambling sites).
It's even gotten to the point where you can buy items on here that would normally take you hours upon hours to get for just $1 (don't forget, this low price is due to pets and how easy it is to obtain a hacked client which pretty much make you immortal when you aren't playing the game drunk or being hit by lag spikes). Anything that's obtainable in-game is being sold by these websites or by individual players on third-party forums. I see accounts being sold on these websites with maxed 100/100 devine pets (& a crap ton of UTs) all the time and I see people selling thousands of life pots on forums for as low as 20 cents each (these are verified life pot sellers as well, I even bought 16 for the sake of this review).
It's great to have items in-game that require alot of skill and grinding to obtain, but the value these hard-to-obtain items hold completely goes out the window when somebody can just whip out their credit card and buy literally everything thanks to microtransactions and third-party websites.
Despite all of these negatives, I still believe there is one last hope for ROTMG to become great like it once was. If DECA doesn't screw up the Unity remake of the game then I think it could easily redeem ROTMG, bring in alot of new players and even restore the game to it's past 8/10 instead of the 4.5/10 it's hanging it at the moment.

I've waited 4 years for this game to come out.
I was really devastated to find out they succumbed and released it out into the Early-Access, because it was around the time
when Early-Access was getting a lot of love, and only so much hate. This was before stuff like Towns development stopped and stuff, people didn't yet see the trouble in it all.
Well, it came out there, and I played it, along with others. I walked around, I killed things, I did the lame penguin boss fights.
I was unimpressed - Rightly so I would think, it's not fully developed yet, it's not released, I couldn't judge it well in it's state.
I noticed things were getting added by community requests, and this is where I started to shy away from it, I didn't want to see what was gonna be one of my dream games, altered and messed around with by the community - for good or worse.
So I ignore the dev blog from there on out, and waited my extra, I guess two years.
Lo and behold, right there on Steam, it's out.
Let's give this a proper go.
(ignore 30 hours of gameplay, that was with the betas, my actual playtime is no more than 17 hours, also, Steam didn't have enough space for my full review, I trimmed where I could)
The intro to the game is very slow and sluggish, it gives you the basic tools you need to get started, and you start mining away at the surface for goodies and oddities, pretty classic compared to another game of this genre.
I amassed my metals and my tools, made myself new weapons and armors, and got to more killing.
Then your first real quest is to go really deep into the planet, get a certain type of material, and teleport to the "hub" of the game.
Well god damn if that didn't take me forever, it didn't feel that exciting.
After you find out about the hub, you find out you have to mine moons for fuel to jump to
new planets out of your reach. Might sound cool at first, but it gets annoying very fast.
You tend to hop planet to planet mining the next tier of resources, and making stuff, but within
this whole mess, you have to go around to certain planets, and find each of the six races and their civilizations, and go into SCAN mode, and start clicking
around for green highlighted objects, and talk to people, to learn more about them, and eventually get the next Mission to go on.
The Missions are like adventure instances, a pre-made map with an objective and puzzles with monsters all over the place.
They're fun, but after you do a few of em, you just want it to stop. They lose their interest quickly, when the bosses later turn into bullet sponges, few of them are unique with cool fights.
The main storyline itself just felt, too forced. I thought this was sort of a primarily exploration and sandbox based game. Well, multiple aspects and shops etc. are blocked from you, until you progress enough in the storyline, so it feels forced and boring right
off the bat. Normally to me, this would have been fine, but this felt unnecessary and everything else just gets flat because of it.
(It gets really annoying trying to find the proper planets to just scan some more and more)
Onto the gameplay aspects and mechanics, progression in the game is done by crafting. You craft the first tier of armor and weapons, and then you tend to go find new, randomly generated weapons to kick♥♥♥♥♥with, and crafting new toolbenches and armor to go along with
the new materials.
It's a little sad, being that making your own weapons is a waste of time, because all the strong - and unique - ones are all out there in the universe, not on your crafting screen. There's only a few tiers of actual equipment as well, it's very short lived. By 8 hours into the game I had already acquired what seemed to be the best armor out of the materials you find in the game.
Onto the UI of the game, it's just, annoying. I don't feel like it's presented very well, it could have been much cleaner. Opening your inventory always gave me a headache, as it opens right in the damn middle of your screen, blocking your character and things around them.
You can move it around thankfully, but it doesn't maintain that position the next time you open it, so it's just a constant struggle trying to open it up in the field. There's a sort function for it thankfully, but not for chests, which gets very annoying, because
there's simply so much♥♥♥♥♥♥you pick up in the game, that you need to constantly reorganize it all if you're picking it all up.
With chests not being able to be sorted, it just causes you a whole hour of frustration, trying to reorganize it all.
The difficulty of the game is modest. When you make your character, you have the choice of Casual, Survival or Hardcore.
Casual has no real penalties for dying, you only drop a small percentage of pixels, and you can just walk on back and get right back to it.
Survival seems to be the "normal" difficulty, you need to eat to survive, you drop certain items on death, and you drop more pixels.
Hardcore is Survival, included that, when you die once, you're dead forever.
In the end, I honestly just felt stupid for playing Survival, my other friends just chose casual because, having to keep up with food all the time just sounded like an annoying chore. It really was. I would constantly just be chowing down whatever I found to keep my meter
happy, and the drop items on death penalty just made it all the while more boring.
There's a lot of other little attractions here and there, you can own a farm, and make shipments (homage to Harvest Moon I would assume), there's
a Pokemonlike capturing system for pets. Upgrades to your ship along with crew. Vehicles to ride around in (though, no promised mech sadly), little challenge rooms out in the world.
They're neat, though ultimately, I never gave em a chance. I got my hotrod and rode around and that was that.
Sadly, there's a lot of bugs in the game, more than I was betting on. Food sometimes became infinite, planets generated too slowly for me to traverse, and I've had the game crash on me and freeze several times when I'm just moving about.
The FPS however, takes the cake. It would CONSTANTLY keep dropping and screwing up, I looked around and tried the fixes people suggested, and
to no avail, and I typically don't have technical issues with games on my end, so this was a huge concern of mine.
Dropping to 30 frames when just walking around, really sucks.
Graphicly/Aesthetically, it's awesome, and the soundtrack is amazing along with it. Good listening in and out of game.
All in all, at the end of the day, the game feels like it's just a bit of a repetitve cycle with no clear reward at the end. Hop from planet to planet, hoping to find something cool next time, and get annoyed that you have to keep mining fuel to continue on. I beat the game, and it just didn't feel satisfying in the least.
I've felt like I haven't covered enough about the game, but at the same time, I can feel (and see) that I've written too much already.
I don't feel like this game is a worthy spirtual successor to Terraria, as some would like to claim. I had that notion back when it was in
development, but no more. I just see this as another blotch on my game list that I want removed.
If you read through and at one point just said "but there's a mod for X" or "wait for an update". Then no, and no.
The player shouldn't have to resort to mods to fix an issue, and I've done plenty of waiting, I thought one of the points of the beta
was so they COULD fix things, and polish it all up. Sadly, it still feels quite raw and buggy, and just not worth my investment. I don't
want to wait around longer for things to get better - That was suppose to be now.
I dunno if the wait was really worth it is what I'm getting at.
tl;dr This is a one way trip out into space. Wether you want to stay up there, or land somewhere else, well, you might get displeased either way.

You are but one person in a game of 15 players, each belonging to a faction and having a unique ability, but you don't know who's who. The "good" faction starts out with the big majority, and must decide who is bad and must be lynched before the bad guys kill them all at night. You have to use your ability to your advantage, figure out who's on your team and who you have to lynch. Or if you're bad, you already know your team and must decide who to kill each night lest they rat you out.
Most of the time you'll die early because you get shot at night (if you're a good role) or discovered and lynched (if you're an evil one), but if you manage to make it to the endgame alive, it becomes an incredibly exciting game to see who can team up and outsmart the other players in order to secure that sweet, sweet victory.
Town of Salem was indeed one of my favourite games to play. I bought the game on Steam because I thought the devs deserved it for making such a good game, and I wanted to show them my support.
Well, all those feelings are gone now.
Long story short, Blank Media Games has made a whole slew of controversial changes to the game in Patch 2.0 and onwards, such as the DLC which is TWICE as expensive as the base game, and removing the Spy's legacy ability which is now monopolized by a bad role. A lot of serious players have left the game because these changes ruin the dynamic of the game. And now, most of the player base is now full of cheaters using multiple accounts and jokers who can't/won't play the game seriously. And in a game where you face off against 14 other people each session, good luck having a game where people are actually sensible.
You have vigilantes accurately killing mafia members with all 3 shots on nights 2, 3, and 4 (the earliest nights they can shoot) and without any suspicion raised. You have games where someone who was resurrected (i.e. a confirmed town member) gets majority-lynched, and proven jokers/evil roles don't get lynched even with 8-10 people still alive (and no, there were no vamps and 3 of the mafia were already in the graveyard). You have games where the jailor randomly executes people and doesn't keep any last will (there's no forger), nor do the town investigatives. You have games where people leave in droves, leaving up to a third of the town dead on day 2. And in most if not all of the games, the only town chat that happens is other people spamming or talking trash, while others are completely silent, not even talking to their teammates as they randomly vote or perform night actions.
I am also leaving the game, possibly for good. Every game is basically an internal rage fest for me now, and I don't see how I can play a proper game anymore. Not just because of the changes the devs made per se, but more significantly the kind of people they're letting into the game, and conversely the people they're chasing away. The devs are only interested in money now, they aren't interested in the player base that actually made the game fun in the first place.

This game is amazing and gorgeous.  The crafting system takes a lil while to get used to becuz you basiacally have to pile all your resources together on the ground to see what items you can craft fom them.  It's actually kinda neat compared to the basic crafting slots method other games use.  It does take a while to learn all the "recipes" if you will, but they're are easy to figure out if you use a lil common sense.
Then there are the beautiful sunrises and sunsets, as well as working at night by nothing more than the moonlight coming thru the trees.  Some days are foggy and others have crystal clear skys.  The ocean water is so clear and blue that you can spear fish from the shoreline, but beware of the occasional shark that swims into the shallows to investigate you.
There is essentially no HUD, other than a small reticule, and if you want to monitor your health, hunger, and thirst, you have to look at your watch which also tells you the time of day and temperature.  The inventory is very small, only 8 slots, but things stay on the ground where you drop them.  This makes sense though because no one can carry 50 rocks and 100 sticks and so on.  It limits you to carrying the amount that any normal person could carry in real life.
Basically, this game is an outstanding survival game, located on a small island all your own, with limited resources, and enviromental dangers that you must avoid.  You get one life and if you die, you start all over on a new island.  This game is very fun and for an early access game, very functional.  There are still things to come such as an end-game where you actually get rescued.  Right now you can just explore, craft, and survive as long as possible, which is a challenge in and of itself as you'll find out.

The concept is sound you have one monster card and you move it around a set arena to defeat the opponent with flanking and cornering. Your deck of 40 cards is made up of spell, weapons, interuptions, etc to add a intense battle experience. But the concept I apprechiated the most about this game is its sheer connection with the player. Let me explain. When playing TCG's or RPG's we gain the most connection when we create the character. For TCG's its deck types. We connect with a type of most or style and make it our own. In RPG's we like to place ourselves in the role of character going on adventures. This game ( be it very little at the moment) dose both. You create a deck to your play style and pick a monster that fits you, but then the game takes it a step further and allows to to alter that creatures apearance. This may seem a small thing but to those of us who watch animes like Digimon or Dragon Drive where you have one monster and thats all you get. This little step allows the player to connect to their "Drako" making it yours. As of right now there are only 6 Drakos in the game but every part from wings, to wing color, to claws, to horns can be changed. This game is only starting out and there are issues with translations but I for one am going to see it through and hope this game can pick itself up and stand tall with the big name TCG's.

Drakerz is definitly a NEW type of card game, not just because it can be played in augmented realty (which is optional), but also because the machanics of the game are something never before seen (Or at least that I have have seen) in a card game and trust me I have played a lot of TCGs. Its all about your one Drako, your monster, your pet, your friend who you try to keep alive in battle. Theres no giant clutter of monsters on the feild that you have to keep track of, just one. The way you play is by moving your Drako across the battle feild, where you have to think very tacticaly on positioning and keeping your resource (Mana) in check to use special move against your enemy.
Now remember this game is still pretty new and it was made in a different country so of course there are going to be some issues, but that dosent mean you should walk away from the game. The team working on this game are actually doing their best to improve the game for others and are always answering questions so dont be afraid to ask too if you get a weird problem accuring.
Drakerz is definitly a game worthy of looking at if you like card games, or even stratagy games and even if you dont it might have some aspects or simplisty that any gamer would like. The best part is that you can play for free with the virtual starter pack and three free drako they give you, even if you go against people who have bought cards you still have a chance to beat them like I have. The cards you get are actually really good and the other cards you can get from the campaign mode only make your deck better. GIVE THIS GAME A CHANCE and if you already left it, GIVE IT ANOTHER CHANCE. I cannot even properly describe how much fun this game can be. Its totally worth it.

I myself had no major problems on Windows 8.1, though I'm reading reviews of problems on Windows 10 and some of the other newer OSes.   One fix I found, and this applies to GTA Vice City and San Andreas as well, is to ENABLE Vsync.  The games aren't really meant to be played at today's ridiculously high framerates, and as such, this can fix a lot of timing and control related issues.
But if you can get it to run, just, holy crap.  There is elegance in this game's design and relative simplicity compared to the later entries that makes it enthralling like few other games out there.  IMHO, it still holds up extremely well, even compared to it's sequels.
Even if this game doesn't work, you can ask Steam for a refund, then use that money to get the PS2 version for like $2 new on Amazon or something.  It won't be AS good as this version, but it'll still be an amazing experience.  So yes, I recommend this game.

Great game. Reminds me of the old, good Settlers games. It does not have as deep supply chain and upgrade mechanics like Settlers had, but it keeps you busy all the time by introducing other factors into the game. Season changes take big part of the gameplay. In Summer you need to stockpile your food and wood supplies for the upcoming harsh Winter. In Winter your clan burn those supplies really quickly and your military troops are less efficient and more valuable during that time*. Many different random events: blizzards, sickness, wildlife, mystic creatures, earthquakes that pose fire hazard. All of those random events can effectively affect your strategy and prosperity of your clan. So far I played about 11 hours in Single Player mode which is basically a Skirmish mode. I really enjoyed it. Game is hard, especially for new comers. Currently there is no advanced tutorial, only some basic tooltips. So I advice to start playing on larger maps with less opponents for the beginning. Game is planned to release sometime in February 2018 and will add Campaign mode and dedicated server for Multilayer mode. Can't wait till they add new goodies to the game. Hopefully more Single Player stuff. I read on forums they might add mod support at some point after release as well.
I rarely buy Early Access games, but this was a good decision.
I highly recommend this game for any Settlers or city/village building game fan.
* - Some clans get military buffs instead of debuffs during the winter.

I'm not a "gamer", but look how many hours I've played. I've never been so obsessed with a game. A game you play so much MUST have lots of commendable aspects to it. If I could, however, I'd both recommend and not recommend this game. Instead, I shall say that it's highly recommended but with some severe caveats, and that my abundant hours of play reflect an intoxicating concoction of amazing (partially realized) potential, pathologic addiction, and an intense frustration that causes you to keep coming back to "avenge" yourself and make the game into the amazing experience it promises to be.
I love the fact that the combat is turn-based, allowing for careful consideration of each action, in contrast to the frenzied 3D mess of many other games. I love the fact that the game revolves around a small number of individuals with their own stats, as opposed to generic "units". I love the process of building up the characters and the company from scratch, one step at a time. But it consumes FAR too much time and forces you to take on too many monotonous contracts, fight too many battles against irritating opponents/terrain, and make too many monotonous journeys across the map to sell loot for the best price at one location, buy new supplies for the best price at another location, treat injuries at yet another, and there encounter new opportunities to grind a tiny bit of extra experience and renown. Contracts and battles, instead of being special, flavoursome affairs, become burdensome chores, taken on just to make your company build a little less slow. With just a little impatience, it's easy for hours and days of meticulous planning to be wiped out, but the attractive aspects of the game suck you in so that you endure the tedious and enraging ones.
The best battles are not easy slaughter-fests, nor irritating affairs against inhumans using magic or trickery, nor stupid ones on terrain that forces the sides to fight in single file. The best battles are tense, evenly-matched bloodbaths that, in the context of the rest of the game (i.e. slow levelling and the need to keep taking contracts), are imprudent to fight owing to the likelihood of injuries and casualties. If levelling didn't demand several real days of continual play, you could make the game revolve around big, exciting, high-risk but high-reward events, not an incessant stream of small errands.
The best battles are those fitting the term "gritty medieval", but you don't get to bask for long in the light (or dark) of this realm. Soon you are forced into a high-medieval, high-fantasy arms race to acquire shining Arthurian armour, magical equipment, and perks to make you almost immune to getting hit or hurt.
The best battles are ones in which ardour and durability can tip the balance, but the RNG-rich nature of the game (and the fact that you have to ignore most stats at each level) means that it is prudent to largely disregard these things for most characters. Instead, the game practically forces you to use a sergeant. You end up with fragile ninjas in suits of scale armour, who want to run away whenever they're scratched, but who continually venture forth into throngs of orc warriors because the sergeant (probably hiding in the bushes) keeps blowing a trumpet to "inspire" them to face the dangers that he so carefully avoids himself.
It is astonishing how often all of your troops miss with hit chances in the 60-80% range, while your enemies pull off a miraculous succession of damaging hits with chances in the 5-30% range. Your perception of the AI being lucky is not "biased", since you never play so as to have low hit chances, and never get to experience the opposite scenario.
There was a time when you had more practical liberty to function as an adventurer, exploring the map, picking suitable targets, amassing loot to sell, ignoring boring contracts. Now, you get less loot and food supplies have limited durability, so that it is almost impossible to function without eternally recurring errands. A plus is that you can now attack caravans and patrols, but the other restrictions (and the fact that every settlement is now tied to a noble house with abundant billhooks and heavy crossbows at command) make this less viable than it would have been before.
The new "ambitions" also take away from the free, adventuring feel from earlier incarnations of the game. You are forced to accept one of only a few options, or sometimes only a single "option". Sometimes, acceptable options that were present before are removed. Some options are presented to you after the conditions have already been met (e.g. "professional" renown), and you just walk a short way down the road before it's "fulfilled". Your troops are such simpletons that their mood automatically improves just because the company met an objective that was imposed on it. It seems so artificial.
The same goes for the "end game" crises, which attempt to impose an artificial "goal" and "resolution" upon the game. That's not how medieval conflicts work. There's never any clear beginning or end, and no clear boundary between one cluster of confrontations and another. Opportunities for freelancing are ever-present. You don't "win" or "lose"; you just stay alive until you die, and hope to have as much adventure and enjoyment as you can in the mean time.
Your "reputation" is displayed alongside your company "renown" and is only affected by a few rare events. No matter how consistently "kind" you've been within a campaign, however, you have to sell out and partake in the mistreatment of peasants, deserters etc. in order to serve the interests of a noble house and thus "win" the relevant end-game crisis.
Some people (probably "gamers") seem to be obsessed with games being framed by "goals", which end up restricting the degree to which you can use your imagination to concoct your own purposes as you proceed. They think that the degree to which you enjoy a game is determined simply by how much you win or lose, which in turn is determined simply by how "skilfully" you play (rather than by how narrowly you play to hit/damage things and not get hit/damaged - an approach that takes all the excitement out of each new level). In reality, the most enjoyable way to play involves more risk and more dramatic tension than you get if you play in the most prudent way, but this way is also more frustrating, since the game forces you to face those risks so often (with so little economic reward) that it's hard to recover and rebuild. In other words, the most enjoyable way to play is when you try to be a hero and NOT a corporate executive.
Comparing the final game to the 0.6.0.21 version ("old version"), my feelings are that the earlier, less "complete" version was about as enjoyable to play. Both have their pros and cons.
The 0.6.x version already had the opening tutorial (time consuming and artificial), and the new world map with ports (a plus), but it still had the old perk tree, and specific injuries (treatable at temples) were not introduced till 0.7.x. "Ambitions", end-game crises and training experience were late additions. The new world map and in-town graphics are impressive, but I also feel nostalgic for the bright green maps, narrow long rivers and masses of forest from the 0.5.x versions. Until quite late, maps were bigger with more mysterious space for exploration between settlements, so that travel did not become stale so soon. The new perk tree is less restrictive and has some exciting new options, but some exciting old ones were removed, and weapon specialism meant that some great game-long utility weapons (e.g. scramasaxes) were degraded into low-grade precursors to other weapons. Injuries add realism and flavour but also more monotonous micro-managerial chores.
Make no mistake: there IS (and already WAS) a lot of greatness in this game. Just beware of the caveats. Play it the way that brings you enjoyment, not necessarily the way it's "meant" to be played.

This is a 3rd person GTA style game with martial arts combat thrown into the mix. The story takes place in Hong Kong and has a strong Asian theme throughout the game, triad gangs with their codes and beliefs, art style, cars, martial arts and lots of food.
You play as a undercover police officer, and a former triad member returning back from USA to Hong Kong, China. Game story evolves mostly around police, you and triads, their constant battle for power. There are lots of side activities, in form of racing, helping people with problems, busting drug deals, stealing vehicles, assassination's, random dating, etc.
There are a lot of collectibles in game, some give you cash, some unlock clothes, melee moves and vehicles, others boost your health. Game plays like any GTA style game, but with some added elements. You can steal and drive cars, bikes, boats (no aircraft), you can shoot firearms, use melee weapons.
A lot of killing in the game is done through martial arts melee combat. You unlock moves, perks, abilities by spending points acquired by doing missions and collecting certain collectibles. I really enjoyed the story, it has many twists and unexpected moments.
Game looks and plays well, there are some low resolution textures here and there, even with high texture DLC pack. Character animations, control was good and easy to use. I really liked voice acting, it didn't have that cheap feel you get in other games where Asian characters are voiced with fake accents. There are some elements of gore in game, that may be unpleasant and not advised for those of under age.

The worlds you encounter are beautiful.  Theres a ton of cool stuff to find if you just explore a little.  You can spend $15 on worse things.

Seriously devs - if you're not goign to develop a character, don't name them or give any impression that you will!  During beta, when there werent' any characters like the old lady, it was easier to focus your attention on the exploration and charm of the world environments.  Having characters with no development just draws attention to their emptyness.
Additional thoughts: The inventory UI is still absolute♥♥♥♥♥♥ Hunger meter drops way too fast, making the mechanic an annoying distraction; Early quests lack flow from one to the other; MM & tech upgrading is poorly explained; action bar usage is not explained (left/right hand equips); The whole game could benefit from a professional writer or storyteller being added to the team.

"b" Is a game changer. It's a life changing experience. I can't look back and say I will ever be the same individual I was before clicking "Play Game" on the store page. "b" Is the greatest computer program on this planet. It's not a game. It's not a story, It's an experience. You write your own story as you traverse the unknown lands as your protagonist, named b. The landscape you traverse is covered with flowers, trees, and you can even encounter a few ladybugs. The soothing music matches the idea of this game being your trancendence to a higher state of existence. As you fly through this world you start to ask questions; "Why are there only ladybugs?" "Why Is this place so barren of predators?" "Where am I?" "Why is this place untouched by humanity?" All these questions you must answer yourself. Personally, I have concluded the game is a metaphor that us as humans are not pure. We are a cancer on this planet and beings like b trancend to the holy land, the place we only dream of uncovering and taking for our own, eventually corrupting it with our factories, and pollution, and other means to make profit out of it. This game teaches us a lesson; We must go back to the primal ages. We must forsake all of our technologies and go back to the times when peace existed. We must uncover the ways to trancend into b-hood.  Someday, maybe the world will go back, and we will be able to go and experience this utopia that "b" shows us, but until then we must suffer and endure the punishment we have earned for disgracing the world and forcing the pure beings such as b into a new plane of existance.

It is these two goals that make b the juggernaut that it is. See, b is an adventure game, but it’s not the kind of adventure game you’ve come to expect. Sure, you’ll need to figure out how to get a flower working and how to distract ladybugs here and there, but the real draw here is a “choose your own adventure.”
As you play through the five episodes, the big moments come when you choose how Barry Benson responds to situations and what he says in conversations with his fellow insects. Choices and dialogue pop up on screen with timers, and you have seconds to pick exactly what you’re going to do or say. Whereas previous adventure games from developer would let you run through every possible line of dialogue, that isn’t the case here. In b, you choose, and the game moves on – adapting its story to each decision.

You need the knife to get started so I had to end it. My second play through which I am currently in is going pretty well. It's not too hard to survive yet but than again I have only been in for a half hour. I just eat and drink coconuts and eat potatos. I have not ventured into the water yet because I am deadly afraid of sharks in real life. So for me this is Deepest Fear Simulator 2015. Other than that the game is pretty good! Not a whole lot of features but It is pre-alpha. Still a fun game with amazing physics and a great physical crafting mechanic.
PROS
----------
Graphics - 8.5/10 The graphics are pretty amazing for an indie game. I know they plan to improve so im sure it will be a 10/10 soon enough! Reminds me of "The Forest" graphics... not to compare the two.
Crafting - 8/10 Not too much to craft but hey.. its just pre-alpha.
Environment - 9/10 Seriously makes me think of Tom Hanks. I found a "DeadEx" package on my island so I will keep it until I find the woman in the farmhouse that creates things out of metal when I become saved.
Gameplay - 9/10 Fun game so far, just needs more features. Which as I have said before is because it is a pre-alpha game. I have nothing but high hopes for this game and I believe the developers will achieve them.
Now im not a usual reviewererer so im not sure if i covered all of the normal category's but I tried my best!!
As for CONS
----------------
Nothing too bad about this game. You have to cut it some slack because it is a pre-alpha game. So as far as a Con list goes I really don't have anything to say. Maybe add in a tutorial so you can prevent idiots like me from trying to bash rocks together hahah.
Now getting to the bottom line.. Should you buy this game? In my opinion yes you should. But keep in mind that it is extremely early in its release. There isn't much to build but there is plently to explore. It's a survival game so it isnt going to be easy. So if you are not patient and if you didnt like games like "The Forest" or "Rust" than probably don't pick this one up. But overall in my own personal opinion I think it is worth a buy. Maybe wait a couple months though if you dont want to get it in such an early state.
Thanks for reading! Like I said this is a first serious review for me!

In the short span of 5.7 hours and over 20 matches I've come to review this Early Access game.
In summary I'd suggest this to any Veteran of RTS games but I wouldn't really do to someone who's pretty new to it or have yet to learn since they might just ragequit from the fact of always getting Resource Shortages, beating themselves up over getting left behind by mere AI and so on.
For a Early Access game like this that's already brimming with potential I have much to hope for.

Okay first of all the Pros of this game are:
- It's Challenging to a degree
- I think Veteran players of RTS would like it
- It's quite simple and easy to understand but requires a ton of management skills
- The Clan diversity can promote playstyles
- Units are very flexible
And the Cons:
- Each game you might (will) suffer from Resource Shortage. Disregarding Winter effects. It might or will happen in most matches. The cause is the second con I'll mention
- Your game can easily turn for the worse the moment you see the layout of your vicinity, so every match is quite a gamble. ie, Getting the first few areas be littered with enemies or enemy spawn areas, No viable source of Food leading to a shortage faster, etc.
- The level of management for this RTS isn't something a newbie can handle easily and might or will pose a challenge. So I believe it might turn off some playerbase because it might be a little too challenging for them, the same way I had after a few matches on Low and Medium Difficulty and even more on Hard. But if you do have a level of comprehension you should be able to figure out how to manage it properly, since I've said before the units are Flexible.
- Clans are diverse and could lead to a playstyle a player might like but I feel it lacks more impact. I guess it's good and bad, because it can lead the player on how to play but not enforcing it as it is the only way to play in a certain Clan. I only wish it would give an even more distiguishable impact on gameplay. A good example would be the Boar Clan and its Lore efficiency.
- Military Units are too straightforward and simple. It is easier to create a Warband considering how simple they are but it's incredibly boring seeing that's the only units there are.
- Valkyries are a force to be reckoned with. Valkyries are a special type of Field Enemy unit that's incredibly strong. And they are a lot harder than conquering an enemy Clan. So I believe it could use some tuning because so far, a Valkyrie is an equivalent of 1 Legendary Unit in your Warband and you will likely face more than 3 Valkyries at a single area in most matches.
That's all I can say for now. If you find my review useful, thank you. I'm quite new to this genre so I'm looking at this from a newbie's perspective and I had to confirm each Pros and Cons I had for this game every match before I made the review.

The environment is much more interesting and feels far more alive than the Mojave and the Capitol Wasteland. The Commonwealth is a joy to explore, and since you need parts for your settlements and power armor, you will be doing ALOT of exploration. Which combined with the combat, is where this game shines.

This is a quite short but challenging game, a minimalist rhythm platformer, where simple geometrical shapes are enough to hook up any player for a few, fun hours.
It feels, initially, like a conceptual game: there's hardly any text, no storyline and every single component in the game, be it stage hazards, enemies and even the player, is represented by a simple solid shape. However, as you play through the first minutes, you notice how much polish went into this game: there are puzzles, platforming hazards and even bosses, all set to some pretty cool electronic music, which requires you to constantly pay atention to what you're hearing, in addition to what you're seeing. The platforming is also very well done: the controls are tight and it's rewarding to advance through the levels, and when you die, you don't feel cheated or tricked by poor controlling or programming - you really feel like you've missed something, which entices you to try again, maybe paying more attention to the background music, maybe trying to watch the patterns of the stage more carefully.
All in all, it's a fun, solid game, which, if you're into platforming, will guarantee you a few hours of entertaining.

If you love Fallout for its RPG aspect, then watch out, your character has a well defined back story written into the game, not a whole lot of quests have alternate endings, and Fallout 3's dialog system of several choices with some opened up because of your high intelligence, or high explosives skill for example have been stripped from the game and replaced with a more Bioware style dialog wheel that essentially has the good guy option, the neutral guy option and the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ option with a fourth option which is usually a question of some sort. The skill system is gone entirely and instead everything is dependant on your special skills which this time start low and must be increased during a level up, the same way that skills have worked in the past. Basically this game is barely an RPG.
The gun play has improved so much and there are so many features and things to do in the game. While there is less replay value than in past fallout games, I did a fallout 3 content in 60 hours, including all DLC. Fallout 4 has taken me 144 hours to do everything except for The DLC. So you don't have to replay it, for those that aren't super hard core there will always be adventures left to be had. The characters are much more fleshed out and more interactive than before as well. The game allows you to slowly bond with your companions over time and implementing an approval/disapproval system that is also seen in many Bioware titles. The world is so dense with content and so much of it is done so well, like the silver shroud quest, there might be fewer quests when compared to a game like skyrim but what is offered is so much more deep and well written.

Battle Brothers is a most excellent blend of, to my experience, The Elder Scrolls: Arena, Darklands and XCOM, and even NEO Scavenger. To me, it is like a mix and blend of some great aspects.
It has strategical features, as well as explorative features. It is in a very early state, so there isn't very much to do (thus, The Elder Scrolls: Arena). Quests get repetitive and the Rogue-like aspects shortly wares off as your party grows in strength.
It is an Early Access title with immense potential, and thus, it deserves all support it can get.
I can't wait to see where Battle Brothers will be a year from now (I also can't wait to see a Battle Maidens Expansion & a Battle Band sequel could bring to the table).
What does it lack, currently, in my opinion?
- More Events, there's countless patrols traveling the world, and an immense potential for thousands of various events happening depending on situation, environments, consequences. Tolls. Reputation. Alignments and Factions. More "Story" or "Narrative" content that the Player can bounce their Band with. Quests are primitive, similarly to Ultima (1) and TES: Arena.
- Caravan "Follow Command", during world map exploration.
- A NEO Scavenger or Project Zomboid Injury system, with added Armor system.
- Crusader Kings" & "Games of Thrones" themed aspects. Factions, alignments, different seats and crowns and shield bands. Intrigues, start as a mercenary band, gain reputation, fame, become a regent, a king, a ruler and so on and forth.
- Relevant or Mirrored Map backgrounds (Fighting inside a city, with Civilians and structures running about). Thus far, Battle Brothers succeeds in delivering a picture of Road-, Forest-, Marsh, -Snow and other basic types of outdoor environments, but lacks in some "city defense" scenarios.

Starbound is a confusing game.  On one hand it has a huge variety of planets, landscapes, blocks, enemies, food, cosmetics, etc.  It's beautiful and a lot of care and a LOT of artists did a ton of impressive work.  You have a spaceship and you can get crew and you can do quests for NPCs and you can catch pets and there's just a very broad set of stuff.
But underneath the pretty art, everything is very shallow.  The differences between planets and landscapes and blocks are largely cosmetic.  All food is basically the same, the enemies are mostly the same dumb "run straight at you" clods, the weapons are almost entirely randomly-generated (and mostly worthless).
The UI itself is extremely primitive in irritating ways: no map, no minimap, no "stack to chests".  You can only place items with the inventory up and the inventory places itself in the middle of the screen directly on top of what you're looking at, so you have to drag it out of the way every time.  You have to eat food in order to regenerate health, but food only lasts a minute or two and it doesn't stack and you can't eat it out of your inventory so every few minutes you have to drag it to your quickbar again, eat it, close inventory.  Over and over, irritating you constantly.
Play more Terraria instead.

Pros:
Good game, lots of fun and a refreshing take on 'open world' GTA-like game. The story has a good sense of itself, in that you see Wei's decisions have gravity and it plays on his internal conflict. Characters are likeably (Jackie, Winston, and Peggy...just to name a few...) And the ending was nice and dramatic and fit well for the build up, felt very epic fight scene-esque. Combat (hand to hand) was great! and the bullet time really helped with (adding epicness) and the inexact feel of the gun control (but i kind of liked this because i think it was meant to portray a gun restricted hong kong). Including the mechanics of lockpicking, bugging, drug busts, taking photos were all novel to me and I enjoyed that little bit, they were well thought out-some may hate this because they do basically just add trivial time sinks into actions.
I've played a lot of this game on ps3 and then I replayed it on PC because I really do enjoy these sort of games. The story is much much better than GTA and feels like it has a real purpose aside from blowing everything up. I think thats an improvement to having such an openworld because you're actually driven to see the next part of the plot and intrigue or whatever. Music was fitting, and the car music was pretty good too with a wide range of genres-this may seem trivial, but im just pointing it out as a way to demonstrate that the studio really put in time and thought into the details.
Cons:
my god, terrible terrible pc port. keyboard controls are unintuitive, clunky, and not nearly as natural or fluid as with a controller. Use a controller. It was sort of annoying to be penalized for running into fences or parking meters and not getting full 'cop' xp for that one mission but I get that it's part of the true crime theme, and adds ~replayability~ but eh. Driving controls needs some improvement. And that karaoke minigame was just ridiculous. Also animation times for getting health upgrades, opening lockboxes and essentially doing any of the upgrade/bonus content were way too long. Doing side missions and earning face xp was pretty laborious-I only really did them because I wanted that shiny new motorcycle/car, but I do have to give it to them that *some* of the side mission were memorably and funny but eh. Oh also, never play the poker mini game, you will lose thousands-the House always wins: you'll have a winning hand, and then in the last round your oppnent will just pull out a last ditch win, but your mileage may vary.

I bought
partially because of its art style, but more because it was being billed as a puzzle game.
As a work of minimalist art,
may well be among the top 10% of games on Steam (though I suppose that's not saying much with con-artists like Digital Homicide on the loose). As a puzzle game, however, Niko not only falls short of the mark, but it drops the arrows before even drawing back the bowstring.
As you'll note, I've only played 35 minutes of this game. Those 35 minutes were enough to tell me that the developer doesn't seem to know very much about puzzle design. Let me spoil the first three levels for you (apparently the developer's packed the game with a good 18 of them, so I should think this to be acceptable spoiler-wise).
First, a few technical notes. Apparently, the resolution in the config tool is the resolution of the *window* containing the game, and the resolution in-game is the resolution the game runs at. Tabbing out doesn't pause the game (I think this is a quirk of Unreal), unlike Unity games. Apparently people have some trouble with save files, and there isn't a level select menu, but I'll be damned if I'm opening up the game again. One thing I will note is that it hasn't overheated my computer (unlike some 3D-, even a few 2D-games), so at least it's optimized reasonably well.
Anyway, having gotten somewhat annoyed at the resolution fiasco that I had when I initially started up the game, I entered the first level. I immediately noted that the walking speed was very slow, and combined with the lack of a "run" button, this indeed is a "walking simulator". Slow walking in video games tends to annoy me, due to the fact that I only have so much time in my life, and putting a slow walk when you could up the walking speed is literally just wasting the player's time.
But puzzles. The first level contains two puzzles; the first one involves looking around the map to find four symbols, and their order. These symbols are etched onto four stones, each one having either one to four markers below it. However, each marker has a different orientation, but the orientation is irrelevant to the actual puzzle. Apparently the puzzle creator likes red herrings?
Having found these four symbols, I proceeded to four buttons that were in a row, in the corresponding order. But the annoying thing is that these four symbols were *just* far enough apart that I had to move the character to click each one. This annoyance could easily have been solved by putting the buttons closer together or by increasing the range of interaction of the character.
The second puzzle in the level is somewhat akin to a simplified Rubik's Cube. No real complaints here, actually
Between the second level's start and the puzzle, there is a really long path that you have to walk down at the snail's pace that you walk, for apparently no reason at all other than to pad out the game, just like how I'm adding irrelevant information to this particular sentence in the review just to pad it out. Not even
(sorry, "
" Match) or Rolling Shapes did this!
But anyway, the second level's puzzle? A maze. Mazes are solvable in log-time, so I don't at all consider these puzzles. But it gets worse; you can actually circumvent this maze by just walking on the thin ledge around the maze, and get to the exit.
Suppose, however that you do decide to enter the maze like I did. You can't reach the exit that easily, because the gamedev put in what can best be described as "slot machines" in the maze with spinning wheels with symbols on them. You have to input the symbols into the machine by stopping each wheel when the correct symbol lines up with the small circle on each one.
I say "correct" because each slot machine requires a different combination of symbols. Which is fed to you right on the adjacent wall.
So in short, this isn't even a puzzle. It's literally a skill test considering the speed at which the wheels spin. And you have to do this with three different machines, in sequence.
And when you do exit the maze and see the level exit, you might just walk towards it... and fall to your doom because you didn't think to jump over that tiny little gap. So you have to do the whole level all over again. Something tells me this game wasn't playtested.
The third level involves lots of water and resurfacing for air. The only thing I would call a puzzle in this level is underwater, really large, and easy, and is made much more annoying by the fact that you have to keep resurfacing for air halfway through solving. Then after this, there's a section where you have to pull four levers and spin a wheel three times all without resurfacing, because the first lever raises the water level to remove the air in the chamber. You can't un-pull the first lever after it's pulled, dying from lack of air just restarts you a long way away, and the fact that you can't even descend directly downwards in a narrow passage makes it seem like there's not enough time to get to the wheel to turn it three times. This is where I gave up, as there was no feedback of "you can't un-pull this lever" when I tried it (making me think I hadn't aligned the reticle correctly).
With regards to art, I do like the minimalist surrealist style (though it doesn't appeal to me quite as much as, say,
or
). There are drawings on some walls that seem to reveal some sort of a narrative about a child growing up and falling off a cliff, but given that I gave up during the third level, I honestly can't say more about this.
I'm a staunch believer in gameplay before aesthetics, and this sort of game is why. Nobody is going to care about your game's narrative if they give up playing because the gameplay is too annoying. Get the gameplay right first, THEN you can think about making your game pretty!
In short, a very much un-playtested piece of art masquerading as a puzzle game. For the price of 7 GBP? Not worth it at all; I would hesitate to even play this for free. While this game is no Flow Match or Rolling Shapes and doesn't deserve a place in my "POS" category, you will get much, MUCH more enjoyment for the same price from Linelight, another minimalist puzzler with abstract narrative, instead.

I love this game. This was my "Game of the Year" for 2012. I genuinely believe that if this were just a tiny bit better, it could have been considered a masterpiece.
Controls are solid, responsive, and the game has plenty to do. Whether it's chasing down dudes from another triad with your sports car - SMG's and pistols spitting hot lead in all directions, or it's smashing a thug's head into a car door, or even slapping a hobo with a fish, this game does not stop being entertaining. There are tons of challenges for one to do - including ones such as races, illegal fighting rings, and even chicken fights.
The city of Hong Kong has never looked so good. At night, the neon lights glow bright, and are complimented by the game's graphical abilities. I'm not very "tech-savvy" (sorry to use that term), but Sleeping Dogs looks stunning, and runs well even on my somewhat old and under-powered setup.
There are very few games that have made me both laugh, and become visibly upset. This is one of them. I don't usually care this much for somebody who doesn't exist. This may sound stupid, but Sleeping Dogs hits true to heart when it needs to, and it will hit
.
Go buy this game (technically, go buy the Definitive Edition, since the original version isn't available on Steam anymore).

If Steam limited reviews to be only one word, I would say that this game is 'beautiful'. Surroundings, soundtrack, artwork, level design and everything about this game is an aesthetic pleasure. There were a lot of times I found myself not caring about the puzzles and simply idling with enjoying the atmosphere the game has to offer.
Puzzle mechanics are quite unique and it never gets repetitive. 18 levels feel like 18 different worlds that you encounter and get through with playing "the dream". Puzzles are not that hard; it only requires a sense of logic with tying things together and you have the "Aha!" moments with several of them.
You are experiencing the conflict between a girl's past and the consciousness with visiting the events that had happened in her past, from which some of them are not very pleasant. Though the devs kept the story part rather obscure and left it up to translation of the player, which is no less than I would expect with such a surreal game.
Pursuing and getting the achievements were also quite the satisfaction. I can say that this is one of the few games that didn't make me complain with starting all over for the missing achievements.
Overall, this game is a hidden gem among the other well-known first person puzzle games. It lacks the love and the attention it deserves in my opinion. With appreciating the developers, I highly recommend this game.

Northgard's trailer video managed to catch me in a way no other game did.
I was so interested in the game and was expecting a moment to buy it. Now I finally did.
The game looks like Civ (happiness, food, gold, wood and science) with a RTS feeling because you have to manage how you allocate each villager.
The game mechanics are great in many aspects:
- You have to manage where you allocate your villagers to get resources
- Harsh winter comes every year and you must plan ahead. You might face a blizzard and it makes things worse. You have to stock food and wood to survive
- Happiness management forces you to keep increasing your territory and constructing new buildings
- Scouting mechanic is fun
- Special area features are nice: relics that a scout must explore, fertile land to farm, stone or silver to gather, wolves, etc
- Battle is simple but still chalenging. It requires micromanagement to survive and falling back to your own territory is a somewhat safe move
Things I feel missing in this game:
- Reasons to come back - the lack of a campaign allows you to play only skirmishes if you're alone and the replay value, although ok, is not awesome
- More races would be a great addition to the game and I believe developers are constantly working on it
- I'd be glad to see a more complex tech tree =D
- Did I mention more races? =P
All in all, if you like Civ and like RTS this is a must buy game, specialy if you have friends to play with! I hope to see more being added to this awesome game!

Long review short: Left 4 Dead is good. Go play it, if you haven't already (which I highly doubt).
Long review long: Left 4 Dead is one of Valve's many titles that is made with the same care and quality they are known to put into a game. Although, to be completely fair, Left 4 Dead is probably my least favorite game by Valve so far.
Left 4 Dead follows a group of 4 humans who have managed to survive the zombie apocalyse and must fight their way through hordes of undead mobs in order to find safety. There's a hardened Vietnam vet, a young girl, a businessman, and a biker who's very obviously faking his masculinity throughout the game. The story and characters are, obviously, not that well fleshed-out (hence why I don't like L4D as much as say... Half-Life or Portal).
What Left 4 Dead is exceptionally good at is co-op zombie killing. The fast-paced action combined with tight FPS controls and multitude of weapons allow for some engrossing, addicting fun. It is designed around you getting online with a group of friends to play together, but since only one of my friends plays this game I decided to make the worst decision possible with Left 4 Dead: I played singeplayer with AI companions.
Now, the AI for the zombies is all well-done and polished. They run wildly at you and go for the first possible route that can lead to them ripping your throats out. But zombie AI is easy. And Valve seriously f***ed up with the ally AI. They're absolutely awful. They stay in the same group and are more of a hindrance than a help to you. I once was on the ground and needed assistance, while all three of my companions stood blindly 5 feet in front of me, staring at each other's feet, until I died right in front of them.
On top of that, the last level "The Sacrifice" is bulsh**. I don't care what anyone else says. I hated the finale. It goes against all intuition that the player has received in the game thus far. When I saw 4 motherf***ing Tanks come out with the hundreds of other zombies, I thought that I'd have to kill them all. It wasn't until I died 5 times that the game explicitly told me to restart the generator, which was an even bigger pain, because the zombies in the area will magnetize themselves to your fleshy body faster than you can say "Oops!". It's just a frustrating last few minutes to an otherwise enjoyable game.
Left 4 Dead is an enjoyable arcade-y zombie game that gives you the tingles whenever you hear the growls of a zombie in the distance, and is both enjoyable and intense to play, which many other zombie games have a tendency to struggle with. I know it's just a simple shooter game, but I still prefer Valve when they actually have stories to tell, but this is stull a fun game. It's worth your money. I'm giving Left 4 Dead a 7/10.

I played Bastion for the first time a few years ago. Now that I've re-played it, I just have to write a positive review about it.
This game is excellent in every possible aspect. The gameplay is fun and extremely adaptable to the player's skill level: if you want to play easy you can just go on with the story without using idols or face challenges, while if you are a completist and look for something more serious you can activate all or few idols (which give enemies various kinds of buffs) and try to beat every proving ground. There's really something for every taste here.
The story is nice and captivating, the kind you appreciate even more when you replay the game a second time. Is incredible with how many details the writers managed to fill the plot considering that everything is narrated by Zulf's voice while you play. Undoubtedly one of the most successful experiments in alternative narration I've ever had the pleasure to play with.
Artistic direction is also really beautiful, the art, the animations, the maps, everything is so polished and detailed that it's simply a pleasure to look at this game running. And the music...is great. Just great.
Really, it's hard to find a flaw in this little masterpiece of indie gaming...Zulf's voice talking over and over can be annoying sometimes, maybe? Honestly it's all I can think of when I ask myself what Bastion's defects are.
What else can I say... hell, just buy this game already. You won't regret it.

I don't normally buy "early access" games, but I made an exception with this game. I definitely got my money’s worth. I bought this game over a three day weekend and dumped hours and hours into it. Following are some the points I like and dislike with this game, which is still an early access game.
-Love the customization of the Battle Brothers, and other RPG elements mixed in with the tactical gameplay.
-Choice of what contracts to take and the ability to drop them (Although a reputation system would be nice. I.e. negative repercussions for dropping a contract. Add a reward system with that. Better the reputation the higher the reward. Maybe even a few contracts that call for unsavory things. All depending on reputation. With this, I also wish the player could be notified of the difficulty of the contract. (Many times I would pick a contract only to see the area I was to raze was rated as impossible.)
- The permanent death of soldiers is a neat take on it since you can easily replace brothers with cannon fodder or with higher quality troops. The only problem is that when your troops die you tend to lose their expensive armor and items. This was supposedly fixed as of 8 September 2015, but I haven’t noticed a difference after multiple character deaths.
- Choice is types of weaponry allow for strategic troop set ups. I like having a shield wall of spearman forming a spear wall. Really satisfying when the AI has no choice but charge the wall. I do wish some more weapons and armor choices were added.
-The only real problem I have with the how the game currently is has to do with how ranged combat takes place. The AI archer will nearly one hit kill my troops with about a 70% accuracy to hit. I find it really frustrating going into a battle with even one archer in the AI’s army. Basically means at least one of soldiers in full armor is going to die in the second round because the AI hardly misses. More than one and you are going to be stuck in a round of retreat and load the auto save and hope for crappy computer rolls until you can make it out with acceptable losses. I’m actually going to stop playing this game until this is fixed. Way too frustrating in its current state.
I do really enjoy this game and would like to continue playing and even donate to help see its completion because I just really enjoy this game. 10/10 would buy again. (Fix the freacking archery! It’s the real reason I’m even doing this review. Please somebody on the development team read this. I just couldn’t besmirch a good game without saying how much I enjoy it because it would give somebody the wrong impression.)
