This might be among the most underrated games I have ever played. Clearly the work of developers who had great ideas, and put them together with care. Deserves much more recognition, especially in the genre of First Puzzle Platformers.
The environments look beautiful, and the soundtrack has many soothing beautiful tunes that in general match the ethereal feeling of the surroundings. The animations might look simplistic, but in no way this hinders the game, or robs it of the soul it has. If anything it seems to show the care the developers had even more. The game is very honest, not pretentious, and that won me over the more I played it, even if I was skeptical about the opening custecene, at first.
Usually games of this genre seem to explore a few mechanics on a large number of puzzles with small variations. This game felt a bit like the opposite, A very large number of mechanics and different patterns scattered in groups of very few, if not unique puzzles that never quite repeated. For me that personally was great, as the game felt like a fun exploration and the experiences always felt fresh. Only two or three puzzles seemed badly designed or "unfair", but that was ok as they were very brief and not repeated exaustively throughout the game.
I think this game belongs with Antichamber, Portal, The Talos Principle, The Witness, and any other First Person Puzzle games, even if it is in some ways more modest (and this is not something bad or to be held against it). It's sad to think a great game like this might not get the recognition it deserves.

This is a summary of my review video, which I encourage you to watch if you are looking for a more in-depth review.
Niko Through the dream proclaims itself to be a first person adventure experience with a puzzle element, but that's not exactly true; there is a lot- A LOT- of platforming throughout this game. I would say 40-60% of the game is platforming; a staggering amount considering there was no mention of platfomring on the games various pages.
The story of the game is supposed to be a narrative experience in a puzzle elemented world; but the narration is not told through vocalization or words, rather relying heavily on the 'dream world' element. It does not do a good job of providing a feeling of connection or emotional suspense. Information about the character and her story is told very abstractly, leaving much to the imagination. I never was able to understand why she was having issues, or even what they were.
How you experience a world through the level design is tied directly into how you enjoy the world, and understand what is happening. Unfortunately instead of walking you through the mechanics one at a time in order to then progress to a more difficult 'puzzle' (platforming element), they are mixed up in difficulty in a nonsensical way. Mechanics are introduced with no warning or time to learn how to use them, instead you are being chased or in a time crunch with no idea how to use the tools you are given. Because you have no clue what to do or no time to figure it out, you have to progress by failure; swimming through tubes without a breath bar, falling off of ledges continuously in order to get a jump perfectly, dying over and over again in order to accomplish the goal. It's not about just figuring out what you need to do, but understanding how to use those mechanics throughout the design. Dying over and over again due to failure in design takes away from the connection to the game, and just adds to the frustration.
The game overall is very lackluster. It doesn't respect your time. The story is vague, and the game drags on with childish puzzles and platforming elements that require many deaths to get through. I cannot recommend this game for it's standing price. If you would like more details on my comments, please watch the video review.

This first-person puzzle game is very atmospheric and tranquil with a unique design, forcing players to choose the correct path to progress. This minimalist game has a major "Wow!" factor and is quite beautiful. The open scenery is jaw-dropping and the puzzles are difficult but fair. The puzzles get harder and harder as the game goes on, leading to the discovery that you have far more power than you once suspected. Discover things you never thought possible and explore a utopian city that feels like a lucid dream!
++
+ Great graphics
+ Astounding sound
+ Fair and unique puzzles
+ Beautiful scenery
+ Flowing animation
+ Easy controls
+ Easy navigation

-+
- No real “skill” involved (This can be good for casual gamers, but the hardcore crowd might not enjoy it.) +
--
- Lacks action
- Very short
- UNREACHABLE PLACES (This is rare but, in a game like this, it can ruin enjoyment.)
You appear in a sky chock full of floating buildings that contain puzzles to be solved, leading to more and more puzzle. You will discover otherworldly architecture and the secrets behind their creation. Find your way through serene mazes and deadly traps to face that which you seek.

This game is good for anyone who loves atmospheric games. It is very peaceful and tranquil with no heart pounding action, so for the action lover it is not a good fit.It can be very exciting and engrossing, but if you repeatedly fail a puzzle, the game can get tedious. Besides that, the game flows very well, pulling you into the dreamlike realm.
My final recommendation is
. The puzzles are good, and the graphics are appealing. The graphics are meant to be minimalist but a bit of detail would have gone a long way to make the game look even better! The easy controls allowed me to jump straight in and begin my adventure with no fiddling with keybinds. The sound effects fit perfectly, and the animation is quite smooth. The unique art design is something I have never seen before and, honestly, it had me awestruck the whole time. I recommend playing the game in a quiet room, where you can properly get your head in the clouds. This is a very solid title. I recommend it to anyone who can appreciate a well put together game but doesn't need intense action.

Here's my take on The Guild 3 on Release Day for Early Access:
Pros:
1. Some new innovations compared to previous games that will make the game flow better. For instance, you start off production in your hut rather than getting a business right out of the gate. Additionally the skill system is interesting and am curious to see how it is in the future.
2. Weather effects are pretty neat.
3. Gameplay is quite very much the same as the previous Guild titles, so it isn't a crazy divergence so if you're a traditionalist you'll like it.
Cons:
1. Bugs (as expected with any EA title). The majority of theses are fairly minor and not crazy huge. For example worker automation was a little funky in the Herb Hut, workers wouldn't start collecting stuff. Additionally some localization issues that need fixing and flushing out.
2. Optimization: performance is a bit low end, but this will most likely be improved once they get to polishing things up near the end.
3. UI Issues: This could be considered a bug, but just a few issues with UI that make it a bit difficult to work on things. Requires some polishing.
4. Unsure on getting married. Not sure if this feature is in yet, but does make a dynasty based game difficult. The previous titles had a list of eligible women for your status and it'd be nice to see something like that for courting them in this title.
Overall it will be a great game. Don't expect anything finished. This is for core die-hard fans who can deal with bugs, even game breaking ones, in the effort of assisting the devs. DO NOT BUY if you expect a complete game, or something that runs smooth. Early Access is NOT for you. Wait until the game is more polished. Follow this game and keep an eye on updates and see when it gets to a point you're willing to deal with.
Will update my review in the future.

As someone who loved the style and controls of Super Meat Boy, but who just couldn't stay engaged due to the difficulty, 140 is the perfect match of difficult gameplay with slow but rewarding progression. Using some very simple mechanics, even simpler visuals, and marrying them with excellent sound and rythm gives you a fantastic 2D puzzle platformer and a highly satisfying experience.
This game reminded me many times of Thomas Was Alone. It has similar very-simple visual styles and simple but satisfying mechanics, but what makes 140 so different and special in its own right is the focus on puzzles and progression. Some sections are relatively easy, some sections are ridiculously hard, but every one of them uses some combination of rhythm, sound and timing to engage the players hands, eyes, ears and brain and delivers with a rewarding one step forward.
* Little things like the respawn noise making the same rythm as sections of gameplay also stand out
* The boss fights are varied and just as fun, they're very well designed
The main complaint against 140 is its short length, and while you'll most certainly be left wanting for more if you're a hardcore platformer or you're expecting something more like Super Meat Boy, 140 is by no means too short for its price, especially considering the more deadly mirrored levels. It isn't given the chance to become unwelcome and I feel it delivers a short, excellent and memorable (given the content) platforming experience.
That said, it's important to understand that if you're not looking for something punishing that requires a lot of patience then the mirrored levels aren't going to add much for you and you'll be left with just an hour to two hours of play time.
Priced at just £3.99/4.99€/$4.99  it's probably fair considering the content is great, and while the main levels can be beaten in an hour, the mirrored levels add another hour, maybe two. If you're looking for a short, engaging experience, this is very much for you. If you want more value for money, it's often on sale for -50% or less, and has been available in a number of indie bundles.

I played Bastion for the first time a few years ago. Now that I've re-played it, I just have to write a positive review about it.
This game is excellent in every possible aspect. The gameplay is fun and extremely adaptable to the player's skill level: if you want to play easy you can just go on with the story without using idols or face challenges, while if you are a completist and look for something more serious you can activate all or few idols (which give enemies various kinds of buffs) and try to beat every proving ground. The story is nice and captivating, the kind you appreciate even more when you replay the game a second time. Is incredible with how many details the writers managed to fill the plot considering that everything is narrated by Zulf's voice while you play. Artistic direction is also really beautiful, the art, the animations, the maps, everything is so polished and detailed that it's simply a pleasure to look at this game running. And the music...is great. Just great.
Really, it's hard to find a flaw in this little masterpiece of indie gaming...Zulf's voice talking over and over can be annoying sometimes, maybe? Honestly it's all I can think of when I ask myself what Bastion's defects are.
What else can I say... hell, just buy this game already. You won't regret it.

140 is a deceptively simple-looking 2D platformer, where you play as a silently morphing geometric shape attempting to collect all the shiny things and dodge all the obstacles. Pretty standard platformer fare, although the little twist on this one is that everything moves to the beat. I enjoy myself a good rhythm game - here's lookin' at you Space Channel 5 - so it's a pet peeve of mine when a "rhythm" title has nothing to show for it other than a few elements moving to a basic pulse. From the screenshots I assumed 140 would be a prime example of that, but was proven wrong almost as soon as I started the first level.
There is no screenshot in the world that can truly demonstrate how flawless the rhythmic aspects of this game are.
responds to the music both technically and visually, whether it's the way an object moves, how it changes aesthetically to "describe" a sound, or how the background music morphs, builds and fires off as you plunge further forward. It also offers a whole lot of rhythmic complexity, so if you were expecting to breeze through by counting 1-2-3-4 then brace yourself - we're talking tied notes, dotted rhythms and syncopation with this one. Finally, I especially loved some of the fantastic audio-visual moments that this game offers up, which I won't spoil but can guarantee you'll love seeing if you happen to be musically minded.
Getting worried that I'm talking about music and rhythm a lot? I wouldn't worry too much. The game is still playable if you find it hard to clap in time; it just means that certain obstacles will feel much, much harder to get through as the answer almost always involves just listening. Thankfully, the default levels come with unlimited deaths and generous checkpointing, so as long as you aren't aiming for every achievement you'll be fine.
So, the final verdict? 140 is a solid testimony to the rhythm-crossover genre, and I would recommend it to anybody who enjoys a rhythm game. I'd also give it a try if you're just looking for something a little different to play, as I'm not sure I've ever seen a game like this before. However... the second I post this review I will be uninstalling the game and never playing it again. Funny considering I'm singing such high praises of it, right? Yeah, well - you know that little 'as long as you aren't aiming for every achievement' disclaimer I made in the previous paragraph?
I have every achievement.
Never.

Reading the reviews(what I usually do before buying a game), I saw that this game had the atmosphere and distinct characteristics I really enjoyed in prior games. Being a fan of games like Final Fantasy Tactics and Tactics Ogre, this hit a strand and stuck with me.
The frustration when you have your combat line in formation, archers/crossbows in the back sniping enemies and your foes have one of your men pinned with many wounds and may die at the next hit. There are twice as many enemies on the map and you have only killed a handful. The line holds this mass of troops back but your one brother has been with you since the first day. Do you break the line to rescue the weakened brother but risk being overwhelmed and attacked on all fronts or do you want to take the risk of watching him dodge attack after attack and may see him fall one turn, never to rise again as that man you once fought with.
In the beginning it can be frustrating, not having the man power nor the equipment so you leave every battle with a loss or two. Later on, its even more frustrating when you have well armored troops who have fought and bled alongside one another for days fall to a chance arrow.
The game does have elements of fantasy, werewolves, goblics, orcs but they are each a separate force with different skills, tactics, and abilities. The human enemies are just as powerful against an underprepared company.
On top of this, weapons have wear which takes time to repair. Health can be healed but after a long period of rest. Plus you carry food and arrows that dwindle with time and  battle AND random occurrence. You need to pay your men(I think maybe they could change this part to once a week) and if there is not enough food/money they desert and leave.
I like the realism, the feel of the game, how gritty it gets. Each battle has me on the edge of my seat because I honestly don't know how it can go. An "easy" battle may have one chance arrow that hits my best fighter in the face and I have to watch him die.
Of all the early access games I  have bought, this one is indeed worth the $20 price. It doesn't have half as much as I could want but at its current state, this game fulfills a need that isn't well addressed in many games today. I actually do feel like a commander of a fierce company which has to pick and choose battles due to realistic limitations.

Set in a kind of low fantasy/medieval open world (the map's not big but it gets the job done), this game is a real treat for any tactical RPG fans out there. Even in early access it gives the player plenty to do and while some of the meatier parts are not yet implemented, the experience is already overwhelmingly enjoyable.
To give you an example - the band of mercenaries you command consists of up to 12 pretty much disposable characters, but each of them has specific traits, portraits and backgrounds that are - and this is truly a testament to the ingenuity of the creators - *just enough* to make you care if one of them dies. In that respect, it's unlike any other tRPG I've seen before, where as a rule of thumb you either immerse yourself in the roleplaying elements fully or don't really give a s**t about any of the characters.
The main reason, however, to get this game even during the EA stage is the gameplay. The battles are already extremely fun, with a much more solid AI than usually in such productions. Your opponents pretty much behave the way you'd imagine (Undead try to swarm you, the Orks just break through anything you might put up against them), but still manage to trap you often enough that the battles don't become stale. On that note, they can be pretty challenging even on the "Even" (or previously known as "Easier") difficulty setting.
The music and graphics, while both quite simple, are pleasant enough, with graphics fixes coming in once in a while.
The game *is* a bit buggy though (a disappearing weapon here and there), but nothing gamebreaking.

EDIT: They have fixed the bug by allowing the option to play in the 32 Bit when you launch from steam. So the earlier bit about it crashing on startup kinda doesn't apply unless you try to play the 64 bit.
A quick thing before I continue; I started playing literally an update or 2, so I can't compare it to anything from before then.
Onto the Review; Do I like starbound? Yes. I really enjoyed the 289 Hours I poured into it, at least to some extent. It kept me busy and took my mind off many things. The soundtrack is pretty good too, as well as the modding community and some of the mechanics, such as the tenant system, missions, quests, and the premise of the story.
Downside is that some of it kinda gets in the way (outside the tenant system).
The story itself seems good, but it kind of forces you into it, rather than easing you in or giving you the option to opt out of it on most of your characters while you do it on only one, you are kinda forced for the first few hours to complete the story quests if you want your ship to be able to fly about the universe. The option to opt out of the story, or only do the story on one character while the rest are just doing their own thing, would fix this problem.
Missions during release as opposed to the last update are optional, but if you choose not to do them you are gonna be locked out of a weapon shop, penguin mercs, etc etc, not just on one character but all of them, even though the option to interact (and get said shop related quests) is available on a new character the moment they get to the outpost.
Bugs are also a big problem, as unless you have a driver that can run OpenGL 2.0, your game is gonna open automatically in OpenGL mode and completely shut down since it can't run it, as opposed to last update where you had the option between standard and Open GL. Although since the launcher is no longer available, it makes it to where you HAVE to run it in OpenGL, meaning an insta-game crash. Best way around this is to go to the Starbound win32 folder and run the game from there, but locking out Steam functionality such as invites.
Good things are that the game still allows exploration and removed the annoying Gear-Lock out from missions, but doesn't offer much room for exploration unless you count the "Find (species) towns and dungeons and scan items to find clues to the next mission!" which yeah is exploration, but as I said the story kinda gets in the way in terms of how urgent the game treats it.
Tenants and crews are a nice addition, allowing you to get crew members on your empty, giant ship. Problem is that upgrading your ship and getting new crew members pretty much means jack-all as it doesn't provide any bonus outside a weak soldier and chemist who only deal about 1-4 damage to creatures (although this may be partially my fault but I have no idea how to get them to actually be useful), and when chucklefish said they fixed the AI, they only made them smarter by a small margin. You have no idea how many times I've had NPCs I had to save from dungeons, or my own Crew, jump into pits off circular saw blades either failing the quest or sending the crew member back to the ship.
Despite all the negativity here, I did enjoy starbound and I probably will still, but this game feels it is far from actually released and definitely needs to fix most, if not all issues by next update and they need to do it pretty darn quickly. When that happens, I'll gladly edit my review but as of Starbound 1.0, and 10 PM EST on 7/25/2016, I will not be recommending the game and implore you to either hold on to your $15+ dollars for now, spend it on something else, or just get the soundtrack for now because that seems like the best part of the game so far.

An intriguing game. A friend showed me some of the game, and it looked rather neat - a puzzle game with platforming interludes, and story that's shown, not told. A lot of it's up to interpretation, so you can take as much or as little as you want from what you see. The hidden scenes and items rewards thorough exploration and expert execution of gameplay; however, some are a bit rude in that reaching them involves doing things that ultimately gets you stuck and requires that you jump off the level to respawn at the last checkpoint.
Gameplay-wise, barely anything is repeated to the point where you feel like you're going through the motions. There's nothing that's done only once in the level, but there's nothing that's re-used in later levels with an irritating twist (ie time limits). Every level holds a new challenge, so you're unlikely to get bored.
The puzzles start out simple, and sometimes have a hint to the solution in plain sight (though you might not register it at first); at other times, they can be rather difficult to conquer, to the point where you'd be tempted to look up a solution. Some of those puzzles guard unlockables, but others guard the way forward, so it can become a bit frustrating. The platforming is the sort of thing you'd expect from something built in Unreal Engine; some sections can be rather difficult to surpass because of finicky jumping mechanics, whilst others are a breeze in comparison.
The graphics are freaking amazing. Lots of eerie backgdrops and landscapes that range from bright and cheery islands to darkened tunnels lit only by glowing mushrooms, distant lights, and the eyes of creatures looking to swallow you whole. It's all thematic, of course - going along with the story, everything is representative of something involving the story being told. Which doesn't stop the game from looking quite wonderful.
The music is quite nice as well - going along well with the themes of the levels, occasionally bringing me back to games I'd played before with the way instruments were used. Going through a factory level, the music reminded me of the old Crash Bandicoot games on the PS1. It, too, plays into the story, though more for setting the tone than anything.
In the time I watched it played by a friend, and in my time playing it, the game only glitched out once - the time I was watching my friend play, a platforming section bugged out and became unwinnable due to a platform reversing its solid state; this was fixed with a reload of the map. The rest of the game was bug-free, which is to be expected.
It's not got a long run-time, but that means you can dedicate a day to sitting down, playing through the game to completion, then finishing it with 100% achievements.
It's definitely worth the low price that the developers are asking for the game, so I highly recommend giving it a look!

Niko: Through The Dream is an excellent example of developer creativity and passion. The game itself is extremely enjoyable to play, as the puzzles involve a large variety of different tasks. One puzzle might deal with colors and colormixing, while another deals with sounds and memorization. The best part is that you aren't sure what to do with each puzzle, and you aren't told how to solve them. You aren't shown what any of the objects in the game do, either, so you're on your own to figure out their purpose and how they work. The puzzles aren't easy, but they're not too hard that you're stuck on one for hours at a time. It's a perfect blend between difficulty and simplicity.
The atmosphere of the game is astounding. It's very simple, but very beautiful. The lighting and skyboxes are really impressive for an indie title, probably my favorite atmosphere in any indie game.
Each area has it's own unique twist that defies logic in it's own way, whether it be floating islands, impossible structures, or insane contraptions that wouldn't exist in the real world.
The story is told through puzzles and sketches (not a narrator), and is easily open for interpretation. One of the most enjoyable ways to be told a story, in my opinion.
Niko: Through The Dream is a puzzle game that really nails the idea of creativity and imagination. It's one of my all time favorite puzzle games, right up there with the Portal series. I recommend this game to anybody looking for a great puzzle game.

I wish there was some way to give a neutral raiting, because this is what AvP 2010 deserves. But I'm going with negative, because while AvP is in no way offensively bad, there are just too many better options out there. Also, this review is for the single player section only. Multiplayer is supposedly good fun, but I've not tried it, and there's not a huge playerbase to support multiplayer these days.
I guess you might consider this the 3rd game in the AvP series, started by Rebellion back in 1999. While that was by no means the first AvP game, it was the first FPS of this nature, and in many ways a groundbreaking game. AvP 2010 keeps many of the mechanics first seen in AvP 1999, and has 3 distinct campaigns, one for each race (Humans, Aliens & Predators). Each race has their unique playstyle which mimics that seen in the movies. Humans are physically weak, but have access to a motion tracker, and strong reliable weapons. The Alien is not very tough, but can climb walls, moves relatively fast and is a beast up close. The Predator is beefy and can take a beating, and has access to a high tech, offense oriented arsenal, which includes the ability to cloak.

AvP 2010 looks good. Even in 2017 it looks good. The environment has a bleak 80's futurustic style to it, similar to that which is seen in the second Alien movie, and looks quite believable. Good use of lighting and real time shadows gives the world a dark and hostile feel to it, something that the official screenshots completely fails to show. The character design is also good, and while technology has advanced since the release of this game, all the characters do look good. It's a technically and artistically impressive game, which stays true to its source material to great effect.
The sound is also quite good. While I would have wished for more ambient noise, the aliens sound like they did in the movies, the classic marine pulse rifle sounds the way it should, and the Predator makes its signature clicking noise. Much like with the graphics, the sound design stays true to its source material to great effect. If you've seen the movies this is based on, in particular Aliens, you'll feel right at home.

Weyland Yutani, "The Company", is as always up to no good. They've decided to breed aliens, and the result is as predictable as can be. The Aliens don't like being confined and break free. You're that alien that breaks free in the Alien campaign. In it your goal is to sabotage for the humans, survive and escape. It's pretty straight forward, as you would expect. You're not really playing a feeling creature, so your motivations are very animalistic.
Something terrible has happened. People are dead, you're alone, and there are aliens everywhere. This is the marine campaign. While there are people on the colony left alive, you're not with them, and all you can do is communicate remotely with your fellow marines. The campaign is underdeveloped, but there are audio logs that you can collect which are mostly really boring, but tell you more about the story, turning it from a mess into something where you can see what they were going for. It's just a shame that the audio logs were not more interesting to listen to.
The great serpent is here. You need to stop them. This is the predator campaign, and the great serpent is of course the aliens that swarm the place. The predators have had a long history with the aliens, and consider them a great threat, and a great prey. This campaign is the one that fleshes out the story the most, surprisingly enough, and you get to learn how the Predators came into contact with the great serpent. The storytelling is not great, but it works.
AvP offers 3 distinct campaigns, with radically different playstyles. It sadly does not offer distinct levels for each, and with one exception, all levels are used for all the races, you just take slightly different paths through. This is not an inherently bad idea, re-threading ground in all campaigns would make the world feel more coherent, but sadly, the it's not done well, and quite often it just ends up feeling cheap. All of the campaigns are really short, at less than 3h each.
The Alien campaign is the one that offers the most unique experience. As an alien you can climb on walls, move through vents and anyone you can sneak up on unnoticed is easily taken down. Sadly unlike the Alien of the previous two games, you're not a fragile but clever hunter, you're a beast who can take a beating, and who moves surprisingly slowly. While the fastest of the 3, you're still slower than in either of the two previous games, or the aliens from the movies. And this does hurt the experience.
The marine campaign starts you off felling vulnerable. The aliens are presented as threatening and dangerous. But this feeling of dread quickly goes away, as you're just incredibly powerful. While the two previous games (but not Primal hunt, for some reason) made you always feel on edge, like you were going up against something scary, in AvP 2010, you're just too darn powerful, so it becomes a simple powerfantasy. A real letdown. Gameplay is mostly like any other shooter, but you've got the nifty motion tracker.
The Predator campaign, my least favourite from the previous two games, is actually the one that works best in AvP 2010. You're a hunter, and you're supposed to feel powerful. With this games emphasis on making you feel like an unstoppable beast, it works quite well. The level design often leaves a lot to be desired, but at least the campaign feels consistent. And the predator has plenty of toys to play around with, most of which are quite fun.

AvP 2010 could have been so much more. It should have been so much more. But two of the campaigns feel rather lackluster, and seem to miss the point of what made the previous two games interesting. AvP 2010 is just so preoccupied with making you feel powerful that that sense of fear or at least unease never really happens. Also, the game has some overly long scripted animations for melee kills. The worst offender is when you take down a civilian as the alien. The first time you see it it's quite shocking. You're doing something terrible to the poor human (offering it to a face hugger who just so happen to wander by), and considering how this has been portrayed in the Alien movies (in particular in Alien 3, which keeps hammering it home to the point where it feels disrespectful to the audiences intelligence) as a♥♥♥♥♥♥metaphor, it should make you feel uneasy. But sadly through repetition it just loses all of its shock value. And it just takes forever. It's not quite as bad for the predator, but it still takes far too long. So in closing, AvP 2010 is a missed opportunity that is not terrible to play, but while it's visually impressive, the way the game mechanics are implemented makes it feel like it's the lesser of the three AvP games. But at least it's not Primal Hunt.

Great rhythm game.
140 is a platforming, rhythm game developed by Carlson Games.
There is no story in this game.
As mentioned earlier, gameplay is a mix of platforming and music. There are three chapters, with each chapter having different objectives. You control a object that can shape shift between a square, triangle or circle. The goal in each chapter is to keep moving forward, collecting items and activating switches and platforming along the way. As you progress through the chapter the music will change. Some of the platforming can be challenging and can take a while to get right. One complaint is that there are no save points during chapters (only inbetween chapters) so when you quit and resume your game, you have to start at the begining of the chapter you were on. There are a total of 3 chapters for campaign as well as 3 challenge chapters which will test your skills.
To be a successful rhythm game you have to have good music. Does this game have good music? Well, yes it does. Audio is electronic pop which is not iritating to listen to.
Graphics are presented in a 2D fashion. The textures aren't well detailed, however this isn't important in a rhythm game.
A good rhythm game.

The average player will likely clear this game in about an hour. Make no mistake, though: This game is well worth your time. Made by Jeppe Carlsen, the lead designer of Playdead's
,
is a slick minimalistic platformer with a gameplay element element that changes the level layout to the rhythm of the game's BGM. If you've played
before, you're already familar with this creator's ability to marry simple controls with extremely clever level design. That same concept applies here. The style of this game is also oh-so appealing: It's an ode to retro gaming that still proves to look entirely modern. The electronic soundtrack—especially that infectious tite screen music—also nalls this ideal perfectly.  Lastly, although the game is about an hour long there is some replayability to be had, as beating the game unlocks a mode in which you can play every level from the opposite direction.
If you're a GTA fan; this is probably the hardest of the 3D franchise to get into, but it is well worth the effort. Behind the dated graphics and controls lies a solid and fun experience.

Bastion is a great game with a great story-telling. The game is actually quite easy to beat, but for hardcore players, no need to worry, because it's quite hard to 100% this game. You also can set a "handicap" for yourself to make the game harder (and to farm more exp). There are several weapons in this game that you can mix and match. Although i said that there are several weapons, you can only use two, which have their own special skills and their own upgrades. All upgrades have 2 different paths which can be switched as you wished (for free), which will be important at some levels, especially if you are not skilled enough.
You can build some buildings which can help you in some way. There are a place to switch your equipment, upgrade your equipment, putting a "handicap" on you, and even just a simple quest to get a currency for either upgrading your equipment or buying stuff. Speaking about buying, you can buy items in this game, although it's mostly just skills, upgrade materials, and drinks (this is a kind of permanent item which can give you a boost when equipped). You will build them all near the end of the game, though, which is good.
All the game story is done by speaking, so for those who are having a trouble in listening might have a hard time in understanding the story. You can make some of it through the image shown on some cutscenes, but you'll miss most of the detail. Despite all that, if you don't really care about the story, this game provides all you need in a game. Beautiful soundtracks, beautiful arts, great gameplay, lots of levels, and much more.

I was gifted Bastion by a friend a few years ago. WHY DIDN'T I PLAY IT UNTIL NOW??? IT'S SO MUCH FUN!!!
Wow. I haven't enjoyed a game this much in a long time. The story is great, the visuals are beautiful and colorful. The whole atmosphere is really lovely. The music is so good and it is fluid in that you can flow from one mood to another easily when the narration changes, you enter a specific area on the map, etc.
But what really keeps me coming back is the combat. I don't usually love hack'n'slash, but these weapons & abilities are SO much fun to use. I love all of them, too bad you can only use two at a time. The option of using spirits and idols to make the combat easier/harder depending on different variables you can choose to control is just brilliant. And the eventual upgrades you get, are awesome.
The (increasingly difficult) maps & monsters are all introduced at a good, flowing pace, and in the end are all super fun to fight. I'm probably going to keep playing and toy with the difficulty and different weapon combinations for a while, even after I've beat New Game Plus.
I was very motivated by the narrator and other rewarding, and interesting parts of the game to keep on playing and complete the story. Too often I don't finish games, but the Bastion called my name every hour of the day since I began playing.
Even after you've completed the story there's still more stuff that you can do. Or, rather you can do other fun things while taking your time with the story. It's cool. The currency, and the rate at which it is acquired, is really in sync with natural progression. Everything about this game is just, "in sync". It flows. It makes sense. Nothing worried me about it. It is most excellently designed.
Whoever came up with the idea to introduce New Game Plus after you've beat it the first time, knew how important that feature would be for people like me who couldn't get enough and wanted to keep playing.
So, you should get this game. It's really perfect, especially if you like rpg's, this is a special one. There's really no way you wouldn't enjoy it, unless you have real poor coordination and fall off the map all the time (but this is just another fun thing about it).
Also. Most of the world is destructible so that's fun (it's so pretty though, why would you want to do that? Maybe to make more room for fighting monsters, or getting past obstacles...) So much fun. Get it!

Battle Brothers is simply awesome.
Some good years back, i was amazed when i discovered Mount and Blade, still in it's beta, and i just loved it, the battles sure, but specially the recruiting and training of your men. Battle Brothers has that same feeling in its recruiting, maybe better, as it's focus is in a small group of men, there are a lot of more characteristics in each of them, and some of them really stand out.

The combat, as you can see in the video, is akin to Final Fantasy Tactics or Fire Emblem. Your equipped itens may present some different moves to use, and it's pretty interesting figuring out who will use which weapon. I think 2 archers and 2 man with weapons with greater reach are advisable when you have the full 12 man team.

I paid the full price, and i don't regret it a bit.

So, it appears to be first person puzzle game set in a weird minimalistic 3-d environment. It starts off with a hand drawn cartoon (not sure what was going on, but hey) before dropping you into the first area. There are no instructions as to what to do, but if you move around (the usual WASD / space) *look* at things and activate things (E), it becomes obvious, though it might take a couple of attempts. The puzzles (so far) have been quite easy to solve, but equally quite satisfying - all (so far) things you'll likely have come across before (pressing buttons in the right order, lining things up, a bit of platforming...) and there are clues as to what to do. There's also some nice sparse background music which adds to the atmosphere & the general surreal feel of it all.
A couple of gripes though - if you hit escape during play, you're presented with some pretty unhelpful menu/symbols one of which just closes the game down without warning (though in hindsight, it does look a bit exit-y). Also there's a bit of 'precision' first person jumping required which I find annoying - the controls are a bit skittish, which isn't helpful when you 10 levels up in the air...
Apart from that, highly recommended!
(Also - a free hint - if you're underwater and hear your heartbeat getting louder, you're about to drown! )

This is a really fun game that is really confusing at first but the more you play the funner it gets and the more you understand. There are 3 parties, the first is the mafia who want to take out the townsman, second is the townsman who are trying to take out the mafia and prevent some characters from being killed like the jester, and third are the stand alones. For example the Jester is a stand alone who wins if he can convince the townsman to hang him. This is an amazing who is who game and if you liked werewolf and/or mafia then you will absolutely love this game! DLC and all! It is every bit worth the $5 and the devs need the money for example to pay for the servers to stay up. And after that you don't have to pay another cent if you don't want to. There is two types of currency. One you pay to add it in to the game and the other you earn by playing games. The beauty of it is that none of it will effect your game and they are all cosmetic items except the DLC just to support the Devs. And most you can earn without paying any real money. The only other thing that you would have to pay for is the one Coven DLC and you don't need that at all if you don't want. It won't effect the game at all before hand it just adds to the game like extra characters for example(And many more). So it's not a cash grab that's trying to steal from you, It's an amazing game that does need to make money (which is why they charged for the base game and Coven DLC) but then made most other things obtainable because they are amazingly fair Devs that love this game and are always involed and watching. If this sounds like the game for you then i wouldn't hesitate! Happy Hunting! ;)
*And just to add, the dlc that adds to the game adds to it in a seperate game mode. So the original game wont change at all. So if you buy Coven and want to experience it, you jump into another game with everyone that has the DLC so that the original doesn't change and it's fair to everyone playing either Coven or original.  Also if you dont want this on Steam or are hesitant, you can try it for free or just play it for free on their website. I personally don't think the $5 is a steal in any way because it is an amazing game that i'm happy to suport and i spend alot more on other games any way. Xenomorphs and the Marines were my main draw towards Aliens vs. Predator, and after finishing the singleplayer campaigns, I am pretty satisfied with the game overall. There are three campaigns in this game - a Marine, an Alien and a Predator-campaign - that all tell slightly different stories from different perspectives, but cross eachother's paths quite regularly to form a kind of loose, overarching plot that all takes place in and around a Weyland-Yutani-colony on BG-386.
What deserves a lot of praise is the wide range of gameplay between the three campaigns. Marines, Xenomorphs and Predators are immediately distinguishable from eachother, each having their own sets of skills to traverse the levels and fight enemies. My personal favorite was the Marine-campaign because it's all good, solid shooter action with all the most well-known and well-loved equipment of the Colonial Marines like the Smartgun, the Pulse Rifle and a Motion Scanner. Fighting Xenos as a Marine reminded me a lot of Aliens with its frantic shooting and the hordes of enemies crawling out of every hole.
However there are also weaknesses to the game, and particularly the campaign where you play as the Xenomorph was a bit disappointing to me. This is in part due to the
long kill-animations that break the otherwise fast and free-flowing alien-gameplay to a jarring degree. The Predator-campaign also suffers from this, but here the problem is alleviated to some extent by the slower gameplay of the Predator and the fact that the Predator is less reliant on melee-kills and can instead use a big array of ranged attacks to fight in addition to his melee-capabilities. Also, to some people the campaigns may be a bit too short and same-y, since they're all a couple hours long at best and take place in largely the same areas of the colony.
On the technical side, Aliens vs. Predator has aged quite well, though the models and textures do look a bit dated. It's not hideous by any stretch though, the levels feel visually coherent and even boast a couple of nice views and effects. Regarding the sound there is little to criticize apart from the rather mediocre voice-acting for the human characters; Aliens screech like aliens, Predators click-clack like Predators and, most importantly, Pulse Rifles crackle with the same satisfying intensity of their movie-equivalents.
All in all it's a fun, diverse, but relatively short experience with a few minor downsides here and there. From my perspective as a fan of the Alien-universe, it's worth it to pick it up on a sale and play it over the course of a week or so.

If you are even slightly bothered by bright and obnoxious colors, avoid this game. 140 is full of excessively contrasting and bright colors, to an extent which can only be sufficiently described as "obnoxious," and there is no way to dim the game in the options. The degree of col♥♥♥♥♥♥ varies by level, but most of my experience was wrought with eye strain. For a very short game like this, you don't want a headache to be your lasting impression on the player.
Beneath the pain is a fairly enjoyable precision platformer. The game doesn't have any real 'puzzles,' aside from figuring out where you need to go and not flunking the jump (which happens often), but the integration of the music is the real selling point. Hitting a checkpoint adds a new instrument to the soundtrack, and a new mechanic to the level tied to that instrument, and the mechanic is then used to progress.
It's a very compact experience, taking only an hour or two and sticking closely to its minimalist aesthetic. However, the levels really drag on; there are only three of them, and if the game runs you two hours, that's about 40 minutes per level. It's not too bad at first, since the checkpoints are quite frequent and there's hardly any delay to respawning and trying again. If the game ended after the third level, with no extra content, this would be an overall positive review; however, completing the main game unlocks a set of 'mirror levels,' and the game falls apart then.
Firstly, the mirror levels invert all the colors, leading to even more obnoxious color palettes than before. Then you replay the same levels, butmirrored - an interesting idea, except now death starts you over from the beginning. Of what might be a 20+ minute level. Which will end with some sort of bullet-hell boss. And good luck spacing your jumps if you're trying to defend your eyes from a painful assortment of hot pinks and sun yellows.
You need to learn these levels deeply, and practice them often, and dedicate lots of time to completing them. This is the core problem with this segment of the game: it is a 1-2 hour experience that then demands significantly more commitment in order to 'complete' it. You don't HAVE to finish the mirror levels, but if you uninstall it then, have you really "completed" the game? Since you need to complete the mirror levels to unlock all the achievements, it suggests the devs don't think you've won until you've gone through that hell.
If you are content to play only half the game, you probably won't regret it. But overall, 140 does not respect the player's time, and as a result I won't recommend it.

Early Access review: As in "Mount & Blade" you travel across a map from town to town, recruiting mercs, buying/selling stuff, running errands for gold. As in "Darklands" there is a medieval German theme with supernatural elements. As in "Disciples" & "Heroes" you switch to a battle map when the action starts. The 2D graphics & music are attractive & work well. The battles are challenging but satisfying. And you gain loot and xp to level up your party. As in "The Witcher" levelling up provides many options & routes for specialization. Keeping your party & its equipment in good order adds a layer of management skill. I'd like to see more variety in faces for party members, as I had 2 or 3 guys who looked identical. And some variation in quests & quest-dialogue text would also be nice. And more variety in clothing. There is music audio, and this is very good, but there's no voice acting. As far as I can tell, there's no interaction between your mercs (as in "Jagged Alliance") but some text-based random events occur to "buff" or "debuff" your party. For an Early Access game it is certainly enjoyable.

Starbound is a confusing game.  On one hand it has a huge variety of planets, landscapes, blocks, enemies, food, cosmetics, etc.  It's beautiful and a lot of care and a LOT of artists did a ton of impressive work.  You have a spaceship and you can get crew and you can do quests for NPCs and you can catch pets and there's just a very broad set of stuff.
But underneath the pretty art, everything is very shallow.  The differences between planets and landscapes and blocks are largely cosmetic.  All food is basically the same, the enemies are mostly the same dumb "run straight at you" clods, the weapons are almost entirely randomly-generated (and mostly worthless).
The UI itself is extremely primitive in irritating ways: no map, no minimap, no "stack to chests".  You can only place items with the inventory up and the inventory places itself in the middle of the screen directly on top of what you're looking at, so you have to drag it out of the way every time.  You have to eat food in order to regenerate health, but food only lasts a minute or two and it doesn't stack and you can't eat it out of your inventory so every few minutes you have to drag it to your quickbar again, eat it, close inventory.  Over and over, irritating you constantly.
Play more Terraria instead.

The ongoing love / hate of SD.
The latest updates did provide a nice change. ( as usual I was on XP branch before the general toss out ) Gone for the moment are finding everything you need to live forever on two islands. The complete removal of buckets, meaning you have to actually plan some water system a bit at first, and be ready for figuing out how to craft the new clay items, such as a water bottle / jug.
However the game still suffers from the most major downfall of all.
There is absolutely no reason to do anything beyond 1 to 2 game days .. 3 tops.
By day three of my new game, I had 4 water stills collecting more than enough fluid for living and stockpiling. A smoker stacked over half full of fish. A box by the stills filled with full coconuts, and of course my bed for save / sleep.
So once agian. 3 days in game of playing. Zero reason to go anywhere for any reason. Explore? Not needed, there is nothing I ' have ' to try and find. Wood? Covered for days. Shelter. Still not needed for any reason at all. Clothing? Not integrated at all.
Love this game for the look, the idea of pure survival with no SyFy elements, no horror.
Hate this game for the simple, there is no survival to it. No drive to do anything beyond the initial setup. It does not even require the " 3 " THREE main elements of actual survival that would make you a hero if you had all established in 3 days really. Food / Water ( has that ) Shelter ( not needed at all still ) Clothing ( not even mentioned )
My ongoing opinion. A neat play for a very casual player. A neat play for an extremely casual survival genre fan. Still think its a neat idea and a cute game. But would have really thought that by now the core of survival would have been in place to build on. Survival involves a lot more than food / water and a save bed.
I have to rate it down now, simply because it's not worth the price with so little gone into making much of a survival genre game.
EARLY ACCESS REVIEW
2/8/17 ** New EDIT **
This game.. and my love / hate relationship.
I WANT to love this game. I really do. I was deep into it on release.. spent all my time then on the old experimental game.. slugged thru' hours of no game to play and testing issues only there..
THEN came the SD as it progresses now..
Which, ' aint ' much.
Its not a survival game... since you have nothing to fear. Not even the need for rest, food and hydration.
Its not a exploration game... well it could be. But only if rowing from one island to the next to the next is your thing.
The building is nice.... but other than a bed to save / sleep.. you dont need to build anything but a water catcher and the occasional new knife or axe.
It would be a really fun casual game, except that there really is no point to do anything. In the last round on experimental with this new update I am trying, trying to enjoy just a calm, peaceful play around game.. and its just simply no reason to even try.. but try I am still.
There is absolutely no reason to do anything now. My smoker is filled with meat. I have two water catchers and rain catching buckets, plenty of fish in shallow water for small meat, a giant crab family on the isle and an easy drop off access to deeper water fish with low danger of sharks. Plenty of wood still to burn.. and the building of the shack I have done was needless.. still no reason to even have a shelter at all. WX has no affect on the player.
SO why play it? I have no idea. Other than for me, I want to see it become something.. I want to like this game. And it is really good for a simple time kill that looks nice, and plays nice.. but has zero challenge. It could have challenge. If there really was a reason to ever venture beyond the first two islands. In 4 starts now before saying.. screw it.. I am going to play for a bit, they were all the same in giving me everything I need to live. Tarps, tools, buckets..... I ve not had to cringe once in hopes of finding survival. Its all on the second beach. I like the idea of it being a casual little play. But having all you need dropped on you at the beginning really removes anything ' game ' about this game. Heck even A' cant play it... as she said " I found everything everytime.. thats boring. "
Well, back to see if I can just linger in it a bit, because if nothing else, it looks nice, and it is relaxing..
I really do hope it evolves a bit tho'.. or at least stops giving you more in the beginning than using cheat codes does.
8/15/2016 ** EDIT**
Well.. been supporting this one since day one.
Now I admit. I am wondering exactly where its heading....
Today, monthly update brought us!! Not much. The ability to craft upgraded crude tools from regular crude tools. The need to make a "NEW" special spear for fishing... and another special spear for defence and hunting.. of which there is really nothing to hunt but some pigs..
AND an amazing SPEAR GUN ( DIYS) made from a component you need to go deep diving to find.... so you can have a SPEAR GUN to go deep diving..
Ok.. thats nice.. BUT:
After all this time, this ' survival ' game still has little to offer survival wise.
You still start on an island where you can find all you need to live in 5 mins.
You can craft all you need to live within 20 ( not counting this fascination that some have with building Aztec sun temples )
Unless you just kill yourself.. or insist on doing everything counter to a ' survival ' game.. you cant die. Which is still moot since its a scrub save / load game.
Weather ( this is a big one to me! ) Still has zero effect, other than fill your buckets ( which today I have 5 of after 30 mins )
NOW THIS IS BIG BIG to me... no drift. You dont even have the worry of things floating away. After all this time, the ocean has no drift. Drop buoys, your raft.. whatever in the ocean.. it wont float away.. So scratch the lose stuff or worry over your raft as you tinker around in the water.. ( which outside of fishing you dont really need to do.. unless you just seek things you really dont need.. medicine... which you only need if you do something to yourself.. etc etc )
Billboards of distant islands.. or close ones even. Dont matter. They are all the same still.
What should be global events do not work. IE Rain storm.. if your not on your island.. your buckets dont fill. Row off your island.. just far enough away to see the billboard.. return.. zero has changed. Time passes, but things like buckets dont fill, fire burns....
God I want to like this game.. I badly want to like this game. A survival game whose premise was survival.. no zombies, no freaky Sci Fi events.. just survival on islands in the ocean.
But after a year.. all we have is, spawn, pick up stuff.. build sun temples.
Unless you just want a zero threat, zero purpose casual island living sandbox.. or really want to support this game.
Not advised at all anymore to anyone.
4/22/2016 NEW EDIT:
THIS is a game I ve supported since it first popped up EA. The team still trudges on, and the game has truly evolved.. slow but steady over the course..
I DO NOT play it alot in sittings still, as even now there is just not that much meat and potatoes wise to hold you if your actually after what the selling point has been.. survival Castaway style...
NO, NO.. SD currently, and most likely even in the end will now be a new category of game.. The Casual Gamers, No Problem, No Stress Survival, Non Survival Game
DO NOT get me wrong.. it IS a good idea, it IS a neat little game.. but unless you just want to build rafts, look for engine parts and build beach houses just to do it.. it has little else to offer.

Aliens vs Predator (2010) is a first person shooter that introduces you to three seperate storylines involving a Human, a Predator, and an Alien. Overall the storylines are decent, while not nearly as difficult as I would have prefered. For example Nightmare Difficulty seems to simply increase the damage and accuracy of your opponents, but not necessarily making them difficult due to one shot mechanics available to Predator and Alien. Boss fights bring a interesting level of difficulty, but are still single meat shields with high health pools that you have to mow down while dodging mechanics and the occassional add. Overall scenary in the game is one of the highest pluses I will give, as the environements truely have the universes feel to them.
TLDR: Singleplayer
Scenary and Graphical Immersion: 9/10
Difficulty: 3/10
Storylines: 6/10
MULTIPLAYER SECTION
If you plan to play the multiplayer on this game this is the section you should read. For those who have played Alien vs Predator (1999) and Alien vs Predator 2 (2001) then the combat of this game is much different as it follows a rock, paper, scissors style of gameplay in melee combat. Both Aliens and Predators can perform Light and Heavy Attacks where the heavy attacks can be interrupted by the light attacks, while  the light attacks can be blocked and countered. Marines can block and light attack to counter. Overall depending on the the skill of the people in game the combat can be quite fast paced, also retaining the executions for both predator and alien, which will one shot from the back, and one shot on low health from a front grab.
TLDR: MULTIPLAYER
Balance: 6/10 (Before the Alien Wall Tail swipe nerf the balance was horrid. While better, Predators are usually a little overpowered compared to Marine and Alien unless the latters have skill advantage).
Maps: 8/10 (Each map usually feels a little different that others, as well as offering different advantages to each of the species. For Example Pyramid and Alien.)
Community: 5/10 (The game has not aged well due to the lack of modding tools. While there is a community still, there have been many reports of hacking throughout the public games. As such playing with a group of friends privately is preferable.)
Gameplay: 7/10 (The one thing I enjoy about this game is the Alien FEELS like an Alien. Your quick, stealthy, and lethal. The Predator also gives you the feel of hunting the other players while using the advanced tech, and Marine keeps you on your heels trying to watch for pings on your motion tracker. Overall the game feels RIGHT, the only cons are lack of Alien Lifecycle and the Rock Paper Scissors limiting the flow of combat.)
OVERALL I do recommend this game simple for the singleplayer if you love the franchise, however the multiplayer should be stuck to friends only unless you want to risk running into a usual hacker ingame. If possible wait for a sale, which usually brings this game down to under 5$ which is well worth the price.

is one of the most delightful
games I have ever played.  As far as game mechanics go, it is just another TD game with no real groundbreaking or innovative dynamics.  But something about the art style, the animations, and the soundscape create a nice blend that is undeniably charming.  This should be a welcome addition to any TD fan’s library.
Like in all good TD games, the core gameplay is extremely addictive.
is well-designed to be challenging, yet not needlessly frustrating.  The level design allows for creativity, but also limits your options enough so it isn’t a total chore trying to figure out what to do.  That said, as you get deep into the game, it can become quite a challenge to 3-star levels; but worst-case scenario you can find guides online to help you out.
There aren’t really that many towers, in truth.  But there is just enough. And they are all diverse, fun to use, and are all useful at one point or another in the game.  I find many TD games with dozens of towers usually still can be beaten with only the best five, anyway.  Nevertheless, to make up for the relatively low amount of towers: there are twelve hero units each with different abilities.  Trying out the different heroes as you unlock them adds that bit of spicy variety to the game.
I feel it is only fair to point out: you can play the original version of the basic campaign for free on the many flash game websites out there… with microtransactions for some extra “premium” content.  The Steam version comes with all content included in the price, as well as a few extra expansion levels; and of course it comes with the benefit of the “meta-aspects” of any Steam game (Steam achievements, trading cards, screenshots, etc.). You can decide what is an acceptable price for this.
If you are an advocate of TD games and can pick up
for a price you are comfortable with, then you absolutely should grab it and give it a go.

I only recently found out about this game and loved the overall idea of it but was a turned off by what I had seen of the combat. Even after watching a few gameplay videos I wasn’t that excited by it and planned on giving it a miss (as much as I loved the rest of the concept).  I was a little surprised to see a demo being offered (as it is rare these days) so I decided to have a look at it and I am glad I did.
The combat system is very enjoyable and feels quite polished already. There are enough subtle nuances to support a range of tactics (depending on equipment and enemy faced..!) and the design is quite well done.
Demo link:
Combat:
-	Characters are represented by busts only, no animations. Don’t let this put you off… the artwork is incredible (armour getting damaged, units getting bruised and bloody etc) and I think it actually fits well with the abstraction of turn based combat.
-	There is no facing/flanking taken into account (allied units always face to the right, enemy always face to the left). While this seems like a significant downside initially, the overwhelm mechanic is actually a relatively elegant way of dealing with this.
-	Fatigue. In addition to action points you also have fatigue (actions add to total fatigue up to a characters max, total fatigue is reduced every turn). If you can’t ‘afford’ the fatigue cost of a move, you can’t do it. Wearing armour reduces your max fatigue, the heaver the armour, the bigger the reduction. This is something that some people don’t like but it is a feature I love. It is a great way to add a little more (abstracted) ‘realism’ to the relatively familiar turn based AP combat system.
Strategic map. Very well done overall. Will be familiar if you have played Mount and Blade but includes day/night cycle.
Interesting points:
-	A lot of the game is randomly generated so locations and strengths of enemy factions, towns, outposts etc will vary each playthrough.
-	A town’s prosperity depends on trade with other towns. If a town’s caravans are continually getting ambushed and/or the town is raided often, it will directly affect the support they can give you (eg. Equipment available)
-	The above point also extends to the games ‘quests’. There are the generic ‘filler’ quests (eg. I need this token package delivered to X town) however the real contracts are based on the towns actual ‘needs’. Eg. If a town’s caravan is continually getting ambushed, they will ask you to escort it (while a town with safer routes won’t offer that contract because they don’t need your help). You can also get contracts to deal with enemy locations (eg. bandit hideouts etc) however it isn’t a static quest; if a force from the local castle/outpost knows about it they may deal with it first.
-	The stronghold/outpost tasks also dynamically evolve based on supply levels/resources, manning, knowledge etc.
-
There is a very interesting video on the world map and simulation here:
More info about world map worth reading
This is a very solid game and leagues ahead of what most games break into early access with. While the final game content isn’t in there, it is a perfectly functional game as is already (and many ‘sandbox’ games have been released with less).
The devs are quite active in the community and maintain an ongoing dev diary. If you are remotely interested in this game, grab the combat demo straight up and check it out (note it is a bit outdated though but does give you a good feel for the combat). Read through some of the other reviews and dev diaries and if you are still intrigued, grab it.
A great purchase; no regrets. (I am actually upgrading to the supporter tier purely for a bit of extra support for the devs.)

Warning, this review contains opinion on the game itself, not Bethesda`s politics regarding extra content. If you are so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, that you don`t understand the difference, go back to minecraft where you belong.
***
Achtung, отзыв содержит мнение касательно самой игры, а не политике студии относительно модов. Если вашего интеллекта недостаточно для понимания разницы, вернитесь в тот майнкрафт, откуда выползли.
In short - I like this game. It`s better than the third part and partially better than New Vegas. Some things Obsidian did better, but most things they screwed up. As always. But they were right about one thing - NV would have been better as a PC exclusive, and if they convince/join forces with Bethesda to create Fallout 5/or New Vegas 2 only for #PCMasterRace I will take back everything I said about them and will also buy their merchandise. Do they have any?
Comparing to New Vegas(because why not?), this is my IMO-opinion:
Pluses:
+ Optimization. To prevent save file corruption, I always disable auto-saves. For Fallout 3&4 I downloaded only 1 unofficial patch just to be safe. No problems during 100% walkthoughs. For New Vegas I used 4! And still it managed to crash and freeze, not to mention eternal loading screens. Sometimes game forgot to render textures, fps dropped to 14, and this list can go on and ooooon.
+ Graphics. Nothing new in NV, same textures and maps, but painted brown.
4-th part is beautifull. Look everywhere - weather, water, faces(not all) armor. Finally everything looks realistic.
+ Gameplay. NV brought a lot of stuff into gameplay like crafting bullets and grenades or breaking them into extra components, cooking, repairing gear with tools yourself and so on. But nothing special. Like in every rpg - go, kill, loot sell, die, repeat. Classic. But Y NO BOBBLEHEADS? :(
Bethesda brought something awesome - building your own Headquarters. Although I didn`t go very far and had only 1 major Fort Nox and a dozen of small checkpoints for resources, I enjoyed every last moment. And with Automatron I had freedom to build my own droid army and not to bother with these whiny humans.
Power Armor. Ooooooowwyeaaaaah! It`s no longer a giant useless piece of junk, now it`s a force to be reckoned with!
+ Combat. Bullets flying in different direction, not where you aim with your scope - almost 60 degree change of direction. Nukes that can`t kill coyotes. Character stuck during reloading and during VATS. Bouncing grenades, like they are made from rubber. NPC`s can deflect swords and axes with bare hands. Nice job Obsidian, how many programmers do you have? 1? 0?
4-th fixed everything. Now we can safely go guns blazing into enemy territory. As a bonus, we can mod our tools of destruction ourselves.
Enemies also learned new tricks. Hiding below ground - scorpions, mirelurks and rats. Climbing on rooftops - deathclaws. Hiding and being useless - Minutemen.
+ Protagonist. Finally we have our own voice. And I don`t understand why ppl prefer mutes? Would Mass Effect/Dragon Age 2&Inq be better without our speaking characters? NOE.
(+/-) Story. That`s an interesting one, because both Obsidian and Bethesda gave were successfull. Partially.
NV had a boring main quest. Seriously, I hate politics, just kept skipping all the dialogues regarding it. Later repeated the same in Witcher 2. DLC`s however were brilliant. Except "Honest Hearts". Why should we care about these savages? Killed both leaders, got a map and left.
4 is vice versa. DLC`s are...strange. Nuka-World is big, but empty and Far Harbor could have been interesting, if we would have been researching The Mist, instead of bothering with someones politics AGAIN. Really, what is it? Anomally from S.T.A.L.K.E.R./Metro 2033? A living creature? We don`t know and it sucks.
Automatron is the only one I liked. Droid army, remember?^^
And now minuses:
- Bethesda nerfed too much and removed some elements, that weren`t so much of a problem for me. Repairing stuff(although we repair our exoskeleton), persuation via perks and abilities(you could hit the Persuade button in the dialogue menu and another menu could have popped up, where you choose what knowledge your character can use), standard levelling like in NV and 3. Thanks for 35435 level cap, but still...
- NV companions were fine, all of them. However in 4 there are some useless- Preston, Cait, Strong, X-synth and MacCreedy.
- No "screenshots" in the end, where we listen what happened to ppl after our role in all of this.
- And no info about Lone Wanderer and Courier #6. They both just dissappeared, like something is happening and they cooperated and went out to investigate.
Bonus: there is a rumor that Obsidian will actually join forces - forever or just for Fallout 5, no idea. But imagine - Bethesda`s skills with programming and a huge amount of resorces + Obsidian`s writing and imagination. This kind of project can be legendary!

Sanctum 2 is one of the few games I can easily sink a few hours into.
It's a simple concept; build tower structures during a build phase to force the hordes of Lumes into a maze and through various turrets/towers of your construction, whilst then during the post-construction phase; fight alongside your towers and try to stop the pesky swarm from getting close to the precious Core. Players can customise thier loadout of perks and tower choices to best suit how they want to handle the horde of fungal monstrosities.
Very fun on multiplayer; particularly with friends to help co-ordinate your schemes and plans. And if you fancy ramping up the challenge; use the Feats of Strength to make levels far more difficult, and reap bigger rewards in XP for your efforts.
And if you fancy absolute tower-defence anarchy/sitting and watching wave after wave of enemy fall into your deadly traps; put it onto Sandbox mode and build hellish labrynths with ridiculous firepower or combinations (personal fav; sticking a Slow-field Mine tower next to a Range tower and feeding them waaaaay too many points; otherwise known as 'Space Time Destruction').
Here's hoping to a Sanctum3 sometime in the near future! :)

What an original and refreshing rts! As we can expect from an early access game, it lacks some important features to really feel like a polished game but its strategical depth already feels so good.
Pros:
- the visual identity
- auto generated map gives a very unique feel to each game (you can not go for the very same build order each game)
- the survival aspect is strategic and challenging
- the "macro" aspect of the game, simple to get your hands on but hard to master
Cons (gameplay):
- lacks comeback mechanics (your units build over time, losing a fight puts you so far behind)
- quite long games including a first half with close to no interactions with the enemy
- the information/vision game is not very deep
Cons (should be coming in the next months ?):
- multiplayer servers and a matchmaking system

Yay, I get to review this now!
Firstly, I am a huge indie games supporter, but check out
as to why these devs deserve all the smacks on their collective wrists they can get. Then check out their metacritic page
and laugh along at its awesomeness. 0.5/10 average user score after 1548 reviews.
Still, it came in the recent Bundle Stars indie game bundle, and surely can't be that bad right? Maybe just a victim of internet hate? And it has Steam trading cards, so it's pretty much me being paid to play it, right? Ha. Haha.
Let's see. The graphics are absolutely awful, simple, low-rez, stock graphics pasted together, primitive character models are pretty much just going through the motions with no facial expressions and really crude, robotic animations. Corpses despawn immediately upon death, though the background corpses that are there are violently graphic.
What little voice acting there is is dreadful, and really is just made up of short snippets (that often doesn't make total sense in the context - like "Uh oh" when you fail a crafting combination, even though you don't lose anything for it) set to trigger when certain events happen. It takes several hits to bludgeon enemies to death and in the meantime they don't sound very perturbed by it.
The AI is deplorable, when you can shoot npcs from range and they often won't come for you as they slowly die, nor do any of their friends around them. You can even sneak right up behind an npc, shoot another one, and none of them will hear it. Even when charging right up to them, half the time they just stand there glitched and let you melee them to death.
Crafting is senseless, and involves a boring little
No, not really, just a mini-animation-thing, with keys to press, that shows off exactly how poor and juvenile their animations are.
The plot makes no sense, the starting video is incoherent (though the guy's utter lack of facial expression or reaction or voice as his plane is crashing is awesome), and there is no plausible explanation why things happen the way they do, like why that plasma weapon was sitting where it was or how the guy knows it's going to float up to attach to his arm or why/how he can still change weapons after that. NPCs will appear out of and walk through solid objects at will, the uneven screen shake during the starting escape portion will give you nausea, and you will find dumb bugs like how boxes during that escape portion can fall on your head and trap you inside their model without the game registering a death and forcing you to load or anything.
Anyway I'm out of negative adjectives, except to say that the game is a pile of snivelporking frumpletops. This smells like a novice-level game programming class project that even for that level came out really badly, yet somehow got developed further after.
Yet, you should get this game. Why? Because it makes every other game on your Steam list look better by association. In fact, maybe it belongs on my Game Collector showcase on my front profile page... hmm. But hey, don't feel too bad about it, devs, some game had to be the bottom of the barrel here at Steam. By submitting this game, you just ensured another game didn't have to be. Very charitable of you.
