But now its a generic "evil has been banished and you need to stop it" story. everyone has the exact same story and there really isnt a reason to choose a race over another other than maybe abilities (if thats even a thing anymore) and looks
-A lot of emphasis is put on the "examin" mode, but it really hasnt changed at all since a year ago. the most interesting things either have super bland and moring descriptions or dont have any at all. the race you play as doesnt change the description much either. for glitch its pretty much just basic descriptions with an emotion tacked on the front. "Intrigued: it is a very nice and sturdy door" and stuff like that
-everyone used to have different AI's. they might have acted the same but at least they looked different. Now theyre just generic hologram men with lines on their face.
-The main story missions are boring. As said before there wasnt much of a story before. Go do some side quests for people to get better stuff and upgrades but that was about it. I am not too far into it but so far the main story has just been "scan these things to get clues on finding the things you need". tedious and boring
-you can no longer do most things on your ship. upgrades and stuff are done at the hub world. some people might like that better, but it makes the ship and the AI that much more useless.
-hunger meter is now a thing. some people like it, some dont. I personally dont like it. you can play on easy and then you dont have one, but then the game is too easy. hunger meter isnt that hard to combat, but when you are sitting there in town talking to people or listening to the main story person babble on, you can starve to death. by the time i realized I was starving I had already died. When you starve, your health drops almost instantly, giving you JUST BARELY enough time to get the food out of your inventory and eat it.
-all around nothing significant has changed since early access to release. a few points I made are about all the have changed, but if you havent played it before, those wont really matter that much, but for a game that was in early access for so long, go without updates for so long and changed so little over that time, it should have been fully released a long time ago.
Thats just half of it.

This game is one of the better open world GTA clones I've played, but it doesn't do much to keep you busy.  There are a lack of side quests & no random events at all.  When older games like True Crime have done a lot more than this one it kind of pales in comparison, especially since this is supposed to be a spiritual successor to the TC series.
You play as an undercover cop in Hong Kong attempting to infiltrate the triad.  You do things that no other cops would in order to fulfill your objective & you eventually become both the cities top cop & the head of the triad.  After you beat the game's story there's really nothing much left to do other than find collectables you missed & once that's done there's nothing left.
The game also doesn't give you guns & you can't carry more than one weapon on your person at any one time.  You have to find/buy a gun & once it's out of ammo it's useless.  You basically treat a gun like it's broken once it runs out of ammo cuz you'll be throwing them away constantly.  Even though the game doesn't focus on guns the gun fights are pretty awesome.  I was in one part where I was at a warehouse riding a Kawasaki Motorcycle & I was shooting guys in bullet time while flying off a ramp then proceeded to jump off my bike onto one of the cars to take out the driver while my bike landed on another car & exploded taking them out.  It's like the best action movie ever made & you're in it.
The real part of the game is in the martial arts & the majority of the game you'll be brawling groups of criminals & executing them in various ways such as putting their head inside an air conditioning fan or grilling them in a fryer.  There's also small fight clubs scattered throughout the game. It can be pretty nasty at times but it's fun.
Overall, the game is good.  Story is something you'd expect from Square Enix but the lasting appeal isn't there.  There is little to no replay value in the game, no NG+, & the world becomes empty of anything to do once you do everything.

The horror genre is dying, unfortunately, it's a very sad fact. Not only in cinematography, but in the whole industry of video games as well. The golden era of horrors is gone. It's been a long time since we've beaten AvP Gold on Director's Cut; discovered the horrible truth of the Covenant family; helped Torque make the right choice in the Baltimore County; saved Earth with Tommy Domasi; barely escaped R'lyeh with detective Jack Walters; fought alongside with young Simon through his darkest nightmares; survived Leafmore High School terror ... The list goes on, for each of us it's different, but we all have something to remember. I've never been to Silent Hill though. Yes, my bad, i regret it very much, too.
But now it's 2016 and i have nothing to play. It's not like i'm asking for a lot, no. Just a simple thriller/shooter. Maybe with a bit of a psychological horror and survival aspects. But i look at the Steam store and what do i see? Acidic pixel "shooters" that have the highest ratings. 2-D Mario-like crap. Minecraft. Filled with agonizing pathos CoD games. Spoiled and ♥♥♥♥ed up AAA titles. All sorts of crap. Then i see something like "A Horrible Horror of a Chainsaw Bloodshed Alien Killer Massive Massacre Gore Zombie Badass Shooting Shooter". I click on it, expecting a nice horror at least, or a cool shooter. And what do i see? A pixel Top-Down game. With highest ratings. And then i realize, that this is it, it's all lost. The genre is practically dead. It's over. The plastic world has won. Noble metal statues and rose-wood masterpieces made with love and care and attention are covered in dust and left forgotten on the shelves of history. Soulless synthetic has replaced the creations of love, mind and talent obeying today's poor taste of a common buyer. The nowadays' generation doesn't need good action horrors, they don't want to be scared. They want to sit there and play addictive acidic ♥♥♥♥ed up ♥♥♥♥♥♥ tasteless meaningless stupid crap. Or pseudo-detective fashionable "camera horrors". Cheap jumpscares and nothing more.
Deep dark stories are not wanted anymore, they are not welcome in today's world. This generation doesn't want a dark action horror with a complicated character, they want simulators. Simulators of fishing, hunting, crafting, building, video taping, of taking a♥♥♥♥♥♥ They are drifting out of touch, and it's more and more visible. Sometimes, very rarely, a single decent horror/action appears. Once in a few years probably. But rarely it happens, and even more rarely it's something playable and enjoyable. The latest one on my mind was Alien Isolation. A good, decent game. But i heard it didn't sell so well, so the sequel is under a big question.

Well, I don't really like doing Early Access "reviews", but I feel I've put enough time into the game and the game itself is already established and fleshed out well enough to warrant a review. Just bear in mind that parts of this review will likely become outdated the further along the development of this game progresses.
Firstly, Battle Brothers, for being an Early Access alpha game, is very stable and polished. Bugs are rare and seem to be fixed rapidly. The game mechanics themselves are already solid and well implemented. As long as development of the game continues, I'd have to say Overhype Studios is doing a fantastic job and is a trustworthy developer.
The game mechanics are typical, but done very well, for this type of game. It's standard fare turn-based combat with a mild amount of role-playing elements. Overall, I'd compare the game to a mixture of Expeditions: Conquistador and Mount & Blade: Warband.
Battle Brothers is brutal. Your troops will die, you'll find yourself frequently frustrated, and sometimes overwhelmed. The game is set in a dark, low-fantasy medieval world, and every battle, no matter how small, is gritty and deadly. If you're someone who doesn't enjoy challenging games, then this isn't really a game for you.
The art and look of this game is awesome. Some people probably won't like it, especially the "game piece" way units are presented on the battlefield. Personally, I like it, and I think it's done exceptionally well. Damage and condition are viscerally and clearly shown on each unit, as well as what armor and weapon they currently have equipped. You can essentially tell how any of your battle brothers are doing just by how they look. It's very cool. As is the fact this is all hand drawn and not your typical indie pixelated mess.
All of this having been said, Battle Brothers does currently have a few issues. This is an Early Access game, that means not everything is implemented yet. Eventually, I found myself bored with nothing to do. It's really only the first few hours that are the most fun. Starting a company, getting through that critical period of making money, buying equipment, barely scrapping by - it's challenging, fresh, and exciting. However, for me, the game tends to hit a point where it begins to feel stale; you're in a limbo where you've cleared much of the map, have a full company of battle brothers, and plenty of equipment and crowns (money). I hope the devs add more long-term and "end game" content to Battle Brothers to alleviate this. There's also another issue I have with this game.
Much of the game is procedural. The map layout, the three battle brothers you start out with, quests; almost everything. This adds replay value to the game, but it also makes it unpredictable in some not so good ways. For example, it's possible to start out with three battle brothers that suck, on a map with towns spaced very far apart, near a city that offers a bad mix of recruitable troops. If you're not experienced with the game, this can prove very frustrating. So, be warned. You may, or may not, like the randomness of the game.
Ultimately Battle Brothers is a solid, challenging, and fun game. It already has a great foundation and shows a lot of promise. I'd definitely recommend it to someone who likes turn-based games or anything in the vein of Mount & Blade.

Sigh. It's really such a shame to say that I wouldn't recommend this game.
I remember seeing this game for the Nintendo DS, but I never got a chance to pick it up. And then this game come to PC with the "HD" version on the title. Saw the negative reviews on the front page but it really can't be that bad right? Since it's horror and everything I figured I might as well try it myself.
The term "disappointment" is a horrible understatement. I didn't expect much graphic wise since it is a port but despite the HD upgrade on the PC, the graphics are still behind the times and everything about it feels outdated. The gameplay is probably better for the Nintendo DS but abysmal for the PC and it's not just the gameplay, it's everything. The sounds repeat for each monster type, the combat music is the exact same loop and the ambiance music is the same. As for the story, well there is a little to no story in the game. You can pick up notes and things but even they do not offer any kind of story, just hints on your current situation. Trust me, there's more story on the description page than the actual game itself.
The monsters are the same warped grotesque things we have seen in the entire Silent Hill franchise and the terror effect no longer exists. Enemies act and look the same to their type. Again there is no explanation for these monsters and why they exist. Most of the game takes place in prison walls, and while there is the occasional town to break up the scenery, most of the game looks pretty flat and dull before long. Colors tend to stick to realistic browns and grays, and while the monsters show some different colors, even they often stick to darker versions of bright colors. Everything looks drab as a result, and the lack of variety in the locations only makes looking at the game that much less interesting.
The walking speed is the speed you should be when crouched or laying down in other games and the run speed is the walking speed. You must hold down the run button the entire time you play but it's okay since you have infinite stamina. You can pick up health pills, medkits, adrenaline shots and poison resistant bottles but I never once used the shots, bottles or medkits and only a couple times used health pills. You can also get a flashlight that flickers on and off constantly, but when it's on a weapon, it stays on.
And then there's the bug. Oh yeah, the gamebreaking bug. You see, I've been playing for three hours and it's all fine and dandy. After encountered the second reanimator monster, I got teleported into the other world and fight against five of those face-spitting acid monsters. Done my business there and finally back to normal world and guess what? I can't get outside of that toilet room! I've tried running, crouching, jumping, slashing, shooting at the open door but the game still won't let me out. There's a machine gun ammo there but it sure as hell didn't help. So here I was thinking, eh maybe I can reload a few saves back and the bug will be gone! But nope, the game decided to say "Well son, that's what you get for not listening to the negative reviews on the store page! Now you get to experience it yourself." And as you can guess, the bug is still there. At this point I already gave up trying and decided to write this review.
It simply baffles me how they can slap High Definition on this when all that was done was barely touching the graphics and adding cutscenes. Within three minutes you can predict when monsters will apear and how the game is going to go pace wise and gameplay wise. And it seems after all these years, the developer didn't even bother to fix their game. The lesson here? Listen to the other reviews before buying anything and it will save you so much time and money. There are dozens of other, better shooters and horror games for your money — ones that make better use of PC controls, sound, and graphical power, so you’re better off steering clear of this game.

Dementium 2 HD is a PC port of a game originally released for the DS. If you compare the game to a lot of other horror games around, you'll find it to be a subpar port - the graphics are bad, voice acting is bad, the cutscenes are bad - even despite considering it's supposed to be a HD remake of the game.
The game itself also has certain issues, with the biggest of them being the terrible hit detection (sometimes you'll shoot an enemy that's standing near a wall or object, but still in clear sight, and the game considers the shot to hit that wall or object) and the character sometimes gets "stuck in nothing" when trying to walk on uneven floor.
Despite these flaws, Dementium 2 HD is still a decent game. It's a game that relies a lot more on making the player feel disturbed rather than relying on jump scares, so it's more disturbing than scary - like the original Silent Hill games (except not as good as them). Story is a bit confusing, but passable at least. The gameplay is decent despite the issues it has. Replay value is, unfortunately, very low - no alternate endings, no extra modes, no secrets, etc. I think probably the biggest letdown of the game is the challenge, as there isn't much challenge - most enemies are very easy to kill even if you lack ammo for your guns, there are a lot of health items through the game, you can get a full health refill at save points and even bosses aren't really challenging. I'd personally recommend playing at the highest difficulty so the game has some level of challenge.
For the cheap price it has, I'd say it's worth it as a one-time experience. If you don't want to get it at full price, wait for a discount or try to get it in a bundle.

I reviewed this game a while ago, and my opinion has has changed twice. It has gone from Negative, to positive and has gone to negative again. I was really happy with the direction that the development was going, but knowing that it is no longer in early access, and may retain it's current state informs this most recent review.
This is a very ambitious passion project, and the developers did an amazing job. It is mind-blowing that the small team at Overhype has produced a game that offers so many hours of entertainment that AAA budget titles can't match. The art is fantastic, the atmosphere is great. The combat and level up experimentation are the strongest selling points for the title, but I don't believe that these positives justify the design flaws.
The player, me in this case, winds up falling into a well packaged skinner box rather than a product that takes the player's time and effort seriously.
There are two core philosophies that are at odds in this game. It wants to encourage the player to be ok with loss. This is highlighted in tips on the loading screen like "expect to lose a few men" and "losing is fun". There are even two achievements for losing. One for losing the first time, and another for losing 10 iron man campaigns. This would be perfectly fine if not for other aspects of the game design.
1. Tips encourage the player to try Veteran mode and Iron man mode, but events, and enemy spawns frequently punish the player with absolutely no avenue for anticipation or counter-play.
Example: maps are procedurally generated and spawns, are absolutely a roll of the dice on who gets high ground, or favorable terrain. Very often a group of 4 archers will spawn above your soldiers with a wall of protection and the enemy AI is set to turtle in every instance that it has this sort of ranged superiority. The same happens for you as well, but it's completely at the whim of RNGeezus. Some contract ambushes during caravan runs will hand you an absolute loss in the form of an enemy spawning right next to the NPC that you have to protect.
2. It takes several hours to get a single brother to a high level, and losing a single high level soldier means hours spent trying to build a replacement while fighting against the same game world that goes out of it's way to the point of inconsistency to make itself difficult.
Example: Most enemy armies can be seen on the world map, but there are several contracts where events force instant encounters with high level enemies. This can be game ending when you decide to take a courier mission as a non-combat option to recover from a rough setback.
The game tells you that you should be OK with losing, while going out of its way to force setbacks and requiring huge amounts of time to reach a position where you as the player can actually contend with the world.
I think the world of the developers. It is an incredibly small team that stuck to a very strict update schedule. At no point during the EA period were purchasers led to believe that the project had gone off the rails or ended. They could write a book on early access handled properly. They were very trainsparent during the whole EA period with their blog over at
. I can't remember how many times a bug was reported and a patch released barely two days later.
I do enjoy some aspects of this game. If further development were announced, I could see purchasing gift copies or the lore book to fund the development. I just can't say "Sure, spend 30 bucks on a game that doesn't respect you or your time" in good conscience. Not without some serious changes in the works.
Don't get me wrong. The game is worth playing, but the price point is rather high. It is not a relaxing experience and requires that the consumer be perfectly ok with a imperfect product full of artificial difficulty spikes.

tl;dr - 8/10 for RPG aspects, 7/10 for Action-based aspects.
Bastion is a great Action RPG that is a great casual game to play. Its style is the type of game that you can either binge a playthrough or take your time and get through in short 30 minute long spurts. In a quick play through, there's about 5-6 hours of gameplay here. For the first playthrough where you take your time and play it a little more thorough than 'barebones', you're looking at a great 10 hour story that unfolds in a great way.
Pros:
-Story is phenominal, and told in a unique way through a narrators eyes.
-Combat is very fun.
-Player/City progression is great.
-Weapon/Skill development is great.
-Replay value. After your first playthrough, you unlock New Game Plus mode, which allows you to continue the game after you play through it. So your second playthrough becomes 'endless'.
-Good variety in weapon loadouts for different combat styles.
-Activating 'idols' for quests increases difficulty. Great that you can do it on the fly if the game gets too easy or too difficult.
-Great sound track. Very rarely do I notice a game's soundtrack. This one definitely stood out to me. Soundtrack does not get repetitive/annoying either.
Cons:
-No DLC or sequel rumors yet for such a great game.
-Wish there was an option for actual 'save slots'.
-Could have been a little more 'side things' to develop character backstories a bit more.

It’s aged horribly, if you are looking to get into GTA start with Vice city then work your way up. Both Vice City and S.A have solid gameplay and story that hold up to this day, this game however does not. Every single critique of this game I have is fixed in Vice City. The story is weak, it’s a revenge tale and yet the main character Claude shows no emotions nor speaks throughout the entire game. You feel empty at the end because it never seemed as if Claude ever cares about anything. You betray characters at a dime for no reason. There is no map, and the mini-map doesn’t tell you where the pay and spray and ammunition are so you have to literally learn the streets. You have hundreds of thousands of dollars to spend on nothing (except guns but good luck finding the ammunation). There are only 3 hideouts and they all look like♥♥♥♥♥♥ for a millionaire Claude sleeps on the floor on the concrete. Every single gang in the game except one is out to kill you and have laser sharp aim. The camera is terrible and will get you killed. The crosshair is not correctly calibrated, bullets go outside of the circle and to the right in the exact same position always, so it is not a glitch but poor programing. The music is terrible, and theirs only about 3 1/2 hours of radio for a 20 hour game. A single station will only have about 20 minutes or about 5 songs each game so it gets extremely repetitive. The map is sectioned off by three bridges, each island is incredibly small. The reason why this is a problem is that there is no map and the game will have missions where you have to travel across islands against the clock. Since there is no map you will fail missions simply because you can’t find the bridge. Cars die in 5-8 hits. The best way to restore your health is to kill yourself because hookers take too long and finding health power-ups is at best random since there is no map and they are not labeled on the minimap. There is armor in the game but I never in 17 hours found it, not once! The handling of the cars is awful and will get you killed since cars can only take 6-8 hits. I played it to see the story and in all honesty it wasn’t worth it. Stick to Vice City, and SA, they are much better games by far. For 3.50 I feel robbed, maybye 0.99, MAYBYE.

They could release this game right now and call it done, if they weren't so perfecting about it.  You can tell the developers are really putting as much part love as they are effort into the development of this game.
Yes, it's early access.  No, it doesn't feel like early access.
Why should you buy it?  I'll tell you!
The game has a level of polish that you rarely see in Early Access, let alone a finished game.  Even for Early Access there is enough to do to get your money's worth out of it.
You start with three mercenaries, and you recruit more as you go from city to town to city to castle.  Want another mercenary?  You see some possible recruits hanging out in the city center, and you read their back stories (because they legitimately have back stories, and you better read them carefully... their stats are tied to them!), you find one possible recruit who used to be a butcher, but he wants more excitement in life... so you recruit him.  His stat bonuses look pretty good!  He's got +melee skill and +fatigue and no negatives, heck, he's even loyal!
You outfit your crew with the available gear at the blacksmith... switching some items around because they're just too heavy for some of your new mercs to wear... gotta work on that fatigue!
With weapons in hand and armor girded you choose a mission and head out into the countryside to fight the Open Graves of the Heimlands Battle.  It's deadly to hit it head on, so you wait for roaming bands of undead to pour forth and engage them one at a time.
After many battles a few of your mercs have learned new tricks, and skilled up.  Your former meat carver looks like he's doing well.  So, you engage the open graveyard head on... it doesn't look so bad now.
The battle is bloody, and you find yourself outnumbered 13 to 5.  The fighting is fierce, and your heroes are only alive because of the new armor you had obtained for them... which is now in tatters.  Shields broken, weapons failing, the last of the undead is slain.
Surveying the battlefield you note your old friends are still alive, and one of the new recruits... but the butcher has fallen.
His memory won't be lost.
Time to return to the town and claim your bounty... it better be worth it.  You've got gear to fix, wounds to heal, and a new recruit to pick up.
Hopefully this one won't die on you.

Im really enjoying myself playing this early access game Battle Brothers. Managing your group of mercenaries going about in this open medieval fantasy world. You are to take up contracts from merchant for earning of your coins and it is up to if you want to fulfill or break the contract, seeing how the situation goes. The towns and cities are randomly generated with every start of a new game, as well as your starting mercenaries.
The combat is a turn base strategy which means combat is RNG and you have to do some management in terms of your AP, fatigue, HP, resolve, initiative and gears. Your mercenaries do level up through combat and you could choose which skills and stats (increasing of stats are interesting as you only could choose 3 stats and it randomly gives you an increase number from 1-5) to increase. Do take note that if one of your men got killed, he remains dead throughout the game, which leads you having to take up new contract with new men and to re-train them from low level up.
Currently, you can have only 12 men at any given time (until further down the dates where the developers will be adding in helpers and might be able to increase the number of roster of your men). Still, having just 12 men doesn't make the game any boring at the current stage, due to the permanent death mechanics.
To add on, I love the graphic details for this game, the weapons, armors, the mercenaries, the monsters, the environment, the showing of wounds and the decapitation. Furthermore, the developers are very active in updating the game and response well to the community.

I've been playing Renegade Kid games for a while, starting with the first Dementium when it first came out on the DS almost 10 years ago. I also finished Moon on DS. And I remember getting this game and playing for about 30 minutes before my DS got stolen one day. I didn't even get a taste of what this game was like.
You see, Dementium: The Ward was pretty amazing, because it's one of the few first person survival horror games I can think of on the DS. Sure, it was buggy, sure, the animations were wonky, sure, one of the worst parts, enemies respawned all the time, and suuure, the game was ♥♥♥♥ing short. I managed to finish it on a single sitting.
Now, I got this years ago. I got to play Dementium II back when it first game out, and when I found out that they were making a PC port, I was excited. I'll be able to finally seal this chapter of my life.
Well, I guess the game didn't age well at all. Unlike Obscure.  The port seems lazy, the visuals look like something out of the PS2 era, the sounds are atrocious most of the time, and the controls feel kinda...Laggy. I swear, it feels like some of your attacks, or even when you stop moving ,there's this momentum before anything happens. Less than a second, but still quite noticeable.
The game is rather short. I managed to finish it in less than 4 hours. The achievements can't be all unlocked in a single sitting, though. Because you need to re-do some of the boss fights with a different weapon to get some of them.
The world is heavily inspired by Silent Hill, and the monsters seem to be, too, yet they don't even come close to being scary most of the time. Same for the ambience.
This game feels lackluster, unpolished, the animations are terrible at times, and all in all, it's not really scary. I think what made the original Dementium amazing was the fact that there was not much like it on the DS at the time, and when translated to the PC (albeit, lazily), where there's MUCH better games out there, this game feels vastly inferior and mediocre. The ending is completely underwhelming, too and the final boss was a pushover. The storytelling was...Not that good. I mean, I enjoyed it. I've got a thing for mediocre games, and I like the dementium games as dumb as they are, but for the average Joe, I wouldn't recommend it.

Oh dear, poor Garry has gotten himself into quite a sticky situation! First, Garry the humble bush pilot had a bit of a mishap during a not-so routine transport job due to Yellowstone’s Mount Saint Helena erupting right as he passed over it, resulting in a crash landing in the middle of...The Amazon jungle? If that wasn’t bad enough, Garry now needs to endure countless lethal cannibalistic natives chasing after him all over the place, puzzles that’ll test your patience and game-breaking bugs that are as hilarious as they are frustrating. Let’s take a look at Garry’s Incident.
So, here we have Day One: Garry’s Incident, Wild Games Studio’s brand new, first person, action-adventure survival game. You play as Garry, a pilot who just crashed into the jungle and soon realizes that, along with the aggressive and possibly very hungry natives, rock-flinging monkeys and badly animated panthers that will devour your heart without a second’s hesitation, there is also something else going on in this place. Something very strange. Something...alien.
That’s basically the whole story summed up. Now that we have that out of the way, let’s look at the gameplay, shall we? So, Day One is, if anything, ambitious. It combines a lot of different gameplay mechanics in an attempt to stand out from the crowd. Though the description of the game might have you believe that this is some sort of open-world, free-roaming survival simulator like Minecraft or Don’t Starve, Day One is much more linear than that. You still have some freedom to move about the lush jungle environments as you scavenge for supplies and resources to stay alive, but this is definitely no sandbox game.
Speaking of Minecraft, there are some comparisons to be made between it and Day One. In a somewhat similar fashion to Minecraft, you have a hunger meter that gradually depletes over time unless you find food via hunting, fishing or plucking fruit from bushes. Day One also has a similar crafting system, where you combine items you find and click a button to convert into new tools and other useful things. Though you can experiment with the system to craft items, you’ll also discover pieces of recipes as you explore the world. You’ll need to memorize these, because the game doesn’t log the recipe for you before you successfully craft an item on your own.
The crafting itself is simplistic and the inventory menu is sub-par, making the crafting more tedious than it has to be. Click the crafting tab, then click the items you wish to use in the crafting process, hit “craft” and you might make something. Every time you craft something you need to go through the exact same quicktime event, over and over again. In fact, QTEs are very commonplace throughout the game and you’ll get annoyed by them faster than you would watching Daniel Tosh do stand-up “comedy”.
Another issue with the crafting, that is also something that goes far deeper than that, is the fact that this and the hunger system are completely arbitrary. You will never really need to catch much food. In fact, you can stay alive on the random fruits you find around the world alone. This is in part due to the fact that the game only has a couple of hours’ worth of gameplay before you complete it. In other words, risking your life hunting panthers or combining dozens of random items in an attempt to make a fishing rod is absolutely pointless. You’ll never need to worry about finding water sources to drink from or refill your bottle for longer treks either. Just click C - the default “drink water at water source” button - and you can drink water directly. Anywhere. Yes, even if there is no water around.
Now, the aforementioned is obviously a bug and not intentional. Bugs are something Day One has a lot of. A LOT. I’ll give the developers some credit: they’ve released about five hundred million patches by now, improving upon the abysmal performance issues players had at launch and many of the worst game-breaking bugs. But even with most of the worst bugs now fixed - hell, BECAUSE many of the bugs are now fixed - it’s just so obvious that the game sorely lacks quality gameplay.
I mean, where do I even begin? Okay, let’s look past the bugs for a second. I’ve already mentioned how the crafting system is pointless. Beyond that, the game’s mandatory puzzles are incredibly tedious and often demand that you backtrack and search every single crevasse in the large environments to find that one thing that’ll let you continue.
At one point, you’ll find yourself trapped inside an enormous maze of underground tunnels, where you need to pull switches in order to align some statues that opens up a gate, allowing you to escape. This simple task is arbitrarily stretched out and made incredibly frustrating by the fact that the switches are scattered around the maze far from one another, and finding them all is a pain because you only have a crude map painted on the rock walls to guide you. There are plenty of dead ends too. Sure, the various traps you’ll encounter are cool and somewhat challenging to master, but walking around for hours looking for switches gets tedious fast. This is not engaging puzzle-solving, people! It’s clearly just a cheap attempt to artificially pad out the game. In fact, the entire game suffers from this problem; you can spend a dozen hours completing this game that only has about three hours of actual gameplay and believe me, that’s not meant as a compliment here.
The extensive list of mind-boggling design choices continues. The game employs a crude stealth system that allows you to sneak up on enemies and kill them in a single hit. However this system is also made pointless because you’ll find so much ammo for your two pistols that you can easily kill every enemy in the game without worrying about ever running out. What is the point of spending three minutes sneaking up on some native - or engaging in close combat with him that exposes the atrocious melee system with broken hit-registration and laughable animations - when you can just shoot him in the head and move on without risking your life? For a survival game, surviving isn’t all that hard. Well, for Garry, anyway. For you, as the player, it can be a tough test to endure the torment of this game.
At least the game looks kind of okay. The graphics aren’t high-end or anything, but the jungles have a lot of foliage, making them feel lush and alive. It’s quite ambitious for such a small game. Animations, however, are not good. The world design is confusing and repetitive. You’ll also get stuck on objects or invisible walls all the time and you can clip through objects and even the ground. The sound design wobbles between mediocre and horrendous. Aiming your weapon feels sluggish. The inventory menu feels like it’s a pre-alpha placeholder. The QTEs are never-ending and...the list just goes on and on. Let’s cut it off here, shall we?
I can sympathise with Garry Friedman. He’s in a pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥ situation. As was I, when I played this game. No matter how hard I tried to look for redeeming factors, I just couldn’t find any. When I finally reached the abrupt ending, I was disappointed that the game just wrapped up before it ever made use of any of its interesting mechanics and before it went anywhere with the story. But, at the same time, I was also happy that I was finally out of that hell. It’s obvious that the developers had a lot of ambitious ideas, but sadly the few mechanics that work are rendered pointless by the level design and the game-breaking bugs. Despite some glints of ambition here and there, even when ignoring the bugs, there isn’t anything here to warrant purchasing Day One: Garry’s Incident.

Fallout 4 is possibly one of the worst failures I have had to endure as a game. Not only did it fail on being delivered as a Fallout game, it fails almost, if not entirely on the rpg aspect. I'm going to get the good out of the way to complain about the bad.
-There are literally two moments in the story that are 'awesome'.
-The settlement system is fun
-The graphics are great, and certainly a leap from Skyrim/Fallout;New Vegas.
-Weapon creation is neat, and power armor customization is cool.
-The companions are great, and do add life to this game, save for a few.
Now for the bad:
The story fails on all fronts to deliver an experience worthy of the Fallout name, and by extension Bethesda. I have seen mods with better story the the steaming pointless trainwreck leading straight to boredom that this game offers as it's focal point. The story didn't start off bad, but then it entered a cliche story which was incredibly obvious from the beginning.
The game has about as much RPG gameplay in it as an open world call of duty. There's quests, sure. "Oh look, a quest to kill 5 of this thing, or a quest to defeat this dude, or that dude, etc., "Go get this item". Which is so sad compared to the beauty that Fallout used to have in its quests, because that beauty is nowhere to be seen here except for maybe 3 questlines(possibly less)
Settlements. serve. no. purpose. Make a chest, dump your stuff in it, leave. Or if you're one of those people that like to make functioning computers in minecraft or something, this is for you I guess.
You can't place yourself in the shoes of the main character either, cause he's a robot that only has four emotions. "Happy!, Sad :(, Convince perk,  Sarcastic.". Compared to previous Fallout/Elder Scrolls games, which had so many options, this is possibly the worst offender, but I understand as the whole game was voiced.
There. is. a. settlement. in. danger. here, l e t m e m a r k i t f o r y o u.

Full disclosure: Jumped in at the start of Early Access, on-and-off over the 3 years of development with a total 47 hours before 1.0.
Solid focus on exploration combined with a large bank of content elements used in a procedurally-generated universe makes this one game that rewards the time spent just looking around checking whats over the next hill, or the next cave branch.
Easy to understand progression and tiering that expands the further out you go, combined with a central story structure that rewards no matter one's playstyle or pace.
Beautifully composed soundtrack that stands on its own as well as suport the beautiful environments and landscapes the game gives you.
Extensive (and optional) colony creation system that is extensible to how little or how far you want to take it, allowing one to be diverse and creative in creating a colony/base.
Launches with Steam Workshop support, combined with a years-old community thanks to its Early Access roots makes it a game that has solid mods right from the get-go, which thankfully it does not need given how well-crafted a game it is.
======
The deep focus on exploration may not be to the taste of some, who may wish to fight for their gains, or keep building instead.
As understandable the progression of the game is and how well-tied it is into one's pace of playing, some of it in the early game are "gated" by what feels like mandatory storyline missions.
The game comes shipped with more soundtracks than actually utilized in the 1.0 release, either because better tracks are now in use, or for future use for future content.
Colony creation system can be somewhat confusing at the start, seemingly requiring arbitrary things such as beautification, use of building materials, and themeing.
The game has been in development for 3 years on Steam Early Access, arguably a very long time in Early Access and has undergone a lot of changes, changes that can be a determining factor in why the game isnt higher rated than it should be, because of disgruntled early adopters or similar.

Without a doubt, this is one of my favorite games. That comes from a guy with about 200 sitting installed on his PC.
Kingdom Rush offers everything I expect from a tower defense game and more; it takes the genre from the base flash games we all played in the school media center as children (which it once was- thanks to the devs, and congratulations for making it this far! I've been a fan since Armor Games.) and improves upon it to truly make it a genre and a game worthy of Steam.
Kingdom rush gameplay is very entertaining, and the wide variety of towers and options made available to you in upgrades outside of levels provide for an individual experience- you decide what strategy is most important to you. Activated abilities can save your rear-end in a close call, or you can use them liberally and as a backbone of your strategy. Footmen can be deployed and placed at your command to stop incoming enemies and maximize the effectiveness of your towers. Do you provide your towers that extra zap potential, or do you instead have them push enemies back down the road?
Though the tower defense is at first glance a seemingly simplistic genre, Kingdom Rush makes it something you can sink days into. I've played through the full flash title, and I bought this copy because I was so fond of it. This Steam copy also provides many more levels and intricacies, such as heroes you can command and chose to fit your playstyle.
Kingdom Rush also provides some astonishing art in my opinion. The game looks terrific, and has an individual indie look to it-and not the hipstery-indie kind, the genuine, we-made-this-for-fun-and-sunk-our-sweat-and-toil-into-this kind.
I can't reccommend this game enough. Kingdom Rush is one of my favorites, and I hope to see more astonishing work from the devs in the future.

The Good:
- Highly addictive, frantic gameplay. Additionally, Kingdom Rush isn’t mired with complexity, and so it is extremely accessible for newcomers to the genre.
-  Kingdom Rush has a high degree of replay value. Every map has three levels of challenges. While the heroic challenge is simply a repeat with more enemies and fewer waves, the Iron Challenges are more creative because they limit you to particular towers only. Additionally, massive amounts of enemies are thrown at you in one consistent wave.
- Excellent music, and the art design perfectly complimented the casual nature of Kingdom Rush.
- During my playthrough, I did not experience any bugs or crashes. Moreover, even with a multitude of enemies and heroes on screen battling to the death, the game maintained a smooth frame without any inconsistencies.
The Bad:
- While I cited Kingdom Rush’s accessibility as a positive, later maps in the main campaign, in addition to the bonus maps, lack creative depth. Specifically, regardless of the map’s environment or layout, the player only needs to construct Tesla Towers in order to completely dominate the enemy. Perhaps if they had included environment specific towers or towers which have increased stats under certain conditions the overall gameplay would have been significantly elevated.
Final Verdict:
I highly recommend this game at full price. I had a blast going through the main campaign and the smaller add-on campaigns.

"140 is a challenging"
Not particularly. Discounting the final "boss" stage, the game simply asks you to be aware of the obstacles changing with the rhythm. As for the final "boss" stage, it's not challenging as much as it is frustrating. The rhythm still tells you when to act, but precicely how to act is randomized.
"minimalistic"
This isn't always a positive descriptor; it certainly isn't here. The extent of your controls are "move" and "jump," and neither of those have any variable function. When you move, you will always move the same speed. When you jump, you will always jump the same height. The entire game can be played through in about one hour, which is good because there's no save function. There's not even a game menu.
"abstract colorful graphics."
The aesthetic feels like a Mondrian fever dream, full of harsh lines and contrasting colors. It's easy enough to understand which square you are and your goals, but that doesn't make it more appealing to look at.
"Rhythmic awareness is required to overcome obstacles"
Can you count to four? Congratulations, you've mastered the rhythm of the game. So much of the game's playtime is spent simply staring at the screen, waiting for the right moment to move rather than actually accomplishing anything. And while the obstacles move to the rhythm, the player icon does not, jarring the musically-inclined from actually relaxing into the music of the game.
"energetic, yet melancholic electronic soundtrack."
That is certainly a complex description of drums. So many drums. If you must play this game, avoid headphones to avoid a pounding headache.

Combines the turn-based tactical gameplay of X-Com with the low-fantasy setting of Mount & Blade, albeit with more fantasy elements such as the undead & orcs. The artwork, music and atmosphere is absolutely spot on in all respects.
The world is completely randomly generated each time you play which gives incredible replay value. Every character in the world (except in the tutorial mission at the start) is randomly generated, so everything always feels fresh, every time you play a new campaign it is like a new game all over again - nothing is the same. But the world itself is very dynamic, in other words the whole thing is like a living simulation. Villages can be burned by orcs, and caravans raided by brigands, and if so then the economy of the town suffers, and the prices will go up and food will be hard to get in that town, and so on. There are all sorts of nasty things going on all around the world in real time whether you get involved or not.
Your men can lose spirit and defect, they can get brutal permanent injuries which affect them permanently, and there is just so much detail here. Every character is different, every weapon has its strengths and weaknesses, every attribute is useful, everything in this game is expertly balanced and there is just constantly challenging and painstaking decisions awaiting you at every turn.
For me, it's just a struggle to keep my men fed and paid while travelling around looking for contracts which won't get us all killed. Because I'm playing on Ironman,The world feels extremely dangerous and you really have to claw your way up from the bottom, as you start out by hiring only the cheapest men you can afford such as beggars, wierdos and country bumpkins from the farm.
Only over time do you become attached to your men as you painstakingly keep them alive with food, heal their injuries, repair their armour, buy them a round at the tavern to keep their spirits up, and slowly level them up and nurture their attributes. But knowing they can be permanently killed at any time if things turn nasty out in the battlefield.
It's these real difficult choices all the time... we only have a small amount of money to keep the men paid for a few days.. but I don't want Heinrich to die... he's only a farm boy but he has some experience now and he's a talented learner, becoming the strong point of our shield wall, we need him badly and he only has a cloth cap for protection.. do we spend the money and get him a helmet which is expensive, or do we risk taking him out and risk getting hit in the head? Perhaps a permanent head injury, or we get unlucky and an arrow gets him in the head? And also, do we pay for the healers to help with Fritz's split shoulder? Or just put him in the back row and hope he will be alright and use the money to buy a helmet for Heinrich? These decisions just keep going on and on and it never gets old and it's always exciting to see how things turn out in the end.
Warning: ball-breaking permadeath and ruthlessly capable enemy AI. The enemies are just absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s to fight against and will give you nothing for free and try to cause you as much pain as possible.
However this is what makes it so exciting and when you die, you really are dead, but there isn't a frustration of repetition because the next game will be in a completely new generated world and so although you may have died, there is a new world around the corner.
If you loved X-Com and medieval fantasy settings, then this game is the game you have always been waiting for. This game has an Ironman mode and this is the way it must be played. So when death comes, the death is real. And when you win a dangerous fight - it really is so satisfying because the danger was real for your men.

TLDR: Game is good enough to make me write my first review - but this is all subjective - your mileage may vary.
Good:
1. Open world - a nice map, somehow invoking a certain Darklands feel. I personally enjoy the fact that not every single nok and cranny has some content - I find the emptiness in some areas create a nice frame for those areas with cities, enemies stronghold etc., a juxtaposition of civilization and wilderness.
2, Squad management - already satisfyingly rich and detailed, with plenty of options and depth to get into. Character backgrounds and traits are nicely described without running too long. They allow one to create a nice impression of one's troops and make your squad more like actual people.
3. Quest/contract system - I find it refreshing that they are not all "save the world from". There is some variation: escorting, scouting, fighting. They don't sseem that much scripted, but rather taking advantage from the open world, e.g. when I took a very handsomely paying escort mission, I htought I will be beset by "unexpected" ambushers the whole way, as per the genre standards. In a surprising twist, the road was calm - but maybe even more stressful because of that.
4. Graphcis - I find them charming, clear to see what is what and pretty enough.
5. Tactical battles - playing on normal difficulty, they were good enough - I don't have experience enough to see if different groups of enemies have widely different tactics (e.g. orks more prone to charging headfirst, while rogues preferring to attack from the flanks) but the AI decently uses its troops and terrain.
UI - the devs say they will improve it significantly, but already I did not have any significant issues with it.
BAD/MY WISHES:
1. A world map would be a huge help, especially when deciding on a contract.
2. I wouldn't mind being able to personalize the leader of the company more - not to put them on the field, more like giving them separate experiewnce based on contracts fulfilled which in turn provided boons like cheaper recrutiment, additional contracts available etc.
3. Factions and standing with them, diplomacy in general - if I say raid caravans originating from one town, it would be nice if they would consider me an outlaw and send their troops after me. Also with the enemies, allowing for a some kind of cease fire or even cooperation with them.
4. I wouldn't mind female characters for players and enemies - just for some variation,
5. Headquarters - a single, fortified camp to call one's own, to return to between contracts and to further customise with trophies after victories and upgrades for the benefit of the company.
OTHER:
Currently, there is only a video tutorial on youtube but I found it easy enough to pick it up from simply playing and reading the tooltips. Be aware that I've learnt this approach on Europa Universalis series with their lack of tutorials, so yeah.
Lack of main quest line - it will be added. I don't actually miss it, it will be something nice to have, but I have fun already as it is.
Some minor bugs - I've had only one gamebreaking bug when in combat AI would not take it turn, other than that there are just a few, such as items going to the bottom of the stash when one unequips them - nothing major.

I am starting to become addicted to these things, these hidden object adventure puzzlers. Maybe its because I’m an old fart, and tiring of the blood and gore of my staples like Fallout and GTA. Or is it because Artifex Mundi actually know how to make a great adventure game, one that at times rivals those of Lucas Arts, such classics as Monkey Island, Loom or Day of the Tentacles.
Story
You play an unnamed female who is in search of her boyfriend Robert, a dashing nautical researcher (I like my men without beards, thank you) who happens to disappear while investigating a supposedly abandoned underwater city called Eden.
In your travels to find Mr Right-half-the-time, you find survivors of the failed aquatic utopia, who are trying to fight a mysterious ancient evil (Look, it’s George Burns!), that was accidentally awakened during construction of new extensions to the city. In the end it’s a typical save the city, get the guy kind of thing (though he needs to be taller, I like my men taller please).
Game Play
Abyss: The Wraith of Eden is still predominately hidden object puzzles but there is a bigger smattering of actual brain teasers that keep you hooked. All the puzzles are logical and down to earth, making you feel more like MacGyver, than mind destroying abstract art-ish ones that need you to take an acid trip just to understand them.
Example, while exploring a submerged room for something to snip some fence wire, I found a toolbox, ‘Excellent’ I thought. Nope, all the tools are broken into pieces and buried under mud and silt. WTF!!!!!, then I investigated the room further and found a hidden metal detector, hoorah! Use the detector to find the parts for a pair of pliers and your done.
Most of the game will have you going back and forth throughout the city, so to solve a puzzle in one room, will sometimes need items collected from either the next or previous rooms, or somewhere else in the complex. This can get you a little lost in you objectives, but thankfully Artifex Mundi threw in a map that keeps you on track and helps you find your way around.
Even the hidden object puzzles are no longer just random useless garbage that you need to find for the sake of finding it. Some of the items you need to advance a puzzle are lost in the pictures, so now the hidden object puzzles feel that they have a purpose to the whole story.
Everything Else
The graphics are a huge improvement over my last Artifex reviewed game, Time Mysteries: Inheritance. Granted TM:I was a remastered older game but Abyss now uses a better graphic engine, thought there are times where the cut scenes tend to look smokey and pixeled.
The voice acting has also been stepped up and gives the game more plausibility to another well written story line. The only let down this time round is the music. Most times it hits the mark and creates the right atmosphere, other times it just loses the tempo and dose not gel with the game, breaking the mood (Well, no candle lit dinner for you pal!).
Ok, so Artifex Mundi is the Mills and Boon of computer games, hey I loved the Twilight series…. Oh♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Did I just say that out loud….. well I’m f%#&ed now, my creditability has just gone down the gurgler.
Look if you don’t mind playing female heroes, love puzzlers and a well written adventure then Abyss:- The Wraith of Eden is a must for your library. Now I must get back to putting these pink ribbons in my beard and ponytail.

How do I start? Where to begin? How is perfection created? Answers that may never see the light of day; although, the product of perfection stands right before us. In this game, starring the amazingly written characters: Sergeant, Jesus, Canada (child), and Egg. This is a story of courage, of love, of friendship, of betrayal, and climbing. Gunplay so incredible, one cannot simply begin to put it into words. However, if there is one major flaw with this masterpiece, is that it is flawless.
Not only are we graciously blessed with an amazing story, but the developers even went out of thier to bestow upon us not one, not two, not three, but FOUR incredible bonus stages; each with their own story, purpose, life lesson, and Egg. Weapon variety unseen, truly the most dedicated piece of work ever created.
Let's begin with the menu. Beautiful art, amazing graphics, intuitive design, and a dog. After entering the game, you are met with a handsome young gentleman who goes out of his way, taking the time out of his day, to teach you the basics. What a kind creator. If only god could be so kind... or perhaps, he was? For creating this masterpiece.
After the short tutorial, you are allowed (ALLOWED, as in given the choice by the great creator) to choose your own path, your own mission.
I begun with the boxing arena. I was expecting a quick boxing fight, but was met with a series of perfect levels, amazing OST, and enemy variety spanning through the ages. Upon reaching the boss, I was met with the battle of my life. So tense, so breathtaking, and yet, over in a flash. Upon beating the boss, I was left to ponder... to wander. And then I went back to the tutorial area.
Level 2. The Egg. There were eggs. And more eggs.
Storymode: You start with an arsenal, and of course, the best weapon of them all: the strongest, the most versatile, the quickest. You are able to pulverise the incoming swarm of Kim's henchmen. After reaching the entrance, instead of doing the cliche of walking through a door, you have scale to the top. Of course, rather than forcing you do a task so difficult, the gracious developers allow a cutscene to do the work for you. And it keeps going. And keeps going. And keeps going. Then you are arrested. Then climb again. And it keeps going. Until you reach the top. The top where Kim himself resides.
After the most intense firefight of my life, I am greeted by 'Sergeant' who brings the biggest, greatest plot twist known to man. After betraying you, the credits roll. The story concludes.
In conclusion, this game. This game. Beauty incarnate. I cannot recommend this game enough. If you are looking for the best game ever made, you have found it my friend. Enjoy.

Abyss: The Wraiths of Eden is another hidden object game from Artifex Mundi which takes us on a journey into an underwater city, searching for our missing boyfriend (we play as a female detective as in most of these types of games). Soon we discover the tragic fate that befell the inhabitants of the city and we must find a way out before it is too late.
As a side note we also learn that the professor who leaves us clues admittedly loves riddles, so there's an actual explanation for encountering so many of them :)
Does the story seem familiar? Wouldn't be surprised if it did. 2K Games made an absolutely amazing first-person shooter in 2007 with a quite similar story and setting. Apparently Artifex Mundi drew a bit too heavily on the concept of Bioshock while making this game and it certainly shows: the Art Deco design and architecture, the flyers and even the letter formats boldly display the source where it came from. As a matter of fact there's no harm in it for me, I love the deep sea environment. The problem is with the plot: after beating the game (and the bonus chapter as well) we are still riddled with questions. What happened to the city exactly, who are these mysterious legates (/wraiths) and where did they come from, why have they been given so many privileges?
It's a shame really, because the game does a great job creating suspense and is thrilling throughout. It feels as if a little more work on the story would have helped the end result greatly.
Of course this doesn't mean the game is bad, actually there are plenty of good things around. First of all this is probably the most eventful HOG I've ever had the fortune to play with: wherever we go something always happens, changes. A warning note appears on the door, the light goes out suddenly or a corpse falls right in front of our feet! So in regard to horror, it is very similar to the previous HOG I've played, Dark Arcana: The Carnival.
Also there's a fair amount of plant horror, which would be interesting, but unfortunately we get no explanation regarding this either, so it feels like a missed opportunity.
While most of the minigames and puzzles have been seen before, they represent the good old Artifex Mundi quality, they are good and fun.The problematic ingredient of the 'twice used hidden object scenes' is present in this game as well, however this time at least these scenes are placed quite near to the target locations (where we have to use that specific item we've just gained). Maybe it's just me, but I had trouble finding some items in a few HO scenes though, some of them didn't really match their names. Also there was a puzzle in which we had to reassemble a fishbone, by putting away the obstacles that were covering the parts. Problem is, there was hardly any space for that, so I spent about 15 minutes trying to jam every unnecessary items into the corners in order to reach the fishbone pieces...
Just like in Dark Arcana: The Carnival, we can exchange the current HO with an alternative method by playing domino. In here we must play according to regular domino rules (by matching the neighboring symbols) and the goal is to reach the tree emblems.
There's another parallel with Dark Arcana: The Carnival, the lack of map travel. I don't usually use this feature, but in this game it would have been handy, as we are going to use the elevator fairly often. Altough there's a point in the game where we get cornered by a [/spoiler]giant octopus[/spoiler], so I can see the logic of not having it implemented, this should still be available in the rest of the game.
There's also a bonus chapter which is fairly short and shows us a snippet what Eden (the city) was like before the catastrophic events. Problem is, we get more questions instead of having answers to the already existing ones. Also the pregnant wife of Gregory caused me a slight confusion (was she carrying the twins or the girl who helps us in the main adventure?). It didn't really help the plot moving forward, so it felt a bit pointless.
The graphics is great for a hidden object game, both the graphic design (thanks to Bioshock ;)) and the realisation look great. The deep sea environments are full of details thus it's a treat to discover all the locations. The backgrounds are nicely drawn with vivid colours, the cutscenes are fluid and hardly pixellated. The sounds are above average, while the music is just mediocre, but it does help keeping up the suspense well enough.
So despite the unanswered questions that remain, the game can still be considered good and is recommendable. If you like underwater scenery and are up for a ~5 hour long adventure, give it a try. And make sure you play Bioshock afterwards, if you haven't already done so :)
PROS
+ interesting (if not very original) deep sea, underwater city setting
+ plenty of minigames with alternative domino game
+ great imagery
+ thrilling cutscenes
CONS
- plot holes
- bonus chapter is lackluster
RATING

I must say, this is one of the best tower defense games out there.  It is simple, but can be very challenging; it is very chill, but can be very involving as well; and it is calm, but can be stressful.
The artwork is what drew me to this game first--it is awesome!  The creatures are excellently animated, and my wife even likes this game more than I do.  It's good for all gamers, IMO.
The only complaint I have is that there are only set stations where you can build your towers.  I would prefer a little more freedom with it.  But that also works into the challenge of the game--you have to deal with limitations and still try to win.  Plus, even with set areas to build, it's WHAT you build there that matters so much.
Lastly, I've noticed that iOS units have TWO sequels for this game..... BRING THEM TO STEAM!!!!!!  I'd buy them all in a heartbeat, as this game is very affordable and still brings many hours of enjoyment for the whole family.

A change to a negative review for this game is long overdue.
This game was freakin' awesome, I loved it. You transformed into monsters to kill your opponents in an Arena FPS fashion and the theme was great, even though most of the music and sound were royalty free which you can find online.
But unfortunately, the developers were aiming solely to become some giant eSport and were so worried of, I quote "being like any other arena FPS" that they never listened to their community - except for literally like 2-4 people who moaned about any change that came with a patch, and would get reverted instantly, effectively making some patches a waste of bandwidth. There was only one game mode, which was a duel where whoever dies first loses but you could also play in the "warmup" lobby, where it's just DM with no score limit and a 10 minute time limit which you could not change.
To make it worse, the master server for this game went down within weeks after launch and the developers still haven't done anything about it, and this was released November of 2014. The servers have literally been down for over a year. When the servers were up, you could only host a dedicated server by emailing your info to the developers to allow your server to even be seen on their master server and you couldn't create a listen or LAN server.
It isn't like the developers are too busy with their lives/not on steam much or anything because the game isn't going on sale all the time all by itself and their Steam account shows that they've been playing other games. Either way it's bad practice. They're blatantly ignoring their forums, not even letting people know if they're really done with the game or not but obviously they are. There's literally no point in buying this game because you can't even play it, unless you consider having bots that literally don't miss a single shot even if just a pixel of you is visible as playing. Oh well, I had fun exploiting console commands to spawn Unreal Tournament 3 guns and powerups in online servers while it lasted. Oh yeah and there's that.

Starts off just okay, but it's the kind of game that takes its time and works you over slowly.
The gameplay is pretty similar to Ys, but you may be happy to hear there's no where near as much grinding. You couldn't even revisit completed levels if you wanted to but the game is of a modest difficulty that, barring some optional stuff and new game plus, won't really push you all that hard. The meat of the gameplay is the variety provided to you, though, and not so much the struggle to progress. Right up until the end of the game, you receive one weapon after another, each one having a pretty neat synergy with others. (you can only have two at a time, plus a consumable attack)
It's also a pretty good play for completion-oriented users. The additional challenge levels will take a few tries, but nothing is absurd. If you manage your upgrades properly and use the right tools for the job, everything will be well within reason to complete, given some getting used to all the difficulty modifiers neccessary for 100%.
A lot of the staying power in this game is in the killer atmosphere. It's usually whimsical, with some somber moments, but whatever mood the game is going for at the moment, it really nails it with the soundtrack, art style, and narration. Seriously, the narrotor really sells the experience. He's a conduit for the developers to joke at your expense, bring the setting of the game to life, and give the whole narrative a strong prescence.
But there are quirks, too. The automatic aiming of your shield/bow/gun towards the nearest enemy will bite you in the keister more than a few times, along with some strange hit detection trickery when parrying blows. The balance of the game isn't always on point, either, whether it be a useless weapon or a trial level where the difficulty isn't what it should be. I tend to find that the little things like choice of different weapon perks or tonic slots help keep these issues down.
If you happen to frequent game bundle sites, you might already have this game. It's aged a little since release, but you really ought to try it out.

Unfortunately, Dementium II HD is not as good a port. I didn’t play it on 3DS, so I have absolutely no opinion on how it was before, but as a PC release, it’s…not so good. It has its moments, but is overall a subpar game in what is already a crowded genre.
Disclaimer: I played for roughly 90 minutes, in which time I got through the village, collected the dagger and returned to the prison, going through it a little bit, before I decided not to keep going. The remainder of the time was letting the game run to collect the trading cards from it.
It might be potentially unfair to review this as a PC game, based on its source material and the limitations of the system. But, the developer has called it HD, which would imply that it’s been improved, at least somewhat, for PC.
That does not seem to be the case. Which is a shame, because it looks like Dementium II has a good story to tell. But, if unlike me, you’ve played and beaten the 3DS version, you likely already know the story, so it may not be a big deal.

TLDR: Game is good enough to make me write my first review - but this is all subjective - your mileage may vary.
Good:
1. Open world - a nice map, somehow invoking a certain Darklands feel. I personally enjoy the fact that not every single nok and cranny has some content - I find the emptiness in some areas create a nice frame for those areas with cities, enemies stronghold etc., a juxtaposition of civilization and wilderness.
2, Squad management - already satisfyingly rich and detailed, with plenty of options and depth to get into. Character backgrounds and traits are nicely described without running too long. They allow one to create a nice impression of one's troops and make your squad more like actual people.
3. Quest/contract system - I find it refreshing that they are not all "save the world from". There is some variation: escorting, scouting, fighting. They don't sseem that much scripted, but rather taking advantage from the open world, e.g. when I took a very handsomely paying escort mission, I htought I will be beset by "unexpected" ambushers the whole way, as per the genre standards. In a surprising twist, the road was calm - but maybe even more stressful because of that.
4. Graphcis - I find them charming, clear to see what is what and pretty enough.
5. Tactical battles - playing on normal difficulty, they were good enough - I don't have experience enough to see if different groups of enemies have widely different tactics (e.g. orks more prone to charging headfirst, while rogues preferring to attack from the flanks) but the AI decently uses its troops and terrain.
UI - the devs say they will improve it significantly, but already I did not have any significant issues with it.
BAD/MY WISHES:
1. A world map would be a huge help, especially when deciding on a contract.
2. I wouldn't mind being able to personalize the leader of the company more - not to put them on the field, more like giving them separate experiewnce based on contracts fulfilled which in turn provided boons like cheaper recrutiment, additional contracts available etc.
3. Factions and standing with them, diplomacy in general - if I say raid caravans originating from one town, it would be nice if they would consider me an outlaw and send their troops after me. Also with the enemies, allowing for a some kind of cease fire or even cooperation with them.
4. I wouldn't mind female characters for players and enemies - just for some variation,
5. Headquarters - a single, fortified camp to call one's own, to return to between contracts and to further customise with trophies after victories and upgrades for the benefit of the company.
OTHER:
Currently, there is only a video tutorial on youtube but I found it easy enough to pick it up from simply playing and reading the tooltips. Be aware that I've learnt this approach on Europa Universalis series with their lack of tutorials, so yeah.
Lack of main quest line - it will be added. I don't actually miss it, it will be something nice to have, but I have fun already as it is.
Some minor bugs - I've had only one gamebreaking bug when in combat AI would not take it turn, other than that there are just a few, such as items going to the bottom of the stash when one unequips them - nothing major.

The minimalistic art style is good and so is the rhythmic timing, but that doesn't make up for the uninteresting controls or bland soundtrack.
Other minimalistic platformers (dust force, super meat boy, electronic super joy) can make up for their minimal graphics with slick, addictive controls. 140 just has move left/right at constant speed and jump. The wall grabs, double-jumps, running, sliding, etc that drive other similar games are lacking here.
Other rhythm games (bit trip runner, beat buddy) are able to make up for their limited controls with an addictive soundtrack. The thumping bass is great at first, but none of the levels have any sort of melodic hook and repetitive percussion can only get you so far.
Since most of the game objects are timed to match the music, you spend a lot of your play time waiting for the right time to jump... and waiting isn't fun.
Although the art style is great, it isn't quite enough to make it fun to play.

is a hidden object puzzle game. Leave on a deep sea dive in search of your missing husband, only to get trapped in an underwater utopia while being tracked by ghostly beings.
: While the setting may appear to be a suburb of
's Rapture, the intrigue is fully original with mysteries and twists of its own. The hand-drawn visuals are as nice as you'd come to expect from
, while the occasional 3D animation doesn't clash too much with the backgrounds. You'll be going back and forth throughout the complex the entire game, but it isn't too tedious as the various paths all branch out from the the same couple of rooms, so going from one location to another is never too long. The puzzles are varied enough, and while you may end up scratching your head to figure out the next step, there are very few frustrations in solving them. If you're stuck in a hidden object puzzle, you can switch to a game of domino as an alternative way to complete your objectives, giving achievement hunters replayability.
: The 3D animation isn't that good, and doesn't offer the same storybook feeling the hand-drawn ones give. The voice acting, while there is little of it, is someone underwhelming and feels forced. The hidden object puzzles often need to be replayed twice, giving the impression the game was being stretched too thin. While the additional content adds a few more puzzles to the game, they are way too easy and merely give uninteresting backgound information to secondary characters.
: ★★★☆☆ - It's up to you
The story had a spooky vibe that kept me interested throughout my playthrough. It's perhaps not the most challenging game of the genre, yet Hidden Object Games aficionados will find what they were looking for. Regardless of the cons, it's a good hidden object game, and a nice way to spend a cloudy afternoon.

If you want a GTA-style game that is mostly serious for a change, then Sleeping Dogs is for you. The game's portrayal of modern-day Hong Kong Island is on point, from the architecture and general street clutter, to the motorists yelling Cantonese profanities at you if you drive recklessly. Gunplay and police escapes are rather rare in this game, since in real life, both Hong Kong and China in general have rather strict gun control laws, and you are an undercover police officer working to infiltrate the Triad gangs. As such, most combat is hand-to-hand, with handheld weapons both bladed and improvised galore. Want to knock a gangster out with a random bystander's dropped hot-pink purse? You can. A main problem with this game is that keyboard and mouse controls are clunky, especially when driving, and hand-to-hand combat is certainly much easier when you have a controller in hand. Otherwise when you have a gun in your hand, aiming definitely benefits from the finer control you get when using a mouse. Fortunately, the game supports autoswitching, and if you swap between controller and kb+m, any button prompts that show up change accordingly with the last input device you used.
If Jirard the Completionist were to rate this game, he'd say "complete it". Get this game and finish it, and if it tickles your fancy, get all the DLC and complete all the content.

The game of 'Battle Brother's is currently in Early Access and may not represent it's final quality. However the game is pretty much in a beta phase - there are some bugs here and there but mostly nothing major. The gameplay is solid as well as completely playable with enough to do. Mostly your mercenary company ends up death though! There is however no 'story' yet besides the initial quest at the start. You can do pretty much everything: Find and destroy ruins of enemies (Orcs, Bandits, Undeads, Werewolves AND Vampires!!!). Deliver packages who seemingly seem to be like, not of importance.
Until you get ambushed by 3 bandit groups who want to kill you for it. >_> Seriously what's in this package?
Furthermore you can escort caravans as well. Sometimes nothing happens and you get a fat paycheck. Sometimes you have to plough through too many to count bandits to escort your caravan-contract to safety. Seriously, what is in THE caravan to warrant 5 groups of bandits to come at me? These also have guards, but they're feeble compared to your mostly better equipped and massive* company. However the 'find [name] building' contract is sometimes confusing as you may not be able to find it at all, thereby wasting valuable time. I wish there was a speedup button as well.
*Depends on how much mercenaries you recruit, and how well you arm them or are armed from the start. No warranty for survival.
+ Combat works great! The enemy has access to the same weapons and equipments you use! Except special type's such as Orc's hammers/axes or special enemies. When you kill them though and you survive you can loot their special equipment. Find out if you want to wear them despite the penalties!
