You know, I bought this game on a whim because I was horribly, horribly bored. But now here I am playing it for the second day straight and loving every second of it. In this Review I'll discuss the Pros and Cons, as well as perhaps maybe what I think would be great to include/change about the game.
Pros
- AI is very simple, yet very well done. AI actually responds to the happenings of the battlefield, causing the enemy forces to employ new strategies.
- The character backgrounds/traits, OH MY GOD. YES, MORE, PLEASE. While you expect to lose characters in the game, it's always nice for them not to be clones of each other, could do with more names though. >_>
- A nice, simple (and hopefully to be expanded upon) selection of weaponry and armor to pick from.
- Resource Management is a constant, but isn't hard if you know what you're doing.
- It's good to know you can run to a town/tower/castle/city to get some backup in the form of ally troops in case you're outmatched, soldiers've saved my company numerous times.
- The diversity in the quests thus far is small, yes, but they're similar yet just different enough to not make it repetitive and boring.
- The skills/level system legitimately does show when in combat, and it's worthwhile to really try to preserve those veterans.
Cons
- Lost Souls, if there's more than five of them, all they seem to do is wail, and make everyone flee regardless of how brave they are. This basically makes a supposed Puny fight so annoying, and so friggin' hard.
-Very hard start off, as there's no real 'sanctuary' from the roaming bands of enemies, and they follow you everywhere. Savescuming is an all to present temptation, on top of that, they keep pace with you regardless of how small your party.
Daily pay is very annoying, and sometimes escorting caravans to long-off cities can bankrupt you if you do it as a starter mission.
- Fleeing enemies do not leave the map, instead they just hide somewhere, causing your group to have to play hide and decapitate with them, for an upwards of possibly ten minutes.
- Orc Youths are probably smaller and weaker...right? So why can they charge and stun my characters like the Warriors/Berserkers? When you're facing a massive Orc force, your entire party can become insta-stunned by a line of shirtless prepubescent Greenies.
- Outside of the friggin' Lost Souls, the other undead seem woefully under-powered, and there's just not enough of them to even it out. Even if there's Fallen Heroes and Necromancers in the group. I'd love to see some Zombie-Knights that basically are complete tanks, or something.
- Citys/towns that are objectives of missions for say, Escort or Delivery, are seemingly at random, causing you to only get 140 Crowns for an across-the-map trek, or 1360 Crowns for going to a town literally half a minute away.
- Lack of overall places-to-be, it would be nice if there was more to do in the towns.
Suggestions
- One thing that would be awesome? That party limit? Yeah, add an option to turn it off, perhaps have multiple levels of it too? As I am a major RTS fan who enjoys large troop counts, and I feel like it would add a new perspective and difficulty to the game in itself (managing a company of 12 men is /waaaaaaay/ to easy after maybe ten minutes of grinding). Besides, it's 2D Graphics, there can't be that much resource-drain on having a 50 v 50 battle (good golly, Ms. Molly), I'd think.
- Undead gaining numbers as they wipe out caravans and perhaps Bandit/Soldier parties? It'd be cool to see that.
- Other Mercenary Parties to interact with. Why not, right? Could be fun if you made a rival, or trusted ally, or crap, just picking a fight to see who's top dog. Mercenaries ain't really that civil, yo.
- Weapons, Armor, and lots of variations! I'd love to see a greater diversity, although the current amount is nice too, but after a short time you seem to get the best stuff (except Coat of Plates armor....can't find that at freakin' all, sorry Alvar.)
- ......A....private.....settlement/Castle that can be purchased? Let's you store soldiers there, perhaps levy taxes and such, also a local place/safe haven to rest, recruit, and who knows what else?
- Rival Kingdoms? Allows you to perhaps pick a side, raid and pillage and plunder as Mercenaries did, while under the banner of a king.
- Different race mercs. It'd be nice to be able to find some Orc Berserker slogging down drinks and hire him, rather than just seemingly commit genocide on his entire race.
- Different races in general?
- While I guess it could be put under the whole 'weapons' suggestion, Muskets/Arqeubus? Slow reload time, but devastating damage, perhaps multiple ammunition types.
- Random Events! A damsel in distress! A friggin' village fire! A chest found in the middle of a forest! A young runaway hiding from his former owners.
Conclusion:
The game is starting off, yes, and it's got a great one at that. I really, really, /really/ like the game. But it would just be nice to have a bit more free-play to it.

In this game, the underwater city is called Eden - but without the peace. Depending on your tastes, the truth might be a bit too unrealistic. I thought it was "believable" because of the general mysticism and dark depths of the game itself. All in all, it was exciting to play and definitely (at least a bit) creepy at some points.

The biggest minus is the animation. I liked the voiceovers, they were full of emotion and that is what I like the most about voice acting. Unfortunately, the animation didn't stand up to the voice actors' performance. The art looks real enough, but when they start talking... The mouth movements look really mechanical. Amazingly deep and smart game. Seems eazy at first glance, but feels really complex and vast at rank 50. The variety of character unique features, perks, weapons and towers allows you to comunicate, plan and make decisions with other players from the moment you've selected a map. But that's only the complexity of gameplay. Sanctum 2 gives you a story and a world with it's own legend. The story is told in comic book style before every next map, and character personalities are filled in with dialogs, your imagination and their in-game voices and phrases. What really surprised me in this game was how vast most of the maps turned out to be. It's not just the play zone, the battlefield, you can explore the world beyond the marked field on minimap. And that's where you discover another side of the game, which rewards your awareness with not just additional supplies, but with extra plot, funny little minigames and simply glorious views. As much as Unreal Engine 3 can be beautiful, game makes sure to deliver. If you aren't in the mood to think through defences, give your resources to your friend and simply enjoy the view and explore the map with mild relaxing electronic music. This game is a marvelous example of what the smart co-op game can be.
Now to the downside. The great big problem of the DLC era. This is really bad way to make DLCs. It's good when they expand and extend the plot of the game, but not this time. DLCs are supposed to be optional, but for some reason the basic game ships with half of the plot (4 chapters) and leaves you with a big cliffhanger (but not as big as HL2EP2 had ;) ). So each one of the DLCs adds a new chapter to the game (5th-8th chapters), allows to unlock new towers and weapons. Yes, you've read right, you need to buy DLCs to get the full game. Except for Britech Skin Pack, this just adds alternative models for 4 basic characters (no extra skin for Tsygan). So in the end, these DLCs are not optional, you will definitely miss out on pretty much half of the game if you don't own them.

All in all, not a bad game for the price.  If you are into side scrollers, this could be a decent addition to your library.

Is this a great game? Yes...Is this a great Fallout Game? No...
I was a fan of Fallout 3 and Fallout NV, and loved the lore surrounding this game series. When Fallout 4 was announced i was like others excited, and when i first played it the excitment was still there. And then slowly..it started to fade. So what is wrong with it?
Well...firstly...i really dont like the conversation system. 4 options? Really limited in explanation of what those options are? What was wrong with Fallout 3 and Fallout NV's system?
Secondly...the town building. Oh god i hate this. Fallout games were about being a hero of the wasteland...not...about being a town mayor. It was not about walking form one settlement to another dealing with problems. I also don't feel it was implemeneted well. Why can't i choose to build a town where i want? Like at Vault 111 for example. Why is it only where Bethesda say im allowed to. Why am i not allowed to destroy eveything in the building range...and only some things?
Thirdly...and joining into the whole town building thing...the new crafting system. Urgh...so...now your weapon choices are limited until your craft the bits for the stock gun. So youve ended up with limited choice over the other games. The crafting system also doesnt make much sense. Why does a large desk fan yeild like one or two screws? If i go to a desk fan and open it up i bet there is far more inside than 2 screws.
But all these issues are secondary to my big one. The story line. Its rubbish.
"Go find your son" the game grandly demands. A son that i have no emotional connection to at all.
"You there...just passing...come save us from raiders and a deathclaw in a heavily scripted fight and then we will make you our saviour"...rigggght...because power armour in Fallout 4 basically might aswell be currency its so common.
"You there...just passing by...you have killed a few ghouls...help us call in our big bad airship so we can impose racism on the commonwealth"...the brotherhood of steel feel more like the Enclave in this game...
And who cares about the institute...havent even got to them because the games story line annoys me too much. But i've seen where the story goes...and i dont think much of it. In the end you install your preferred dictator and thats basically it. It doesnt feel that there is enough uniqueness in the endings (like it did in fallout NV) and it also doesnt feel like theres anoy point being evil in this game...its not so much good vs bad...more like...smart over stupid.
The game feels like its been watered down in order to sell it to the call of duty generation. Its lost its best elements just to make it easier for you to go shoot stuffs. It doies get better with mods (actual mods not those paid ones) and some of the DLC looks interesting...but the game persistantly fails to keep me into it.
Sorry fallout 4...better luck next time?

Despite being an RTS, Northgard plays more like a Civ game, in which your primary focus is maintaining balance between happiness, food, wood, lore (science), krowns (money), and military power. Since each map is randomly generated, you'll find that your approach to victory depends not only on your chosen faction but also the resources available near your starting position. This map generation is what keeps this game replayable and repeatable.
However I must admit that combat can be repetitive, since at the moment there are only three types of fighting units. Some factions have unique warchiefs (general unit) but their attack power is more or less the same. Their uniqueness affects resource management instead.
CONS
- Right now, there are no hotkeys yet for units, which make defending and microing against attacks a chore.
- Repetitive combat, needs more unit types, with more unique mechanics.
- Needs customizable victory conditions. Whenever you start a game, you can tick boxes if you want a fame victory, trade victory, domination victory, etc. But the magnitude of these victory conditions are fixed. For example, fame victory requires 1200 fame---I wish there was a slider that allows me to change this to mayble 1400 or 1000 fame. I really think these victory sliders would allow players to decide how long each game lasts, since each game lasts roughly about an hour.
PROS
+Randomly generated maps, map objectives and map events make each playthrough challenging and unique.
+System requirements are quite low. The game can run on low end PC's and laptops
+Decent comeback mechanics. Being beaten in a fight does not mean you lose the game.
+Easy to learn, hard to master.
DEPENDS ON TASTE
+/- Economy management requires IQ. Not only do you have to sustain your town's needs in a summer/winter cycle, you also have to prepare for game events. Thankfully these events have early warnings (usually several months ahead of such catastrophe) so if you mess up, it's probably your own fault for mismanaging your resources. I like this challenge, though I know of others who hate it.
I recommend this game, especially if you like Civ and would like to play a more casual, RTS version of it.

Dementium II HD is a Survival-Horror game ported from the Nintendo DS and released for Windows in 2013. It is a sequel to Dementium: The Ward, and expands on the original with more enemies, abilities, weapons etc. Playing Dementium II felt like a cross between Silent Hill and The Evil Within. You switch from a normal environment to some kind of demented horror environment, which overlaps your reality. You play as William Redmoor, who is trapped in a Prison mental health facility and is experiencing waking nightmares.
Visually the game isn't as modern looking as The Evil Within, but it's not bad either. It's got some good moments where something jumps out and scares you, or you encounter a monster and have to fight with a knife, but the AI seems rather simple even on harder difficulties. The story is interesting, but drawn out and you get pieces of it at a time. All in all not a bad game for the genre.

Let me state this first: This is an HD release of a NINTENDO DS game. Don't expect the graphics to be amazing, you will see some pixels. Dementium II is one of the only (good) survival horror games on the Nintendo DS. It started out as a Silent Hill game on the DS but Konami turned it down twice. The developer went back and created their own game, which was well-received. This is the HD re-release of it.
You start off in a prison after going through some brain surgery. Head trauma? You are being led back to your cell by some guards and start experiencing illusions. Before you know it you pick up a postcard and are in some hellish world. You pick up a shank and start killing Silent Hill-like monsters. That is the basic plot that you are given, which considering the DS, is not too bad.
The graphics look good for a DS re-release. They put a little effort into the PC port with a lot of resolutions, v-sync, and a graphics slider. On my 970 (About a 980) Dementium II runs really well. I would expect that due to this being a DS re-release. Yes, I know I am using DS re-release a lot, but that is because it is. I don't know much about the game.

A lot of horror games seem to forget that at the end of the day, their game is supposed to be fun. You can cram it full of weird monsters and spooky notes and jumpscares all you want, but if it's not fun to play, no one's going to care. Dementium feels like it really takes that to heart, balling up a bunch of common elements and a few cliches in a package entertaining enough that you won't care about the details.
You play William Redmoor, apparently the same guy as in the original Dementium, whose brain problems have landed him in an oddly secure mental hospital. You have a habit of hallucinating some very Painkiller-looking monsters, and indeed your perception shifts between the hospital and its baton-wielding security guards and some gritty, monster-filled hell dimension. It's a pretty good hook, if not a terribly original one, but the game throws in a bunch of neat details to spice it up. You have a full map of each area, and there are all sorts of side rooms and locked doors that you need additional weapons or items to access. It feels almost Metroidy, except for that the core path is quite linear and there are no real secrets, just places to remember to backtrack to.
There's a pretty good spread of monsters as well, though they tend to lean towards melee types and aren't particularly fast or threatening. They have a ton of health, which can make fights tedious, but to be fair, so do you, hence the lack of threat. Outside of their Clive Barkery appearance they're not particularly scary. Dementium also likes setting up enemy arenas and gauntlets to work through, and with the generous amounts of health the enemies have these can really bust up the game flow, and not in a good way. New weapons and foes come quickly enough to keep you interested and moving forward, though.
What really got me about Dementium was how fleshed out it is as a game, despite the core gameplay and combat being a little cheap and weak. There's a perfectly good tutorial baked into the opening of the game that gets you right into the action. You have an inventory screen where you can fiddle with items and check your selection of health and buff supplies. You get to leave the hospital behind after the first chapter and explore some outdoor areas. The cutscenes are clean and frequent, even if the animation quality is lacking. And even the story tries to be a little different, with a mysterious antagonistic doctor talking about his plot to create the very real monsters from your own brain.
For a title originally released on the DS, Dementium II HD is a solid, well-rounded FPS adventure that really doesn't suffer for its console origins. Each of its many parts is polished and arranged with the others to form a legitimately entertaining package. As long as the combat doesn't wear you out, you'll find plenty of fun in this one, something that can be hard to find in other horror games.

It turns out you can make a hidden object game out of just about anything, and Bioshock is no exception. I'm not being facetious here either, you can only have so many art deco steampunk underwater cities before someone starts making the connections between them. But Abyss manages to go a bit beyond Rapture with its own supernatural angle, and makes a pretty entertaining and relaxing game of it to boot.
You play a professional diver on the trail of her husband who disappeared on a routine excursion. The tutorial scenes get you to the gates of Eden, a sprawling underwater metropolis that just kinda flew under the radar, I guess? The place has been overrun by the titular wraiths, ghastly cloaked things that really do not want you finding your beau. To thwart them, you're going to have to pick up every piece of garbage you can find and solve the brain-teasers that people used to lock things in Eden instead of, y'know, actual ♥♥♥♥ing locks.
This is all very standard fare for a hidden object game, and in particular an Artifex Mundi one. As you travel about the undersea burg you'll come across hidden object scenes to solve. Each has 12 items to find, most just by clicking them but some by combining other items. Those scenes grant you an inventory item which, along with other loose objects you find, allow you to open up new areas and progress the plot. Abyss has an interesting pace to its collecting, where most of the items you need for a particular area are found in or near that area. You'll often fill up and then clear out your entire inventory in a single wing of the city, which helps cut down on laborious backtracking.
That's true until the last hour of the game, at least. Once you identify the source of the wraiths and how to defeat them, you're set on a city-wide scavenger hunt to assemble the bits and bobs to do it. This last leg involves a LOT of backtracking, almost enough to make up for the excellent pacing earlier on. There's also a central elevator you'll be using a lot that cycles through three floors without being able to select which floor to go straight to, and by the end of the game I was about sick of pulling that particular lever.
Despite these gripes, Abyss is a very solid adventure. The scenes are crisp and colorful, the puzzles are fun and have a few unique elements, and the story has a few welcome twists to keep you involved. I mentioned that it's not a straight Bioshock rip and I meant it... fans of Lovecraft might want to consider this one more seriously, in fact. There are even some good spooks to be had here, an uncommon feature for hidden object games. Your protagonist has an unfortunate habit of disturbing corpses and not noticing hostile beings until they're up in her face, and a few of those gave me some embarrassing starts.
The quality-of-life elements are all in place for a satisfying experience as well. The map is very clear with where you need to go, though it doesn't allow for fast travel. The hint system works fine, and much like many Artifex Mundi games there's an optional domino game mode that you can play in lieu of the actual hidden object scenes. It's a nice consideration for folks who want to enjoy the adventure without all the item hunting. That means that even if you aren't a HOG enthusiast, Abyss is a great way to relax and puzzle through a deep-sea city of mysteries.

All the hype around this game and my general interest in a space exploration game in which the player can do as they please on top of the fact that it was recently fully released finally compelled me to play Starbound. And guess what? It's♥♥♥♥♥♥
You're able to farm, build, fight, explore or sell things in this game. I couldn't stand playing it for long enough to try farming but from what I've seen it looks pretty dull.
The building mechanics are actually decent as there's a good amount of options that allow for the player to really make whatever planet side structures they want. Sure, it would have been nice to be able to build things in space but it's too much of an issue.
From what I've played fighting is a fairly mixed bag. The diversity in the weapons and the special abilities they each have is pretty cool and it was always quite exciting to finally find a new weapon to use. Problem is, the actual combat is... lacking. It's a desperate flurry of spamming left click in the hopes that your weapon will make contact with the rejected pokemon charging towards you. It's so imprecise that it just becomes a chore.
Exploration is god awful and by far the most disappointing aspect of the game. Each planet is just a reskin of the last and there is quite literally nothing to do except trade, fight and get loot (and build, of course.) After adventuring around a couple of planets with my mate I was beginning to suspect that there really wasn't much to this game at all.
Which just leaves you with selling. To be honest, I don't think I need to go to in depth with this one: You drag and item into a UI panel and press a button.
So what else really is there? Well, mining of course!
At the start of the game you get chucked onto a boring Earth-like planet and have to find 20 "core fragments" in order to get into the space part of the game. There is only one tiny little problem:
Hunting for the core fragments is the most soul crushingly dull experience I've ever dragged myself through.
It really comes down to running through a bunch of empty caverns in the hope that you can get deep enough into the planet to find a cluster of orange flowing tic-tacs in the ground. ♥♥♥♥ing riveting stuff. Add to that that you'll be dying from huge drops into empty caverns and hoards of the rejected pokemon chasing after you and you've got one hell of an irritating start to a game.
For one the "100 best games ever made" you must be thinking that this game has some kind of saving grace. Well, there is one more thing... the story.
And my god is it dreadful.
Imagine the most generic science fantasy story line just being straight up told directly to the player instead of letting them slowly uncover the game's mysteries for them self. And that's the story. It's just some vague way of stringing together the quests you get given in the game.
So surely, surely there has to be something here to enjoy, right? Right?
Yes! There is! The art direction, graphics and animation quality are excellent. It is a really beautiful game. The soundtrack is also quite decent. So if all you want is a pretty slide show with cool music, then go for it!
But if you're looking for a game with real substance and content, stay away. At best, it's just an average Terraria-esque game with space bits tacked on. At worst, it's slow, repetitive and just really empty.
"In Starbound, you create your own story - there’s no wrong way to play!"
Yeah... not quite.
Final verdict:
45/100

Had this game for three years now, since it first came out on EA. Spent a bit less than 30 hours on this current build. Honestly can't say I'll be back.
If you're the type of person who likes building things, namely colonies, you'll probably love this game. I like building, but it's not something I'll sit around and do forever. And honestly, outside of building, the quality of my moment-to-moment experiences go downhill very quickly.
The most difficult monsters are the ones that just run or fly at you and try to occupy the same pixel as you; this ends up with the most boring monsters being the most difficult and the more interesting monsters being fairly rare and inconsequential.
While the EPP (enviro protection pack) is an interesting idea on paper, in-game it negates any and all side-affects of the planet you go on, with VERY few exceptions. Either you freeze to death with absolutely no recourse to survive, or you have the right EPP and the planet mechanically plays exactly the same as every single other planet. It feels like an unfortunate black/white decision that actually tended to make the very earliest planets far more difficult and equally as interesting as the very 'hardest' planets.
After all is said and built, there's really nothing to keep me in this game: mechanics aren't quite deep enough, planets play too similarly, time spent mining is quite and empty. In my 30 hours back with the game, I built a sick underwater palace for my shark man... And I left. Too much empty space left me feeling like there's better, more mechanically interesting things to spend my time doing. Not a bad game. Just boring, really.

I'd say Floating Point is a good game to play spontanously while waiting for something else, as it requires no "getting into", allows for frequently checking the clock and lets you quit at any time without penalties of any kind. I wouldn't play it for longer than thirty minutes at a time.

Never thought I would enjoy a hidden object game but Abyss showed me that HOG can be very enjoyable. Abyss has typical but engaging hidden object gameplay which is just the right difficulty and it has an engaging and interesting story. I really enjoyed playing it and was never bored. I played it as a casual alternative to other more "hectic" games such as Borderlands and that job it did just perfectly. The story was so good that it kept me wanting to play on just to see what happens next. There are minigames one can play (which I did not do much) and they are ok too (such as dominoes) - puzzles can be skipped and those minigames be played instead so that progress can still occur (which is a good idea but I believe is quite standard in HOG these days)
There was not too much going back and forth which I really thought was positive (a lot of backtracking is something I do not enjoy in games). I guess the only downside is that the bonus which unlocks upon completion of the game is rather short but still good - after all it is a bonus and one cannot expect a fully fledged experience again as a bonus.
In summary, I strongly recommend this game. It is well made, has an interesting story and has a good length (not too long or too short). If you have never played a HOG or do not know if you like, give this one a try - you might just get into the genre of HOG. Artifex Mundi has done a really good job and I am looking forward to playing the other Artifex Mundi HOGs in my library.
Definitely a recommendation. $10 might be a little pricey - get it when it is on sale for $5 or less or when in a bundle. You will definitely get your money's worth out of it then as the game takes about 3 - 4 hours to complete including the bonus (my time is inflated as it was paused for a long while - it did not take 26 hours to finish!)

Well, isn't this a little diamond in the rough. I don't know where this game came from, or how the development team knew that there were people like me out there looking for an unforgiving, turn-based combat rpg in a medieval fantasy setting. Don't get too attached to that level 6 character with the pimped out gear, either. You will die. A lot.
Pros:
* Great turn based-combat system
* Good RPG/skills system
* Unique graphical style - the "egg soldiers". It's really grown on me.
* Yes, it's early access, but this feels polished already.
* Your hardwork will eventually pay-off - you will equip and skill your guys to a level where they can actually survive consecutive battles.
* Already been three bug updates just a handful of days after initial release.
Cons:
* Start of game is tough - took me about 8-9 attempts where my squad wiped in the first or second battle.
* Not a great deal of content as yet outside of the combat - be prepared to escort caravans and run errands from one side of the map to the other for a pittance.
* The best gear - armour/weapons/etc - don't respawn very quickly. By day 50 in my current game, most the stores are generally quite bare. This may be by design.
* Once you get a solid core of 6-8 guys who are armoured up and at or around level 8, it's currently fairly easy to make money and win battles with minimal loses - again, this is probably due to an overall lack incontent outside of the start game period.
* Some minor bugs - dead battle brothers turning into zombies who I can't target, the unpassable water tiles bleeding over into the grass/non-water tiles a little too far and making you stuck, etc.
Overall:
If you like turn-based combat RPGs with a Mount & Blade-esque world map, this is the game for you. I've already sunk a number of hours in it, and I'm looking forward to more content.

Northgard is a nice little indie strategy game that deserves more praise. The Norse-inspired RTS brings some interesting mechanics to the genre that I would love to see in larger titles, such as dividing the land into territories and assignming laborers to buildings.
By far the most unique aspect of the game is that you only have one unit - the villager. Assigning a villager to a building changes their role - whether that be a woodcutter, a runemaster, or even your sailors and warriors. It brings to the game an extra layer of strategy when you account for the opportunity cost of turning your farmers into soldiers.
Good things aside, the game is still an early access game and has some problems. The AI isn't very intelligent and the maps are always a round-shaped single landmass. Fortunately the territories themselves tend to differ quite a bit, and each map has a map-specific victory condition to add some flavor.
Overall, it is a fantastic game for where it is right now. I got it on sale for USD $14.99 and it is well worth the price. They have added two new clans (factions) since I bought it, and their dev team has laid out plans for a campaign, multiplayer updates, and more as they speed towards a planned full-release around March 2018.

140 is about as minimalistic as a platformer can get. It makes other minimalistic games look complicated.
The entire game is made out of the three most basic shapes: circles, triangles, and rectangles. These shapes are all colored very simply and don't even have any texture (except for the grey static that kills you). There's a reason no artists were needed to develop this game; calling the graphics in here "art" would be a bit of a stretch.
However, what saves this game from being as boring as its graphics is the exceptional soundtrack. After all, it's a rhythmic platformer, so the music
be good, since it's essential to the gameplay. Fortunately, the music is great, and it fits the gameplay perfectly.
Ironically, for a game that has such an amazing soundtrack, you won't find an official OST
. This is because the music is truly part of the gameplay, and so it's not as simple as just playing one long sound file in the background like most games do; the music is affected by what is happening in the game. The result is that the music you hear will vary slightly each time you play the game.
Unfortunately, that means we are left with no soundtracks to listen to, apart from the title screen and level select music, which are probably the only real tracks you can listen to without actively playing the game. To listen to any of the music that plays during the actual game, you'll have to settle for watching videos on YouTube. An unofficial OST put together by fans can be watched
. While these videos are very well done, it's such disappointment to have no "real" tracks for each of the three levels.
And yes, you heard that right; the game only has three levels. Each one takes about seven minutes to run through, maybe 15 if it's your first time. That's means there's less than an hour of gameplay for the entire game.
But what about the mirror levels? Well okay, there are actually three more levels after you beat the first three, but I'd hardly consider them new levels. They're literally exactly the same as the first three levels, but reversed (instead of moving right, you move left). They have no new content, no new music, and no new bosses. It's just the same thing over again, except that this time, you move backwards. Oh and one more thing, the mirror levels have no checkpoints at all.
And that's the reason only about 2% of players have actually completed the mirror levels: no checkpoints means that one mistake will send you
to the very beginning. At this point, the game turns from fun into frustrating. I guess that may appeal to some hardcore gamers, but for most people, it's not worth their time doing something that isn't even fun.
I really wished there would be more levels, since having only three is just pitiful. After you beat the third boss, the game looks like it goes into a "3D" mode for a bit. That could've been a cool way to start off the next levels. Too bad it didn't.
As much as I wanted to write a positive review for this game, because I
the three levels it did have, I simply cannot recommend a game that has so little content.
TL;DR: Great game, but there's not even an hour of content (unless you're a masochist willing to play the mirror levels, then there's a few more hours of
content). Now I know $5 isn't very much, but neither is <1 hour of gameplay. If the game had an OST bundled with it, then it might be worth it. But sadly it doesn't.

I wish that Steam would add a "meh" thumb as opposed to just the thumbs up and thumbs down rating. Because I kinda feel guilty of giving this game a thumbs down. But at the same time, I don't.
Is the gunplay better than it's predecessors? Yes. Are the graphics better? Yes. Is the overall experience of the game better? Although the "experience" part is entirely up to you, the overall game itself is, sad to say, not as great as it was hyped up to be. Is it necessarily a horrible game? No. But for a Fallout game, myself and many others would agree when I say that this is not a Fallout game. Whereas good fallout games like New Vegas and even Interplay's Fallout 1 & 2 were roleplaying games for the most part, Fallout 4... isn't.
Character creation (excluding the new "perk system") is much better than it was in previous Fallout games, but it ultimately ends up becoming an unecessary waste. Why? Because no matter how much time you spend creating your "character", you just end up playing out the same "role". You're a father. The nukes come. You and your family stay in a vault and your son gets captured. You get out of the vault many years later. Then you spend the rest of the game either doing side quests or inevitably following the mainstoryline and looking for your son.
In a game like New Vegas, rather than having an all-encompassing story, you have multiple stories. Sure, there's a main questline in New Vegas, but the "main" part ends up becoming the basis for multiple branching paths, both major and minor. In Fallout 4, you end up finding out about your son the exact same way everytime you play. Even if there are different factions, you just pretty much get the same ending were you to join a different faction (with minor "differences" here and there).
Some people hate this game. I personally think that hate is too strong a feeling to have toward this game. As long as you take the game for what it is (an arcade shooter, with a loot-based system and very few rpg elements), then you just might have some amount of fun with this game. Despite the negative things I mentioned, it still shines in some aspects. For instance, the Silver Shroud questline was kind of fun. And even the fact that your companions can butt in on your conversation with other npcs is a nice little touch that adds some form of substance to the game. But ultimately, this game isn't all that great.

+ Pros
+ Great combat System - While no CS or CoD, it handles very well for being the giant, open world RPG that it is. If you chose to ignore VATS entirely and just play it like a shooter or hack and slash, the option is definitely there. Conversely, if shooters aren't your thing, the VATS system allows you to play the game as an RPG and sidesteps the whole shooting system entirely. It's the best of both worlds.
+ Immersive world - No one does open world like Bethesda. In an age where many games are trying to unnecessarily and uninterestingly shoehorn in Open World because it's a hot button selling point, Bethesda always pulls it off perfectly. There's plenty of interesting and unique places you come across, plenty of interesting random encounters, etc. The world is just fun to explore.
+ Interesting Characters and Companions - While I would argue that there are not as many interesting characters as previous FO games, same of the coolest and most iconic yet are definately introduced in FO4. Not a reason to buy it on its own, but if FO lore is your thing, there's lots of cool stuff in here.
+ Morally Gray Factions - As much as people complain about the story (and believe me, there's a lot to be desired), there is one thing that Bethesda nailed with the faction choices: moral ambiguity. Without giving away any spoilers, I'll say this; Every faction thinks they are doing what is best for humanity. Every faction has their problems. There is no black or white, good or bad decision. That adds a level of depth (especially for your first play through) to really think about what the best thing for mankind is.
+ Mods. Lots of mods. Lots of free mods. Lots of good mods.
- Cons
- Little RPG for an RPG - This is by far the biggest complaint about the game, and it's true. Compared to other FO games (Namely NV, but even FO3) this game lacks heavily in the RPG department.
1. They really limited the RP options for you. You're pretty much stuck playing a good guy or a sarcastic good guy no matter what. Unless you just decide "screw the story entirely" and just start killing everyone, there's really no way to play an evil character, or even a morally gray character within the RP system of the game. You're always pretty much stuck being the good guy, regardles of what faction you choose.
2. No more Karma system. While I think everyone could agree the karma system could use some tweaking, it was still a fun system. Taking it away entirely was kind of a let down. I would have much rather seen a more fleshed out karma system than none at all.
- The game is easy. Even on survival difficulty, the game just isn't that challenging. It can be, for the first few levels, but once you learn what talents are good (namely damage talents and VATS talents) the game is never that challenging again. About halfway through my most recent play through, I tried survival for the first time. In about 50 hours played since enabling survival, I've maybe died 5 times. The plus side is, there are mods to increase the difficulty, so this can be helped to an extent.
TL:DR - Fallout 4 is a great game with problems. While it doesn't stack up in the RPG category compared to its predecessors, it has far surpassed them in game play mechanics. There's plenty of fun Fallout fluff to discover and Boston has proved to be an interesting setting for the franchise.

Well, the situation is quite simple...
Arena shooter with a twist - you don't pick up weapons, you pick up "beasts".
Each beast has different attacks, just like primary and secondary fire in "normal" first person shooters.
The beasts are the different weapons, basically.
Every beast has its own health. If the health gets to zero, the beast is "defeated" and disappears (or dies, not sure, you see a strange reddish fountain, I don't know what to make of it.. ).
If you lose a beast, you'll be instantly switched to another beast you have picked up before.
If all beasts are gone, only the mere mortal remains. That is what you spawn as, a simple human. But you have a crossbow (fully automatic). At least something.
The thing is, you don't just have to watch the health of your beasts, no, your mortal form takes damage too. And if your human health reaches zero you are dead, no matter how many beasts you picked up before..
Interesting concept for a multiplayer shooter, I have to say. Innovation is still possible in that genre, it seems.
Here is the thing: I have found no other games, no other players, nothing, zero, nada..
This kinda defeats the whole point of a multiplayer game, I would say...
Until this situation changes: Not recommended.

I've supported this game for a very long time; since 2014, according to my reciept. Since then, it has gotten worse. I don't deny that the developers have put an immense amount of effort into this game since I started playing it, but they put a lot of that effort into missions, which, in my opinion, make the game worse. Back in 2014, when you started playing starbound, it started in a very similar fashion to how it starts today; stuck in your ship, above a random planet. However, if you got yourself enough coal, you could immediately start exploring the planets in the local system, and eventually the rest of the universe, which was why I played most of those 112 hours currently displayed on my profile. However, now that missions have been implemented, I can't explore. I've sunk several hours into the most recent version of this game over the past few months, and the furthest I ever got was another planet in the same solar system as I started in! For a game whose most redeeming feature, in my eyes, is an infinite number of procedually generated worlds to explore, trying to force crafting, mining, and RPG mechanics on me in the first few hours I play it is a really great way to put me off.
To fix this, the developers should either make the story/tutorial stuff optional, and let you start the game with all of the game's mechanics in play, or they should let the story happen spontaneously and naturally; don't just put the teleport temple thing on the planet I start on, put it on some other, random planets, and let me find it myself. The great thing about making the only restriction on exploration your supply of coal is that you naturally come across the supplies you need to make advanced tools while looking for coal; I don't need to be told to dig down to the core of the planet to find gold and silver! Anyway, the mining mechanic is the worst one in the game; if I want to play minecraft, I'll play minecraft; resource-mining is a really akward mechaninc to put in a space exploration game.
Again, I don't doubt that this is a really good game once you get past those starting missions, but getting to the exploration part of the game is now such a chore that I just can't be bothered anymore. At least no man's sky is coming out soon; hopefully it can satisfy my hunger for exploration.
I've noticed that some people are having trouble launching the game, and for them, I'd suggest trying to launch in 32 bit: steam library, right click on starbound, properties, local files, browse local files, win32, starbound.exe (for windows. Apologies to other os users). A little addition to my review; they removed the launcher with option to launch in opengl! Why?! That was the go-to solution for game launch problems that most people could figure out themselves, and it's completely gone. I don't know when they did this, but I'm surprised that no one else seems to have pointed this out.

While decent on its own, I can't call this game is an improvement over the previous games in series. Sure, it looks pretty and sports high production values, it's modern and cinematic in a sense, but it's also very been there done that. Especially the Marine single-player campaign, which is just unbelievably boring. Predator campaign, however, is noticeably better. The gameplay is somewhat bogged down by lots of melee vs. aliens and the clunkiness of melee combat mechanics in general, but Predator's campaign feels fresh and shakes things up, putting a surprising emphasis on mobility. Boss battles are more creative too. But the real deal is the Alien campaign, which is even more stealth-heavy and genuinely fun to play through.
Levels and environments are detailed and generally well-made, but they are recycled throughout each campaign, completing the single-player experience means that you'll tread the same paths three times, albeit in a different order.
Multiplayer is still alive at 2017, every time I've checked there was a couple of populated servers online.
PC port-wise game is meh. FOV for Marine and the Predator is headache-inducingly low, which can be fixed through an external utility. But refrain from using it online, for it could lead to a VAC ban. Interface suffers from chronic consolitis too.
Considering the fact that it's dirt cheap nowadays, it's worth getting in my opinion. There is nothing else to scratch that AvP itch that is not also very, very old...

Nothing has changed about my support for this game. I bought the supporter edition back when Battle Brothers finally went into Early Access. It was worth every Cent even back then and it is even more so now.
The devs put much love into every detail of the game.
You have your band of mercs you are traveling with across the map, doing jobs here and there always trying to hold your money together (atleast in the beginning of the campaign this can be challenging if you take some losses). There is never really a feeling of being overpowered. All the time you can loose a good man to a stray arrow. Even the weakest brigand archer can bring down your battle hardened veteran if he already took some beating.
And this is only when fighting the normal rubbish on the roads. There are much more sinister things around. Undead legions which never fatique and never loose morale, moving tanks of ironclad orc warriors and sneaky little goblins with their poisoned arrows and deadly marksmanship.
What i love the most about this game is equipping my mercs. Especially finding rare or even unique pieces of amor is great.
The combatsystem which is the core of the game is turnbased while initiative dictates the order in which your own mercs as well as the foes attack.
The different foes i mentioned earlier do come with their very own tactics each. So you are forced to adapt to their abilities if you want to go out of the fight without losses.
The weakest part (if you can even call anything weak) of the game is the worldmap which can feel a bit too little interactive. You wander around from vilage to vilage or chase down (or getting chased by) enemies in the wilderness or search for hidden layers to attack.
I can only recommend this game.
I have never seen another Early access done as good as this. The devs were highly receptive to suggestions for improvements and the final product shows they have done a great job.
Unfortunately not everything they wished to be able to put in was possible do to time and finacial reasons so I do wish them best luck with todays release to then be able to further improve this gem of a game to brings us a worthy expansion :)

I got this game on sale ($3.50 instead of $10) and I recommend getting it while it's cheap, but buying it full price is fine if you're a fan of hidden-object and/or adventure games. It's a really neat mix of both (and puzzle games) that I enjoyed. Takes roughly 4 hours to beat with the bonus content.
The Cons: Voice acting is kind of flat in places, and the lip sync on the 3D model is horrific. It’s the stuff of nightmares. Also, some of the hidden-object game lists use terms that I didn’t recognize or wouldn’t have used, so that can be frustrating (it turns out there’s a mini-game in those parts you can use to skip if you’re having trouble, tho!). The hidden-object parts are sometimes a little iffy in terms of application (why do you spend all this time picking up 20 things when the one thing you wanted was on top?) and there's the "your knife broke after one use" adventure-game tendency, which is a pain.
The Pros: Story is fairly interesting, if a bit clunkily delivered, scenery is a gorgeous and interesting mix of 3D (moving parts) and somewhat painterly 2D… it’s a little hard to describe but it generally works well. The adventure-game components are like 90% logical and easy to guess, and the rest can be picked up on pretty fast. It's very fun, easy to play while still being challenging and interesting.
While the con section is visibly longer, this is still a fun game, and I recommend it, especially on the cheap.

Elegant and intuitive. The game has no menus, no text, no pause function. If you want to wait before taking your next move, just stop where you are. Go make a sandwich. 140 is a series of system introductions that reminds us what gaming has lost -- remember when there was no tutorial, and no one read the manual? But we didn't need either, the game taught us by letting us make mistakes, letting us explore. Here we have a rhythm-oriented platformer that begs the question "Why did we stray?" Screw twelve hour tutorial mission sets. If you don't learn the rules, you die, and try again, until you do.
This game is graphically simplistic, but beautiful. The soundtrack is the same thumping piece for the most part, and yet you never mind. Nothing feels repetitive, and you always want "one more try." I haven't beaten the three permadeath levels yet, but I haven't stopped trying, and I likely won't stop trying until I've 100%ed this thing, even if it takes me a dozen hours. It's that sensation-- "oh! I know what to do next time!"-- that defines some of the best games ever. When you fail, but don't regret it.
Fun, simple, elegant, recommended.

The additional story let you play a Eden citizen who will need to rescue his wife and their baby.

The game features an inventory where you can store items to combine with the environment to go deeper in the story.
The game has several difficulties and have a guest feature: all the family can play the game and resume it where they left. Also you can use the Hint/Skip hourglass whenever you want and wait until its refill to use it again. But be warned that you may not skip or use a hint in any puzzle or hidden objects scene if you wish to have some achievements.

The first Hidden objects scene features the name of the objects to find some are found easily (normal one) and some others need you to interact with the environment or to combine two items to found them. Another achievement requires you to find 3 objects in 3 seconds or find all objects with only 5 or fewer miskicks in the hidden object scenes. A beautiful (and sometimes infuriating) minimalistic rhythm puzzler that I'm absolutely terrible at but keep coming back to. 140 tests your patience and puzzle-solving skills against a colourful background, fitting music, and a geometrical theme that any design kid would acknowledge. There is no tutorial but the aim is straightforward: collect small, circular objects to unlock the next stage without making contact with the static (you'll die and get blasted by a quick dubstep drop if you do).
The rhythm-synced puzzles are unique and steadily increase in difficulty as you go along. "Bosses" mark the end of each level and are appropriately challenging. There are save points before most (if not all) of the puzzles so there's no need to worry about redoing the entire level after a death; if you quit in the  middle of a level and close out of the game, however, you
have to restart the stage. The controls are simply the directional keys and the set-up options should ensure smooth play on any machine.
140 is an indie gem that warrants a play by any lover of challenging platformers. Though the levels may be somewhat short, mirror mode will keep you occupied for the times those beat-'em-up/FPS/hack-and-slasher what-have-yous just won't cut it. Snap this up at half price and entertain the little masochist in you.
: 140 features bright colours and quick-moving, flashing, and/or warping sequences. Anyone who may be sensitive to these sorts of things should tread with caution and do the appropriate research before jumping in.

The Settlers 2 was one of the first games I ever played. Any one who played this strategy builder will feel instantly at home. Northguard expertly catches this nostalgic feel and spices it up with elements that seem to be inspired by another Settler classic, the Catan board game to be precise.
Exploring territory, claiming it, building up your settlement, managing resources and fighting your way through the harsh nature of Northguard until you finally meet the opponent you actually wanted to fight are key elements to the game. There is a strong emphasis on juggling your food and wood store as well as keeping your villagers happy enough to grow your settlement. Randomly created maps and areas with special traits spice things up enough to keep the game interesting after the third or fourth playthrough. The subtle yet meaningful differences between the factions of Northguard do the rest.
As of writing this review the singleplayer campaign is just a grey button in the main menu. Multiplayer lacks many stock options like setting up custom teams and the game interface could use some additional convenience features. However if you are looking for a well done strategy builder with a good mix of economy and combat features I can already recommend the game as it is. Just testing out the different factions in skirmish was already more entertaining for it's price tag than what my last AAA strategy builder title offered for me, and there is still a lot of promise in this game's future.

This is a really simple, yet surprisingly fun and relaxing game. It's perfect for doing something when you're talking to people or just taking your mind off things without trying too hard.
You basically control a red dot that grapples onto blocks and swings around the level, trying to fly into bars that rise and fall with your momentum that are on top of the blocks. When you're moving faster, the bars rise higher, making them easier to hit, and they award more points. In addition, there is also a bottom part of the level submerged in water that basically works the same way except gravity is reversed.
When you start out, it's a bit tricky but you get the hang of it quickly and the movement becomes very smooth and enjoyable. The levels are randomly generated, so on occasion you'll get a really hard level with lots of block clusters, but even if you aren't done with a level, you can keep advancing to new levels until you get one you like.

Fantastic game. I bough this when it first came out on Xbox 360 and played it until it was stolen a few years later in 2015. So 2 years roll by and I see AVP on Steam. I figured I'd give it a go, see if its as good as I remember it to be.  To my surprise it is just as good as I remember. The graphics still hold up really well on my laptop and the gameplay is just as engaging and intense. Whether you are the rough and tumble Marine trying to save him and his friends while you discover some secrets about your employer Weyland-Yutani, the stealthy Predator cruising through the jungle as he tries to restore honour lost to the humans or the ferocious Xenomorph dodging and ducking through vents as you slaughter human and Predator alike.
The game really gets the universe of AVP. The smart guns and sentry guns from Alien are here and ready to use and all of Predator's gadgets and gizmos are present as well. Everything from his cloaking devices to his smart disc to his Combi Stick are here.
While the Marine's campaign is very much similar to your standard FPS, it does try to spice things up with by adding a motion tracker from Aliens. The tracker will quickly become your best friend as the Xenomorphs will  know your location and try to sneak up on you. I would have liked to see more variation of firearms though. There isnt many in the campaign. Maybe only 6 or so are there to use. Thankfully the flamethrower and smart gun keep things interesting. I loved watching the Xenomorphs stop, drop and roll as they tried to put out the fire that was rapidly burning them to death. Other than these few things, the Marine campaign isn't that memorable. Thankfully this doesn't really take away too much from the game.
The Predator's story is much better. They did a good job on this section of the game, in this section, you truly feel like you are the extraterrestrial hunter as you leap from vanatge point to vantage point and stalk your prey with precision. The story isn't very compelling here as you try to kill an abomination and remove the stain upon your honor that the humans have placed. But the finishing and stealth kills here are gory and satisfying, It is great fun to use your Predator strength and snap a human's neck before you remove his head, spine and all or to impale a Xenomorph on your wrist blades as your tear it's inner mouth out. The gadgets here are done well and fun to use. The plasma caster is capable of completely vaporizing enemies from long range and the smart disc is able to decapitate and injure multiple enemies in one throw.
The Alien's campaign is great fun. While the story here is pretty much absent, you don't really seem to notice as you crawl across ceilings and through sewers and ambush your prey. It was really something else to sneak up on a civilian and pin him down while a facehugger comes in to finish the job. The Alien doesn't really have any gadgets here other than her  tail, claws and teeth. But combat is better to be avoided as the Marines will turn you into swiss cheese at the drop of a dime. It is much better to use the shadows and vents to your advantage and take them out one by one.
So all in all, the game is good. The gameplay is fun, the kills are gory and the graphics still hold up really nice for a 7 year old game. The only real complaints I have is the the AI can be absolute idiots sometimes as they just stand out in the open and stare at a wall. But other than that, the game is solid and just as fun as I remember it to be. The final score is 8/10. It is a good game but could have been better if the AI was smarter and if they did a better job on the campaign.

Cliver Barker's Silent Hill... almost.
Unfortunately, not Undying and Silent Hill 2, but Jericho and one of the more recent, crappy Silent Hill games.
A port of a Nintendo DS game, I can't imagine how much of a pain it'd be to play on that system.  Much of it feels rather stiff (obviously dictated by its original platform), especially in the movement - and I say this as some who thinks the movement in System Shock 2 is completely appropriate for the respective game.
Further perplexing is how much focus there is on combat, given the system it was first developed for.  While there are times where just running away is an option, they often put you in situations where you must destroy all the enemies in an area to proceed.  This feels like it works against the general vibe of the game, which seems to be shooting for (and accomplishing to some extent) a true survival horror quality.  I feel they should've focused on more of the Resident Evil-like puzzles the game had, and leaving combat as a secondary option.
The classic Silent Hill inspirations are very prominant, right down to the nightmare world changes.  Mix in some Hellraiser, and you've got the general visual design.  This and the audio design are where the game shines the most.  Still hampered by being an up-rezzed port of a DS game, but you can definitely feel the artistic ability the team has in these areas.
In all, it reminds me of Blue Stinger - a game that's not horrible, but having a few poorly thought out aspects that hold it back from being a great game.  If you need something to at least scratch that survival horror itch in these days of action horror games, this will do alright, giving you about three to four hours of relief.
(Those jumping puzzles near the end though, Jesus Christ.  Just horrible game design, especially for a game with terrible jumping.)

Oh man, where do I start? I absolutely LOVE this game. It is one of my favorite indie games that I've ever played (though I do still have a lot left to get around to!).
The story of Bastion is definitely an interesting one, and the way you learn more of the details is relatively simple but intriguing. For instance, learning through the Dream levels turns out to be more fun than you would expect. The perspective of the characters shifts as the game goes on and it definitely has you wonder what is going on.
I liked the frame of everything with the narration, but I don't want to spoil any of the story so I won't say any more. The graphics of the game are great; it is straight up beautiful to look at. Very nice sound all around, and I love the music it has. The actual vocal songs they created were amazing as well and fit the style of their scenes almost perfectly.
Gameplay-wise, Bastion still continues pulling things off. There are enough unique enemies and bosses in the game to keep things interesting, and the weapons available also allow for you to test out different builds. The development of the Bastion is nice, even if you end up building everything in one playthrough (meaning you can't necessarily make a "bad" choice of what to build). But it helps tie everything into the world as a whole. Each level has a unique feeling to it and definitely keeps me focused. The training grounds for the weapons give you some nice challenges to overcome, and all of them are certainly doable. The potions you can equip further your build for Kid.
All in all, Bastion is just an amazing game. It keeps you focused and interested, with next to nothing wrong with the game at all. I never got bored with it, and I never will. I have played it multiple times since it was released, and I am always excited to play it every time I return.

Started my mercenary company with my old battle comerades, a disowned noble and two shrewd hunters.. employed some riff raff, from strange Cthulhu cultist to a craven thief and a wild man, who was to dumb to hold his sword right, but could bash your head in with his mace.

This is surely not for the player who can´t lose some of his men, the difficulty is very high and one (un)lucky hit, can decapitate your main warrior. Besides the high mortality rate, this game is a unique mix (i would name Mount & Blade from setting and map movement with a bit of Darkest Dungeon regarding the characters .. and their likeability to die ;) ) with many possibilities to establish your merry band of mercenaries.
The characters are randomly generated but with enough background to make them unique enough, also if they live long enough there are different experience paths to take. The combat is strategic, turn based. The story, as far as already implemented is nicely written too.
That said there is still much left of the game, many features which are already in the official list, as well as some usability ones, which hopefully will be implemented. Also you will have to like the graphic style, which surely is not for everyone.. and sometimes makes it hard to differentiate on the battlefield imo.
Conclusio i´m really looking forward to how this game will envolve and i´m sure that i will send many more mercs to their deaths.. and hopefully some to riches ;)
edit: I really have to compliment the team behind this game, they are a perfect example of how to do an Early Access Game. Regular updates and good communication, lead to a continually improved game.

This is a good tower defense game.  The towers, mobs and maps are well-designed.  Also the scale of the maps allows for decent sized towers and mobs that are easily distinguishable, i.e. you are not looking at dots on a huge map.  I also like that there are many building locations -- I don't like the games where you only get a few preset locations for builidng towers.   There is some repeatability because there are different modes and levels of difficulty (and different loadouts of towers and commander abilities to choose from), and your commander unit slowly levels up.

This is the squad-based tactics game I've been waiting for. Even in Early Access, Battle Brothers provides an eminently playable, thoroughly engrossing experience. The combat is more visceral, satisfying, and believable than any other turn-based tactical game on the market. $20 for this game is a steal. It is currently great and only going to get better, because apparently the folks at Overhype Studios know what they're doing.

This is a fantastic tower defense title.  It includes multiple playable characters along with numerous weapons, towers, and perks.  These various possibilities, along with the maze creation in each map, give the game a very creative feel.  You can create a build to play close-range, long-range, or anywhere in between.  You can play the entire game in co-op, creating complementary builds.  The base game itself is a good length, and each DLC adds not just more content, but enemies which fundamentally change the way that you play.  Until now, Orcs Must Die 2 was my favorite title of this nature.  Sanctum 2 has overtaken it for the top spot.  My only gripe with the title is the final level of the base game, which sends multiple "bosses" (enemies that can destroy your blocks and towers) without a chance to re-build.  I was eventually able to beat this map with the help of an online guide, but I found the solution to be very unintuitive, requiring towers which I had not needed before and would not need again.

To be fair, this is a decent game. I'm making a thumb down review because Steam doesn't allow for neutral reviews, and they are many Tower Defenses that I would recommend before this one. The game has most of the basics of TD right, but it lacks anything special that would make it stand out of the crowded TD genre. On sale this could be an ok pick.
+ The game as a fair amount of content, with 2 separate campaigns, 2 commanders with different abilities (you can play either campaigns with either commander), and 3 different play modes.
+ The economy model is decent rewarding players who spend the less they can for each enemy waves.
- The main issue, is that the various levels are a little too generic, this feeling is increased by the fact that waves are only made of one type of enemy at once, the game merely increasing the number and strength of those enemies. Overall many levels feel too long and repetitive. This may be fine for mobile gameplay but on PC it doesn't work so well. Several times, confident in my defense, I just pressed ALT-TAB and went on reading my mail or browsing the web, just monitoring the game from times to times in the taskbar with aeropeek and switching in only for the occasional boss waves. Here I should point that the second campaign was a bit better in this regard and offered a little more variation and slightly more interesting action.
- Towers can only be placed on specific locations, no “mazing”. The background graphics sometime makes it hard to say if a specific square is build-able or not, this is an unfortunate oversight.

starbound is probably a prime example of how, in my opinion, most survival sandbox games should feel like, bring you in with the thoughts of just going in and adventuring the first time you play. its style in art and game mechanics really pulled me in, though at the alpha launch it felt lack luster after about 100 hours, personally.
its first year in alpha was really lack luster and i probably wouldn't have recommended the game at the time, but now i feel with its proper story and diverse play styles of adventuring, combat, and building really shows how a sandbox game can really appeal to alot of its player base.
the planets feel more diverse in its biomes and sub-biomes, also the villages and outposts are more than just another thing to just walk past with its simple quests from villiagers and the mini dungeons are great to find and make you wonder why it was made and its purpose in the world.
combat feels fun with all the weapon mechanics and how they synergize with your skills and other weapons. monsters dont just walk toward you and deal damage by touching you since they have attacks of their own, which means you can capture them with the pet system and use them in battle.
finally, the building is simple point and click to place blocks and items, but with all of the styles of blocks and decor items you find or build you can really make a house or colony really feel unique. there's alot of options to choose from and its not hard to use or get creative with.
overall, starbound is a pretty good game that can appeal to a good chunk of people. the 1.0 release touched it off with a nice story and intro to your protagonists story and the worlds lore as a whole. the mechanics feel fun and overall its a pretty well designed game.

I cannot recommend this game in it's current state. It's just not "there" yet. The core idea behind it is cool. It mixes elements from many other RTS into one. It's sort of like a mix of settlers, age of empires, civilization, and many more. Howerver, there are multiple issues.
Food is an important game mechnaic. You have to balance food with your resources and armies to prevent your clan from starving. However, food is extremely hard to get by, especially in the late game, and the lack of food hinders any advancement, prevents progress, and kills all enjoyment.
It is actually very possible, to end up in a locked stalemate with AI, with no way to break through and win. There are many scentarios where both sides control a similar amount of resources, but AI cheats, and somehow manages to have BOTH a huge army and huge amount of resources, while a human player can only have ONE of these at a time, which the other lacking, at least somewhat. It is because of this, that such stalemates happen. You have just enough strength to hold him back from killing you, but you can never beat him, because he kicks your♥♥♥♥♥every time you try.
There are plenty of small bugs and oddities. For example, I am somehow able to get by wit hjust ONE woodcutter, while event 20 food gatherers arent enough. Sometimes, food will start going down without any reason for it to do so.
The constant cycling between summer and winter, although a hugely important game mechanic ends up being more annoying than fun. It's just such a grind to be ALWAYS in a state of "preparation for winter".
The devs kinda locked themselves in, by focusing the game around "Norse Mythology/Culture". Because of this, they can never meaningfully introduce more races or cultures, except for maybe the ENGLISH? It would make sense for a DLC.
Skirmish vs. human or AI is fine, but I cant imagine how they can create any sort of an enjoyable, meaningful campaign with a good storyline. I just dont see it at this point in time. Prove me wrong please!
It feels like a game which, if it was much cheaper, all it's faults could easily be forgiven, but at it's current price, although not very high, it's probably not worth it, at least not yet.

Here are pros and cons after finishing around 95% of game quests.
[+] GUN PLAY. This is where this game excels. Comparing to New Vegas Fallout 4 is a huge step forward. Shooting outside VATS is fun. You get lots of weapons, apparel, items, power armor with the ability to customize them. It’s a solid FPS.
[+] SETTLEMENTS. Building settlements have no purpose for the main game whatsoever. But it’s still enjoyable minecraft-like construction simulator.
[+] GRAPHICS. This game looks fantastic (especially with the high resolution texture pack). I love the art direction of this game although mood tones are all over the place. The other downside are human face and dialogue animations. Not a lot of emotions.
[-] RPG SYSTEM. Practically non-existent. Did you enjoy SPECIAL system in previous Fallout games? Well, forget about it. Bethesda cut out the traits AND the skills. Now there are only stats which allow you to get perks. And perks are something like perks combined with skills in previous games.
[-] PLOT. Oh boy, did they screw it up. It's not only that you don't care about it but it's also insultingly stupid and very hard to believe in. By the time you get to see your son you have zero emotions about this whole affair.
[-] DIALOGUES. It's just a mess. Only 4 reply options which usually don't even matter. No roleplay, no skills/stats checks, no variety whatsoever. You can just as well spam the sarcastic options. At least it can be mildly entertaining.
[-] ROLEPLAY. Again there ain’t none. You can’t even be evil. It’s like Mass Effect. You can be a♥♥♥♥♥♥in dialogue all you want but in the end you’ll still help everyone.
[-] QUESTS. Fallout 4 quests are probably the laziest I’ve ever seen in a RPG game. It’s literally “GET THERE, KILL X BAD GUYS, GET Y ITEMS”. That’s all. If you are looking for interesting quests get Fallout 2 or New Vegas.
[-] TECHNICAL. Like every other Bethesda game it’s buggy as all hell. Without customizing the config files you WILL get performance drops on EVERY PC. I have a fairly powerful PC: i7-5820k, 32Gb RAM, GTX1080Ti and M.2 SSD. With the high resolution texture pack I dropped to 30 FPS in downtown area of the game. And that’s in 1080p. Without pack I’ve managed to get 60 FPS in 4K in most areas but downtown still is a challenge for hardware. Unless you have extremely beefy PC I suggest you to look up config file tweaks on Reddit/forums.
TL;DR
As a FPS game inspired by Fallout universe I’d give this game 8/10
As an actual part of Fallout RPG games series I won’t give more that 5/10.
